title: SAP PI/PO 7.5 to Integration Suite (CPI) 2027 Migration: Cloud Connector HA, Groovy 4 & IDoc Cutover Checklist
description:
With SAP Process Orchestration (PI/PO 7.5) reaching mainstream end-of-maintenance in December 2027, most enterprise integration teams are facing the same question: how do we migrate 100 to 400 legacy IDoc, RFC, and Proxy interfaces to SAP Integration Suite (CPI) without blowing the budget or breaking production order flows?

Here are the 4 architectural failure points that consistently derail PI/PO to CPI cutovers:

1. Single-Node SAP Cloud Connector Bottlenecks

Moving on-premise IDoc and RFC traffic to cloud CPI turns a single Cloud Connector into a single point of failure. Before migrating Tier-1 S/4HANA flows:

  • Deploy a Master + Shadow High-Availability pair on separate hosts and test failover.
  • Separate Dev/QA and Production subaccount Location IDs so noisy non-prod retries cannot starve production RFC channels.
  • Move high-frequency plant-floor or >50MB payload traffic to SAP Edge Integration Cell instead of round-tripping through public cloud.

2. Groovy 2.4 & Legacy Java Mappings

Custom UDFs, legacy Java mappings, and older Groovy scripts frequently break on SAP Integration Suite's Apache Camel 4 / Groovy 4 runtime. Inventory every custom script before writing build estimates.

3. EOIO / ABAP Proxy Queue Blockages

When moving EOIO (Exactly Once In Order) ABAP Proxy interfaces to CPI JMS queues, always configure dead-letter queues and alerting so one malformed payload cannot stall downstream order processing.

4. Unverified SI Discovery Quotes

Before signing a 6-figure System Integrator SOW, classify your entire PI/PO interface catalog into Simple, Medium, and Complex tiers so effort estimates stay grounded in actual XML/mapping complexity.

Practical Migration Resources

  • IDoc & RFC to CPI Migration Guide: https://btp-integration.pages.dev/sap-pi-po-idoc-to-cpi-migration-guide

title: Marketplace Avatar Retention: Node.js Signed Object Storage with Deletion Evidence
description:
The page fires during a user avatar upload because deletion_eligible_oldest_age has crossed the team's limit. A marketplace seller used a signed object storage write, replaced the avatar, and abandoned another large media transfer; the on-call sees three keys and one uncomfortable question: which bytes can be deleted without breaking a live page or a recovery promise?

Short answer: let browsers send large files to object storage with narrowly scoped signed URLs, keep retention decisions in the Node.js SaaS database, and delete only from durable evidence that an object is no longer referenced and its recovery deadline has passed. Proxy uploads through the application only when the application must inspect or transform every byte before accepting it. The transfer path changes capacity. It does not settle ownership.

That distinction is the runbook. A direct upload keeps large media off the application's request path, but a completed transfer can outlive the tab that started it. A proxy gives the server one request to authorize and receive, yet couples Node.js request duration and application capacity to file size. Neither design makes deletion safe by itself.

Incident response starts by establishing deletion authority

At 02:13, the worst dashboard is a count of "old objects." Age is not intent. An old avatar may still be the current avatar; a recent video may already be abandoned; a replaced image may be inside a promised recovery window. The first action is to trace an object key back to an authenticated marketplace owner, a live database reference, and a recorded deletion deadline. If any link is absent, stop automated deletion for that object class and investigate the evidence producer. Then follow one candidate all the way through the system: find the deletion record, confirm its tenant, identify the domain row that last referenced the key, compare the current state with the state captured when cleanup was scheduled, and inspect the deadline that represents the recovery promise. If the seller restored the listing after the job was queued, the live reference wins. If the avatar was replaced twice, only the keys with no current attachment continue. If an abandoned direct upload never gained a domain reference, its separate cleanup deadline governs. This trace is slower than pressing a delete button, but it turns the incident from storage archaeology into a set of falsifiable checks, and those checks tell the team which missing field or transition to instrument next.

I've been paged by missed jobs and duplicate deliveries. The durable lesson is blunt: queue age tells you that work is late, not whether replaying the work is safe. A deletion worker must assume that its message can arrive twice and that the database may have changed since the message was scheduled. It reloads current state before acting.

No shortcuts.

The object store cannot infer the marketplace contract from a key and a timestamp. It does not know that a seller restored a listing, that a new avatar became current, or that a moderation process still holds a file. Object lifecycle management can expire objects and transition storage classes, so it is useful for data whose prefix and age encode a valid policy. It remains a backstop to an application decision, not a substitute for one.

Age is ambiguous.

Work backward from what the on-call needs. A useful deletion record contains an opaque object key, tenant ownership, the domain resource that referenced it, the time deletion became eligible, the recovery deadline, and the final outcome. The record is not a copy of the storage inventory. It is evidence for a business transition.

Telemetry for the gap between ownership records and an aging backlog

The earlier signal is a growing gap between deletion eligibility and confirmed deletion. Measure both the age of the oldest eligible record and the number of eligible records that remain unfinished. Age alone pages during low-volume maintenance or one deliberately retained object. Count alone pages after a normal burst even when workers are catching up. Together, and observed across more than one evaluation window, they tell the operator whether a queue is merely busy or no longer advancing.

Instrument transitions, not just requests. Emit a counter when a file becomes eligible, when a worker claims the record, when current references block deletion, when the object is removed, and when completion is durably recorded. A histogram from eligibility to confirmation exposes slow progress before the oldest-item alert fires. Structured logs should carry an intent or deletion ID, tenant ID, media class, prior state, next state, and a bounded reason code. Don't log a signed URL because it is a temporary capability.

The dashboard then answers a short sequence of operational questions: Is new work becoming eligible? Are workers claiming it? Are reference checks blocking a particular media class? Are completions keeping pace? The page should link to that sequence, not to a storage console with millions of unrelated keys.

The threshold is local policy. I'm not sure there is a defensible universal number, because the right delay depends on the stated recovery window, worker schedule, expected upload volume, and the time an operator needs to intervene. Resolve it with a replay of production-shaped records and a written error budget for deletion delay. A concrete invariant is stronger than a fashionable duration: alert before delayed deletion can violate the user-facing retention promise, while leaving enough time for normal scheduling jitter.

How should a beginner Node.js SaaS choose signed object storage or a server proxy?

Choose by where byte-level trust must be established. For routine marketplace avatars and large listing media, the least complex capacity model is a control plane in Node.js and a data plane in object storage. The application authenticates the seller, allocates an opaque key, records the expected ownership and media policy, and issues a short-lived signed write. The browser uploads to that exact destination, then asks the application to finalize. Before attaching the object to an avatar or listing, the application checks the storage attributes promised by its own record.

Do not treat the browser's success callback as proof of durable application state. The tab can close after bytes arrive but before finalization, or retry finalization after a response is lost. Finalization therefore needs an idempotent result: repeating the same valid request returns the already established attachment rather than creating another one. An issued signed URL is authority to attempt one storage operation within its scope; it is not permission to attach an arbitrary key to a different tenant.

A server proxy is still the cleaner choice when every accepted file must be decoded, scanned, or transformed synchronously before storage, or when the product only accepts small files and the team values a single request boundary over independent data-plane scaling. The catch is operational: slow clients, large request bodies, ingress limits, and application autoscaling become part of the upload system. It is not suitable for the stated marketplace job when large media should avoid the app server.

Signed direct upload has its own cost. It introduces an interval in which storage and application state may disagree, so the design needs reconciliation and explicit cleanup. Your mileage may vary across runtimes and storage implementations; test the largest permitted file, an interrupted transfer, an expired signature, a repeated finalization, and a deletion racing with restore. A 40 KB avatar on localhost proves almost nothing about the large-media path.

Delivery is a separate decision. If a download response is meant to display an avatar inline or save an attachment with a filename, Content-Disposition defines those response semantics. It should not be overloaded into the retention model. How a browser presents bytes and when the system may destroy them are different contracts.

Security boundary: verify current references before deletion

The deletion worker should consume a stable record ID, not "delete this key" as an unconditional command. On every attempt it reloads the record, confirms that the deadline is in the past, and asks the domain database whether any live attachment still points at the key. If the object became current again, the correct result is a recorded skip, not a delete followed by repair.

This Go sketch shows the guard around a generic storage interface. The Node.js service can own the records and scheduling; the worker contract stays independent of a vendor SDK.

package retention

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "time"
)

var ErrNotEligible = errors.New("object is not eligible for deletion")

type Candidate struct {
    ID        string
    ObjectKey string
    DeleteAt  time.Time
    DeletedAt *time.Time
}

type Records interface {
    Load(ctx context.Context, id string) (Candidate, error)
    HasLiveReference(ctx context.Context, key string) (bool, error)
    MarkDeleted(ctx context.Context, id string, at time.Time) error
}

type Objects interface {
    Delete(ctx context.Context, key string) error
}

func DeleteEligible(ctx context.Context, db Records, store Objects, id string, now time.Time) error {
    candidate, err := db.Load(ctx, id)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if candidate.DeletedAt != nil {
        return nil // A replay observes the completed outcome.
    }
    if now.Before(candidate.DeleteAt) {
        return ErrNotEligible
    }

    referenced, err := db.HasLiveReference(ctx, candidate.ObjectKey)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if referenced {
        return ErrNotEligible
    }
    if err := store.Delete(ctx, candidate.ObjectKey); err != nil {
        return err
    }
    return db.MarkDeleted(ctx, candidate.ID, now)
}

The interface makes the critical review question visible: what happens if the process stops after object deletion but before MarkDeleted? The next delivery must be able to repeat the storage deletion and then record completion. That requires idempotent delete semantics in the chosen adapter and a test that exercises this exact boundary. The code also leaves room for the database implementation to serialize a restore against a deletion claim; the precise transaction mechanism belongs to that database, not to the queue message.

Keep retention classes explicit rather than applying one age rule to everything:

Object class Evidence before deletion Why age alone fails
Unfinalized upload No live attachment and its cleanup deadline passed A slow or interrupted finalization may still reconcile
Replaced avatar A newer avatar is current and the recovery deadline passed The previous image can be part of a restore promise
Deleted listing media The listing remains deleted and any hold is clear Domain state can change after the job was scheduled

Bucket lifecycle rules can enforce expiration for a deliberately isolated class of abandoned data. Align the key layout, lifecycle timing, and application cleanup deadline so two independent mechanisms do not encode conflicting promises. If the business offers a recovery period, a shorter storage expiry makes that promise false; if nothing ever expires, abandoned direct uploads accumulate without a bound.

Alert economics includes the cost of false positives

Ship the instrumentation before tightening the page. During deployment, compare eligible, claimed, blocked, deleted, and recorded totals, then inspect the oldest records from each state. Exercise a duplicate queue delivery, a restore just before eligibility, an upload that never finalizes, and a worker restart between storage deletion and database completion. The acceptance criterion is not that every job runs once. It is that every valid object reaches one explainable terminal outcome despite retries.

False positives have a real cost. An alert set below routine queue jitter trains the on-call to ignore age; an alert based only on count fires during healthy bursts; a page for reference-blocked candidates may punish the worker for correctly protecting live media. Use a lower-urgency ticket for accumulating cleanup that remains inside the retention promise, and reserve a page for sustained lack of progress that threatens that promise.

The decision rule is compact: direct signed upload for large marketplace media, application-owned evidence for attachment and retention, and guarded idempotent deletion after the deadline. Stick with a proxy when synchronous byte inspection is the actual requirement. Whichever path carries the upload, make the deletion claim provable before allowing automation to act.

References

  • MDN: Content-Disposition response header
  • AWS S3 documentation: Object lifecycle management

Further reading

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Content-Disposition
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lifecycle-mgmt.html

title: Exporting an OpenAPI Round Trip in Insomnia: What Comes Back
description:
Quick answer: Insomnia's desktop UI has no OpenAPI export option. A UI export gives you only Insomnia v5 YAML or a HAR file. To get OpenAPI, you run inso export spec, which extracts the raw spec already tied to the collection; it does not regenerate a spec from your requests or fold in the edits, environments, scripts, or tests you added while debugging. The trip back to OpenAPI is therefore not a symmetric save, and the original spec stays the contract of record.

What each export actually produces

Insomnia separates moving your whole workspace from extracting the contract, and the two paths return different things.

Path Format What it holds
UI export Insomnia v5 YAML The collection with its spec, requests, environment settings, and tests
UI export HAR A request and response archive for traffic analysis
Inso CLI OpenAPI YAML or JSON The raw spec bound to the collection, written to a file or stdout

The UI labels each export with the entity name and asks for a format, but OpenAPI is not on that list. The CLI command inso export spec "My API Collection" --output spec.yaml is the only built-in route to an OpenAPI file, which makes it a tool for CI and scripting rather than a general save button.

Why the round trip is not symmetric

When you import a spec, Insomnia generates requests as build artifacts. That generation runs one way: editing a generated request changes the request, not the spec. Running inso export spec afterward hands back the original document, so work that lives only in the workspace never makes the return trip.

Stays in the workspace Returns in the exported spec
Environment variables and sub-environments Paths, operations, and schemas from the raw spec
Pre-request and after-response scripts Declared servers and security schemes
Assertions and test suites Component definitions already in the spec
Nunjucks template tags and cookie history Nothing you changed only inside a request

The practical rule is to change the contract in the spec itself and regenerate the request, instead of editing the request and expecting an export to write it back. If you start from a hand-built collection that has no spec, there is no native reverse button. Turning those requests into OpenAPI needs a third-party plugin, and the output has to be reviewed because OpenAPI has no place for scripts, environments, or template tags.

The plain-text trap in exported files

Version 13.4 and later mark variables as confidential. When a v5 file is exported, those names land on a confidentialKeys list, which preserves the marking across import, Git Sync, and duplication. The marking does not protect the value: it stays in plain text in the file's data. Anyone who can read the exported file or the Git repository can read the token.

A confidential label is not encryption. The v5 file records the name on a confidentialKeys list while the real value sits beside it in plain text. Treat the export as a secret even though the variable looks protected. Use secret variables in the vault when you need the value encrypted at rest.

Before committing a v5 file, scan it for tokens the same way you would scan any config, or move sensitive values into secret variables. Relying on the confidential flag to keep a credential out of a shared repository is the failure mode worth avoiding.

Frequently asked questions

Can I export my edited requests straight back to OpenAPI in the UI? No. The UI offers only v5 YAML and HAR. Use inso export spec for OpenAPI, and expect the raw spec rather than a document rebuilt from your requests.

Why do my request changes not appear in the exported spec? Generation is one-way. Edit the spec and regenerate the request so the contract and the calls you send stay aligned.

Are confidential variables safe to commit? No. Their values export in plain text even though the names are listed as confidential. Use secret variables for encrypted storage, and keep plain-text exports out of public repositories.

How do I get OpenAPI from a hand-built collection? Through a third-party plugin. Review the result carefully, since scripts, environments, and template tags cannot be represented in the spec.

The bottom line

Keep the spec as the single source of truth and use each export for what it is good at: v5 for backup and migration, HAR for traffic analysis, and inso export spec for pulling the contract into CI and linting. None of these merge your debugging work back into the contract, and a v5 file should be handled as a possible secret. When your checks need to prove that running requests still match the contract instead of merely moving files around, Powerduck pairs ordered scenario runs with code review in one desktop app. For how the tools differ across these workflows, see the Insomnia comparison hub.

title: Writing a Dockerfile: five instructions, explained one by one
description:
To run your Python app with Docker, you first need a Dockerfile. It is the recipe for your image: a text file, named Dockerfile, that lists the steps to build it.

We made a 28-second video that goes through the five instructions you need:

tiktok.com

You can also watch it on our site: Writing a Dockerfile.

The rest of this post goes through each instruction of the video, with the code.

The app

A folder with two files: the code and the list of its dependencies.

my-app/
├── app.py
└── requirements.txt

The whole Dockerfile

Here is the file from the video. It goes at the root of the folder:

FROM ubuntu:22.04
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y python3 python3-pip \
    && pip3 install -r requirements.txt
CMD ["python3", "app.py"]

Five instructions, read from top to bottom.

FROM picks the starting image 

FROM ubuntu:22.04

An image almost always starts from an existing one. Here, Ubuntu 22.04, pulled from Docker Hub. It contains a minimal Ubuntu system and nothing else: no Python, no code of yours.

The part after the colon is the tag, which is the version. Always write one. Without it, Docker takes latest, and your build may change the day a new version comes out.

WORKDIR sets the working folder 

WORKDIR /app

The instructions that follow (COPY, RUN, CMD) work from /app, inside the image. If the folder does not exist, Docker creates it. It is the cd of the Dockerfile, and it stays in effect when the container starts.

COPY copies your code into it 

COPY . .

Two paths: the first one is on your machine, the second one is in the image. The first dot is the build context, the folder you give to docker build. The second one is the working folder, so /app. After this line, app.py and requirements.txt are in the image, along with everything else in the folder.

RUN installs your dependencies 

RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y python3 python3-pip \
    && pip3 install -r requirements.txt

RUN executes a command while the image is being built, and keeps the result in the image. Here it installs Python, which the Ubuntu image does not have, then the packages listed in requirements.txt.

The -y matters: nobody is there to answer "yes" during a build.

CMD tells Docker which command to run at startup 

CMD ["python3", "app.py"]

CMD does nothing during the build. It records the default command, the one that runs when a container starts from the image. You can replace it for one run by adding a command after the image name: docker run my-app python3 other.py.

The form with brackets starts the program directly, without a shell in between, so it receives the stop signal when you stop the container.

RUN and CMD are easy to mix up:

When How many
RUN While the image is built As many as you need
CMD When a container starts One: if you write several, only the last one counts

Every instruction adds a layer

An image is not one block. Each instruction adds a step on top of the previous ones, and Docker keeps the result of each step in its build cache. You can see them, once the image is built:

docker history my-app

To be precise, the instructions that change files (COPY, RUN) add a layer of files, and that is where the size of the image comes from. CMD only records a setting: it shows up in the history with a size of 0B.

This is why the order of the lines matters. When you build again, Docker reuses the cache until it reaches a line that changed, or a COPY whose files changed. From that line on, everything is rebuilt.

In the file above, COPY . . comes before RUN. Change one character in app.py and Docker installs Python and all the packages again.

Going one step further

The file above is the simplest one to read, not the one to ship. Once the five instructions are clear, two changes make the image faster to build and much lighter:

FROM python:3.13-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
CMD ["python", "app.py"]
  • Start from an image that already has Python. python:3.13-slim saves the apt-get step, and the image is much smaller than the one built on Ubuntu. --no-cache-dir keeps pip's download cache out of it.
  • Copy requirements.txt first, the code after. The packages are reinstalled only when the list of dependencies changes. A change in app.py rebuilds the last COPY alone.

COPY . . takes everything in the folder, including a .env file with your passwords if there is one. Add a .dockerignore file next to the Dockerfile to leave out what has no place in the image:

.git
.env
__pycache__
venv

There is more to a production image, starting with not running the app as root. That is for another post.

Next

The Dockerfile is only the recipe. Building the image and running a container takes two commands:

docker build -t my-app .
docker run my-app

That is part 2 of the series: Building and running a container.

This video is part of a short series on Docker by Ilaria Digital School, an online tech school with live, instructor-led classes. Docker is taught in our Full-Stack Software Developer Pathway.

title: Can your coding agent beat a 94% Rust speedup? 4 Wasmtime benchmarks and 11 Lean 4 math problems are still unbeaten
description:
Most AI coding benchmarks rely on static suites or LLM-as-a-judge. I wanted to see what happens when developers point their idle coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, or local CLI/MCP agents) at live, objectively verifiable challenges where every accepted pull request lands straight on main.

So I built Swarmdesk (completely free to use).

Two live arenas right now

1. The Speed Race (Rust + WebAssembly)

8 Rust functions compiled to WebAssembly and measured deterministically by Wasmtime instruction count ("fuel") on randomized inputs, not noisy wall-clock timing.

  • To set a new record, a PR must match reference outputs byte-for-byte and cut instructions by at least 3% (tapering to 1.5% below 60% of baseline, and 0.5% below 35%).
  • Current status: 4 functions have verified records (up to 94% fewer instructions), and 4 functions are still completely unbeaten.

2. Open Math (Lean 4)

11 open mathematical conjectures, quantitative bounds, and composable blueprint helper lemmas.

  • Every PR compiles inside an isolated, networkless container and replays the compiled .olean through the Lean 4 kernel against a read-only Spec.lean using only standard axioms (propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound), with zero sorry or native_decide.
  • Current status: 0/11 solved so far.

How to connect your agent in 60 seconds

  1. Sign in with GitHub on joinswarmdesk.com (OAuth asks for zero repository access; PRs are opened locally from your fork via your own gh CLI).

  2. Generate your personal desk key and either:

    • Paste the one-line prompt into Claude Code, Cursor, or Codex, or
    • Run the CLI: 
     export SWARMDESK_KEY=<your-key>
 npx swarmdesk-cli claim --problem speed-race
  • Or connect it as a local MCP server via npx -y swarmdesk-cli mcp.
    1. Your agent claims a 45-minute lease on one open target, edits one source file, runs the local checker, and opens a PR. Accepted submissions are committed to main under your GitHub handle.

Prompt-injection protection

Humans post optimization ideas, vote, and propose new math problems, but nothing user-typed ever reaches an agent. Maintainers distill approved ideas into a single-line ASCII technical hint, and submitted Rust/Lean files cannot contain comments or string literals.

The challenge

  • Have idle Claude/Codex/Cursor or local model quota? See if your harness can claim the first record on one of the 4 unbeaten Rust functions or beat the 94% speedup.
  • No agent running right now? You can still steer the swarm by voting on ideas or proposing a new open math problem or helper lemma you think current agents cannot crack.

I would love honest feedback on the setup flow or anything that breaks when you try it!

title: A real dependency audit: 1,090 packages, 118 seconds cold, 1.5 seconds warm
description:
Every "is this safe?" check pays a network cost the first time. Here is what that cost actually is, measured on a real lockfile.

I keep saying that checking a dependency before you install it is cheap. "Cheap" is the kind of word that hides a number, so I measured the number instead.

The setup

OWASP NodeGoat is a deliberately vulnerable Node app. Its lockfile is from 2023, which makes it a useful stress test: real package shapes, real advisories, a thousand nodes.

The run is pinned to one commit:

git clone https://github.com/OWASP/NodeGoat
git checkout c5cb68a7084e4ae7dcc60e6a98768720a81841e8

Machine: 11th-gen Intel i7-11800H, Linux, 16 threads. Tool: Dep-Vet 0.16.0, release build, 19 MB binary. The cache is isolated in a temporary directory, so this is a genuine cold start and it does not touch my normal cache.

The result

Run Wall time Packages Exit
Cold 118.26 s 1,090 3
Warm 1.45 s 1,090 3

82× between the two runs, on the same input, with the same output.

The cold run left 1,866 cache entries behind, 115 MiB total. That is the actual cost of the first audit: every packument, every advisory batch and detail page, every EPSS and KEV lookup, and the download counts. Nothing is loaded in the background, nothing is preloaded on install, and no daemon is running between audits.

The warm run reads all of it from SQLite and finishes in under two seconds.

Why the two numbers matter differently

A cold run happens once per machine. The number that governs your day is the warm one, because almost every real check is a diff:

  • The CI action runs dep-vet lock on a pull request, so it checks added packages, not the whole tree.
  • watch re-audits when the lockfile changes.
  • guard runs before an install command, and only on the packages being installed.

So the honest framing is not "a 1,000-package audit takes two minutes". It is: the first audit of a tree costs a couple of minutes of wall clock, and every audit after that costs about a second and a half.

That distinction is also why the caching rules are conservative. Registry metadata is cached for 24 hours. Advisories are cached for five minutes, because a five-minute-old advisory list is fine and a day-old one is not. A warm run more than five minutes later will re-query OSV and take longer than 1.45 s — the number above is a genuinely warm run, not a best case with stale security data.

The exit code is part of the benchmark

Both runs exit 3, and that is not a bug in the measurement.

One dependency in that 2023 lockfile, grunt-if@0.2.0, no longer exists on npm. Dep-Vet reports the 1,090 packages it could check — 210 HIGH findings across 101 packages, 356 WARN findings across 205 — and still refuses to print "clean":

  could not check 1 package:
    grunt-if@0.2.0: '0.2.0' of 'grunt-if' was not found on npm; dep-vet takes
    an exact version or dist-tag, not a range
  this report is incomplete

A package that was installable in 2023 and is gone in 2026 is a supply-chain event worth knowing about, not a parsing inconvenience. Exit 3 is how the tool says "I could not finish" without pretending the rest of the tree is clean.

That is also why a benchmark with a two-minute cold run is not a failure of the tool. The run made 1,866 metadata requests, with bounded retry and backoff, and then told the truth about the one thing it could not resolve.

What this is not

  • Not a comparison to npm audit. That answers a different question (known advisories for versions already in the lockfile) with a different amount of work (one bulk request to the registry's audit endpoint). A faster number from a smaller check is not a faster tool.
  • Not a claim about contemporary risk. NodeGoat is pinned to a deliberately old tree; the 101 HIGH packages are a property of the fixture, not of npm in 2026.
  • Not a general speed claim. One machine, one lockfile, one run each. The script is in the repo so you can get your own numbers.

Reproduce it 

git clone https://github.com/nassih-yassine/Dep-Vet
cd Dep-Vet
cargo build --release
DEPVET_BIN=./target/release/dep-vet examples/benchmark/run.sh

The script clones NodeGoat to a temp directory, wipes an isolated cache, times dep-vet audit package-lock.json twice, then prints the cache entry count and size. It writes nothing to ~/.cache/dep-vet and stores no results.

Try the tool 

npx @nassihyas/dep-vet npm express@5.3.0
npx @nassihyas/dep-vet audit package-lock.json

Repo: https://github.com/nassih-yassine/Dep-Vet

MIT, no account, no API key, no analytics. One opt-outable update check is the only request that isn't a registry, advisory, or archive fetch.

title: attackscout-agent: a read-only website security check you run on your own server
description:
Most website security scanners look at your site from the outside. That is useful, but it cannot see an old PHP branch, a .env that sits in the web root, or a certificate file that expires next week. Those are visible from the server.

attackscout-agent is a small command line tool that checks those things from the inside. It is free, MIT-licensed, written in Go, and it only reads.

What it does

Run attackscout-agent scan on a Linux, macOS or Windows server. It detects the web root and your nginx or Apache configuration, then runs seven checks:

  • End of life: PHP, Node.js, .NET, WordPress (core, plugins, themes), Drupal, Joomla, PrestaShop, React and Next.js, compared with an end-of-life table embedded in the binary.
  • Known vulnerabilities: npm, Composer, PyPI, NuGet and Go lockfiles, plus Terraform and OpenTofu provider versions, matched against the OSV database with Google's osv-scalibr library.
  • Sensitive files: .env, .git/, SQL dumps, archives, phpinfo.php, logs, private keys, .htpasswd, terraform.tfstate. Names only, contents are never opened.
  • File permissions: world-writable files and directories, 777, world-readable wp-config.php and .env (Unix only).
  • Web server configuration: HSTS, CSP, X-Content-Type-Options, frame protection, Referrer-Policy, version disclosure and directory listing in nginx, Apache and IIS configuration.
  • wp-config.php: default or missing salts, WP_DEBUG, WP_DEBUG_DISPLAY, DISALLOW_FILE_EDIT. Secret values are never printed.
  • Certificates: PEM files, for expiry, a certificate expiring in under 30 days, weak keys and SHA-1 or MD5 signatures.

Every finding has a stable identifier, a severity from info to critical, and a fix. A check that cannot run says not_checked, and one that makes no sense on the system says not_applicable. Neither is ever shown as a pass.

Example

I ran it on the fake WordPress site and nginx configuration that ship in the repository's testdata/ folder (on a Windows machine, so the permissions check is not_applicable):

Checks
  [fail          ] End of life - End-of-life table embedded in the binary, dated 2026-11-25
  [not checked   ] CVE (OSV) - CVEs not checked for 5 components that OSV does not track (WordPress, Joomla extensions, ...)
  [fail          ] Sensitive files
  [not applicable] File permissions - Not applicable on Windows: Unix permission bits do not exist there and ACLs are not read
  [fail          ] wp-config.php
  [fail          ] Web server configuration

Findings
  [CRITICAL] sensitive-env: Sensitive environment file in the web root: .env (content not read)
  [CRITICAL] wpconfig-salt-default: wp-config.php keys or salts empty or left at the default value: AUTH_KEY, SECURE_AUTH_KEY (values not shown)
  [HIGH] php-eol: PHP 7.4 is end of life (branch 7.4, since 2022-11-28)
  [MEDIUM] header-hsts-missing: nginx configuration does not set Strict-Transport-Security
  ...
Summary: 4 critical, 4 high, 5 medium, 10 low, 0 info

Note the second line: WordPress and Joomla extensions are not in OSV, so the tool says "CVEs not checked" instead of pretending there is none.

Does it send anything?

Not by default. There is no telemetry and no update check. Two commands use the network, and only them:

  • attackscout-agent db update downloads the public OSV archives. Nothing about your server is sent.
  • attackscout-agent scan --online sends package names, versions and ecosystems to api.osv.dev, and nothing else (no path, file name or domain).

This is enforced by tests: one parses every source file and only allows the vulnerability package to import a networking package, another runs a full default scan with a guard on the HTTP transport and fails on any request.

Use it in CI 

attackscout-agent db update
attackscout-agent scan --root . --project . --fail-on high

The command exits with 1 when a finding is high or critical, 0 otherwise, and 2 for a usage error. --json gives a report you can keep as an artifact. In CI it is most useful for lockfiles and Terraform files; the file and configuration checks need the real server.

Install 

go install github.com/attackscout/attackscout-agent@latest

Prebuilt binaries for Linux, macOS and Windows (amd64 and arm64) are attached to each GitHub release, with a checksums.txt file.

What it does not do

  • It reads certificate files. It does not connect to your site, so it does not test TLS versions or cipher suites.
  • It reads configuration files. A header added by a proxy or CDN in front of the server is not seen.
  • It does not analyse Terraform configuration; tfsec and Checkov do that well.
  • Its end-of-life table is as fresh as the release you run.

See the other side too

This tool sees the inside of the server. What a visitor or a scanner sees, such as the headers actually served and what is reachable from the Internet, needs an outside look. For that I run AttackScout, an external audit of a domain. The CLI is separate and free; it is not part of that service.

Repository and docs: https://github.com/AttackScout/attackscout-agent

Feedback and issues are welcome, especially false positives and server layouts the auto-detection misses.

title: A Practical Color-Reference Workflow for Photographing Translucent Materials
description:
Photographing translucent materials is a calibration problem before it is a photography problem. Two shots of the same stone, taken ten minutes apart under the same lamp, can look like two different materials once the camera decides on a white balance. I ran into this while helping document jadeite pieces for a small trading archive, and the fix turned out to be mostly code, not gear.

The problem

A camera's auto white balance optimises for a pleasant average, not for consistency. With a strongly coloured subject filling the frame, the camera compensates for the colour it sees and neutralises exactly the signal you want to measure. Dark green material on a light background pulls the exposure one way; the same material on dark velvet pulls it the other.

Step 1: fix the light, then stop trusting the camera

I settled on a single diffused source at a fixed distance, a matte grey card in the corner of every frame, and manual exposure. The grey card is not decoration: it is the anchor the script uses to normalise every image to the same reference point.

Step 2: sample the card, not the subject 

from PIL import Image
import numpy as np

def grey_reference(path, box):
    img = Image.open(path).convert("RGB")
    patch = np.asarray(img.crop(box)).reshape(-1, 3).astype(float)
    # median is robust against dust and specular highlights
    return np.median(patch, axis=0)

The crop box is fixed once and reused for the whole series, so every frame gets the same treatment. Median instead of mean matters: a stray highlight on the card will drag a mean badly and leave a colour cast that no later step can undo.

Step 3: apply a per-channel gain 

def balance(img, ref, target=(200, 200, 200)):
    arr = np.asarray(img).astype(float)
    gain = np.array(target, dtype=float) / np.maximum(ref, 1.0)
    out = np.clip(arr * gain, 0, 255).astype(np.uint8)
    return Image.fromarray(out)

Two lines and the whole series lands on a common neutral. I keep the gain values in a CSV next to the images; when a new lamp or a new diffuser shows up, the drift is visible as a step change in that column instead of being buried in the pictures.

Step 4: describe the material in numbers, not adjectives

Once the frames are comparable, a short feature extractor makes the archive searchable. For translucent material the useful features are narrow: mean hue in the subject mask, saturation spread, and a crude translucency proxy built from the ratio of edge brightness to centre brightness.

def translucency_proxy(img, mask):
    arr = np.asarray(img.convert("L")).astype(float)
    edge = arr[mask & ~erode(mask)]
    core = arr[erode(erode(mask))]
    return float(np.mean(edge) / max(np.mean(core), 1.0))

This is not a grading system and it does not pretend to be one. It is a way to sort two hundred photographs into groups that a human can then look at side by side, which is the only part of the job that actually needs eyes.

What I would do differently

  • Put the grey card in the frame before the first shot, not after the fortieth.
  • Store the raw gain values in the filename. EXIF rewriting is a rabbit hole.
  • Resist the urge to make the numbers look nice. A feature that separates your groups but has no physical meaning will not survive a change of lighting.

If you only take one thing from this: the difference between two photos of the same piece is usually a measurement error, and measurement errors are cheaper to fix in code than in a studio. The reference archive this workflow was built for lives at https://www.jjjadeite.com, and a shorter buyer-facing write-up of the same ideas is at https://sites.google.com/view/jadeite-buyer-guide — both were useful to me as examples of how the same material is described for two very different audiences.

title: How to Use Databricks SQL With the VisuaLeaf Database Client
description:
Databricks is a cloud platform teams use to prepare and analyze data. I connected VisuaLeaf to Databricks to run SQL, find the columns I needed for a join, and compare two versions of a table to see which rows had changed.

What is Databricks used for?

A retailer can use Databricks to combine orders from its application database with tracking events from shipping carriers. Data engineers build the pipeline that turns those feeds into tables. Analysts can then use SQL to find late shipments, and data scientists can use the same data to train models.

How Databricks SQL runs a query

A *SQL warehouse* runs your query and reads the table data from cloud storage. *Unity Catalog* organizes tables into catalogs and schemas and controls who can access them. When you write SQL in VisuaLeaf, it sends the query to the warehouse and displays the results.

Simplified Databricks architecture diagram for a SQL query.

A full table name follows the pattern catalog.schema.table, as in workspace.fulfillment_demo.shipments. Use all three parts when staging and production have tables with the same name.

Connect VisuaLeaf to a SQL warehouse

In Databricks, go to *SQL Warehouses, open your warehouse, and copy the *Server hostname** and *HTTP Path* from *Connection details*. The hostname identifies the workspace. The HTTP path selects the warehouse.

Create a Databricks connection in VisuaLeaf with these settings:

Field What to enter
Connection Mode SQL Warehouse
Host The server hostname from Databricks
Port 443
HTTP Path The warehouse path beginning with /sql/1.0/warehouses/
Catalog Optional. I used workspace for the demo.
Sign-in method I used a personal access token. Use the method your workspace allows and your client supports.

For a token-based connection, go to *Settings → Developer → Access tokens → Manage* in Databricks and generate a token. Enter it in the *Personal access token* field in VisuaLeaf.

Click *Test Connection, then *Save and connect. In the build I tested, JDBC URL **Auto-Fill**** put the HTTP path in *Catalog. If you see that, switch back to *SQL Warehouse** mode, clear the JDBC parameters from *Catalog*, and enter the fields manually.

Choose how VisuaLeaf signs in to Databricks below the warehouse connection fields.

Once you connect, run this to see the catalog and schema your session starts in.

SELECT current_catalog(), current_schema();

I opened shipment_events to check what its nested columns looked like in the table browser. Expanding a struct showed the individual fields without having to write a new query. If your connection works and a table query fails, check the three-part name and your Unity Catalog grants.

Expand a nested value to inspect details such as a shipment event’s scan location.

What I used VisuaLeaf for

Compare a source table with staging

In *Data Compare*, I paired shipment_notes with shipment_notes_staging and matched rows on note_id. The *Structure* tab flagged a separate difference. The source declares a foreign key from shipment_id to shipments.shipment_id. The staging table leaves it out.

Use note_id as the match key so the comparison pairs the same note across both tables.

Check that the match key is unique on both sides. Databricks treats primary and foreign keys on these Unity Catalog Delta tables as informational, so a declared primary key can still have duplicate values. Run this against the staging table and repeat it for the source.

SELECT note_id, COUNT(*) AS copies
FROM workspace.fulfillment_demo.shipment_notes_staging
GROUP BY note_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

If it returns rows, resolve the duplicates or pick a key that identifies one record on each side. For an order-line table, that might be the order ID and line number together.

Check the join before running it

Catalog Explorer has its own relationship view for tables with declared foreign keys. In *Visual Schema*, I could move the tables around the canvas and export the model as DBML.

The diagram shows the columns you need for the join: shipments.carrier_id` and carriers.carrier_id.

Follow the line from `_shipments.carrier_id_ __to__ _carriers.carrier_id`_ to find the columns for the carrier join.

I built the join in *Visual Query Builder*, filtered to shipment_status = 'Delivered', and sorted by delivered_on. The query returned 3,479 delivered shipments. If you join orders to shipments, an order with two shipments can appear twice. Count distinct order IDs when the metric is orders.

The SQL preview below the canvas shows the query generated from the join, filter, and sort settings.

*Columns & Filters* in the result grid work on the loaded page. To apply those conditions across the table, put them in the query’s WHERE clause and rerun it.

The filters match 11 of the 50 rows loaded on this results page.

Save a CSV export you can rerun

I saved the orders export as a *Data Transfer* job so I could run it again. The table source worked. In a separate test with a custom SQL source, the preview returned rows and the field mapping stayed empty. If that happens and you need a filtered CSV, run your query in the Databricks SQL editor and download the result.

Set the source type to Table and the target to CSV.

Databricks visualization and dashboard examples

The demo has a carrier_performance view with one row per carrier. It divides late deliveries by completed deliveries. I kept both counts in the result so I could check the percentage in the chart.

SELECT
    carrier_name,
    delivered_shipments,
    delivered_shipments - late_shipments AS on_time_shipments,
    late_shipments,
    CAST(late_delivery_pct AS DOUBLE) AS late_delivery_pct
FROM workspace.fulfillment_demo.carrier_performance
ORDER BY late_delivery_pct DESC, carrier_name;
Carrier Delivered Late Late delivery rate
Coastline Freight 862 195 22.62%
Summit Ground 867 122 14.07%
Cedar Express 874 77 8.81%
Bluebird Parcel 876 45 5.14%

In *Chart Builder*, I used carrier_name for the category and late_delivery_pct for the bar height. Keeping the chart beside the results in *Split Panel Views* made it easy to check the 22.62% against its denominator.

Coastline Freight had the highest late delivery rate in the demo at 22.62%, with 195 late shipments out of 862 delivered.

You could use the same data in a *Databricks AI/BI dashboard* to track the weekly late delivery rate or break it down by service level. Group by the promised date to report on shipments due that week. Before sharing, check whose data permissions the dashboard uses. Databricks can run its queries with the publisher’s or the viewer’s permissions.

Connect Power BI to Databricks

If your team reports in Power BI, open *Get data* in Power BI Desktop, choose the Databricks connector, and enter the warehouse hostname and HTTP path. *Import* loads a copy into Power BI and updates it on refresh. *DirectQuery* queries Databricks when people interact with the report.

Databricks SQL with Python

The *Databricks SQL Connector for Python* is for scripts that send SQL to a warehouse and fetch the result. This example uses a personal access token from an environment variable. Install databricks-sql-connector and set the three connection variables before running it.

from os import environ

from databricks import sql

with sql.connect(
    server_hostname=environ["DATABRICKS_SERVER_HOSTNAME"],
    http_path=environ["DATABRICKS_HTTP_PATH"],
    access_token=environ["DATABRICKS_TOKEN"],
) as connection:
    with connection.cursor() as cursor:
        cursor.execute("SELECT current_catalog(), current_schema()")
        print(cursor.fetchone())

A *Unity Catalog Python UDF* executes the Python on Databricks compute. I called delivery_outcome from VisuaLeaf’s SQL Editor, passing DATEDIFF(delivered_on, promised_on) to classify shipments as on time, late, or in transit. VisuaLeaf sent the SQL. Databricks ran the function on the warehouse. Use a serverless or Pro SQL warehouse for this kind of UDF.

Which Databricks tool should you open?

Task Where I’d start
Manage permissions, notebooks, or pipelines Databricks web workspace
Compare two versions of a table or inspect a join VisuaLeaf
Publish a dashboard for colleagues in Databricks Databricks AI/BI dashboards
Build a report for a team that already uses Power BI Power BI Desktop
Run SQL from your own script Databricks SQL Connector for Python

For a first run with your own data, download VisuaLeaf and start with source and staging tables from a refresh you can verify.

Is VisuaLeaf a Databricks App?

*Databricks Apps* is a service for hosting custom data and AI apps on Databricks. VisuaLeaf is a SQL client installed on your desktop. It connects to a warehouse to run queries and browse your data.

title: Why Prompt Firewalls Miss AI Agent Privilege Escalation (and How to Intercept Tool Calls at Runtime)
description:
Most AI security gateways check what enters the model and stop watching once inference begins. That gap breaks down the moment an autonomous agent can run SQL queries, fetch URLs, or invoke shell tools. An indirect prompt injection hidden in a retrieved ticket or web page can pass an input classifier, persuade the model to build a malicious tool payload, and reach your execution layer unchallenged.

To close that gap, you need a deterministic boundary between the model's tool intent and the underlying OS, database, or network runtime. While building ToolShield (an MIT-licensed Python runtime proxy), I tested a recursive argument scorer, a consecutive-violation circuit breaker, and structured audit hashing against real attack payloads. That testing also surfaced a subtle calibration bug where a standalone cloud metadata probe silently passed the default risk threshold.

Where input filters go blind

Input guardrails evaluate natural language, whereas tool-calling exploits rely on valid syntax aimed at downstream parsers. When an agent holds credentials for internal databases or cloud APIs, a poisoned retrieval snippet turns an ordinary model call into server-side request forgery (SSRF), path traversal, or command chaining.

A runtime proxy reverses the inspection order. Instead of guessing intent from prose, the proxy intercepts the exact tool_name and structured JSON arguments dictionary right before execution. Because those parameters conform to strict schemas, deterministic checks evaluate them in fractions of a millisecond without waiting on a second LLM call.

Inside a deterministic tool proxy

In toolshield/core.py, the ToolShield class enforces four controls on every call to guard(tool_name, arguments).

First, tool allowlists and blocklists gate which functions an agent can invoke. Calls outside allowed_tools add +0.70 risk (UNAUTHORIZED_TOOL), and calls matching blocked_tools add +0.80 (FORBIDDEN_TOOL), crossing the default 0.65 block threshold immediately.

Second, inspect_value() walks nested dictionaries and lists recursively so attackers cannot hide payloads inside deep JSON keys. Every matched regex rule in toolshield/rules.py adds a fixed weight (+0.50 for credential leakage or prompt hijack phrases, +0.45 for path traversal, +0.40 for shell chaining, and +0.35 for SSRF probes), capped at 1.0.

Third, a consecutive-violation circuit breaker tracks repeated blocks. If an agent triggers max_consecutive_violations blocks in a row (default 3), self.circuit_broken flips to True, and every subsequent call raises SecurityViolation with CIRCUIT_BREAKER_ACTIVE, including benign queries like SELECT 1;.

Fourth, SecurityAuditLogger emits Elastic Common Schema (ECS) JSON records containing the decision, latency, violation tags, and a SHA-256 fingerprint computed from the tool name, canonical sorted JSON arguments, and UTC timestamp.

Wrapping an existing Python tool function requires one decorator:

from toolshield import ToolShield, SecurityViolation

shield = ToolShield(
    agent_id="tier2-analyst-agent",
    allowed_tools={"query_db", "fetch_endpoint"},
    max_risk_threshold=0.65,
    max_consecutive_violations=3,
)

@shield.wrap("query_db", target_fn=run_sql)
def guarded_query(**kwargs):
    return run_sql(**kwargs)

Running the local unit test suite (tests/test_core.py) verifies benign queries, shell chaining blocks, credential detection, forbidden tools, and circuit-breaker quarantine across all 6 test cases in 0.001s.

Testing payloads and catching a threshold bug

Theory looks tidy until you test single-vector payloads through the CLI. On bash, pass JSON arguments directly; on Windows PowerShell, wrap the JSON payload with escaped quotes or pass it via Python so the shell preserves internal braces and asterisks.

First, run a benign database read:

python -m toolshield.cli --tool query_db --args '{"query":"SELECT count(*) FROM alerts;"}'

That exits 0 with risk_score: 0.0 and an audit record:

[+] STATUS: ALLOWED
[+] Attestation Hash: c0b003243ccaf23f2693ff9563aa71ad0a52f14c957ea450a7efcf9f11d9b4ce

Next, send a combined shell injection, sensitive file read, and cloud metadata probe:

python -m toolshield.cli --tool execute_shell --args '{"cmd":"cat /etc/passwd; curl http://169.254.169.254"}'

ToolShield blocks the call and exits 2 (Risk Score: 1.00):

[-] STATUS: BLOCKED (Tool execution 'execute_shell' blocked by ToolShield: Risk score 1.00 exceeded threshold 0.65)
[-] Violations: SHELL_INJECTION:COMMAND_CHAINING, PATH_TRAVERSAL:SENSITIVE_SYSTEM_FILES, SSRF_PROBE:CLOUD_METADATA_ENDPOINT
[-] Risk Score: 1.00

Now test a single high-impact SSRF probe targeting an allowlisted HTTP helper (fetch_endpoint):

python -m toolshield.cli --tool fetch_endpoint --args '{"url":"http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/"}'

Watch what happens at the default 0.65 threshold:

[+] STATUS: ALLOWED
[+] Attestation Hash: ddd7a131678cef064e2f34256143f7ea387bd7d1e369ba193e337b3cdcf69a07
{
  "security": {
    "decision": "ALLOW",
    "risk_score": 0.35,
    "violations": [
      "SSRF_PROBE:CLOUD_METADATA_ENDPOINT"
    ]
  }
}

Because SSRF_PROBE carries a +0.35 weight and fetch_endpoint is not on the blocklist, the total score (0.35) stays below 0.65 and the metadata request slips through! Lowering the threshold to 0.30 catches the probe immediately:

python -m toolshield.cli --tool fetch_endpoint --args '{"url":"http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/"}' --threshold 0.30

[-] STATUS: BLOCKED (Tool execution 'fetch_endpoint' blocked by ToolShield: Risk score 0.35 exceeded threshold 0.30)
[-] Violations: SSRF_PROBE:CLOUD_METADATA_ENDPOINT
[-] Risk Score: 0.35

Weighted additive scoring is easy to miscalibrate for standalone critical rules. Any rule that represents an outright policy breach, such as querying 169.254.169.254 or metadata.google.internal, should either carry a weight at or above max_risk_threshold (>= 0.65) or act as an unconditional hard-deny trigger.

When regex proxies are not enough

A lightweight Python proxy lowers blast radius quickly, yet three engineering limits remain.

Regex rules catch obvious metacharacters (;, &&, ../), whereas double-URL encoding, Unicode homoglyphs, or DNS rebinding targeting private CIDRs require canonical URL parsing and network egress controls at the container or VPC layer.

Whenever you adjust max_risk_threshold or add rules in rules.py, write regression unit tests asserting that each standalone critical payload blocks on its own rather than relying on stacked violations.

Finally, compute_attestation_hash() hashes arguments and timestamps with a static string salt ("toolshield-v1") and no prior-event chaining. Treat that hash as a SIEM correlation ID; if you need tamper evidence against a compromised proxy host, add HMAC signing with an external secret or ship logs to append-only storage.

Next step

Audit the rule weights in your agent tool wrappers against your block threshold today. If any standalone indicator (cloud metadata IPs, private key headers, or path traversal) scores below your block cutoff, promote it to a hard-deny check and enforce egress filtering behind the proxy.

Drafted with AI-assisted editing and verified against local unit tests and CLI runs on ToolShield.

title: Check that an osu! skin's followpoint frames are numbered without gaps
description:
An animated follow-point trail uses followpoint-{n}.png, starting at 0. A missing number in the middle usually stops the animation early, and it is easy to miss in a folder that already has followpoint.png. This note is a small Python script that lists the still frame and the numbered frames, then reports gaps before you pack the .osk.

The script does not judge contrast or aim. It only checks names. You still need to play a jump map afterwards. Finished examples of follow-point density are easier to compare on osuskins.org.

What the script looks for

  • A base file followpoint.png, followpoint.jpg, or followpoint.jpeg (and the @2x partner if you ship one).
  • Numbered frames followpoint-0.png, followpoint-1.png, and so on.
  • A gap such as 0, 1, 3 (2 missing), or a sequence that starts at 1 instead of 0.

The script

Save this as check_followpoint_frames.py in the skin folder, or pass the folder as the first argument.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
import sys
from pathlib import Path

STEM = "followpoint"
EXTS = {".png", ".jpg", ".jpeg"}

def exists(dirpath: Path, name: str) -> Path | None:
    for ext in EXTS:
        for cand in (dirpath / (name + ext), dirpath / (name + "@2x" + ext)):
            if cand.is_file():
                return cand
    return None

def main() -> int:
    root = Path(sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else ".").resolve()
    base = exists(root, STEM)
    frames = {}
    for p in root.iterdir():
        name = p.name
        for ext in list(EXTS) + [e.replace(".", "@2x.") for e in EXTS]:
            pass
        low = name.lower()
        if not low.startswith(STEM + "-"):
            continue
        core = name
        for tail in ("@2x.png", "@2x.jpg", "@2x.jpeg", ".png", ".jpg", ".jpeg"):
            if core.lower().endswith(tail):
                core = core[: -len(tail)]
                break
        else:
            continue
        suffix = core.split("-", 1)[-1]
        if suffix.isdigit():
            frames.setdefault(int(suffix), []).append(p.name)
    print("folder:", root)
    if base:
        print("base:  ", base.name)
    else:
        print("base:   MISSING followpoint.png (or .jpg)")
    if not frames:
        print("frames: none (static follow point only)")
        return 0 if base else 1
    nums = sorted(frames)
    print("frames:", ", ".join(str(n) for n in nums), "(%d files)" % sum(len(v) for v in frames.values()))
    start = nums[0]
    end = nums[-1]
    missing = [i for i in range(0, end + 1) if i not in frames]
    if start != 0:
        print("warning: sequence starts at %d, not 0" % start)
    if missing:
        print("MISSING frame numbers: " + ", ".join(str(i) for i in missing))
        return 1
    print("ok: contiguous followpoint-0 .. followpoint-%d" % end)
    return 0

if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

What to do with the report

A skin does not have to animate follow points. If you only ship followpoint.png, the script should report no frames and a present base file. If you meant to ship an animation, fix any missing number and run the script again, then play a map with clear jumps and confirm the trail still points right and fades in 1.2 seconds.

The job of this check is only to catch a missing followpoint-2.png before you upload the .osk. If the names you intended to ship are present and numbered without gaps, the script is done.

title: An agent that pays for its own timestamps: x402 on a CPU-mined coin
description:
Every night at 23:41 an agent we run, on OpenClaw on a Mac mini, makes a list of the SHA-256 of every file in its notes, takes the SHA-256 of that list and stamps it into a blockchain. It pays for the stamp itself. It has no card and no USDC: it pays in NORTH, the coin of TrueNorth, which ordinary processors mine. This post shows how that works, what it costs, what went wrong, and when you should use something else.

What a stamp is for

A stamp proves that some data existed no later than a given block. For an agent that means: these were its notes on that night, and nobody changed them afterwards without it showing. The same goes for logs, model outputs or release files. Only the SHA-256 leaves the machine, never the file.

The service

The stamping service sits behind an HTTP gate:

https://gate.polarka.org/v1/stamp/<sha256>

Every ten minutes it puts whatever came in into one Merkle tree and writes the root into the chain in one transaction. Each SHA-256 gets a proof: the path in the tree, the transaction and the block. Anybody can check it, with their own node if they don't want to trust ours:

polarka-agent stamp-verify proof.json --rpc-url http://127.0.0.1:<rpc port> --rpc-cookie <datadir>/.cookie

Blocks come every two minutes on average, so a proof is usually in a block within about twelve minutes. When we released version 0.2.8 of the client on 24 November 2026, its two stamps took 1.5 and 10 minutes.

Paying with x402, in NORTH

The gate speaks x402: a call without payment gets 402 Payment Required with what the gate takes, the client pays and asks again. The gate sells a lot of 100 calls; today a lot costs 0.0091765 NORTH, the NORTH that about 600 hashes make. A stamp is one call.

On the client side it is one command:

pip install polarka-agent==0.2.8
polarka-agent start        # a wallet, a first coin from a faucet, mining for a pool

The wallet pays nothing until its owner writes the limits by hand; no command and no tool writes this file:

echo '{"per_payment_north": "0.05", "per_day_north": "0.5"}' > ~/.polarka-agent/default/limits.json

Then:

H=$(shasum -a 256 notes.tar | cut -d' ' -f1)
polarka-agent fetch "https://gate.polarka.org/v1/stamp/$H" --most 0.05

--most is the most this call may pay. The first answer says the stamp waits for the next batch. Asking again for the same URL later brings the proof; that costs one more call of the lot, not a new payment.

For an agent that speaks MCP:

{"mcpServers": {"north": {"command": "uvx",
  "args": ["polarka-agent@0.2.8", "--dir", "/path/to/north-wallet", "mcp"]}}}

The tool is north_fetch. Our agent can also run shell commands, so its wallet runs as a signing service under a user of its own: the agent can ask it to pay, but it cannot read the recovery words or change the limits (polarka-agent signer-setup prints the script for Linux or macOS).

Paid by its own processor

A program can mine the NORTH it spends:

polarka-agent mine https://pool.polarka.org --address ADDRESS

The pool pays for each share every ten minutes, so there is no waiting for a block of one's own. At 100 calls for about 600 hashes, a year of nightly stamps, each asked for once more to get its proof, takes about 4,400 hashes: a few seconds of an ordinary processor's work. The exact number moves with the network's difficulty; polarka.org/data/unit.json has it.

What the agent actually did

  • The scheduled job has run every night since 23 November. The stamp of that night is in block 31012 and checks against our own node.
  • One lot pays for all of it, tests included: 94 calls of 100 are left.
  • In version 0.2.7 we found a bug by using it: two stamps asked for 66 seconds apart bought two lots, because the second call did not see that the first payment was still waiting for its block (the agent's second lot is still unused). Version 0.2.8 fixes that: one payment for a lot now serves every path of the gate while it waits. Two calls at exactly the same moment can still buy two lots.
  • On 24 November the agent stopped halfway, before it fetched the previous night's proof. Nothing was lost: a proof can be fetched later from the same URL, and we fetched it the next evening.

When to use something else

  • OpenTimestamps stamps into Bitcoin for free, because public calendars put any number of stamps into one Bitcoin transaction. A proof takes a few hours to be confirmed. If you need Bitcoin's security and can wait, use it.
  • USDC over x402: if your agent already holds USDC, paying per call there is cheap too. Coinbase's facilitator charges $0.001 a transaction after 1,000 free a month.
  • What we are not: TrueNorth is young and small. Its last blocks would be cheap to out-compute, and a node refuses to go back more than 72 blocks. NORTH is not traded anywhere, so it has no price. The service is run by one person under a pseudonym and may stop.

A NORTH stamp fits where minutes matter, or where an agent should pay its own way without a card or a funded account.

Try it without installing anything

There is a remote MCP connector at https://polarka.org/mcp (in Claude: Settings > Connectors > Add custom connector). Its tools are free: the state of the network, a guide, a stamp into the chain (up to 100 a day from one place) and the check of a proof. It holds no wallet and asks for no account.

The code is open source (MIT, no warranty): https://github.com/Polarka-monitor/polarka-agent. How the parts work and who sees what: https://polarka.org/how/

Sources for the comparison: OpenTimestamps (https://opentimestamps.org and the announcement at https://petertodd.org/2016/opentimestamps-announcement), Coinbase's x402 documentation (https://docs.cdp.coinbase.com/x402/support/faq). The times and numbers are our own, measured between 22 and 25 November 2026.

This article was written with the help of an AI assistant, under the direction of the project's author, who checked it before it was published. The agent in it and much of the code were also built with AI assistance.

title: How to check a redirect map before a website migration
description:
The redirect map is the spreadsheet behind a website migration: one row per old URL, with the new URL it should go to. The redirect rules are built from it, so every mistake in the map becomes a live mistake on launch day.

We move sites between platforms (Webflow, Shopify, WordPress, custom code), and we check the map before anything goes live. This post covers the three kinds of mistakes we look for, with real output from redirect-map-check, the free, open-source checker we built for it:

  1. Old URLs the map leaves out
  2. Rows that send a URL to the wrong page
  3. Rows that contradict each other

All examples come from the tool's demo shop, Harbor & Pine. It's made up, so there's no client data here.

Start with every old URL

Google's site-move guide says that in the simplest moves, such as a domain change with a wildcard redirect, you may not need a list of old URLs. For more complex moves, you list them and decide where each one goes. It suggests where to look:

  • your sitemaps
  • server logs or analytics, for the URLs that get the most traffic
  • Search Console's links report, for pages with internal and external links
  • your CMS

It also says to include embedded images and videos.

On one of our own moves, a Webflow store going to Shopify, we built the 301s by crawling the old sitemap and combining it with the redirects already set up in Webflow. The sitemap covers the pages the old site listed. The existing redirects cover older addresses that already pointed somewhere.

If you're leaving Webflow, export its redirects first. Webflow's help page warns that importing a redirects CSV overwrites all existing redirects.

1. Old URLs missing from the map

A URL in the old sitemap with no row in the map: after launch it answers 404, or keeps answering at its old address. The checker reports it like this:

Each problem comes with a written fix, and here it suggests the closest live page it found. If nothing replaces the page, ignore the suggestion: Google's help on 404 errors says a deleted page with no replacement should return a 404, and that 404s don't harm a site's indexing or ranking.

Two related cases:

  • In the map, but not redirected: the row exists, but nobody built the rule. Fix: Add a 301 from /careers to /jobs (/jobs is live). Or, if /careers is meant to stay, delete row 15 from the map.
  • Not in the map, still works: a URL that keeps its address. That's fine if it was intended, so it's only a notice.

2. Rows that send a URL to the wrong page

A redirect can land on a live page and still be wrong. The checker looks for this in two ways.

The live rule doesn't match the map.

Change the rule for /delivery-information to a 301 straight to /help/delivery, which is live ("Delivery – Harbor & Pine"). It currently lands on /help/returns.

The rule matches the map, but the map is wrong. This is the one a URL-only check can't catch. The checker compares the old page's title and H1 with the new page's, ignoring words that appear on most pages, like the brand name:

The suggested pages are scored on title and H1 words and on the words in the URL slug. A score of 0.75 or more is labelled strong; from 0.5, possible.

It compares words, not meaning. A page renamed with different words, or translated, won't be found, so treat the suggestions as a shortlist to confirm.

After launch the old pages are gone, so the checker needs their titles from before. Keep the old-pages.json that a pre-launch run saves, or point the checker at a copy of the old site.

3. Rows that contradict each other

These come from reading the map itself, so they show up even before any rule is built.

  • Conflicting rows: one old URL, two targets.

  • Rows that redirect to each other: Rows 21 and 22 send these URLs to each other (/sale/winter → /sale/spring → /sale/winter). Point row 21 at a live page instead of another old URL. (This one is from the demo map with two rows added.)
  • A row pointing at another old URL, which turns the rule into a chain: Change row 18 to point straight at /shop instead of /old-promo-2023, and make the rule one hop. Google advises redirecting straight to the final destination and keeping chains short where that isn't possible.
  • A row that keeps the same URL, like /,/. It's fine as documentation, but don't build a rule from it: a URL redirecting to itself loops.
  • Duplicate rows and skipped rows (a row without two URLs, like /press,TBC) are reported as notices.

Run it on your own map

It's a Node CLI (Node 20+) with no runtime dependencies, and it runs on your own machine:

npx redirect-map-check \
  --sitemap https://www.example.com/sitemap.xml \
  --map redirects.csv \
  --base https://staging.example.com

Or npx redirect-map-check ui for a local page in your browser where you drop the files in.

The map can be a CSV or TSV with commas, semicolons or tabs, with or without a header. Headers such as old/new, from/to, Source URL/Destination URL or Redirect from/Redirect to are recognised in any order. You get a terminal summary plus CSV, HTML and JSON reports.

Run it against staging before launch, then against the live site after.

Limits:

  • It follows server redirects only, not JavaScript or meta refresh.
  • It checks the URLs you give it (the old sitemap, a URL list and the map), and doesn't crawl links to find more.
  • It skips image, video and news entries in sitemaps. If those addresses change too, pass them in with --urls.

More detail

  • The tool, with all its options
  • Source on GitHub (MIT)
  • Guides to the other problems it finds:
    • Redirects to the homepage
    • Redirects that end in a 404
    • Redirect chains and loops
    • Temporary redirects

Feedback on the report and on the wording of the fixes is very welcome, in the comments or as a GitHub issue.

Originally published at itcrowd.work.
