title: Start with 100 traces, not a better model
description:
Subtitle: If you are building with AI in a real product, the scarce work is not prompting. It is deciding what "good" means, and checking for it on every change and on live traffic.

It is now easy to get a convincing demo. A model answers the sample questions. A prototype looks fluent. A stakeholder says it feels better than last week.

That is not the same as having a product.

The gap is measurement. Generative systems do not fail the way ordinary software fails. They degrade quietly. A prompt change, a model update, or a tweak to retrieval can improve some cases and quietly worsen others. If the only quality signal is a handful of examples someone eyeballed, the team will ship the 5% regression and never see it.

This is not a new observation from me. It is the conclusion that keeps showing up in public writing from teams that have had to run these systems in production.

Look at the data before you build the harness

Airbnb's engineering team put the starting point as plainly as I have seen it. In their 2026 guide to eval-driven development, Rohit Girme, Dan Miller, Mia Zhao, Lifan Yang, and Clint Kelly write that when in doubt, you should look at your data. Their recommended first habit is to run a prototype through about 100 examples, read the outputs and the traces, find the mistakes, categorize them, and only then build an evaluation. They argue that this habit will do more for product quality than any framework.

That sequence is the opposite of what a lot of early teams do. The common path is to pick a generic "helpfulness" score, or a public benchmark, and treat a rising number as proof. Airbnb's warning is that this produces false confidence: the metric looks fine, you ship, and it did not capture the failure mode users actually hit.

They also recommend a golden set of 50 to 100 examples that must include bad examples, not only good ones, because you cannot test whether an evaluator has any discernment if it has never seen a failure. For LLM-as-judge setups, they target agreement with human labels in the high 80s to 90s before trusting the judge at scale, and they keep the evaluator set small: three to five well-calibrated judges, each aimed at one dimension, rather than a pile of noisy ones.

Two other details from that piece are worth taking seriously even on a small team. First, appoint a final human decision-maker for what counts as good or bad system behavior, because people will disagree. Second, evaluate the trajectory of an agent, not only the final answer. A correct answer reached by the wrong tool call, or by leaking data into a sub-call, is not a pass.

In production, they describe sampling 5% of live, de-identified traffic each day, running programmatic checks and virtual judges, and sending flagged outputs to human review, with a weekly product review to close the loop. New failure modes become new evals. That is the product work.

Evaluation has to be continuous, not a launch gate

A CSIRO-linked research group made the same argument at the systems level. In a paper last updated in November 2025, Boming Xia, Qinghua Lu, Liming Zhu, and colleagues argue that traditional evaluation, built around fixed benchmarks and static test suites, does not capture the way LLM agents behave after deployment. They propose treating evaluation as a continuous, governing function across development and operations, not a terminal checkpoint, and they describe a closed loop between offline, development-time evaluation and online, runtime evaluation.

MLflow's November 5, 2026 guide translates that into a practical sequence a production team can actually run. The pieces are a versioned dataset of real cases, automated scorers, a CI gate that blocks regressions, and sampled evaluation of production traces. It describes three loops:

  1. A pre-merge loop: every change to a prompt, model, tool, or retrieval step runs against an offline dataset in CI.
  2. A post-deploy loop: a sample of live traffic is scored, and low-scoring traces are flagged.
  3. A learning loop: production failures are added to the dataset, so the suite grows with the system's real failure modes.

The same guide, citing Airbnb, repeats the 50-to-100 example starting point, and it adds rules that hold up well: prefer real traces to synthetic ones, stratify examples by intent and failure mode, version the dataset like code, and write an expected fact or required tool call into each case, not just an input. For scoring, it separates deterministic code checks (format, required tools, policy rules) from LLM judges (relevance, tone, groundedness) and from human review, which remains the reference standard and the way judges get calibrated.

It also warns against a single average score. An average can hide a collapse in one intent. Compare per scorer, against a baseline, and fail the build with a clear message about which cases dropped.

Public benchmarks are not your eval

There is a temptation to skip all of this and cite a model leaderboard instead. That is a weak substitute for measuring your system.

On November 22, 2026, Eugene Yan published a teardown of 12 public evals. In eight of the twelve, he found evidence that the grader failed work that should have passed. Even when the grader was right, he argued, many benchmarks measure what is easy to check rather than what matters in real use, such as reliability, work velocity, or multi-turn collaboration.

That does not make public evals useless. It makes them a poor stand-in for a private, versioned set built from your own traces and failures. A benchmark tells you something about a model on a generic task, at one moment. Continuous evaluation tells you whether the application you actually shipped got better or worse for your users.

What this means for a small team

You do not need Airbnb's scale to use the same order of operations.

Start by instrumenting the system so every run leaves a trace. Run about 100 real or realistic examples, and read them. Label the failures. Build a small golden set that includes those failures. Put deterministic checks in first, then one or two judges, and calibrate those judges against a person who is allowed to make the final call. Run the suite on every change to the prompt, the model, the tools, or retrieval. Sample live traffic, even if the sample is small. Every new failure that matters gets added to the set so it cannot pass unnoticed again.

The teams that get this right will look slower in the first month, because they are reading output instead of polishing the demo. They will be faster after that, because they can tell whether a change helped.

I invest in and advise Drytis. The work I pay attention to is not the first draft a model can produce. It is the judgment that turns a promising system into something you can measure, catch in regression, and stand behind.

If you are building with AI this quarter, how many of last week's failures are now in a versioned set that would block the same mistake from shipping again?

Author

Thomas Eide is an AI investor and a hands-on advisor in Drytis. He has also invested in Drytis Academy as philanthropy. He's on X as @tahoehokie and on LinkedIn at linkedin.com/in/drytis.

title: Download Rank Isn't Revenue: What 90 Days of App Store Charts Say About Mobile Games
description:
Hi DEV 👋 This is my first post here. I run GameQuant, where I record the App Store charts in 170+ countries every day and turn them into pages, estimates and articles. Most of my time goes into data pipelines, but every so often the data shows something worth writing up for people who actually build games.

This fall it showed a clean example of something every mobile game developer hears and few get to see: a game can lose most of its new players and keep its revenue.

Three games, two scoreboards

The App Store has two charts that matter most for a free-to-play game. Top Free moves mostly with recent downloads. Top Grossing moves with recent spending. For a new game the two usually rise and fall together. For a mature one they can split.

Here are three of the biggest casual games in the US, from Oct 16 to Nov 24, 2026:

Game US Top Grossing Games US App Store revenue, Oct 2026 (estimate)
Monopoly GO #1 on 37 of 40 days $23M to $66M
Royal Match #2 to #5 every day $18M to $54M
Royal Kingdom #6 to #9 every day $13M to $38M

Revenue estimates are ranges for the US App Store only, in-app purchases before Apple's fee.

Royal Match: falling installs, flat revenue

Royal Match was #21 in US Top Free Games on Oct 17. By Nov 10 it was #105. From Nov 22 it sat at #177.

Over the same five weeks it never dropped below #5 in Top Grossing Games, and it was #1 in Top Grossing Puzzle on 26 of the 40 days.

A game that loses 156 places in the download chart and holds its revenue rank is living on the players it already has. For developers that is the whole argument for retention and live ops in one chart: once you have a large base of long-term payers, revenue can hold long after new installs slow down. Install rank on its own tells you very little about how a mature game is doing.

Royal Kingdom: the reverse

Royal Kingdom is the sequel from the same studio, Dream Games. On Nov 24 it was #64 in US Top Free Games, more than 100 places above Royal Match. It still earns less: #6 to #9 in Top Grossing Games, and an estimated $13M to $38M in October against Royal Match's $18M to $54M.

More installs, less revenue. A newer game has not yet built the base of long-time spenders the older one has. If you compare your game with a competitor by downloads alone, this is the trap.

Monopoly GO: the live ops machine

Monopoly GO lost #1 in US Top Grossing Games on only three days in that window, Nov 15 to 17, and took it back on Nov 18. It was #1 in the Top Grossing Board Games and Family Games charts every single day.

Two details stand out from the store data:

  • 14 updates in 90 days, the latest on Nov 19. That is an update roughly every week.
  • In-app items from $1.99 to $99.99 in the US. A wide price ladder lets casual players and big spenders both find something to buy.

Try it yourself

If you want to dig into chart data like this, there is a free sample of our rankings: the US App Store charts by category, positions 1 to 25, for 30 days (Oct 19 to Nov 17, 2026), as one CSV with the columns date, country, chart, category, rank, app_id, app_name, app_store_url. It is linked from gamequant.github.io, CC BY 4.0.

A few lines of pandas show where each of the three games appears and how high:

import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("gamequant_appstore_top25_us_2026-10-19_2026-11-17.csv",
                 dtype={"app_id": str})

games = {
    "1621328561": "Monopoly GO",
    "1482155847": "Royal Match",
    "1606549505": "Royal Kingdom",
}

sub = df[df["app_id"].isin(games)].copy()
sub["game"] = sub["app_id"].map(games)

# days in the top 25 and the typical rank, for every chart and category
summary = (sub.groupby(["game", "chart", "category"])["rank"]
              .agg(days="count", median_rank="median", best="min")
              .sort_values(["game", "best"]))
print(summary.to_string())

In this window you can watch Royal Match drop out of the top 25 of the Top Free Puzzle and Casual charts around the end of October, while it stays in the Top Grossing ones every day.

The full write-up

The complete article has the 90-day Top Grossing chart for all three games, their ranks in the UK, Germany and Japan, and the lifetime revenue figures Scopely has published:

👉 Monopoly GO revenue in 2026 vs Royal Match and Royal Kingdom

If you build mobile games, I'd like to hear how you read these charts for your own titles, or what you'd want to see in data like this. Comments are open.

title: What an Intermittent SQLite Lock Taught Us About Building Local-First Software
description:
Building a local-first application for a single user sounds simple enough. No distributed infrastructure, no thousands of concurrent users, no complicated database servers.

Yet even an ordinary editorial workflow can reveal an unexpected concurrency problem.

While developing LORQAI Studio 3, a creative content management application built with Go, SQLite, React, and TypeScript, we encountered an intermittent error:

database is locked

It appeared when saving an article after generating a website preview.

That small error led us to reconsider not only database concurrency, but also how we create and verify backups.

Reproducing the Problem

The application generates previews from existing content while allowing users to continue editing.

We suspected that an active read transaction might overlap with a subsequent save operation.

Instead of relying on additional retries, we isolated the suspected mechanism in a disposable test database.

The test followed a simple sequence:

  1. Create an article revision.
  2. Open a read-only transaction and read the revision.
  3. Keep the read transaction open.
  4. Attempt to save an updated revision through a separate writable connection.

With rollback-journal mode, the writer reached the configured three-second busy timeout and returned database is locked.

Even though each connection pool was limited to one open connection, the separate reader and writer could still compete for access to the same database.

We had reproduced a plausible failure mechanism, although the precise sequence behind the original intermittent UI error remained unconfirmed.

Moving to WAL

The architectural adjustment was to enable SQLite's Write-Ahead Logging mode for writable database connections.

The relevant setting is:

PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL;

Unlike rollback-journal mode, WAL allows readers to retain their existing snapshots while a writer commits new changes.

The journal mode also persists across database connections and restarts.

Our configuration uses:

  • Go driver: mattn/go-sqlite3
  • Busy timeout: 3000 milliseconds
  • Synchronous mode: FULL
  • Foreign keys: enabled
  • Maximum open connections: one per connection pool

After the change, the writer successfully committed a new article revision while the existing read transaction continued to see the original title.

That was the behavior we needed.

However, WAL does not turn SQLite into a multi-writer database. Write transactions remain serialized, and long-running readers can interfere with checkpoint progress.

WAL addresses an important concurrency problem, but it does not eliminate every possible source of contention.

The Backup Question

Changing the journaling mode introduced another consideration: backup integrity.

When WAL is active, committed changes may still reside in the associated WAL file. Simply copying the main database file is therefore not a reliable general-purpose backup strategy.

Our implementation uses SQLite's Online Backup API to create a separate, consistent database snapshot.

The backup workflow then:

  1. Creates an isolated database copy.
  2. Converts the destination database to DELETE journal mode.
  3. Confirms that the journal mode has changed.
  4. Closes the database connections before cleaning up the destination's remaining sidecar files.
  5. Verifies the resulting backup.

The live application continues using WAL.

Backup verification includes SQLite's PRAGMA integrity_check, SHA-256 payload verification, schema consistency checks, and validation of restored content and media.

Creating a backup is one thing. Demonstrating that it can be restored successfully is another.

What the Tests Confirmed

The recorded development results included successful targeted concurrency, backup, recovery, and restart tests.

The subsequent end-to-end editorial workflow also completed successfully without requiring a save retry.

These were controlled tests using disposable data, not a long-term production benchmark.

The results demonstrate that the reproduced reader/writer conflict was addressed under the tested conditions. They do not establish that all possible database contention has been eliminated.

What We Learned

Local-first does not mean concurrency-free.

A single-user application can still have background jobs, preview generation, database writes, and backup operations competing for shared resources.

Our experience reinforced four practical engineering principles:

  • Reproduce a failure before attempting to fix it.
  • Understand the database's concurrency model.
  • Consider the consequences of configuration changes beyond the immediate problem.
  • Verify recovery and the actual user workflow, not just individual components.

The most valuable outcome was not enabling WAL itself.

It was recognizing how a seemingly small database configuration change could affect the reliability of the wider application.

Sometimes the smallest error messages lead to the most useful architectural lessons.

References

  • SQLite Write-Ahead Logging
  • SQLite Isolation
  • SQLite Online Backup API

Based on documented LORQAI Studio 3 development experience and recorded regression tests. AI-generated drafting and editorial review were used in preparing this article.

title: The registry said 127.0.0.1. Docker went.
description:
Shipkeep is an open-source platform to deploy apps on your own servers. You give it an image reference, and an agent on the server asks the Docker daemon to pull it.

The control plane refuses a registry whose host is, or resolves to, an address that is not public: no loopback, no private ranges, no 169.254.169.254. That check has tests, and they pass.

Then a security review asked a simple question: who actually makes the connection? Not the control plane. It checks a name, then sends the server a reference that still names that host. The Docker daemon on the server does the pull, with none of those checks.

So I built a lab to see what the daemon does when the registry is the attacker.

The lab

One real node: Docker Engine 29.10.0, containerd image store, Ubuntu 24.04. A small HTTPS registry with a valid certificate for its name, the kind anyone can get for a domain they own. Plain HTTP servers on 127.0.0.1 and on the node's private address, logging whatever reached them. Every pull went through POST /images/create, the call the agent makes.

Four things reached places the control plane would never allow.

  1. The name is resolved again, on the node. I pointed the node's answer for the registry name at a private address. The daemon pulled from it. A name that passed the control plane's check can answer differently a minute later: DNS rebinding.
  2. Redirects are followed anywhere, in plain HTTP. A blob request answered 307 Location: http://127.0.0.1:8099/…. The daemon sent the GET there. Same with the node's private address.
  3. The token service is called anywhere, in plain HTTP. A 401 with Bearer realm="http://127.0.0.1:8099/…". The daemon called it, with the repository scope in the query string.
  4. A name that resolves to loopback, on any port. Docker treats 127.0.0.0/8 as an insecure registry by default. Version 29 does not fall back to HTTP, but it still opened the TCP connection and sent its TLS handshake to the port I chose.

This is not a Docker bug. The daemon is a client, and it trusts the registry you name. That is fine on a laptop. It is not fine when "the registry you name" can be typed by any user who can deploy an image.

These requests are blind: the response never reaches the user, and the pull fails on the digest or the token. But the path, the query and the port are the attacker's choice, and a closed port fails differently from an open one. That is enough to map the node's network, and to send a GET with side effects to an internal service: a cloud metadata endpoint, an admin page, a database's HTTP port. On a single-machine installation, the control plane itself is on that loopback.

An egress proxy, and why it is not enough

Docker reads HTTP_PROXY and HTTPS_PROXY for its registry traffic. Point them at a proxy you control, and every connection goes through something that can say no.

So each server now runs shipkeep-egress, a small mode of the agent binary, as its own systemd service and its own user, on 127.0.0.1:7480. It does very little:

  • CONNECT only. Registry traffic stays HTTPS end to end, and the proxy never sees a path, a header or a token. A plain HTTP request, which is what cases 2 and 3 become, is refused.
  • Public addresses only. It resolves the name itself and refuses if any answer is not public, using the same list as the control plane. A test reads both lists, the Go one and the TypeScript one, and fails if they differ.
  • The check runs in the dialer. Not on the DNS answer, but in net.Dialer.Control, on the address the socket is about to connect to. A second answer, a cache or a retry cannot change what is reached. 
func guard(_, address string, _ syscall.RawConn) error {
    parsed, err := netip.ParseAddrPort(address)
    if err != nil || !Public(parsed.Addr()) {
        return errNotPublic
    }
    return nil
}
  • Bounded. 64 tunnels, 10 seconds to connect, one hour per tunnel. Each tunnel logs its host, its port and its outcome.

With the proxy in place, cases 1, 2 and 3 to a private address were refused. Cases 2 and 3 to 127.0.0.1 still reached the probe.

Go's proxy support never sends a request for localhost, 127.0.0.0/8 or ::1 to a proxy, whatever NO_PROXY says. The daemon is written in Go. A redirect to a loopback literal bypasses any proxy you configure.

A firewall rule for one process

Loopback had to be closed in the kernel, for the daemon only. Other services on the host must keep talking to each other, and containers have their own network namespace anyway.

nftables can match the cgroup of the process that owns a socket. So: reject new connections from the Docker daemon to loopback, except the proxy and the local DNS resolver.

table inet shipkeep_egress {
  chain output {
    type filter hook output priority filter; policy accept;
    socket cgroupv2 level 1 "shipkeep.slice" ct state new jump docker
  }
  chain docker {
    ip daddr 127.0.0.1 tcp dport 7480 return
    meta l4proto { tcp, udp } ct original ip daddr 127.0.0.53 ct original proto-dst 53 return
    ip daddr 127.0.0.0/8 reject
    ip6 daddr ::1 reject
  }
}

ct state new matters. docker-proxy, which serves published ports, runs in the daemon's cgroup too, and its replies to local clients must still get through.

That rule is not what I wrote first.

The first design broke in the lab

The first version matched system.slice/docker.service and was loaded by an ExecStartPre of the Docker unit. It worked, and it survived two restarts of Docker. Then the lab kept going.

nftables resolves a cgroup path to a numeric ID when the rule is loaded. The path must exist at that moment. The cgroup of docker.service is created at each start and is gone while Docker is stopped, at boot in particular. Restarting Docker gives a new ID, and a rule loaded earlier matches nothing.

nftables.service starts by flushing the whole ruleset. Ubuntu's /etc/nftables.conf begins with flush ruleset. A restart of that service removes the guard while Docker keeps running. It removes Docker's own NAT rules too, which is a separate surprise.

The fix is a slice. The Docker unit gets Slice=shipkeep.slice, a slice that holds the daemon and nothing else. It starts at boot, before nftables and Docker, and its cgroup exists whether Docker runs or not. Its ID does not change when Docker restarts.

The guard is then loaded in the same transaction as anything that could remove it. A drop-in for nftables.service replaces its start and its reload with one file that includes /etc/nftables.conf, then the guard. Its stop flushes, then loads the guard again. One nft transaction, so there is never a moment without the rule.

Two smaller ones:

  • The DNS exception failed when the node itself ran in a container. Docker's embedded resolver answers on 127.0.0.11:53, then DNATs to a random port. The rule saw the translated port. Matching ct original, the destination before translation, fixed it.
  • The proxy could not run, and the installer did not notice. The egress service could not execute the binary inside the agent's private directory. The daemon reports its proxy settings whether or not anything listens there, so every check looked green. The service now runs from a root-owned copy, and the installer waits until the proxy answers.

Settings drift

The proxy settings can change after the installation: someone edits daemon.json, which Docker applies before its environment, or adds a drop-in. So the installer refuses to continue when daemon.json sets a proxy, and the agent reads the daemon's settings (GET /info) before every pull. If they are not exactly the proxy's, it refuses with a cause of its own, egress_unguarded, and the deployment says why.

I checked that too: with NO_PROXY=* added later, the next deployment stopped before any download.

What it costs

  • A registry that redirects to plain HTTP stops working. Docker Hub, GHCR, ECR and GCR redirect to HTTPS, so they keep working.
  • A registry on a private network is unsupported. It already was. When it is supported, its exception will be an explicit server setting.
  • Every pull of that daemon goes through the proxy, including docker compose pull for the control plane on a single machine. The guide says so.
  • Servers installed before this change need to run the installer again, and Docker restarts with it.

Results

On the lab node, after the change:

  • A pull from Docker Hub went through the proxy, including the redirect to its CDN.
  • The four attack registries were refused, and the probes received nothing.
  • A deployment from the control plane succeeded.
  • Loopback stayed refused for the daemon after Docker restarts, after every start, reload, restart and stop of nftables, and after reboots.

The design, the alternatives and the lab are in ADR 0023. The proxy is under 400 lines of Go, comments included, with nothing outside the standard library.

Where it stands

  • Released in v0.1.0-alpha.5. It has run in test containers with systemd, not on a real server yet.
  • If you installed an earlier release, run the server installer again on each server.

Where you can help

  • You know nftables or systemd better than I do: read the guard and its drop-ins and tell me what I missed.
  • You have a disposable Ubuntu 24.04 VM and a domain name: follow the installation guide and tell me where it breaks.
  • First contribution: the good first issues each say what to change and when it is done.

And a question for the comments: what does the Docker daemon on your servers reach when a registry tells it to go somewhere else?

title: Public vs Private in Go: How Visibility Works (Without public or private)
description:
If you come from Java, C#, or TypeScript, you're probably used to writing public and private all the time. In Go, those keywords don't exist. Visibility is defined in a much simpler way: by the first letter of the name.

In this article we'll see how this works in practice, with examples of functions, structs, and methods, along with some best practices.

The golden rule

  • Uppercase letter → exported (public): can be used by other packages.
  • Lowercase letter → unexported (private): can only be used within the same package.

This applies to functions, variables, constants, types, methods, and struct fields.

package example

var Version = "1.0.0"   // public
var debug = false       // private

const MaxItems = 100    // public
const timeout = 30      // private

type User struct{}      // public
type cache struct{}     // private

Public and private functions

Let's create a simple project with the following structure:

myproject/
├── go.mod
├── main.go
└── calculator/
    └── calculator.go

calculator/calculator.go

package calculator

// Sum is public (starts with an uppercase letter): other packages can call it.
func Sum(a, b int) int {
    return validate(a) + validate(b)
}

// validate is private (starts with a lowercase letter): only the calculator package can see it.
func validate(n int) int {
    if n < 0 {
        return 0
    }
    return n
}

main.go

package main

import (
    "fmt"

    "myproject/calculator"
)

func main() {
    fmt.Println(calculator.Sum(2, 3)) // works: 5

    // calculator.validate(5) // compile error
}

If you try to call calculator.validate(5), the compiler complains:

cannot refer to unexported name calculator.validate

In other words, the compiler itself enforces encapsulation. No conventions or code review needed.

Structs, fields, and methods

The same rule applies to struct fields and methods. A very common pattern is to keep the field private and expose access through public methods:

package account

type Account struct {
    Owner   string  // public
    balance float64 // private
}

// NewAccount is a "constructor": the idiomatic way to initialize private fields.
func NewAccount(owner string) *Account {
    return &Account{Owner: owner, balance: 0}
}

// Deposit is a public method.
func (a *Account) Deposit(amount float64) {
    if a.isValidAmount(amount) {
        a.balance += amount
    }
}

// Balance is a public getter to read the private field.
func (a *Account) Balance() float64 {
    return a.balance
}

// isValidAmount is a private method.
func (a *Account) isValidAmount(amount float64) bool {
    return amount > 0
}

Using it from another package:

acc := account.NewAccount("Maria")
acc.Deposit(100)

fmt.Println(acc.Owner)     // ok
fmt.Println(acc.Balance()) // ok: 100

// acc.balance = 1000      // error: unexported field
// acc.isValidAmount(10)   // error: unexported method

Notice that you can't change the balance directly. Every change goes through Deposit, which validates the amount. This protects the data integrity of your struct.

Important points (and gotchas)

1. The unit of privacy is the package

In Go, "private" means private to the package, not to the file or the struct. If two files are in the same folder and declare the same package, they can see each other's private functions.

This is different from Java, where private restricts access to the class.

2. There is no protected

Go has no class inheritance, so the concept of protected doesn't exist. There are only two levels: exported and unexported.

3. Getters don't use the Get prefix

The Go convention is to name the getter for the balance field Balance(), not GetBalance(). Setters, if they exist, are usually named SetBalance().

4. JSON only sees exported fields

This is a classic mistake for beginners. Private fields are not serialized by the encoding/json package:

type Product struct {
    Name  string  `json:"name"`
    price float64 `json:"price"` // will NOT show up in the JSON!
}

If the field needs to appear in an API response, it must start with an uppercase letter:

type Product struct {
    Name  string  `json:"name"`
    Price float64 `json:"price"` // ok
}

The same goes for ORM libraries like GORM: unexported fields are ignored.

5. The internal/ folder

Want to restrict an entire package? Put it inside a folder named internal/. The compiler only allows code from the parent module (or parent directory) to import that package.

Public vs Private in Go: How Visibility Works (Without public or private)

myproject/
├── go.mod
├── cmd/
│   └── api/
│       └── main.go
└── internal/
    ├── handler/
    ├── service/
    └── repository/

Anyone importing your module from outside cannot access anything inside internal/. It's great for hiding implementation details without having to expose everything as public API.

6. Document what's public

Everything exported should have a comment starting with the name of the identifier. go doc and pkg.go.dev use it to generate documentation:

// Sum returns the sum of two integers, ignoring negative values.
func Sum(a, b int) int {
    return validate(a) + validate(b)
}

Best practices

  • Start private. Export only what really needs to be used by other packages. It's easy to make something public later, but making something private again is hard (and breaks compatibility).
  • Keep your public API small. The less you expose, the less you have to maintain and document.
  • Use constructors (NewX) when the struct has private fields that need to be initialized correctly.
  • Use internal/ to organize larger projects into layers without leaking details.

Summary

Characteristic Public (exported) Private (unexported)
Name starts with Uppercase Lowercase
Accessible from Any package Only the same package
Appears in JSON Yes No
Appears in go doc Yes No

Conclusion

Go's approach is minimalist: a single rule, checked by the compiler, with no extra keywords. At first it may feel strange to depend on capitalization, but after a few projects it becomes natural, and the code gets cleaner to read, because you know whether something is public just by looking at its name.

I hope you enjoyed it; if you have any tips, feel free to share them in the comments.

title: A security audit found 11 issues. Five of my fixes had bugs of their own.
description:
Shipkeep is an open-source platform to deploy apps on your own servers. An agent on each server runs containers and routes, and a control plane tells it what to do. Last week the agent learned to ship container logs, and the browser learned to open a shell in a container.

Then a security audit of main filed eleven issues. Three were P1:

  • secret values could reach the log store unredacted, in two different ways;
  • one WebSocket message, under 64 KiB, could crash the API process. I had written that code the same day, while answering review comments.

I fixed each issue with a test that failed on the old code first. Then I reviewed each fix the way I would review someone else's pull request. Five of the eight fixes had a real bug of their own.

Absence is not "no secrets"

The agent removes secret values from log lines before shipping them. To know which environment variables are secrets, it reads a container label, sk.secret_env, which lists their names. The agent writes that label when it creates a container.

Containers created before the label existed have no label, and the shipper read "no label" as "no secrets". After an agent upgrade, an application that printed its token got that token stored as written.

Worse, a new container with no secrets also had no label: the agent only set it when there was something to list. Missing and empty meant the same thing, so the shipper could not tell an old container from one with nothing to hide.

The fix:

  • The label is now always set, empty when there are no secrets.
  • A container without the label is treated as one whose secret names are unknown: every environment value of 8 bytes or more is redacted, PATH and NODE_ENV=production included, until the application is redeployed.

Over-redacting is ugly in logs. Leaking a token is worse.

Logs come one line at a time

The second P1: a secret containing a newline, like a PEM key, was never redacted. Docker output is split into lines before redaction, and the redactor searched each line for the whole value. No single line ever contains a multiline value.

Each line of a multiline value is now a value of its own. Then a related case: lines are cut at 16 KiB. A line cut in the middle of a secret ends with its first half, which no whole-value match finds. So for a cut line, the redactor also masks the longest start of a secret that the line ends with.

My first version ran that cut-start redaction before the normal one. The review found the hole:

TOKEN=abcdefgh_abcdefgh
cut line:          ... abcdefgh_abcdefgh
cut-start first:   ... abcdefgh_[redacted]

The last 8 bytes of the secret are also its first 8 bytes. The cut-start pass masked them, and the whole-value pass then had nothing left to match. Half the secret shipped.

Running the passes the other way round fails too: a shorter secret inside the cut start hides the rest of it. The version that holds does not chain replacements at all. For each secret, one pass over the line with the Knuth-Morris-Pratt failure function finds every occurrence, overlapping ones included, plus the start the line ends with. Then the union of those spans is redacted:

for _, value := range r.values {
    found = value.match(found, line, cut) // every occurrence, and the cut start
}
// sort, merge overlapping spans, replace each with [redacted]

It also makes the cost linear. Secrets can be 64 KiB, and a naive suffix scan of a crafted 16 KiB line is quadratic. A randomized test compares the spans with a byte-by-byte scan on 20,000 cases over a two-letter alphabet, where values overlap themselves and each other.

64 KiB of braces

The browser terminal sends control messages over a WebSocket: {"type":"resize","cols":80,"rows":24}. My code turned each message into a class-validator DTO with plainToInstance, and only then validated its fields.

plainToInstance walks the whole object recursively. A resize message with an extra field nested 3,000 levels deep fits in 64 KiB, and it overflows the stack. A WebSocket message listener runs outside the framework's exception handling, so that RangeError could take down the process, and every session in it.

The fix checks the message's shape before anything transforms it: exactly the expected keys, each a primitive. Each message is also handled inside its own try, so a failure ends only that session.

The review of that fix found a weakness, not one of the five bugs: my try also wrapped the shape check. If the check itself ever threw, the message would be silently dropped instead of ending the session as the spec says. Worse, the tests still passed with the shape check deleted, because the broad catch hid the overflow. Now only JSON.parse is caught there. I checked that deleting the shape check makes three tests fail.

Read, compare, write

GitHub tells Shipkeep when the GitHub App is installed, suspended or removed. An event applies only if it is newer than the last one applied. Two problems:

  • Two deliveries at once. Both read the same row, both pass the time check, and the older one can write last. An older unsuspend undid a newer suspend.
  • A delayed event after a removal. The removal deleted the row, and with it the time of the last event. A delayed unsuspend then recreated the installation, active.

Each delivery now takes a transaction-level advisory lock per installation before reading. A removal keeps the row as a tombstone. GitHub gives a reinstalled App a new installation id, so nothing legitimate ever follows a removal.

The test forces the interleaving. A third PostgreSQL connection holds the installation's row while both deliveries start, and releases it once both are waiting. The old code lets the older unsuspend win, and with the fix the newer state stays, in both orders.

The review found what the lock broke. Before the lock, each delivery purged expired delivery records, locking those rows. A delivery waiting for one busy installation kept them locked, so a delivery for any other installation blocked behind it. The purge now uses FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED. With the old purge, the new test hangs until its timeout.

Refuse, and ask

Deleting an application after a failed first deployment could free its domain while a server still routed it. The cleanup of the failed deployment was queued but had not run yet. Another application could then claim the hostname.

The first fix refused the deletion until every server had confirmed the cleanup. The review found the dead end. A creation that failed after reaching the server gets no cleanup at all. A cleanup that expires can never be queued again under the same key. Either way, the application could never be deleted.

So a refused deletion now asks: it queues a removal for each container or route a server may still hold, audits that, and answers 409. Once the servers confirm, the next attempt goes through.

Then the automated review on the pull request caught what that change broke. The deletion queued those removals before it looked at the confirmation token. Deleting an application requires a confirmation, and any token, valid or not, could now make a server remove containers. The token is now checked first, without being spent, so it stays usable for the deletion that follows.

What the reviews were for

None of these bugs were in code I hadn't touched. Every one was in a fix: a fix makes an assumption about the bug, and the review checks that assumption. Each fix started with a test that failed on the old code, and that test passed every time. It just did not cover what the fix itself broke.

Reviewing my own fixes cold, a few hours later, caught five of them before merge. The automated review on the pull request caught the sixth: the confirmation token.

Where it stands

  • Released: v0.1.0-alpha.5, with all of the above, on refreshed base images. The release scan, which stops on any high or critical finding that has a fix, passed on both architectures with no exception.
  • Not v0.1.0-alpha.4. That release stopped halfway. The workflow pins the image of the tool that copies the control plane image by digest, and quay.io no longer served that digest. The binaries were published, the image and the installer bundle were not. Pinning by digest protects you from an image that changes, not from one that disappears. A published release is never replaced, so alpha.4 now says so at the top, and alpha.5 is the same code plus a one-line fix.
  • The control plane image still has high findings in Debian packages with no fix yet. The triage checked what the process actually loads: Node carries its own zlib and zstd, and nothing in the container uses PAM, util-linux or Perl. Each one is recorded in docs/security/image-triage-2026-11.md, with the pinned PostgreSQL image's one high finding, accepted until December 18.
  • Installing the published alpha.5 from scratch, the way the guide says, still found three things no test had: a documented command without a terminal that stops at a question it did not expect, a misleading error when the agent starts before the control plane is ready, and a restore that leaves a container running. They are #499, #500 and #501.
  • One more thing from the release day: GitHub squash-merged a pull request during an API incident, never marked it merged, and never ran CI on the commit. I did not tag that commit. I waited for the next merge, and tagged once CI was green on it.

Where you can help

  • You run self-hosted apps: follow the installation guide on a disposable Ubuntu 24.04 VM and tell me where it breaks.
  • You like breaking things: the exec WebSocket, the log shipper and the GitHub webhook endpoint are all new. Issues are welcome, and the security policy says how to report privately.
  • First contribution: the good first issues each say what to change and when it is done.

And a question for the comments: when you fix a security bug, who reviews the fix?

title: I tested 78 AI-agent pull requests for cheating. Here's what I found.
description:
Coding agents like Copilot, Devin, Cursor and Claude are rewarded for one thing: a green build.
So I assumed they would sometimes get one the wrong way. Delete the assertion that caught their bug.
Add .skip to a failing test. Loosen tsconfig. Add a package that doesn't exist.

I built a tool to catch that, then tested whether it actually happens.

The tool

Isoklo is a CLI and GitHub App that checks pull requests with fixed rules.
No AI model, so the same change always gets the same verdict. It looks at the diff and checks things like:

  • assertions removed from tests with nothing added in their place
  • skipped or .only tests
  • weakened type-check or lint config
  • new packages that don't exist on npm or PyPI
  • secrets, and hidden Unicode instructions in files like CLAUDE.md

You can try it in any git repo:

npx --yes isoklo@latest check --base main




The test

I searched GitHub for recent pull requests opened by agents, and kept only active team repos
(organisations or 3+ contributors, pushed in the last 30 days).

  • 78 agent pull requests across 18 repos
  • Devin: 47 PRs · Cursor: 22 · Claude: 5 · Copilot: 4

I ran every PR through Isoklo and checked each finding by hand.

The result

  • 0 real problems. No agent deleted a test to get a green build.
  • 2 blocks, both false alarms:
    1. A Go test check (t.Fatalf) moved into a helper function looked like a deleted assertion. It was a refactor.
    2. Passing os.Environ() to a subprocess looked like leaking environment variables. It wasn't.
  • Most other output was low-value notes like "a workflow file changed".

What I learned

  1. Agents in real team repos behave better than the internet suggests. Maybe because teams review agent PRs closely, or because agents are mostly given small, safe tasks.
  2. The scary demos are real, but rare. It's easy to build an agent that cheats on purpose. It's much harder to find one doing it in the wild.
  3. Test your assumption before your second feature. I spent weeks building rules and only one day testing whether the problem was common. I should have done it the other way round.

What I'd love to know

If you use AI agents at work: what's the sneakiest thing one has actually done in a pull request?
I'd rather build checks for real failures than the ones I imagined.

Links

  • Code: https://github.com/isoklo/isoklo
  • A live blocked pull request (demo): https://github.com/isoklo/isoklo-demo/pull/1
  • GitHub App (free for public repos): https://github.com/apps/isoklo
  • Website: https://euklo.com/isoklo
  • npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/isoklo

If you try it and it flags something wrong, please open an issue.
False positives are the most useful feedback I can get.

title: Cloudflare Now Suggests D1 Indexes. Test Your Imports Before Applying One.
description:
Cloudflare launched D1 Insights index recommendations on November 25, supplying suggested SQL, affected queries, and usage metrics. Before accepting a recommendation for an operational database, test the work that keeps its records current. An index that helps a pricing lookup also needs maintenance when indexed records change. The useful comparison includes the supplier import, not just the search screen.

Disclosure: This article was generated with AI assistance from the linked public sources. The proposed pricing exercise below is illustrative.

The feature makes a good starting point for investigation. It does not supply a finished migration decision. Cloudflare's recommendation documentation says D1 checks that the suggestion is a single valid CREATE INDEX statement, but does not check it against the schema or execute it. The operator still owns the change.

Start with the work surrounding the query

The TMC Price Intelligence case study describes Keith's delivered 2023–2025 engagement: extracting product, size, price, region, and supplier information from emails and attachments, then connecting a pricing repository to reviewable reports, quotes, and invoice work. Implementation, rollout, production support, processing speed, and infrastructure cost were all part of that engagement.

Those responsibilities make a useful setting for an index review. The case study does not identify D1 as its database. The following is a proposed D1 exercise for a comparable pricing system, rather than a description of TMC's schema or a completed benchmark.

Suppose staff regularly look up offers for a product, package size, and region. Meanwhile, an import process adds supplier offers, and a reviewer corrects extracted fields. A demonstration that repeatedly searches an unchanged database measures only one part of that working day.

Write down the operations before changing the schema: adding a new supplier list, correcting an offer's indexed fields, looking up comparable offers, and producing the report staff need. Keep the same review rules and output requirements throughout the comparison.

Give the recommendation a concrete job

Review which query the suggestion is meant to improve. Compare its filter and join columns with the actual table definitions and existing indexes. A plausible name is insufficient evidence that a proposed index fits the current application.

Cloudflare's index guide explains that indexes are maintained automatically as referenced data is inserted, updated, or deleted. They also consume storage. It recommends using EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN to inspect whether a query uses an index.

For the proposed pricing exercise, retain the current query and its expected offer records. Apply the candidate through a migration in an isolated test database. Inspect the plan and compare the returned records as well as execution behavior. Faster output that omits a required supplier is a failed change, regardless of its timing.

Use the application's explicit sort rules when comparing ordered results. The test should establish that the same offers remain available under the same business criteria, without relying on an accidental display order.

Keep unrelated SQL changes out of this comparison. Otherwise, a new index and a rewritten filter can produce a result that is difficult to explain.

Replay the import and the correction

Prepare fictional supplier lists with varied product names, package sizes, regions, and prices. Include a larger batch and a smaller follow-up correction. These are synthetic fixtures, with no customer records or private supplier correspondence.

Run the same sequence against equivalent starting data with and without the candidate index. Record the time until the imported records are available for review, query timings, and the database work associated with each operation. Correct an indexed field through the normal application path and confirm that later lookups reflect the correction.

Separate the initial index build from ongoing ingestion. A one-time construction cost and a recurring import cost answer different operational questions. Keep both in the review instead of folding them into one unexplained average.

D1's billing metrics expose rows read, rows written, and storage. Use those categories alongside application timing. A reduction in reads alone cannot establish the total usage change, and a synthetic rehearsal cannot establish a future production bill.

The decision depends on the workload. A lookup used throughout the day may justify additional maintenance work. An occasional report over a frequently changing table may produce a different result. Record the expected frequency of each operation rather than declaring every index either cheap or expensive.

Leave the next operator a decision they can inspect

Cloudflare's recommendation guide calls for testing the migration locally and checking that the affected queries return the same results while reading fewer rows. Its recommendation metrics are estimates from sampled query analytics. Treat them as evidence for prioritizing the investigation, then retain the evidence from the application's own rehearsal.

A useful change note identifies the candidate index, the queries it serves, the import and correction fixtures, and the observed tradeoff. Include the migration revision so the note describes a specific schema change.

For a pricing team, the practical outcome is whether reviewed supplier information is available when people need to compare offers and prepare a quote. An index recommendation can point to a costly lookup. Shipping it requires following that lookup back to the process that keeps its records usable.

title: RAG Evaluation Guide: Separate Retrieval Quality from Answer Quality (Runnable Node.js Example)
description:
Original guide + downloadable runnable script: Read on umutgungorr.com · Download rag-evaluation.mjs

A runnable Node.js example covering recall, precision, answer omissions and out-of-corpus questions. Synthetic data, actual test output and limitations.

What are we measuring?

RAG evaluation asks two separate questions: did retrieval find the necessary evidence, and did the answer convey the necessary information? Fluent answers can hide missing evidence; complete evidence does not guarantee a complete answer.

The example was prepared and run locally on Node.js v24.19.0. It uses three synthetic documents, two questions and keyword matching, without embeddings, a vector database or an LLM. It is a small evaluation fixture, not a full RAG system or a production benchmark.

Dataset and expected evidence

The release question needs two documents: build covers test/build and secrets covers the secret check. The media question needs only images. Expected document IDs and answer facts are stored in the evaluation fixtures, not read by the retrieval function.

Recall is relevant evidence retrieved divided by relevant evidence expected. Precision is relevant evidence retrieved divided by all evidence retrieved. factCoverage checks only whether expected strings appear in the answer; it cannot establish semantic correctness or hallucination rates. It can miss valid paraphrases or accept a phrase inside a negation.

Run the example

Save rag-evaluation.mjs from the source links and run node rag-evaluation.mjs using Node.js 24. No package, account, API key or network access is needed. A failed assertion terminates the command with an error.

// Synthetic documents; no LLM, API key, embedding model or external request.
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
const corpus = [
  { id: 'build', text: 'Yayın öncesi test ve build çalıştırılır.' },
  { id: 'secrets', text: 'Yayın öncesi gizli anahtar kontrolü yapılır.' },
  { id: 'images', text: 'Blog görselleri WebP biçiminde saklanır.' },
];
const cases = [
  { id: 'release', query: 'yayın test build gizli anahtar', expected: ['build', 'secrets'], facts: ['test ve build', 'gizli anahtar'] },
  { id: 'media', query: 'blog görselleri', expected: ['images'], facts: ['WebP'] },
];
const tokens = text => new Set(text.toLocaleLowerCase('tr-TR').match(/[\p{L}\p{N}]+/gu) || []);
function retrieve(query, k) {
  const terms = tokens(query);
  return corpus.map(doc => ({ ...doc, score: [...tokens(doc.text)].filter(t => terms.has(t)).length }))
    .filter(doc => doc.score > 0).sort((a, b) => b.score - a.score || a.id.localeCompare(a.id)).slice(0, k);
}
function evaluate(item, docs, answer) {
  const hits = docs.filter(doc => item.expected.includes(doc.id)).length;
  return { recall: hits / item.expected.length, precision: docs.length ? hits / docs.length : 0,
    factCoverage: item.facts.filter(fact => answer.includes(fact)).length / item.facts.length };
}
for (const item of cases) {
  for (const k of [1, 2]) {
    const docs = retrieve(item.query, k);
    // This is evidence concatenation, NOT an LLM-generated answer.
    const result = evaluate(item, docs, docs.map(doc => doc.text).join(' '));
    if (item.id === 'release') assert.equal(result.recall, k === 1 ? 0.5 : 1);
    else assert.equal(result.recall, 1);
    assert.equal(result.precision, 1);
    console.log(JSON.stringify({ case: item.id, k, retrieved: docs.map(d => d.id), ...result }));
  }
}
const release = cases[0];
const fullEvidence = retrieve(release.query, 2);
const incompleteAnswer = fullEvidence[0].text;
const incomplete = evaluate(release, fullEvidence, incompleteAnswer);
assert.equal(incomplete.recall, 1);
assert.equal(incomplete.factCoverage, 0.5);
console.log(JSON.stringify({ case: 'answer-omission', ...incomplete }));
assert.equal(retrieve('pasaport yenileme', 2).length, 0);
console.log('PASS: retrieval, answer omission and out-of-corpus checks');

Observed results

For the release question, k=1 retrieved only build: recall 0.5, precision 1 and factCoverage 0.5. k=2 retrieved build and secrets, giving 1 for all three ratios. Both k values returned only images for the media question. These are fixture results, not overall accuracy claims.

The answer-omission case intentionally uses only the first retrieved document despite complete evidence. Recall remains 1 while factCoverage drops to 0.5, reproducing the distinction between retrieval and answer completeness. An out-of-corpus query returns no evidence; a real product still needs a separate abstention policy.

{"case":"release","k":1,"retrieved":["build"],"recall":0.5,"precision":1,"factCoverage":0.5}
{"case":"release","k":2,"retrieved":["build","secrets"],"recall":1,"precision":1,"factCoverage":1}
{"case":"answer-omission","recall":1,"precision":1,"factCoverage":0.5}

Moving to a real system

Two questions cannot establish that larger k is always better. Real evaluations need varied questions, irrelevant documents, missing evidence and contradictions, alongside cost, latency and context-noise measurements. Review evidence labels and avoid tuning on the same cases used to claim success.

Do not accept real LLM answers using substring matching alone. Review grounding, abstention and domain risk separately. Traces can retain document IDs and versions, but private text and credentials must not enter public logs.

Your first evaluation record

Record question ID, corpus version, expected and retrieved evidence IDs, ranks, k, answer and separate evaluation results together. Identify the failing layer, change that layer and rerun the same cases. The linked debugging guide complements this with one hypothesis per change.

Related engineering guides on umutgungorr.com: Original RAG Evaluation Guide | Debugging Shared-State Bugs with Hypotheses | Interfaces for Uncertain Systems

title: Matching Riders in Real Time over WebSockets
description:
Originally published at aharshit123456.space.

A student with a scooter is about to leave the hostel gate. Another student wants to get to the library, which is on the way. The app has a few seconds to notice, propose the pair, let both sides agree, and then show the co-pilot a moving dot as the pilot approaches. Two things must never happen along the way: one pilot promised to two people, and one slow phone freezing the live view for everyone else. This post is about how the Go backend of Kurukuru does live matching, scheduled matching for repeat commutes, and the WebSocket hub that streams a trip, and about the concurrency bugs each of them taught me.

Kurukuru is a gamified, college-first, peer-to-peer ride-sharing app I built at CosQ. A pilot is already going somewhere with a free seat; a co-pilot needs a ride and pays the pilot in in-app coins. The co-pilot gets on at a Kuru in point and off at a Kuru out point along the pilot's route. The backend is a single Go service on Postgres with PostGIS (the architecture post covers the rest of it).

Three speeds of "real time"

"Real time" turned out to mean three different things, and each got a different transport:

What Latency it needs Transport
The pilot's position during a trip a few seconds, both directions WebSocket per trip
"Has anyone matched my ride yet?" a couple of seconds, one question HTTP polling every 2 s
Suggestions for next week's commute minutes background matcher plus a queue the app reads

The temptation is to push everything over the socket. I didn't, because a match is a decision that must survive a closed app, a network change or a server restart. A poll against the database always returns the truth; a missed push silently doesn't. So the socket only carries data that is fine to lose: positions superseded three seconds later.

The geometry of a good match

Before any concurrency, the matching rule itself. Both riders submit a plan: start, destination and departure time. The question is whether the co-pilot's trip fits along the pilot's.

Pilot start → Kuru in co-pilot's start, projected on the route → Kuru out co-pilot's destination, projected on the route → Pilot destination

Fig. 1 — a match. Both of the co-pilot's points are projected onto the pilot's route; the projections become the pickup and drop-off.

The evaluation is a pure function with no database access:

  1. Time. The two departure times must be within 20 minutes of each other.
  2. Distance off route. Project the co-pilot's start and destination onto the pilot's route segment. Each must lie within 600 m of it, or the pilot would make a real detour.
  3. Direction. The drop-off projection must come after the pickup along the route. A co-pilot going the opposite way can sit perfectly close to the line and still be a terrible match.
  4. Worth it. The shared stretch between pickup and drop-off must be at least 250 m.

Projection uses a local flat approximation around the pilot's start (metres per degree of longitude scaled by the cosine of the latitude), which is plenty accurate at campus distances and far cheaper than spherical geometry. Each candidate also gets pickup and drop-off times from an average campus speed of about 21 km/h, a detour estimate and a fare from the shared distance. The score adds the two off-route distances to ten points per minute of departure gap; lower is better.

t1, d1, in := projectOnSegment(pilot.From, pilot.To, copilot.From)
t2, d2, out := projectOnSegment(pilot.From, pilot.To, copilot.To)
if d1 > maxOffRouteM || d2 > maxOffRouteM {
    return Candidate{}, false
}
if t2 <= t1 { // co-pilot is travelling against the pilot's direction
    return Candidate{}, false
}

Keeping this pure paid off twice: it is unit-tested without a database, and the scheduled matcher later reused it unchanged.

Note: The route is a straight line for matching, roads for display. Matching treats the pilot's route as the segment from start to destination. The screens show real road paths from a self-hosted OSRM routing server. Running a road route for every candidate pair would put a network call inside the matching loop; on a compact campus the straight line is a good enough filter, and the 600 m tolerance absorbs the difference.

Live matching: one lock, one decision

When a co-pilot opens the matching screen, the app polls GET /api/rides/{id}/match every two seconds. If no live match exists, the handler tries to make one:

  1. Begin a transaction and take a transaction-scoped advisory lock: SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext('kurukuru-matching')).
  2. Load up to 200 open plans of the opposite role that are in the same college pool, not blocked by either side, not already in a live match, and never paired with this ride before.
  3. Evaluate each in Go and keep the best.
  4. Insert a proposed match and commit, which releases the lock.

An advisory lock is a named mutex inside Postgres. It isn't tied to any row, and the xact variant releases itself when the transaction ends, so a crashed request can never leave it held. Serialising all live matching behind one lock is blunt, and that is the point: without it, two co-pilots searching at the same moment both see the same free pilot, both evaluate it as their best option, and both insert a match. Row locks can't prevent this because the conflict is over the absence of a match row. A global lock turns "check, then insert" into one atomic step.

Note: The cost: matching is single-file. Every search waits for the one before it. Each search is one indexed query plus some arithmetic over at most 200 rows, so the critical section is milliseconds. On a campus that's fine; on a city I'd shard the lock by area or cohort instead of dropping it.

A proposal is not a ride. The pilot must accept and the co-pilot must confirm, in either order. The respond endpoint locks the match row with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, records one side's answer, and when both flags are true, creates the trip and marks both plans matched in the same transaction. Each action is allowed only for the right role (a co-pilot can't "accept" on the pilot's behalf), and responding to a match that is already settled just returns its current state, so a double tap is harmless.

In the app — a proposed match from the co-pilot's side, rendered from test data: who the pilot is, the fare, and where and when Kuru in and Kuru out happen.

The other path: nearest available pilot

An older flow skips plans: a pilot toggles "available", storing their position as a PostGIS geography point, and a co-pilot asks for the closest one within a radius.

SELECT u.id FROM users u JOIN user_cohort uc ON uc.user_id = u.id
WHERE u.is_available AND u.id <> $1
  AND uc.college_id IS NOT DISTINCT FROM $5
  AND ST_DWithin(u.last_location, ST_MakePoint($2, $3)::geography, $4)
ORDER BY ST_Distance(u.last_location, ST_MakePoint($2, $3)::geography)
LIMIT 1

With geography, distances are in metres on the real Earth, and ST_DWithin uses a GiST index, so only pilots inside the radius are sorted.

The WebSocket hub, and the bug that could crash the server

Once a trip starts, the pilot's phone sends its position, heading and id over a WebSocket every three seconds, and the server fans each message out to everyone subscribed to that trip. The server also pushes system events into the same channel: "trip started", "trip finished", and "pioneer" events when someone uncovers a never-seen part of the map.

The first hub was the version you write in an afternoon: a map from trip id to a slice of connections behind a read-write mutex, and a Broadcast that looped over the slice calling conn.WriteMessage. It worked in testing. It had two serious problems.

Concurrent writers. gorilla/websocket supports exactly one concurrent writer per connection. Broadcast ran on whichever goroutine called it: the reader goroutine of each subscribed client, plus HTTP handlers pushing system events. Two clients sending at the same instant meant two goroutines writing to the same connection, and the library detects that and panics. An unrecovered panic in a goroutine takes down the whole process, so every trip, every request and every user would go with it.

One slow phone stalls everyone. Broadcast held the hub's read lock while writing. A phone that stopped reading (in a tunnel, backgrounded, on a dying network) made its write block, the read lock stayed held, and every join, leave and broadcast for every trip queued up behind it.

The fix is the standard pattern for socket servers, and it is worth knowing by heart:

Any goroutine calls Broadcast → non-blocking send into each client's queue (32) → one writer goroutine per connection → socket 10 s write deadline

Fig. 2 — the hub after the fix. Broadcast never touches a socket; it only queues. A full queue means the client is too slow, and it is disconnected.

func (h *Hub) Broadcast(tripID string, payload []byte) {
    h.RLock()
    clients := h.tripSubscriptions[tripID]
    msg := append([]byte(nil), payload...) // one copy, shared by every queue
    var slow []*client
    for c := range clients {
        select {
        case c.send <- msg:
        default:
            slow = append(slow, c)
        }
    }
    h.RUnlock()
    for _, c := range slow {
        c.close() // its reader then fails and removes it from the hub
    }
}
  • One writer per connection. Each client gets a writePump goroutine that is the only code allowed to write to its socket. It also sends the keepalive pings, so pings can't race with data either.
  • Bounded queues, never blocking. Broadcast does a non-blocking send into each client's 32-message channel. If the channel is full, that client is closed rather than waited on. The hub lock is held only for in-memory work.
  • Close exactly once, from anywhere. Closing is wrapped in sync.Once, closes a done channel and the socket, which unblocks both the reader and any write stuck in the writer. The send channel is deliberately never closed, because a broadcast may still be sending to it; closing it would turn a race into a panic.
  • Liveness and limits. Pings every 50 seconds, a 60-second read deadline extended by each pong or message, a 10-second write deadline, and a 64 KB read limit (a GPS message is a few hundred bytes).
  • No leaks. When a trip's last client leaves, its entry is deleted from the map.

Tests reproduce both failures under Go's race detector (four clients each sending 200 messages at once, and a subscriber that never reads), and a benchmark showed delivery latency unchanged.

Scheduled matching: a queue inside Postgres

Live matching only works while both people are staring at their phones. Commuters want something else: "I go from the hostel to the library at nine, Monday, Wednesday and Friday, for the next four weeks; find me someone." That became scheduled matching, designed in a short spec before any code.

The data model reuses as much as possible. A series holds the route and repeat pattern; each dated occurrence is an ordinary ride row linked to it. Proposals between series live in their own table, so the live flow is untouched. When both people accept, the backend creates one normal confirmed match and one trip per shared day, so chat, ratings and trip screens work without knowing scheduling exists.

Two series are compatible when they share at least one calendar day and every shared day passes the same evaluate function from live matching. "Same day" is computed in India Standard Time with a fixed zone, so the answer doesn't depend on the server's clock settings or on time-zone data being installed in the container.

Create or edit series + insert job, same transaction → match_jobs table → matcher goroutine claims with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED → up to 5 suggestions per series

Sweep every 3 min → retire dead series, expire stale suggestions → re-enqueue open series with room in their queue

Fig. 3 — the scheduled matcher. Events produce jobs; a periodic sweep is the safety net for anything an event missed.

SKIP LOCKED as a job queue

The producer side is trivial: creating a series inserts its rides and a job row in one transaction, so a series can never exist without a job. The consumer is a goroutine started from main that polls every two seconds and claims the oldest ready job:

UPDATE match_jobs SET claimed_at = now()
WHERE series_id = (
    SELECT series_id FROM match_jobs
    WHERE run_after <= now()
      AND (claimed_at IS NULL OR claimed_at < now() - interval '5 minutes')
    ORDER BY run_after LIMIT 1
    FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED)
RETURNING series_id

FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED makes a worker skip rows another transaction has locked instead of waiting for them, which is exactly the semantics of a work queue. Several Honbu instances can run the matcher at once and never process the same job twice. A claim older than five minutes is treated as a crashed worker's and becomes claimable again. Re-enqueueing a series clears its claim, and a finished job is deleted only if it is still claimed, so an edit that arrives mid-processing isn't lost.

Each run fills the series' queue up to five suggestions and also offers itself to the other series' queues. The cap is enforced inside the insert statement, not in Go:

INSERT INTO series_matches (pilot_series_id, copilot_series_id, score)
SELECT $1, $2, $3
WHERE (SELECT count(*) FROM series_matches WHERE state = 'proposed'
        AND (pilot_series_id = $1 OR copilot_series_id = $1)) < 5
  AND (SELECT count(*) FROM series_matches WHERE state = 'proposed'
        AND (pilot_series_id = $2 OR copilot_series_id = $2)) < 5
ON CONFLICT (pilot_series_id, copilot_series_id) DO NOTHING

A check in Go followed by an insert is a race between two workers; a guard inside the statement narrows that window to almost nothing. The unique pair constraint also makes rejection permanent: a rejected suggestion keeps its row, so the pair is never suggested again.

In the app — a pilot's suggestion queue for a repeating ride, rendered from test data. "They said yes" means the other side has already accepted; one more tap confirms all four days.

Accepting: where the races live

Accepting is the most concurrent operation in the system. Two people might accept different suggestions for the same series at once; the other side might skip a date or cancel while you tap. The accept transaction:

  1. Locks both series rows, ordered by id. Every accept takes these locks in the same global order, so two accepts touching the same pair of series queue up instead of deadlocking.
  2. Locks and re-reads the suggestion. If it is no longer proposed, or either series is no longer open, or the riders have blocked each other since, it is marked expired and the caller gets 409.
  3. Records this side's accept. If the other side hasn't accepted yet, commit and stop.
  4. If both have accepted, reload the dated rides (some may have been skipped since the suggestion was made) and re-run the pairing. For each shared day, create the confirmed match and trip and flip both rides from open to matched.
  5. Mark the suggestion confirmed, supersede every other proposal touching either series, and mark both series matched.

Two guards catch the races the locks don't:

  • A partial unique index allows at most one confirmed suggestion per series (... WHERE state = 'confirmed'). If a concurrent accept confirmed one of these series first, the update fails with a unique violation, which the handler maps to 409 rather than a 500. The database settles the race; the code just reports the verdict.
  • A row count on the ride update. Each day's rides are flipped with WHERE status = 'open', and the code requires exactly two rows to change. A concurrent "skip this date" that canceled one of them leaves only one row, and the whole accept rolls back. An earlier version happily overwrote a just-skipped date back to matched.

Failing softly

A background goroutine inside a web server is a liability if it can crash the process. Every unit of matcher work runs inside a small safely wrapper that recovers panics and logs them, so one malformed series costs one log line, not the server.

The sweep also turned out to need a garbage collector. A series whose every remaining date had passed (or was within the 30-minute matching cutoff) stayed open forever, showing "nothing ahead" in the app and being re-examined every three minutes. The sweep now retires such series, cancels their leftover dates and drops their queued job, reusing the existing canceled status so nothing new needed a schema change.

Routing degrades the same way: a three-second timeout, a 24-hour in-memory cache of up to 2,000 routes, and a straight line when the routing server is down. A routing outage changes how a line is drawn, never whether a ride happens.

What I'd reuse

  • Match the transport to the consequence. Decisions go through the database and can be polled; disposable streams like GPS go over the socket.
  • Keep the matching rule a pure function. It's easy to test, and the second matcher reused it unchanged.
  • When the conflict is over a row that doesn't exist yet, take an advisory lock. It's the simplest correct answer to "check, then insert".
  • One writer per WebSocket, bounded queues, drop the slow. Never write to a socket from a broadcast loop, and never hold a shared lock across network I/O.
  • Postgres is a fine job queue. FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, a stale-claim timeout and a periodic sweep go a long way before you need a broker.
  • Let constraints settle races. Partial unique indexes and "exactly N rows changed" checks catch what careful locking misses.

Stack in this post: Go (net/http, gorilla/websocket, lib/pq), PostgreSQL with PostGIS, OSRM, Flutter. Figures come from the backend's code, its scheduled-matching spec and plan, and its history, March to November 2026.
