title: Quest Books, an In-App Editor and Road Watch
description:
Originally published at aharshit123456.space.

A game lives on its content, and content is always slightly wrong: a cafe closed last month, a park pin sits in the middle of a lake, a new food stall nobody has added yet. A road safety tool lives on trust, and trust breaks the first time the app claims something that is not true. Both need to change faster than an app store review allows, and both need the phone and the server to agree exactly on the rules. This post covers three features of the Kurukuru app that sit on that line: quest books, an editor for them inside the app, and Road Watch, a way for riders to report road problems.

Kurukuru is a gamified peer-to-peer ride-sharing app I built at CosQ for college campuses. A pilot who is already going somewhere offers a seat; a co-pilot who needs one pays a few coins. The map of the campus is a pixel-art world with a fog of war that clears as you travel. The app is Flutter; the backend is one Go service on Postgres and PostGIS.

Quest books: places as collectible stamps

A quest book is a curated list of real places in an area, organised like a passport. Each book has chapters (one per neighbourhood or campus zone) and five sections: food and drink, culture and arts, nature, adventure, and games and play. Every place is a stamp, and you collect it by being there. There is a book for the campus and one for Bengaluru; the Bengaluru book started from a community-curated list of about 9,000 places, credited in the app.

The interesting design choice is what you see before you collect something. A hidden place shows only its kind and distance: "a bakery, 140 m". You can ask for directions and the map draws a path to it, but the name stays secret until you arrive. That turns a list into a treasure hunt, and it means the book itself is a reason to go somewhere new.

GPS fixes batched on the phone → Sync request impossible jumps dropped → PostGIS: within a place's radius, inside the book's region → New stamps slam onto the map

Fig. 1 — stamping. The phone never decides that you collected something; it only reports where it has been.

Stamping rides on the same GPS batches that clear the fog. The phone sends timestamped fixes; the server drops fixes that would need more than about 144 km/h to reach from the previous one, then asks PostGIS which uncollected places those fixes came within range of:

cand AS (
  SELECT p.id, MIN(ST_Distance(p.geog, f.g)) AS dist
  FROM quest_places p
  JOIN quest_books b ON b.id = p.book_id AND b.active
  JOIN f ON ST_Covers(b.region, f.g) AND ST_DWithin(p.geog, f.g, p.radius_m)
  WHERE p.active
    AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM quest_stamps s
                    WHERE s.user_id = $1::uuid AND s.place_id = p.id)
  GROUP BY p.id
)

Each place has its own radius: 50 m by default, 150 m for parks, lakes, stadiums and other places whose coordinate is a centre rather than a door. Nearest places are stamped first, with a cap per sync and per day so a bus ride through a dense neighbourhood does not empty a chapter. Stamps give XP and badges at 1, 10, 50 and 100, but never coins. Coins are what co-pilots pay pilots with, so a reward that a GPS spoofer could farm is kept out of the ride economy.

On the phone, the book is a leather cover that swings open at the chapter you are standing in, with category tabs on the page edge and round ink stamps. Asking for a chapter you are not in gets a distinct "not here" answer, so the app can explain instead of showing an empty page.

The campus quest book, closed. Tapping the cover swings it open at the chapter you are standing in.

Editing game content without shipping the app

Fixing a quest place used to mean a staff member editing a draft in a web editor and someone running a seeding script from a terminal. I wanted two things: people we trust (a campus ambassador, say) should be able to fix places from inside the app while walking past them, and going live should be a button, not a script. And under no circumstances should an app user be able to change what everyone sees.

The answer is the classic draft and publish split.

Action Who Where
Edit the draft Staff editors, plus app users switched on individually Web editor or the app
Validate the draft Everyone, continuously Web, app and server, same rules
Publish draft to live Admin staff only Admin panel button

App users reach the editor API with their normal sign-in token, but only if a per-user switch is on for them. If it is off, the API answers exactly as it would for a bad token. Every admin route refuses app tokens outright, so there is no path from the app to publishing.

Publishing copies the draft to the live tables in one transaction, with rules chosen to be safe for players:

  • Places are upserted by a stable external id, so editing a place never orphans the stamps people already hold.
  • A place missing from the draft is switched off, never deleted. Its stamps survive.
  • Chapters are rebuilt from the places in them: a 400 m buffer around the convex hull of each area's points.
  • A draft with validation errors is refused, and so is an empty one, which would otherwise switch every live place off.

Optimistic concurrency, two people, one cafe

Two editors can open the same place. Each row has a version, and a save carries the version it started from:

UPDATE quest_editor_places
SET name=$3, category=$4, ..., version = version + 1, updated_at = now()
WHERE view = $1 AND id = $2 AND version = $12   -- the base version
RETURNING ...

Zero rows updated means someone else got there first; the server answers 409 with the row as it is now. The app shows the edit immediately, and on a conflict it rolls back, reloads and says "Someone else changed this. Reloaded." It never overwrites. The API client returns a sealed result rather than throwing, so every screen has to handle every case:

switch (await _api.putPlace(_view, place, base)) {
  case Saved(:final value):  _places = replaceById(_places, value);
  case Conflict():           _places = before; _notice = conflictNotice;
  case Failed(:final code):  _places = before; if (code == 'no_access') _noAccess = true;
}

The web editor gets live updates over server-sent events. The app polls every 20 seconds while the editor is open, which is simpler on mobile and plenty for a handful of editors. One subtle bug to avoid: a poll that lands while a save is in flight would replace the optimistic edit with stale server data. A counter of saves in flight makes the poll skip that round.

One set of rules, three languages

What counts as a valid place has to be identical in the web editor (JavaScript), the app (Dart) and the publish step (Go), or an editor sees green in the app and the publish refuses it. There is no shared runtime between the three, so the rules are ported, not shared, and the tests carry the same cases:

  • the book needs a slug, a name and a region with at least three points;
  • a place needs a name, an area (its chapter), one of the five categories and a position;
  • the radius, if set, is a whole number from 10 to 500 m;
  • a place outside the book's region is an error (ray casting on the polygon);
  • two places with the same name within 15 m is a warning, not an error.

The duplicate check groups places by name first, so it stays fast on a 9,000-place book. Picking a position uses the map with a fixed crosshair in the centre: you move the map, not a pin, which works one-handed and never needs a long press. If the crosshair is outside the book's region, the screen says so before you save.

The in-app editor: the draft banner and error counts, a form with problems listed at the top, a conflict after someone else saved first, and the crosshair picker outside the book region.

Road Watch: road reports from riders

Students who share rides know exactly where the potholes are. Road Watch lets anyone plant a warning flag where the road has a problem: a pothole, a damaged surface, waterlogging, illegal parking, vending blocking the road, a broken light, a jam. Others back it (+1 per person) and later confirm when it has been fixed. Every issue shows how many days it has been open.

The report flow: type (one tap moves on), an optional photo, place and severity with a plain example for each level, and the duplicate check.

The flow is four steps: type, photo, place with severity and an optional note, then review. A duplicate check sits before the review: a report of the same type within 40 m is offered as "Back this report" instead, because one issue with fourteen backers is worth more than fourteen issues. You can still file yours if it really is a different problem. There is a cap of three reports a day, and reports are accepted only inside the area the map covers.

Honest by construction

The design prototype for Road Watch was beautiful and slightly too optimistic. It said new reports were "Reported to the city office", that the right office owned each issue, and that faces and number plates were blurred automatically. None of that was true yet, so none of it shipped:

  • A new issue is "open", not "reported". Nothing forwards reports automatically. It becomes "reported" only when a staff member actually passes it on, and only then does the "reported to" line appear.
  • Ownership is a field, not a claim. Every issue says "Owner: unconfirmed" until someone confirms it.
  • Photos are moderated, not blurred. The copy says a moderator checks photos before other people see them, because that is what happens.

Widget tests assert that words like "blurred" and "reward" never appear on these screens, so the prototype's promises cannot creep back in through a later copy change.

Never while driving

The most important rule: a pilot never interacts with Road Watch while a trip is moving. Typing a report is exactly the kind of distraction a road safety feature must not cause.

The app enforces it with a check that says yes only when it is certain the user is not piloting a trip in motion:

bool mayReport({required bool stateKnown, required bool isTripActive,
    required TripDto? trip, required String? myId, bool matchPilotInProgress = false}) {
  if (!stateKnown || matchPilotInProgress) return false; // unknown counts as blocked
  if (trip == null) return !isTripActive;
  if (trip.status != 'in_progress') return true;
  return myId != null && trip.pilotId != null && trip.pilotId != myId; // co-pilots may report
}

The key is stateKnown. The ride-state lookups return a small Lookup type that tells "there is no trip" apart from "I could not find out". A failed network call never opens the gate. The check also runs again right before any action, not just when the screen opened.

Instead of the report button, a pilot in motion gets one big gold button: Mark spot for later. One tap stores the position and time on the phone, with no network, no photo and no typing. Marked spots last 24 hours. When the trip ends, the trip summary offers to finish them, which takes a few taps each while parked.

The server enforces the same rule independently: creating a report or uploading a photo as the pilot of a trip in progress is refused with 409 trip_in_motion. Client checks are for experience; server checks are for safety.

Mark spot for later while piloting, finishing marked spots after the trip, and a report saved offline.

Photos on a phone budget

Phone cameras produce multi-megabyte images full of metadata, including the GPS position of wherever the photo was taken. The app shrinks every photo before it leaves the phone, in a background isolate:

static Uint8List shrink(Uint8List bytes) {
  var im = img.decodeImage(bytes) ?? (throw const PhotoTooLarge('not a readable image'));
  im = img.bakeOrientation(im);                       // apply EXIF rotation to the pixels
  if (max(im.width, im.height) > 1280) im = resizeLongEdge(im, 1280);
  im.exif.clear();                                    // re-encoding drops EXIF and GPS
  for (var q = 75; q >= 35; q -= 10) {
    final out = Uint8List.fromList(img.encodeJpg(im, quality: q));
    if (out.length <= 560 * 1024) return out;         // server allows 600 KB; keep headroom
  }
  throw const PhotoTooLarge();
}

Orientation has to be baked into the pixels before the metadata is cleared, or portrait photos arrive sideways. Up to three photos are uploaded after the report is created, each with its own client-generated key, so a retried upload never creates a second copy. The server checks the JPEG magic bytes rather than trusting the content type, refuses a file that still carries an EXIF GPS block (a best-effort scan that never rejects a file just because it could not parse it), and keeps each photo visible only to its author until a moderator approves it.

Offline first, without duplicates

Roads with problems are often roads with bad signal. A report that fails to send goes into a queue on the phone and is sent again when the app resumes. The danger with retries is duplicates, so every report carries a UUID made on the phone, and the server has a unique constraint on author plus that key. Sending the same report twice is harmless.

The queue flush has a few small rules that each fixed a real failure mode:

  • A network error stops the flush (try later); a permanent refusal such as "outside the area" or "daily limit" drops that report so it cannot block the rest.
  • Two flushes at once share one run instead of sending twice.
  • The queue is re-read at the end, so a report added while a flush was running is kept.
  • A corrupt stored value reads as an empty queue instead of wedging the feature.

There are no push notifications, so status changes reach people through an inbox derived from data: the phone takes the newest status event of each report you made or backed and turns it into an alert. Nothing is sent; the inbox is computed from the same data as your report list. Only events done by staff are worded as "Kurukuru staff marked it"; a fix confirmed by riders says so. A public "oldest open" list ranks unresolved issues by age, which is the accountability half of the feature.

An issue with its timeline (future steps shown as waiting) and the public oldest-open list.

One model, two codebases

The app and the backend share no code: one is Dart, the other Go. What they share is a contract, and I found it holds up best when it is made of three things.

Outcomes, not exceptions. Every API client returns a sealed type that names the cases the server can produce: Created, Duplicate(existing), Rejected(code) for reports; Saved, Conflict(current), Failed(code) for the editor. The compiler then makes every screen deal with every case.

Stable error codes as strings. HTTP status codes are too coarse (two different 409s mean different things), so the server returns a short code and the app maps each one to a behaviour:

Code Meaning What the app does
duplicate Same type within 40 m Shows the existing issue and "Back this report"
trip_in_motion Caller is piloting a moving trip Closes the flow; suggests Mark spot
outside_area Outside the mapped area Explains that reporting is limited here
daily_limit Three reports today Says so; the queue drops it
conflict Stale editor save Rolls back, reloads, shows the notice

Constants owned by the server, mirrored by the app. The daily cap, the 40 m duplicate radius, three confirmations to verify a fix, the 600 KB photo limit: the server enforces all of them, and the app mirrors them only to give a better answer sooner. If they ever drift, the server wins and the app shows the server's answer.

Code generation from a schema would remove the duplication. For a two-language system this size, hand-written models with tests on both sides of every code were faster to change and easier to read, and the written design spec that listed every endpoint and code did the job a schema would have done.

Takeaways

  • Separate draft from live, and make publishing an admin action that is safe for players: upsert by stable ids, deactivate instead of delete, refuse empty or invalid drafts.
  • Version every editable row and let the database decide conflicts with WHERE version = $base. Roll back and reload; never overwrite.
  • Port validation rules deliberately when you cannot share code, and keep the same test cases in every language.
  • "Unknown" must fail closed for anything safety-related. Model "could not find out" separately from "nothing there".
  • Give the risky user one safe action (Mark spot for later) instead of just a disabled button.
  • Shrink, strip and key every upload on the device: bake orientation, drop location metadata, attach an idempotency key.
  • Ship only the promises that are true. Write tests that keep the untrue ones out.

Stack in this piece: Flutter, Dart sealed classes, image and image_picker, shared_preferences; Go with Postgres and PostGIS on the backend. Quest data for Bengaluru from a community-curated list; map data © OpenStreetMap contributors.

title: Fog of War on a Real Map with PostGIS
description:
Originally published at aharshit123456.space.

In strategy games the map starts dark. You only see what your units have walked through, and the black slowly peels back into terrain. It is one of the oldest tricks for making a map feel like something you earn. So what happens when the map is your actual campus, the unit is you, and the fog only lifts where your phone's GPS has really been? This post is how Kurukuru's backend turns a stream of noisy GPS fixes into a personal explored area, serves it back as a single shape, pays out progress for it, and draws a blocky world from OpenStreetMap underneath.

Kurukuru is a gamified, college-first, peer-to-peer ride-sharing app I built at CosQ: a pilot with a free seat gives a co-pilot a lift and earns in-app coins. The game layer exists to give people a reason to open the app on days they don't need a ride, and to make every ride also count for something. Exploration is the core of that layer. Its backend is a few hundred lines of Go and some well-chosen PostGIS calls (the architecture post covers the rest of the service).

  • ~36 × 19 m size of one fog tile at the campus's latitude
  • ~75 tiles lifted around a single GPS fix (120 m radius)
  • 23,750 tiles in the campus area, the denominator of "% explored"

Pick a grid before you pick a shape

The naive fog stores the user's GPS trail and buffers it into a polygon. That breaks quickly: trails are huge, buffering a long line on every request is slow, and "how much have I explored?" has no stable answer because two overlapping walks count twice unless you union them.

The standard alternative is to discretise the world into tiles and store, per user, the set of tiles they have seen. Membership is a primary-key lookup, overlap is free (a tile seen twice is still one row), and "explored percentage" is a count. The question is which grid.

I used geohash. A geohash encodes a latitude and longitude by repeatedly halving the world: the first bit says east or west of the prime meridian, the second north or south of the equator, then the same again inside the chosen half, alternating. Every five bits become one character from a 32-letter alphabet. Each extra character makes the cell 32 times smaller, and every cell has a short, stable string name.

Eight characters (40 bits, 20 for longitude and 20 for latitude) give a cell 360/2²⁰ degrees wide and 180/2²⁰ degrees tall. Near the campus that is about 36 m east to west and 19 m north to south: big enough that a walk produces a manageable number of rows, small enough that the fog's edge still follows paths and buildings.

Note: Why not hexagons? Hex grids such as Uber's H3 have nicer neighbour properties and equal-area cells. But PostGIS can turn a geohash straight into its polygon with ST_GeomFromGeoHash and back with ST_GeoHash, the encoder is fifty lines of Go with no dependency, and the merged outline only needs edges that line up. Rectangles were enough.

From GPS fixes to tiles

The app collects fixes in the background and uploads them in batches: every 5 seconds while it is on screen and every 20 seconds when it isn't, keeping at most the newest 200 fixes. A failed upload puts the batch back at the front of the queue, so walking through a dead zone costs nothing. Each fix carries the time it was taken, not the time it was sent.

The server first makes the fog lift in a radius rather than in the single tile under the fix. GPS on a phone is often off by tens of metres, and a 36 m wide tile under a wobbling dot looks like a broken trail. Revealing everything within 120 m of each fix gives a smooth band along the path you walked.

// tiles whose area intersects the circle of radiusM around (lat, lng)
for la := lat - dLat; la <= lat+dLat+cellLat/2; la += cellLat / 2 {
    for lo := lng - dLng; lo <= lng+dLng+cellLng/2; lo += cellLng / 2 {
        dy := (la - lat) * mPerDegLat
        dx := (lo - lng) * mPerDegLng
        if dx*dx+dy*dy > radiusM*radiusM {
            continue
        }
        seen[geohashEncode(la, lo, 8)] = struct{}{}
    }
}

Sampling at half a cell in each direction guarantees every tile inside the circle is hit at least once; the set removes duplicates. One fix produces about 75 tiles, and a batch of fixes from a walk shares most of them, so the server collects the distinct tiles for the whole batch before touching the database. A straight one-kilometre walk with a fix every ten metres reveals about 440 distinct tiles.

Learning which tiles are new, in one round trip

Then come two bulk statements, each passing the whole tile list as one Postgres array:

INSERT INTO grid_tiles (id, geom)
SELECT t, ST_GeomFromGeoHash(t) FROM unnest($1::text[]) AS t
ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;

INSERT INTO user_explorations (user_id, grid_tile_id)
SELECT $1, t FROM unnest($2::text[]) AS t
ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING
RETURNING grid_tile_id;

The first lazily creates global tile rows with their polygons, so the grid only ever contains places someone has actually been. The second is the useful trick: ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING ... RETURNING returns only the rows that were actually inserted. Tiles the user had already seen are silently skipped, so the result is exactly "tiles newly revealed by this batch", with no read-before-write and no race between two uploads from the same phone.

The newly revealed tiles go through one more conditional update to find pioneer tiles, the ones nobody in the whole app has seen before:

UPDATE grid_tiles SET first_discoverer_id = $1
WHERE id = ANY($2) AND first_discoverer_id IS NULL
RETURNING id

Because the IS NULL check and the write happen in one statement, two people walking into the same unexplored corner at the same moment can't both be first. If the upload belongs to a trip in progress, the server pushes a "pioneer" event into that trip's WebSocket channel, and both riders see a toast that they just mapped a new corner of campus.

# fog sync · illustrative request and response
$ curl -X POST $HONBU/api/explore/sync -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" \
    -d '{"trip_id":"","gps_trace":[{"lat":20.35,"lng":85.81,"t":1763100000000}, …]}'
{
  "status": "synchronized",
  "new_tiles_unlocked": 132,
  "total_unlocked": 1250,
  "pioneer_tiles": ["tgt5…"],
  "discoveries": 2,
  "xp_gained": 100,
  "coins_gained": 20,
  "stamps": []
}

The response also carries the user's new XP, level and coin totals, so the app can animate a reward without a second request. The user id in the body is ignored and replaced with the token's subject: a client can report where it has been, but never on someone else's behalf.

Serving the fog as one shape

The map screen needs the inverse: everything this user has explored. Sending thousands of rectangles and letting the phone draw each one would be slow and would leave hairline seams between tiles. Instead the server merges them:

SELECT ST_AsGeoJSON(ST_Union(t.geom)), COUNT(*)
FROM user_explorations e
JOIN grid_tiles t ON e.grid_tile_id = t.id
WHERE e.user_id = $1

ST_Union dissolves the shared edges and returns one (multi)polygon: an outline with stepped edges, plus holes for unexplored pockets enclosed by explored ground, like a courtyard you walked around but never into. The app receives a single GeoJSON shape and the tile count.

user's tiles rows of rectangles → ST_Union one outline + holes → GeoJSON rings and pockets → app: screen-sized fog, outline cut out (even-odd), pockets painted back

Fig. 1 — from rows to fog. The server does the geometry; the client draws one path.

Drawing it is then cheap. The app builds one path containing a rectangle the size of the screen plus every explored ring, fills it with the even-odd rule (so the rings become cut-outs in the fog), and paints the pockets back in. Before the first outline arrives it clears a small circle around the player, so a new user never starts in total darkness.

Note: The trade-off: the union is recomputed on every map load. For one user on one campus that is a few thousand small polygons and stays fast. A heavy explorer of a whole city would make it expensive; the obvious next step is to cache the outline per user and invalidate it when a sync reveals new tiles, or to union only the new tiles into the cached shape.

In the app — the exploring sheet, rendered from test data: percentage of campus, tile count, and the opt-in switch for background exploration.

Turning tiles into progress

The percentage needs a denominator. The campus is a fixed bounding box, so the number of geohash-8 tiles inside it is a constant computed once: 23,750. Tiles revealed off campus still count toward your total and your rewards; the percentage is simply capped at 100.

Rewards are paid in discoveries. Each user has a small counter of newly revealed tiles that haven't been paid for yet. Every sync adds the new tiles to it; every full 60 tiles converts into one discovery worth 50 XP and 10 coins, and the remainder stays banked for next time. The increment, the conversion and the grant happen in one transaction, so two overlapping syncs can't both cash in the same 60 tiles. That one-kilometre walk is worth about seven discoveries.

Levels are deliberately dull: one level per 500 XP, computed from total XP whenever needed. Badges are not stored at all. Each badge is a definition (a metric and a target, like "explore 500 tiles" or "finish 10 trips"), and a user's badges are evaluated from live counts of their tiles, flags, trips and stamps. "Newly unlocked" is computed by evaluating the counts before and after an action and diffing. With no badge table there is nothing to migrate when a badge is added or a target changes, and nothing that can drift out of sync with the underlying data.

What the fog doesn't defend against

An open question in any location game is cheating. The fog trusts the positions it is sent, apart from dropping impossible coordinates. Quest stamps, the part of the game where you collect specific places, are stricter: they drop any fix that would need more than 40 m/s (about 144 km/h) to reach from the previous kept fix, cap stamps per sync and per day, and pay only XP, never coins. For the fog itself I accepted the risk, because what you gain by spoofing it is a prettier personal map and a slow trickle of coins. If exploration ever paid real value, the same speed filter would be the first thing to move over.

Flags

The other way to mark the map is to plant a flag with a short note. The tile under it is computed in SQL with ST_GeoHash(point, 8); if you are that tile's first discoverer, the flag is marked as a pioneer flag. Flags are anonymous by design: the API never returns an author, only whether a flag is yours. Nearby flags are fetched with a bounding-box prefilter on plain latitude and longitude columns, and a flag disappears for everyone after three reports, and immediately for the person who reported it or blocked its author.

The world under the fog

Fog needs something to hide. The first map was a standard tile map; the current one is a pixel-art block world baked from OpenStreetMap, so roads, water, parks and buildings each have their own block type and buildings rise according to their height.

The baker is a Python tool that runs offline:

  1. Download OpenStreetMap features for the area: land use, water, roads, railways, buildings and trees.
  2. Rasterise everything onto a grid three times finer than the target, in painter's order (land use first, then water, then roads at their real width), with proper even-odd filling so courtyards and ponds become holes.
  3. Downsample each cell from its 3×3 subsamples by weighted majority, with boosts for roads and water so a 5 m lane or a narrow canal survives on a 10 m grid instead of being voted away by the grass around it.
  4. Classify buildings by kind (house, flats, shop, institution, religious, industrial) and height class, from OSM's height or floor count where present and a per-kind default otherwise.
  5. Encode each row with run-length encoding (g12r3g40 is twelve grass, three road, forty grass) and gzip the result.

One region file was fine for one campus. A whole city was not: a public OSM query server can't serve that much data, and a single file would be tens of megabytes. So the city baker clips a regional extract locally, cuts the city into square tiles that all sit on one shared grid (so neighbouring tiles meet on exact cell edges), and writes a manifest listing each tile with its size and SHA-1 hash.

Map Levels of detail Tiles
Campus 4 m and 2 m cells 30 and 99
Bengaluru 10 m and 5 m cells 650 per level

The Go server embeds all of it with go:embed, about 21 MB in total, and serves a tile with its hash as the ETag. A request that includes the hash from the manifest gets Cache-Control: immutable for a year, because a tile's content can never change under the same hash; anything else gets an hour. The app switches from the coarse level to the fine one past a zoom threshold given in the manifest. Tiles that would be nothing but grass are never written; a 404 for a tile means "open grass", which keeps the city's outskirts free.

Toward an open world

The block map is top-down. The next design walks around in it: a real-time 3D world built from the same kind of map data, where you move a voxel character through the streets near campus. The design splits it cleanly. An offline builder precomputes the area as JSON tiles, 500 m square, in local metres east and north of one origin, so the renderer never handles latitude and longitude. Roads are polylines with their real width and class, buildings are footprints with heights, and land cover, shops, trees and lamps ride along. A three.js renderer streams tiles around the player, turns roads into ribbon meshes along the real polylines, extrudes buildings and checks collisions against footprints.

The tile JSON, with a version field in every file, is the only contract between the two halves: the renderer knows nothing about where the data came from. Terrain height, traffic, pedestrians and interiors were explicitly left out, because the area is flat enough and each would have doubled the scope. A trial of it sits behind a feature switch in the app.

What I'd reuse

  • Discretise before you geometrise. A grid turns "where have I been?" into set membership, makes overlaps free and gives you a stable denominator.
  • Let RETURNING tell you what changed. INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING answers "which of these are new?" in one race-free round trip.
  • Put the geometry on the server and send one shape. ST_Union plus an even-odd fill beats thousands of client-side rectangles.
  • Bank progress in a counter and pay out in whole units. Thresholds like "every 60 tiles" stay atomic inside one transaction and never double-pay.
  • Derive badges from facts. Definitions in code evaluated against live counts can't drift out of sync with the data.
  • Content-address static tiles. A hash in the manifest lets clients cache forever and lets you redeploy without invalidation headaches.

Stack in this post: Go, PostgreSQL with PostGIS, geohash, OpenStreetMap with Overpass and osmium, Python, three.js, Flutter. Figures come from the backend's code and baked map manifests, the open-world design spec and the app's exploration code, March to November 2026.

title: Kurukuru: A Ride-Sharing Game on One Go Binary
description:
Originally published at aharshit123456.space.

Two students leave the same hostel gate every morning for the same library. One has a scooter and an empty back seat; the other is about to pay for an auto. A ride-sharing app could pair them, but on a campus the hard part is not the matching maths. It is trust (who is this person?), money (who pays whom, and how much?), and giving people a reason to open the app on a day they don't need a ride. This post is about the backend I built for that app: one Go binary that handles identity, trips, a coin wallet, live matching and a map game.

Kurukuru is a gamified, college-first, peer-to-peer ride-sharing app I lead at CosQ. A pilot is a student already going somewhere with a seat to share; a co-pilot needs a ride. The app finds a pilot whose route passes near the co-pilot, picks where the co-pilot gets on (Kuru in) and off (Kuru out), and the co-pilot pays the pilot in KuruCoins. Around that sits a pixel-art map of the real campus covered in fog that clears as you move, flags you can plant, quest books of places to find, and levels and badges. The backend, called Honbu, is mine end to end: every commit from the first one in March 2026 to the latest in November.

  • 1 Go binary serving the app, two staff tools and the map tiles
  • ~12.6k lines of Go, plus ~5.6k lines of Go tests
  • ~21 MB of baked map tiles embedded in the binary

In the app — the onboarding card that explains the vocabulary the whole backend is built around: pilot, co-pilot, Kuru in and Kuru out.

Why one binary

The usual advice for a product with this many moving parts is to split it: an auth service, a trips service, a payments service, a realtime gateway. I went the other way, for three reasons.

One person, one deploy. Every service you add is another thing to deploy, monitor, version and keep compatible. With a single developer, the cost of a service boundary is paid entirely in my evenings.

The interesting operations cross domains. Finishing a trip debits the co-pilot, credits the pilot, writes two ledger rows, marks the trip complete and grants experience points to both riders. Planting a flag inserts the flag, grants XP and coins, and writes a ledger row. In a monolith with one Postgres database, the money movement and state change in each of these is a single SQL transaction (the trip's XP follows in its own small one). Split across services, each becomes a saga with compensation logic, and a bug in it costs real (or at least virtual) money.

Go makes a monolith cheap to keep tidy. The standard library's net/http is enough; there is no web framework. Each domain is a package under internal/ with a RegisterHandlers(mux) function, and main.go is little more than a list of those calls. Packages can only reach each other through exported functions, so the boundaries are real even though they share a process.

Flutter app Supabase login → Honbu (Go) one http.ServeMux, ~20 domain packages → Postgres + PostGIS (managed, Supabase)

Staff web tools quest editor, admin → same binary separate staff logins → Routing service (OSRM, private network)

Fig. 1 — the whole system. The app talks only to Honbu; Supabase is used for sign-in and as the database, never as a data API from the app.

Package What it owns
auth, cohort, staffauth verifying app logins, deciding a user's matching pool, staff tool logins
rides, trip, copilot, pilot ride plans, matching, the trip lifecycle, the live trip socket, pilot availability
wallet, payments, progress coin pricing and ledger, coin top-ups and cash-out, XP, levels and badges
exploration, voxel, routing fog of war and flags, baked map tiles, road paths
quests, editor, roadwatch quest books, their collaborative editor, road problem reports
features, admin, account, verification feature switches, staff panel with audit log, account deletion, pilot verification

Shared plumbing lives in pkg/: the database pool and the WebSocket hub.

A walled garden on top of someone else's login

The product promise was that you only ride with people from your own college. That makes identity the most security-sensitive part of the system, and I didn't want to own passwords or email verification. So sign-in is delegated to Supabase Auth (email with confirmation, or Google), and Honbu's job is to verify the token the app sends, not to issue it.

Verifying someone else's tokens

A JSON Web Token is a signed claim: "this is user sub, valid until exp". The signature can be symmetric (HS256: both sides share a secret) or asymmetric (ES256: the issuer signs with a private key and publishes the public half as a JWKS, a JSON Web Key Set, at a well-known URL). Asymmetric is the better fit for a third-party issuer because the verifier never holds anything that can mint tokens.

Supabase signs access tokens with ES256, so Honbu's verifier looks at the token header, picks a key by its kid (key id) from a cached JWKS, and verifies. HS256 tokens are still accepted under a server-side secret, which is what the end-to-end test suite uses to impersonate users without a real login.

token, err := jwt.Parse(raw, func(t *jwt.Token) (interface{}, error) {
    switch t.Method.Alg() {
    case "ES256":
        kid, _ := t.Header["kid"].(string)
        return jwksKey(kid) // cached; refetched at most every 30 s on an unknown kid
    case "HS256":
        return []byte(secret), nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("unexpected signing method %v", t.Header["alg"])
}, jwt.WithValidMethods([]string{"ES256", "HS256"}))

Two details matter. WithValidMethods pins the algorithms, which closes the classic "alg: none" and algorithm-confusion attacks. And the JWKS cache refetches on an unknown kid (so key rotation just works) but at most once every 30 seconds, so a flood of tokens with random key ids can't turn Honbu into a request amplifier against the identity provider.

The endpoint I deleted

The first version of Honbu did run its own register and login endpoints, minting its own HS256 tokens. Registration only checked that the email string ended with the college domain. It never proved the person owned that mailbox, so anyone could create an account for any student's address and receive a token Honbu fully trusted. The campus-only gate was a text filter.

The fix was to stop serving those routes entirely, and a test now asserts they stay unregistered. Identity comes only from the provider, which only issues a session after the mailbox is confirmed. Removing code was the security fix.

Cohorts: the college is derived, never stored

Later the app opened to anyone with an email address, while keeping students of one college matched only with each other. Everyone else lands in a public pool called the Kurukuru Commune. The rule is one SQL view:

CREATE VIEW user_cohort AS
SELECT u.id AS user_id, c.id AS college_id
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN auth.users a ON a.id = u.id AND a.email_confirmed_at IS NOT NULL
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT cc.id FROM colleges cc
    WHERE lower(split_part(a.email, '@', 2)) = cc.domain
       OR lower(split_part(a.email, '@', 2)) LIKE '%.' || cc.domain
    ORDER BY length(cc.domain) DESC LIMIT 1
) c ON TRUE;

Three choices are deliberate. The email comes from the auth provider's own table, not from the profile the app sends, so a client can't claim a college. Only a confirmed email counts. And the domain match is anchored on a dot, so cs.college.ac.in belongs to the college but college.ac.in.evil.com does not. Because the cohort is computed rather than stored, adding a college to the colleges table takes effect for existing users immediately.

Every matching query then joins the view and requires college_id IS NOT DISTINCT FROM the searcher's own. IS NOT DISTINCT FROM is the null-safe equality: two Commune members (both NULL) match each other, which plain = would not do.

Staff logins with separate audiences

The two staff tools, a quest book editor and an admin panel, do get tokens minted by Honbu: a bcrypt-checked shared password per tool, then a short-lived HS256 token. Each tool has its own password hash, its own signing secret and its own aud (audience) claim, so an editor token is useless on the admin API and neither works on the app API. Failed logins are rate limited both per client address and across all addresses, so rotating IPs doesn't buy unlimited guesses. Every admin change and every user lookup goes to an audit table.

The trip lifecycle as compare-and-set

A trip moves through a small state machine, and every transition is a conditional UPDATE:

matched both sides agreed → in_progress either rider starts → completed coins settle, XP granted

Fig. 2 — the main path. An older on-demand flow also enters as requested and moves to in_progress when a pilot accepts; any open state can end as canceled.

UPDATE trips SET status = 'in_progress'
WHERE id = $1 AND status = 'matched' AND (pilot_id = $2 OR copilot_id = $2)

If zero rows change, the trip was not in the expected state or the caller is not on it, and the API answers 409. This is optimistic concurrency without a version column: the WHERE clause is the precondition, and Postgres evaluates it atomically. Two taps on "start" can't both succeed, and nobody can start a trip they aren't part of.

Completion is the one transition that needs more than a single statement. It locks the trip row with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, re-checks the riders and status, prices the trip from the stored distance (never from the client), locks both balances, writes the debit, the credit and two ledger rows, and finally flips the status with the same conditional-update trick. If anything fails, the whole thing rolls back.

In the app — the end of a trip as a co-pilot sees it, rendered from test data: coins out of the vault and XP toward the next level, both from the same server response.

When "active" needed a time window

One surprise came from scheduled rides. Confirming a repeating ride creates one matched trip per shared day, up front, so chat and ratings work the same as for a live ride. But the home screen asked for "the newest trip that isn't finished", and a ride three days away suddenly showed up as a live trip with a pilot en route. The fix was to define active in time: a trip linked to a match counts only from an hour before pickup to three hours after, or whenever it is actually in progress. "Open" and "happening now" are different questions, and the schema had only answered the first.

Coins in one paragraph

KuruCoins are the app's currency. Fares are priced from fuel cost (distance over typical two-wheeler mileage times the local petrol price, with a five-coin minimum), so a pilot is reimbursed roughly what the trip cost them. Balances live on the user row, and every movement also appends a row to a wallet_transactions ledger carrying the delta and the balance after it, written in the same transaction as the balance change and under row locks, so a debit is refused rather than allowed to go below zero. Coins also come from playing: exploring and planting flags pay a few. Buying coins through a payment gateway and cashing them out exist in the code but are dark-launched: off unless switched on, and in test mode the app says plainly that no real money moves. A cash-out only debits coins and queues a request for a person to pay out by hand.

One database doing five jobs

Postgres with the PostGIS extension is the only stateful component, and it does more than store rows:

Job Postgres feature
Nearest available pilot geography points with ST_DWithin and ST_Distance
Fog of war geohash tiles as polygons, merged with ST_Union and served as GeoJSON
Serialising live matching a transaction-scoped advisory lock
Background job queue FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED on a jobs table
Race-proof confirmations partial unique indexes (one confirmed match per series)

None of these needed a new piece of infrastructure: no Redis for locks, no queue broker, no separate geo service. The trade-off is that the database is a single point of failure and the main scaling limit. For a campus-scale app that is the right trade.

Deploy shape

The deploy is deliberately boring. A multi-stage Dockerfile compiles a static binary (CGO_ENABLED=0) and copies it into a small Alpine image with CA certificates and time-zone data. A container PaaS runs it and injects PORT. The routing server runs as a second, private service that only Honbu can reach. Configuration is environment variables. A missing database URL produces a clear error at boot naming the variable and the kind of URL to use, never a silent fallback to a default connection string in the source.

Two details were learned the hard way:

  • The database's direct host was IPv6-only, unreachable from Docker on many laptops and from the PaaS. Connecting through the provider's session pooler fixed both.
  • Static data rides inside the binary. Baked map tiles for the campus and a whole city, region files and editor data are compiled in with go:embed. A deploy can never ship code that expects tiles it doesn't have, and serving a tile is a read from memory with an ETag.

There are two health endpoints: /health says the process is up, and /health/db pings the pool and runs a read-only count on the ledger table, so a broken connection string shows up as a failing check rather than as the first user's error. Feature switches are read from environment variables, overridable at runtime from the admin panel with a ten-second cache; if the flags table is unreachable, the environment value wins, so the app never loses its switches because of a database blip.

What the monolith costs

It isn't free. Handlers reach a package-level database handle instead of receiving it, which makes some handlers harder to unit test; the newer packages take a store interface instead and test against an in-memory fake plus a real PostGIS database. The WebSocket hub keeps its subscribers in process memory, so two replicas would each see only half the clients of a trip (the background matcher, by contrast, was built to run on several instances at once). And a sibling project's small API shares the binary and the database, which is convenient until its traffic or its bugs affect Kurukuru. I'd split along those seams first, and only when one of them hurts.

What I'd reuse

  • Start with one binary and real package boundaries. Cross-domain operations like "finish trip, move money, grant XP" stay a single transaction for as long as you can keep them there.
  • Delegate identity, verify strictly. Pin the accepted algorithms, cache the JWKS, throttle refetches. Never let your own endpoint mint tokens the identity provider wouldn't.
  • Derive membership from the authority, not the client. A view over the provider's confirmed email is harder to fool than a profile field, and it updates itself.
  • Write state transitions as conditional updates. UPDATE ... WHERE status = 'expected' plus a row count is a concurrency control you get for free.
  • Use the database's own tools before adding infrastructure. Advisory locks, SKIP LOCKED, partial unique indexes and PostGIS covered locks, queues, race safety and geo queries.
  • Close the doors your platform opens. If your server is the only client, turn the managed data API off with deny-by-default security.

Stack in this post: Go (net/http, gorilla/websocket, golang-jwt, lib/pq), PostgreSQL with PostGIS on Supabase, Supabase Auth, OSRM, Docker, Flutter. Figures come from the backend repository's code, schema and history, March to November 2026.

More from Building at CosQ

  • Fog of War on a Real Map with PostGIS: turning GPS trails into an explorable, game-like map.
  • Turning a Real Map into a Pixel World: the Kurukuru app's map, 3D world and pixel UI in Flutter.
  • Quest Books, an In-App Editor and Road Watch: game content you can edit in the app, and road safety reports.
  • Everything Else I Built at CosQ: WHAM! OTT, MemoChan, PreviouslyOn, Gothicco and more.

title: Why Motion Should Never Be an Afterthought Added in Sprint 4
description:
When motion lives in the same code-native canvas as layout, choreography ships on day one.

For years, product teams accepted a strange ritual: designers drew static pictures of software in Figma, wired together fragile click-through prototypes, and handed them off to engineers to rebuild from scratch. That prototyping era is over.


Figure 1: ExodeUI replaces static vector handoffs with a unified code-native UI & motion studio.

Why the Old Prototyping Workflow Breaks Down

In physics & springs vs dead keyframes, static vector tools hit a hard ceiling:

  1. Duplicate Work: Every screen is built twice—once as a vector illusion, once in production code.
  2. Missing Runtime Truth: Static frames can't model real browser layout, async states, or interruptible gesture physics.
  3. Permanent Drift: The moment code ships, the Figma file becomes outdated documentation.


Figure 2: Closing the gap between visual design and production execution.

How ExodeUI Replaces Figma

Instead of drawing dead rectangles, ExodeUI lets you design with real layout primitives, deterministic state machines, and spring physics that compile straight into production TypeScript:

// ExodeUI velocity-preserving spring configuration
export const drawerSpring = {
  type: "spring",
  stiffness: 380,
  damping: 32,
  mass: 0.9,
  restDelta: 0.001,
} as const;

What Changes for Your Team

  • Designers work visually with live data, real responsive rules, and 120fps spring choreography.
  • Engineers receive clean, idiomatic React, Vue, Svelte, Solid, or Vanilla TypeScript components—not position: absolute guesses.
  • Product Teams skip the throwaway prototype phase and iterate directly on real software.

Build Without the Handoff Tax

The prototyping era taught teams to draw software twice—once as static pictures, and once in code. ExodeUI collapses both into a single code-native canvas.

title: # 56 seconds to 0.7: when per-line cost grows with the number of sources
description:
logscry is my open-source log triage tool in Go. Before a line is templated and scored, a grouping stage folds multi-line stack traces into one event. To do that it keeps a small buffer per log source and stream, and releases each one after 200 ms of silence.

On my laptop's real logs it never held more than 20 buffers at once. Then I replayed a capture with 80,000 distinct source names on a single timestamp. It took 57 seconds.

Why would anyone have 80,000 sources?

Because the source name is not always yours to choose. A journald entry carries its own identifier, so any program can log under as many names as it likes. A Docker host running docker run --rm loops creates a new container name every few seconds. And a log tool should assume that a stream can be hostile.

The bug

On every line, the grouper looked for buffers that had gone idle:

// per line, before main's fix
for _, key := range inOrder(g.buffers, true, expired) { // walk the map, filter, sort
    g.emit(g.buffers[key], ...)
}

inOrder walked every buffer, kept the expired ones and sorted them. That is O(n log n) per line, which makes a stream of distinct names quadratic overall. Live, the timer walked all the buffers a second time to find the next deadline. And on a single timestamp nothing ever expires, so all 80,000 buffers stayed in memory until the end of input.

The fix, in three parts

1. A deadline heap with the old order. A container/heap sorted by (deadline, arrival sequence), which is exactly the order the old sort used. The idle flush pops while the top has expired, and the timer only peeks at the top. This matches the old behaviour because expiry is monotone in the last-seen time: if one buffer has expired, every buffer with an earlier deadline has expired too.

2. A bound that emits instead of dropping. At most 4,096 buffers and 16 MiB. Past either limit, the least recently touched buffer is released early. I deliberately did not use the heap's top for this: on a single timestamp the top is the oldest header even if a stack frame just landed on it, so evicting the top would split the trace in progress every time. An early flush emits the event, so no line is ever lost. The worst case is a trace split in two.

3. The nil. This is the classic container/heap trap:

func (h *deadlines) Pop() any {
    old := *h
    n := len(old) - 1
    p := old[n]
    old[n] = nil // without this, the backing array keeps every popped buffer alive
    p.index = -1
    *h = old[:n]
    return p
}

Without that line, the heap held 17.4 MiB after every buffer had already been emitted, and the version with the nil held 0.68 MiB. A test now checks that nothing emitted stays reachable.

Proving nothing else moved

A performance fix that changes output is a bug fix you didn't ask for. So:

  • The old grouper is copied verbatim into a test file as a reference. A differential test feeds both implementations random interleavings of sources, streams, folds and timestamps, and compares every emitted line, timestamp included.
  • A fuzz target runs the same comparison: 8.6 million executions, 0 differences.
  • Ten real journald boots (63,017 entries) replay byte-identical: export, stdout and stderr.

Results

before after
Replay, 80k sources on one timestamp 56.9 s 0.72 s
Live, distinct sources 14,358 lines/s 1,522,116 lines/s
Live, one source 1.09 M lines/s 1.10 M lines/s
Heap, 80k pending sources 20–330 MiB 1.6–17 MiB
One ordinary line 771 ns 861 ns

The last row is the honest one: an ordinary line now costs about 90 ns more. I'll take that in exchange for a cost that no longer depends on how many sources are open.

Takeaways

  • Per-line work must not depend on the size of your state. The tests count the buffers each line touches, so this can't come back unnoticed.
  • Keep the old implementation as an oracle. A verbatim copy in a test, plus fuzzing, beats "the tests still pass".
  • When you bound something, decide what eviction costs. Here an evicted buffer is emitted early, never dropped.

logscry is Apache-2.0: https://github.com/maxie7/logscry

title: Stop, don't guess: the rules I give my AI for reading lab reports
description:
For a medical client, I built the part of a system that reads lab reports. A PDF comes in from a laboratory, the system pulls out the values (blood tests, mostly), converts them, and puts them in front of a doctor.

Over 99% of the values that are in the reports are read automatically. This post is about the other part, the small one, because that's where the real design lives. And it's where my AI assistant, left alone, writes code that is plausible, tidy, and wrong in a way that matters: when it doesn't know a number, it makes one up.

The code that looks right

Ask an AI to "extract the values from the report, and handle missing data gracefully", and you get something like this:

function readValue(text: string, test: string): number {
  const match = text.match(new RegExp(`${test}\\s+([\\d.,]+)`));
  if (!match) return lastKnownValue(test) ?? 0;   // "graceful"
  return parseFloat(match[1].replace(',', '.'));
}

Nothing crashes. Every test gets a number. The dashboard is full. A reviewer sees a sensible fallback.

Now read it as the doctor. A missing value became the patient's last known value, or zero. The unit was ignored. And the code can't tell you which numbers were read and which were invented, because they all have the same type: number.

Jim Shore described this pattern in 2004, in a short IEEE Software column called "Fail Fast". His example is a configuration reader that returns a default when a property is missing: the program keeps working, and fails in strange ways later. In a config file that's a debugging problem. In a lab report it's a wrong number in front of a doctor, looking exactly like a right one.

Four states, not one

The fix starts with the type. A value pulled from a report is not a number. It's one of four things:

type Reading =
  | { kind: 'read'; test: TestCode; value: number; unit: CanonicalUnit }
  | { kind: 'absent'; test: TestCode }                       // the document doesn't contain it
  | { kind: 'unreadable'; test: TestCode; reason: string }   // it's there, we couldn't read it
  | { kind: 'estimated'; test: TestCode; value: number; unit: CanonicalUnit; basis: string };

The difference between absent and unreadable is the whole point. "The lab didn't run this test" and "my parser failed on this line" look identical in a database column (an empty cell), and they mean opposite things. One is a fact about the patient's report. The other is a bug in my system.

I learned how much this matters by looking at the empty cells. Many of them were tests that had simply never been performed: correct, nothing to fix. But some came from a wrong upload: a test request form, uploaded where the report should have gone. A request form lists test names with no results next to them. A naive parser reads it as "a report where everything is missing", and that's a lie told with a straight face.

So one rule is cheap and catches it: a document with no values at all is not an empty report. It's a stop. Someone has to look at it.

Password-protected PDFs belong here too. They exist, and they arrive. A locked file must never become "zero values found": it gets its own outcome, locked, and goes to a person, who can get the password from the lab or ask for a new copy.

Some values are never estimated

Is an estimate ever acceptable? Sometimes, and the doctor needs to know when. The rules I work with are:

  • A critical value (an inflammation marker, for example) is never estimated. If it's missing, the report stops.
  • At most one estimated value per report, and it is always declared, with a visible mark next to it. Never a silent one.
  • Everything else that the machine can't read goes to support.

Which tests are critical and how many estimates are allowed are not decisions for the code. They are medical decisions, so they live in configuration, and the code only applies them:

type ReportOutcome =
  | { kind: 'ready'; readings: Reading[] }
  | { kind: 'stopped'; reasons: StopReason[] };

function decideReport(readings: Reading[], policy: ReadingPolicy): ReportOutcome {
  const reasons: StopReason[] = [];
  if (readings.every((r) => r.kind === 'absent')) reasons.push({ kind: 'no-values-at-all' });

  for (const r of readings) {
    const critical = policy.criticalTests.has(r.test);
    if (critical && r.kind !== 'read') reasons.push({ kind: 'critical-not-read', test: r.test });
    if (r.kind === 'unreadable') reasons.push({ kind: 'needs-a-person', test: r.test, why: r.reason });
  }

  const estimates = readings.filter((r) => r.kind === 'estimated').length;
  if (estimates > policy.maxEstimatesPerReport) reasons.push({ kind: 'too-many-estimates', estimates });

  return reasons.length > 0 ? { kind: 'stopped', reasons } : { kind: 'ready', readings };
}

The shape matters more than the details. The function never returns a number pretending to be a reading. It returns ready or stopped, and stopped always carries its reasons, so the person who picks it up knows what to look at.

Units are where plausible numbers come from

The system recognises and converts 123 units of measure automatically. That number sounds like overkill until you see the same value written two ways by two labs, a factor of 10,000 apart.

Think about what that means for a parser. Same patient, same test, same result: one lab prints a small number, another prints a number ten thousand times bigger, and both are correct in their own unit. Skip the conversion, or guess the factor, and you get a value that is perfectly readable, perfectly plausible as a number, and off by four orders of magnitude. The AI will happily guess the factor from the unit's name, because the name looks familiar.

NASA lost the Mars Climate Orbiter in 1999 to a cousin of this bug. The investigation board's report gives the root cause as a "failure to use metric units" in one ground software file: one side produced data in English units, the other expected metric, and nothing between them checked. Every individual number looked fine.

So the rules for units are strict:

type Conversion =
  | { kind: 'converted'; value: number; unit: CanonicalUnit }
  | { kind: 'unknown-unit'; written: string };

function toCanonical(value: number, written: string, units: UnitTable): Conversion {
  const known = units.lookup(normalise(written));   // the table lives in configuration
  if (!known) return { kind: 'unknown-unit', written };
  return { kind: 'converted', value: value * known.factor, unit: known.canonical };
}

An unknown unit is not converted "by similarity". It becomes unreadable, and a person sees it. When they confirm what it means, add it to the table once, with a test, and from then on the machine handles it. A table can grow to a hundred entries and more that way without a single guess in it.

The person is part of the system

It's tempting to think of support as the exception handler. It isn't. When the data isn't enough, the system stops, and someone on the support side corrects it from a console: a value, but also a patient's name, date of birth, or email. That's not a failure of automation. It's half of the design.

Lisanne Bainbridge wrote about this in 1983, in "Ironies of Automation": the more you automate, the more the human is left with exactly the cases the machine couldn't handle, the hardest ones, often without the practice or the context to handle them well. So the console has to make the hard case easy: show the piece of the page next to the empty field, say why the machine stopped, and accept only the correction it asked for.

And every correction is recorded in a log that can't be rewritten. Pat Helland's paper "Immutability Changes Everything" has a section title that says it all: "Accountants Don't Use Erasers". A wrong correction is fixed by a new entry, never by editing the old one:

type Correction = {
  reportId: string;
  field: string;
  previous: string | null;
  corrected: string;
  correctedBy: string;
  correctedAt: Date;
  reason: string;
};

// append is the only write: give the app's database role INSERT on this
// table, and no UPDATE or DELETE.
await corrections.append(correction);

Put the rule in the permissions, not just in the code. If the app can't run an UPDATE on that table, neither can the next feature your AI writes.

And then you lock it in

A rule in a comment is a rule the AI will forget. Next month I'll ask for support for a new lab format, the assistant will add a parser, and somewhere in it there will be a friendly ?? 0.

So the guardrail is a test, and the test needs real data. Build a bench of real reports, anonymised, with an answer key for each one: which values are there, which are absent, which tests are critical. Include the ugly ones: the locked PDF, the request form uploaded by mistake, the lab with the odd unit. Then the test reads them all and counts:

it('never estimates where an estimate is not allowed', async () => {
  const results = await readBench(anonymisedReports);
  const tally = countReadings(results, answerKey);

  expect(tally.estimatedCritical).toBe(0);
  expect(tally.reportsOverEstimateLimit).toBe(0);
  expect(tally.absentButActuallyPresent).toBe(0);   // "not there" must mean not there
  expect(tally.read).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(baseline.read);
});

Each line guards a different lie. An estimate on a critical value: red. Two estimates on one report: red. A value the answer key says is on the page, reported as absent: red. A parser change that silently reads less than before: red. When a future change brings back the graceful fallback, this test fails, and the AI has to explain itself.

The rule, in one line

When a system reads data for a doctor, stopping is a feature and guessing is a bug: every value must say whether it was read, absent, unreadable, or estimated and declared.

It works well beyond medicine: invoices, bank statements, delivery notes, any document where a plausible wrong number costs more than a pause. Your AI assistant is very good at making code that never stops. Your job is to tell it where it must.

Further reading

The ideas here come from people who thought about them long before me:

  • Lisanne Bainbridge, "Ironies of Automation", Automatica, vol. 19, no. 6, pp. 775-779 (1983).
  • James Shore, "Fail Fast", IEEE Software, vol. 21, no. 5 (2004), in the Design column edited by Martin Fowler.
  • NASA, Mars Climate Orbiter Mishap Investigation Board Phase I Report (November 10, 1999).
  • Pat Helland, "Immutability Changes Everything", CIDR 2015, section 2: "Accountants Don't Use Erasers".

What I added is small: four states instead of one number, and a bench of real reports that turns red the moment a guess sneaks back in.

I'm Matteo Mazzocchi, an Italian developer. I build CRMs and back-office systems for small businesses, with an AI pair and a lot of tests that say no. More about my work: mazzocchimatteo.com.
