title: Unit tests caught 2 of 5 tax bugs. A real browser caught all 5.
description:
I built Tickmark for the KaneCLI Hackathon: an invoice maker for India (GST) and the US (sales tax) where an AI coding agent isn't allowed to say "done" until a real browser has checked every invoice.

The bug that started it

I asked Claude Code to apply a teammate's "one-line refactor". The unit tests stayed green.

But the change made the place of supply default to the seller's state. So every client in Mumbai, billed by a company in Bengaluru, got CGST + SGST instead of IGST. In India that means the client can't claim their tax credit and the invoice has to be re-issued.

The unit tests never saw it, because the tax logic was fine. The bug was in what the customer sees.

How Tickmark works

  1. Tax rules are plain English. Each rulebook is a Markdown file anyone can read and edit: > 8. If the supplier's state and the place of supply are different states, every tax line must be IGST and no CGST or SGST line may appear.
  2. Kane CLI checks them in a real Chrome. It opens each invoice the way a client would and checks every rule as its own assertion.
  3. A Claude Code Stop hook closes the loop. When Claude tries to finish, the hook runs Kane. If a check fails, Claude gets Kane's bug title, root cause, evidence and a suggested fix, fixes the code, and Kane checks again.

Lesson 1: Kane reads brilliantly and adds up badly

In testing, Kane passed "each amount equals quantity × rate" on a line showing 12 × $45.00 = $450.00.

So I split the job: Kane reads, code does the math. Kane copies the numbers and dates off the page, and plain code re-adds every sum and counts every due date.

Even better, Kane can export a test it wrote to Playwright. So Kane writes the "reader" once, and from then on the math check runs offline, in about a second, for 0 credits.

Lesson 2: test what the customer sees

I planted 5 realistic tax bugs, one at a time:

Planted bug Unit tests Kane CLI
IGST only for registered buyers ✅ ✅
Place of supply defaults to the seller's state ❌ ✅
Resale certificate ignored ✅ ✅
Sales tax charged on the whole subtotal ❌ ✅
Amount in words uses the wrong number ❌ ✅

Kane 5/5. Unit tests 2/5. Three of the bugs lived in templates and UI defaults, not in the tax logic.

Lesson 3: try it on code you didn't write

I pointed Tickmark at a popular open-source GST billing app (531★) and audited a PDF it exported.

  • Its GST was correct: IGST for an inter-state client, matching GSTINs, the right amount in words.
  • But the invoice contradicted itself: "payment due within 7 days" in the terms, and a due date 15 days out. Both were the app's own defaults.

It also showed me my own mistakes. My rules assumed my own invoice layout. And Kane missed the 7-vs-15-day contradiction until I moved date counting into code. I wrote all of that down in the repo, including a bug Kane didn't confirm.

Use it from any agent

Tickmark is also an MCP server. Ask Claude Code, Claude Desktop or Cursor:

"Does this invoice match the contract we signed?"

…and Kane flags things like a $165/hour rate against an agreed $150, or Net 15 instead of Net 30.

Try it

No account needed for the demo:

npm install
npx playwright install chromium
npm run demo
  • 💻 Code: https://github.com/N-45div/Tickmark
  • 🌐 Live app: https://tickmark-invoices.vercel.app

Built with Claude Code for the #KaneCLIHackathon by TestMu AI. Feedback and new country rulebooks are very welcome. 🙌

title: Web Monitoring Explained: Why Vector Search Cannot Answer Questions Alone
description:
TL;DR: Vector search returns passages whose embeddings are close to a query; it does not determine what changed, compose an answer, or prove that each claim came from a captured page. A reliable media-monitoring system therefore treats retrieval as one stage in RAG: capture and normalize a page, record a verifiable diff, retrieve the relevant evidence, ask a generator to answer only from that evidence, and reject output whose citations do not resolve to stored passages.

Start with the bill. For a page-change watcher, its useful approximation is fetches + retained bytes + embedding work + index residency + generated tokens. Suppose an illustrative workload watches 10,000 pages hourly. That is 7.2 million fetch attempts in a 30-day month; if every attempt retained a 200 KB representation, snapshots alone would add about 1.44 TB per month before replication. Conditional requests can reduce transferred bodies when validators are available, but they do not remove scheduling, metadata, or verification work. The material change is to retain content-addressed baselines and normalized diffs instead of another full copy after every poll.

That choice has a cost of its own: deleting intermediate full snapshots limits later visual reconstruction and parser forensics. This is retention engineering, not a claim that one storage policy is universally cheaper.

What does a page watcher actually need to retain?

A raw HTML page is poor evidence by itself. Navigation timestamps, ad slots, recommendation widgets, and tracking parameters may change while the article does not. Before comparison, extraction should identify the editorial region, normalize insignificant markup, and preserve the source URL, observation time, response validators, parser version, and a cryptographic digest of the exact retained representation. A changed digest says that bytes differ. A structured diff says where and how they differ.

I model each observation like a ledger entry because the same invariants are useful: an idempotency key prevents a retry from creating a second event, an append-only record preserves ordering, and derived artifacts point back to their inputs. This does not make distributed processing magically exactly once. It makes duplicate delivery observable and makes repeated processing converge on the same event identity.

The retention unit should match the question. If editors ask, “Did the headline or named claim change?”, retain field-level before-and-after values plus the source captures required by policy. If they may need pixel-level proof, a DOM diff is insufficient. Keep screenshots or a replayable capture, knowingly accepting the larger storage and privacy surface.

For pages that may contain personal data, retention also has a compliance boundary. The GDPR principles of data minimisation and storage limitation apply when the regulation is in scope; “we might need it later” is not a retention schedule. Access controls, deletion rules, and audit records belong beside the index design, not in a cleanup ticket.

Why can't vector search answer the question by itself?

Vector search ranks stored items by a similarity function over embeddings. Its output is usually an identifier, a score, and a passage. None of those fields is an answer, and a high-ranked passage is not a factual verdict. Similarity does not establish temporal order, entailment, completeness, or provenance.

Retrieval stops there.

Consider the query “What changed in the acquisition announcement?” The nearest passages could include yesterday's announcement, a related analysis, and today's correction. The search layer cannot infer that the correction supersedes one sentence while leaving the rest intact unless the stored records carry versions and the application applies that relationship. It also cannot safely turn the three passages into a concise explanation. That is the generator's job, constrained by retrieved evidence and an answer contract.

RAG names this composition: a retriever supplies external context and a generation model conditions its output on that context. The original RAG paper describes the combination of parametric and non-parametric memory; it does not convert retrieval scores into guarantees that generated claims are supported. Grounding is an application invariant. Enforce it with passage identities, prompt constraints, citation validation, and abstention when the evidence set is inadequate.

Silence is valid.

If retrieval finds yesterday's text but the current capture failed, the correct status is “change not verified,” not a fluent summary built from stale evidence. Imagine that the source returned a truncated body during a timeout, the normalizer nevertheless emitted a short document, and semantic search ranked yesterday's intact paragraph above it. A generator could write a plausible “no change” alert unless accepted-capture state and temporal filters exclude both the broken observation and superseded evidence. The alert would be readable, cited, and wrong. That sequence is why capture validity must be settled before similarity ranking and why citation presence alone is weaker than end-to-end grounding.

The evidence path is a small accounting system

The cleanest architecture separates observation from interpretation. A scheduler issues conditional HTTP requests where supported. The capture worker records status and validators, then normalizes content using a versioned extractor. A differ compares the current artifact with the last accepted baseline. Only meaningful changed regions become retrieval documents; each document carries page_id, capture_id, diff_id, timestamps, and a content digest.

Retrieval then filters before it ranks. The tenant or publication, page identity, language, time window, and accepted-capture status are exact constraints; semantic similarity operates inside that set. This ordering prevents an excellent semantic match from the wrong publication or an obsolete version from entering the prompt. The generator receives immutable passage IDs and produces claims tied to those IDs. Finally, a validator checks that every citation exists in the supplied context and that cited text still hashes to the recorded content.

Stage Durable fact Failure that must not become an answer
Capture URL, observed time, HTTP validators, body digest timeout or partial body
Normalize extractor version, normalized digest parser drift mistaken for editorial change
Diff baseline and successor IDs, changed spans duplicate retry emitted as a second change
Retrieve query, filters, ranked passage IDs stale or cross-publication evidence
Generate model/config identifier, cited claim set uncited prose presented as fact
Deliver idempotency key, destination, attempt state repeated alert from redelivery

This trail supports reconciliation: count accepted diffs, grounded answer records, and delivered alert identities over the same interval, then investigate mismatches. Do not use a single “pipeline succeeded” counter. It hides gaps between stages.

A minimal grounded path in Go

The following sketch leaves fetching and embedding behind interfaces so the important contract stays visible. Retrieval returns immutable evidence, generation returns claims with passage IDs, and validation fails closed. The digest check catches accidental or unauthorized mutation between indexing and answer assembly.

package grounded

import (
    "context"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "errors"
)

type Passage struct {
    ID        string
    DiffID    string
    Text      string
    SHA256Hex string
}

type Claim struct {
    Text       string
    PassageIDs []string
}

type Answer struct {
    Claims []Claim
}

type Retriever interface {
    Search(ctx context.Context, pageID, question string, limit int) ([]Passage, error)
}

type Generator interface {
    AnswerFrom(ctx context.Context, question string, evidence []Passage) (Answer, error)
}

func GroundedAnswer(ctx context.Context, r Retriever, g Generator, pageID, question string) (Answer, error) {
    evidence, err := r.Search(ctx, pageID, question, 8)
    if err != nil {
        return Answer{}, err
    }
    if len(evidence) == 0 {
        return Answer{}, errors.New("no verified evidence")
    }

    allowed := make(map[string]struct{}, len(evidence))
    for _, p := range evidence {
        sum := sha256.Sum256([]byte(p.Text))
        if hex.EncodeToString(sum[:]) != p.SHA256Hex {
            return Answer{}, errors.New("evidence digest mismatch")
        }
        allowed[p.ID] = struct{}{}
    }

    answer, err := g.AnswerFrom(ctx, question, evidence)
    if err != nil {
        return Answer{}, err
    }
    for _, claim := range answer.Claims {
        if len(claim.PassageIDs) == 0 {
            return Answer{}, errors.New("uncited claim")
        }
        for _, id := range claim.PassageIDs {
            if _, ok := allowed[id]; !ok {
                return Answer{}, errors.New("citation outside retrieved evidence")
            }
        }
    }
    return answer, nil
}

The limit of eight is an example configuration, not a quality threshold. Tune candidate count against a labeled set of real page changes, including corrections, deletions, boilerplate churn, near-duplicate syndication, and failed captures. Measure retrieval recall separately from claim support: an answer can cite every claim and still omit the passage that contained the decisive change.

Test retry behavior too. Replaying the same capture, diff, and delivery message should preserve one logical event identity, while a genuinely new observation receives a new identity even when its visible text happens to match an older version. That distinction keeps deduplication from erasing history.

What should the system deliberately forget?

Keep immutable metadata and evidence long enough to meet the defined editorial, legal, and operational purpose; expire material that no longer serves it. A practical policy may retain accepted normalized versions and meaningful diffs while dropping unchanged response bodies quickly, then keep aggregate operational metrics longer than content. The exact periods must come from jurisdiction, contracts, newsroom requirements, and incident-response needs rather than a generic RAG recipe.

The trade-off is direct. Less retained content shrinks privacy exposure and storage growth, but it weakens the ability to reproduce an old parser decision or prove how a page looked between accepted baselines. Record the policy version applied to each deletion so an auditor can distinguish deliberate expiry from missing data.

Vector retrieval remains valuable here because language varies: a correction about “revised guidance” may answer a query phrased as “forecast changed.” It still occupies one bounded box in the design. A trustworthy alert is a reconciled chain from capture to cited claim, with an explicit unknown state whenever that chain breaks.

Further reading

  • Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks: https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • HTTP Semantics, including conditional requests and validators: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110
  • Robots Exclusion Protocol: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309
  • W3C PROV-O, an ontology for provenance: https://www.w3.org/TR/prov-o/
  • GDPR Article 5 principles relating to processing of personal data: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj

title: Wan 2.1 cloud image: 28 flows, native VACE, Triton and SageAttention
description:
This episode is a cloud-image update for Wan 2.1 rather than a single model release. The image grows from 18 to 28 flows, adding seven native VACE workflows plus more mature Phantom, ATI trajectory control, and Uni3C camera-reference paths.

Watch the episode: https://youtu.be/XPonYGLEBAc
Chinese original: https://www.bilibili.com/video/BV1M7TxzpEZm
Image entry: https://www.compshare.cn/images/compshareImage-1crfjcsablzi?referral_code=A7fTQUYY9lCDFJwA6MMvoq

What is in the image

  • Seven VACE flows: single/multi reference, control plus reference, first-last frame, extension, reference editing, and related combinations.
  • Phantom multi-image subject reference.
  • ATI trajectory control.
  • Uni3C camera movement from a reference video.
  • The previous 18 flows remain available.

The practical value is coverage: one deployed environment contains the major Wan 2.1 video tasks, so you do not assemble model loaders and node dependencies from scratch.

Deployment path

The episode uses the U Cloud image entry, deploys an instance, opens JupyterLab, enters the ComfyUI directory, and starts the interface. A 4090 is the recommended rental in that test. Any trial credit mentioned in the video is a point-in-time platform offer, not a current guarantee.

Acceleration settings

CausVid is the general accelerator in this image. The recommended starting point is 10 steps and CFG 1. AccVideo is less universal across the included flows, so swapping it in requires per-flow testing rather than a global replacement.

The image mainly uses 14B or 720p models. Block swap and model compilation are enabled to manage VRAM; Triton and SageAttention are installed and working in the tested environment.

Known limits

  • A 420GB-class image is large; deployment and startup take time.
  • Flow count is not quality count - each task still needs its own reference and settings.
  • Cloud pricing, availability, and trial credits change.
  • No workflow JSON or weights are bundled with this article; the episode provides an image entry.

title: How ExodeUI Brings Game-Engine Spring & IK Physics to Everyday Web UI
description:
Tune stiffness, damping, and mass visually while exporting pure, tree-shakeable TypeScript.

For years, product teams accepted a strange ritual: designers drew static pictures of software in Figma, wired together fragile click-through prototypes, and handed them off to engineers to rebuild from scratch. That prototyping era is over.


Figure 1: ExodeUI replaces static vector handoffs with a unified code-native UI & motion studio.

Why the Old Prototyping Workflow Breaks Down

In physics & springs vs dead keyframes, static vector tools hit a hard ceiling:

  1. Duplicate Work: Every screen is built twice—once as a vector illusion, once in production code.
  2. Missing Runtime Truth: Static frames can't model real browser layout, async states, or interruptible gesture physics.
  3. Permanent Drift: The moment code ships, the Figma file becomes outdated documentation.


Figure 2: Closing the gap between visual design and production execution.

How ExodeUI Replaces Figma

Instead of drawing dead rectangles, ExodeUI lets you design with real layout primitives, deterministic state machines, and spring physics that compile straight into production TypeScript:

// ExodeUI velocity-preserving spring configuration
export const drawerSpring = {
  type: "spring",
  stiffness: 380,
  damping: 32,
  mass: 0.9,
  restDelta: 0.001,
} as const;

What Changes for Your Team

  • Designers work visually with live data, real responsive rules, and 120fps spring choreography.
  • Engineers receive clean, idiomatic React, Vue, Svelte, Solid, or Vanilla TypeScript components—not position: absolute guesses.
  • Product Teams skip the throwaway prototype phase and iterate directly on real software.

Build Without the Handoff Tax

The prototyping era taught teams to draw software twice—once as static pictures, and once in code. ExodeUI collapses both into a single code-native canvas.

title: React Email States: A Typed Fixture Contract
description:
Email verification looks like a small React feature: render an input, submit an address, then wait for a message. In a real product, it quickly becomes a state machine. The user can submit twice, the message can arrive late, a test fixture can expire, or the API can return an error after the component has unmounted.

The pattern I keep reaching for is a typed UI contract. It gives the component a short list of states and makes impossible combinations harder to represent. That matters for production flows and for test fixtures, where an email inbox may behave like a burner email: useful for a short scenario, but not something the UI should trust forever.

Why email UI becomes a state problem

A boolean such as isLoading is rarely enough. The screen may need to distinguish between:

  • no address has been submitted yet;
  • a verification request is running;
  • the app is waiting for a matching message;
  • a message was found and accepted;
  • the fixture expired;
  • the user can retry after a temporary failure.

If these are represented by several independent booleans, combinations like isLoading: true and hasError: true become possible. The code still compiles, but the UI can show a spinner beside a stale error. It feels random to a user and is hard to reproduce in a test.

I also avoid putting provider-specific terms directly into the component. Whether a team uses a shared test inbox, a mock server, or a temporary mailbox, React should receive the same small contract. This keeps the feature focused on user feedback instead of inbox plumbing.

For a related integration concern, version invite emails across React and Node is a useful reminder that the client and server need to agree on event shape, not just endpoint names.

Define the contract before the component

Start with the events the UI actually understands. A minimal contract can look like this:

type EmailState =
  | { kind: "idle" }
  | { kind: "sending"; address: string }
  | { kind: "waiting"; address: string; startedAt: number }
  | { kind: "verified"; address: string; messageId: string }
  | { kind: "expired"; address: string }
  | { kind: "failed"; message: string; retryable: boolean };

type EmailEvent =
  | { type: "submit"; address: string }
  | { type: "sent"; startedAt: number }
  | { type: "matched"; messageId: string }
  | { type: "expired" }
  | { type: "error"; message: string; retryable: boolean }
  | { type: "reset" };

The kind field is the important bit. TypeScript can narrow each branch, so code rendering a verified state can safely use messageId. There is no need to guess whether it exists because another boolean happened to be true.

Keep the contract small. I don't put the full email body, provider response, or an access token in this state. A short message ID is enough for diagnostics, and the server can keep sensitive details outside the browser when possible.

Model the states with a discriminated union

The transition function should be boring. Boring is good here because it makes retries and fixtures easier to reason about:

function reduceEmail(state: EmailState, event: EmailEvent): EmailState {
  switch (event.type) {
    case "submit":
      return { kind: "sending", address: event.address };
    case "sent":
      if (state.kind !== "sending") return state;
      return { kind: "waiting", address: state.address, startedAt: event.startedAt };
    case "matched":
      if (state.kind !== "waiting") return state;
      return { kind: "verified", address: state.address, messageId: event.messageId };
    case "expired":
      if (state.kind !== "waiting") return state;
      return { kind: "expired", address: state.address };
    case "error":
      return { kind: "failed", message: event.message, retryable: event.retryable };
    case "reset":
      return { kind: "idle" };
  }
}

Notice that a late matched event is ignored unless the screen is waiting. This is a small guard, but it prevents an old polling request from verifying a newer attempt. At the API boundary, idempotent email verification APIs add the server-side version of the same idea.

Build a small React hook

The hook can own the reducer while the component only renders the state. A production implementation would add an AbortController and clear its timer in the effect cleanup:

function useEmailVerification() {
  const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(reduceEmail, { kind: "idle" });

  const submit = async (address: string) => {
    dispatch({ type: "submit", address });
    try {
      await api.startVerification(address);
      dispatch({ type: "sent", startedAt: Date.now() });
    } catch {
      dispatch({ type: "error", message: "Could not start verification", retryable: true });
    }
  };

  return { state, submit };
}

The example leaves polling out on purpose. Polling belongs behind a small adapter that emits matched, expired, or error; it should not leak timer details into every button and status label. Also, spellings like tamp mail com or fake e mail com may appear in search-driven test input, but they are not valid states or validation rules by themselves.

Test transitions instead of screenshots

Reducer tests are quick and tell you more than a large screenshot suite. Cover the happy path, a duplicate event, expiry, and a retryable failure:

it("ignores a late match after expiry", () => {
  let state: EmailState = { kind: "waiting", address: "qa@example.test", startedAt: 1 };
  state = reduceEmail(state, { type: "expired" });
  state = reduceEmail(state, { type: "matched", messageId: "old-1" });

  expect(state.kind).toBe("expired");
});

This style also makes fixtures clearer. A fake inbox can emit a deterministic sequence without pretending to be a browser. The test says what happened and what the UI should show, which is much easier to debug when CI is busy.

Q&A: practical tradeoffs

Should every email flow use a state machine?

No. A one-shot “send again” form may be fine with local state. Use an explicit union when there are asynchronous steps, retries, expiry, or more than one source of events.

Should the UI poll the inbox directly?

Usually no. Keep provider credentials and matching rules on the server or in a test adapter. The browser needs a safe status event, not the full mailbox.

What if the backend already has a state machine?

Share event names and IDs where practical, but don't force the frontend to mirror every backend state. Translate server responses into the smaller set of states the user can act on.

A shipping checklist

Before merging an email verification screen, check that:

  1. Every visible state has one kind value.
  2. Late events cannot update a newer attempt.
  3. Retry and expiry are explicit, not inferred from a timeout alone.
  4. Timers and requests are cleaned up on unmount.
  5. Tests cover transitions, not only the happy screenshot.
  6. Test inbox details stay out of browser state and logs.

Typed contracts are not ceremony for its own sake. They give React a stable boundary around an unreliable async workflow, so the feature is easier to ship, easier to test, and less confusing when email arrives a little late.

title: The 12 checks I run on every page before I call it done (free tool)
description:
A page can look finished and still be broken in ways nobody notices until it is live: a title that is empty, a missing viewport tag, an image with no alternative text, a script that fails on a phone. None of these show up in a screenshot. All of them cost you visitors.

So we wrote down the checks we actually run, and turned them into a free tool. Here is the list, and why each item matters.

The 12 checks

  1. Page title — the headline in search results and in the browser tab. Empty or duplicated titles are the most common self-inflicted SEO wound.
  2. Description — the sentence under the headline in search results. Without it, the search engine picks a random fragment.
  3. Main heading — one h1 that says what the page is. Pages with three h1s and no h2 structure are hard for both people and machines.
  4. Picture and text for shared links — Open Graph tags decide how a link looks in WhatsApp, Facebook, LinkedIn, X and most chat apps. A missing og:image makes your link look broken.
  5. Mobile settings — without the viewport setting, a phone renders the page at desktop width and shrinks it.
  6. Page weight — a heavy page is slow, above all on a mobile connection.
  7. Pictures — every image needs a description for people who cannot see it, and must actually load.
  8. Links — every link needs a working address and a name that says where it leads.
  9. Encrypted address — an address starting with https protects the visitor's connection.
  10. Search engines — this check reads the instructions a page gives to search engines.
  11. Language and forms — a page states its language; every form field has a label.
  12. Scripts and styles — every script file is one more request before the page is ready.

Why a browser cannot just check another site

Browsers block one site from reading another, for good reason. So the tool asks a public relay service to read the page you enter, and everything else — the checks, the report, the printing — happens in your browser. Nothing is stored, no account is needed.

If the relay cannot read the address, you can paste the HTML source directly and the checks still run.

What a good result looks like

Every check passes, or fails with a specific instruction: not "image missing alt" but "3 of 14 images have no description — add a short sentence for each". A check you cannot act on is not a check, it is a scolding.

Use it

The tool is free, works on a phone, and prints a report you can send to a client or a developer:

Website Audit — free tool

It is the same checklist we run on every page we build at Harbor Digital Studio. If the audit finds something you would rather have someone fix, that is what we do — websites from $800, fixed price, written scope.

title: Inheritance type in java
description:
Introduction

When we start learning Java we come across many important concepts in Object Oriented Programming (OOP). One of those concepts is Inheritance.

Inheritance is a concept that allows one class to acquire the properties and methods of another class. In simple words instead of writing the same code again and again we can create one common class and allow other classes to reuse its functionality.

We can understand inheritance using a real world family example. A child may inherit certain characteristics from their parents. Similarly in Java a child class can inherit properties and methods from a parent class.

What Is Inheritance in Java?

Inheritance is an Object-Oriented Programming concept in which one class acquires the properties and methods of another class.

The class that provides its properties and methods is called the Parent Class or Superclass. The class that inherits those properties and methods is called the Child Class or Subclass.

Example imagine a father has a house. His son wants to use that property. in Java the Son class can inherit the properties and methods of the Father class.

class Father {

    void house() {
        System.out.println("Father has a house");
    }
}

class Son extends Father {

    void bike() {
        System.out.println("Son has a bike");
    }
}

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Son obj = new Son();

        obj.house();
        obj.bike();
    }
}

Output:

Father has a house
Son has a bike

The Father class contains the house() method. The Son class uses the extends keyword to inherit the Father class.

When we create an object of the Son class, we can access both the inherited house() method and its own bike() method.

** Why Do We Use Inheritance?**

Imagine you are developing a school management application. In that application you need to create three classes: Student Teacher and Staff.

All three classes have some common information such as name, age, and address.

Without inheritance we might write the same properties in all three classes. This creates code duplication.

Instead, we can create one common class called Person and allow Student, Teacher and Staff to inherit it.

Example:

class Person {

    String name;
    int age;

    void display() {
        System.out.println(name);
        System.out.println(age);
    }
}

class Student extends Person {

}

class Teacher extends Person {

}

class Staff extends Person {

}

Now Student, Teacher, and Staff can reuse the common properties and methods from the Person class.

The main advantages of inheritance are:

  1. Code Reusability – We can reuse existing code instead of writing it again.
  2. Code Duplication Reduction – Common properties and methods can be maintained in one parent class.
  3. Easy Maintenance – Changes to common functionality can be managed in one place.
  4. Extensibility – We can create new child classes using existing parent classes.
  5. Method Overriding – Child classes can provide their own implementation of inherited methods.

Types of Inheritance in Java

Inheritance can be implemented in different ways depending on the relationship between classes.

Java commonly discusses five types of inheritance:

  1. Single Inheritance
  2. Multilevel Inheritance
  3. Hierarchical Inheritance
  4. Multiple Inheritance
  5. Hybrid Inheritance

1.Single Inheritance

Single inheritance means one child class inherits from one parent class.

For example, imagine a Father has a house and a Son inherits the property.

Java Example:

class Father {

    void property() {
        System.out.println("Father has a house");
    }
}

class Son extends Father {

    void vehicle() {
        System.out.println("Son has a car");
    }
}

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Son obj = new Son();

        obj.property();
        obj.vehicle();
    }
}

Output:

Father has a house
Son has a car

Here the Son class inherits the Father class. Therefore, the Son object can access the inherited property() method and its own vehicle() method.

This relationship between one parent and one child is called Single Inheritance.

2. Multilevel Inheritance

Multilevel inheritance means one class inherits another class, and a third class inherits the second class.

We can understand this through a family relationship:

Grandfather → Father → Son.

The Father inherits from Grandfather and the Son inherits from Father.

Java Example:

class Grandfather {

    void land() {
        System.out.println("Grandfather has land");
    }
}

class Father extends Grandfather {

    void house() {
        System.out.println("Father has a house");
    }
}

class Son extends Father {

    void bike() {
        System.out.println("Son has a bike");
    }
}

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Son obj = new Son();

        obj.land();
        obj.house();
        obj.bike();
    }
}

Output:

Grandfather has land
Father has a house
Son has a bike

Here the Son class directly inherits Father but it can also access the inherited method from Grandfather because Father already inherits Grandfather.

3. Hierarchical Inheritance

Hierarchical inheritance means multiple child classes inherit from one common parent class.

For example one parent has two children: a Son and a Daughter.

Both children can inherit common properties from their parent but they can also have their own individual properties.

Java Example:

class Parent {

    void property() {
        System.out.println("Parent has property");
    }
}

class Son extends Parent {

    void bike() {
        System.out.println("Son has a bike");
    }
}

class Daughter extends Parent {

    void car() {
        System.out.println("Daughter has a car");
    }
}

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Son s = new Son();
        Daughter d = new Daughter();

        s.property();
        s.bike();

        d.property();
        d.car();
    }
}

Output:

Parent has property
Son has a bike
Parent has property
Daughter has a car

Here both Son and Daughter inherit the same Parent class.

The Son can access the parent's property and his own bike method. Similarly, the Daughter can access the parent's property and her own car method.

4.Multiple Inheritance

Multiple inheritance means one child class inherits from more than one parent class.

For example imagine a child wants to access properties from both Father and Mother.

However Java does not support multiple inheritance through classes.

Why? Imagine both parent classes have a method with the same name. If the child inherits both classes it may become confusing to decide which parent's method should be executed. This situation is related to the Diamond Problem.

However Java provides another way to achieve multiple inheritance using interfaces.

Java Example:

interface Father {

    void house();
}

interface Mother {

    void car();
}

class Child implements Father, Mother {

    public void house() {
        System.out.println("Father has a house");
    }

    public void car() {
        System.out.println("Mother has a car");
    }
}

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Child obj = new Child();

        obj.house();
        obj.car();
    }
}

Output:

Father has a house
Mother has a car

Here the Child class implements two interfaces: Father and Mother.

Java allows a class to implement multiple interfaces. This is how we achieve Multiple Inheritance in Java.

5.Hybrid Inheritance

Hybrid inheritance means combining two or more types of inheritance.

For example, we can combine hierarchical inheritance and multiple inheritance.

Java does not support hybrid inheritance using classes alone when it requires multiple class inheritance.

However we can achieve hybrid inheritance by combining classes and interfaces.

This is useful when an application needs to reuse functionality from different types of relationships.

Difference Between All Types of Inheritance

Inheritance Type Meaning
Single One child inherits one parent
Multilevel One class inherits another class in a chain
Hierarchical Multiple children inherit one parent
Multiple One child inherits multiple parents
Hybrid Combination of two or more inheritance types

In Java, Single, Multilevel and Hierarchical inheritance are supported through classes. Multiple inheritance is supported through interfaces and Hybrid inheritance can be achieved using classes and interfaces together.

** Important Keywords Used in Inheritance**

When working with inheritance in Java two important keywords are extends and implements.

extends: We use the extends keyword when one class inherits another class.

class Son extends Father {

}

implements: We use the implements keyword when a class implements an interface.

class Child implements Father, Mother {

}

Remember:

  • Class to class – extends
  • Class to interface – implements
  • Interface to interface – extends

** Where Is Inheritance Used in Real Time Projects?**

Inheritance is not only used for learning Java concepts. Developers also use it when building real world applications.

For example consider an online banking application.

A banking application may have different types of accounts:

  • Savings Account
  • Current Account
  • Salary Account

All these accounts have some common features such as account number, account holder name, deposit and withdrawal.

Instead of writing the same code in every account class, developers can create a common BankAccount class.

Then Savings Account, Current Account, and Salary Account can inherit the common properties and methods.

This makes the application easier to develop, understand, and maintain.

title: MongoDB to Redshift Without a Load Job: A Change Stream Tutorial on AWS Glue
description:
Two questions sit inside every MongoDB to Redshift project. What does a document look like once it is a row in a SQL warehouse? And how does an order that was edited an hour after the first copy ever get there?

A first attempt usually answers neither. A script exports the collection, COPY loads the file, and the edit shows up tomorrow, provided the whole table is reloaded.

These are the routes people usually take:

  • mongoexport to JSON, then COPY. You keep a script, a scheduler and a staging bucket. Freshness is hours to daily, and only full reloads are possible, so an update or a delete never arrives as a change.
  • AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) with its MongoDB source. Change data capture (CDC) through the oplog or change streams into native Redshift tables, in document mode or table mode. You run a replication instance and a task, plus a staging bucket in Amazon Simple Storage Service (S3).
  • Debezium, Kafka and a Redshift sink. Changes land within seconds. The cost is Kafka, Kafka Connect, Debezium and one sink connector per collection, plus merge logic that you write.
  • Managed extract, load, transform (ELT) services such as Fivetran, Estuary or Airbyte Cloud. Nothing to host, and minutes of lag depending on the plan. They charge per row, per GB or per connector for a second copy inside Redshift.

This tutorial takes another route. OLake Go, an open source (Apache 2.0) replication tool, follows the MongoDB change stream and commits each collection as an Apache Iceberg table in the AWS Glue Data Catalog, with the files in a bucket you own. Redshift maps the Glue database onto an external schema and queries the tables where they sit, and Athena and DuckDB read the same files.

I ran every step on 2026-10-30 against MongoDB 7 as a single-node replica set in Docker, OLake Go v1.1.0 and a Redshift Serverless workgroup at 8 Redshift Processing Units (RPU) in ap-southeast-1. The first sync took 14 seconds and the change sync 11 seconds. Every figure below is from that run.

You need: MongoDB 4.0 or later as a replica set (self-hosted or Atlas), an AWS account where you can create a bucket and Identity and Access Management (IAM) entities, Redshift Serverless or an RA3 cluster, Docker, and about 40 minutes.

Step 1: A replica set, a user and two collections

OLake Go reads changes through a change stream, which MongoDB offers only in replica set mode. One member is enough, and that is what I used. Launch mongod with --replSet rs0, connect with mongosh and run:

// 1. A single-node replica set (self-hosted only)
rs.initiate({ _id: "rs0", members: [{ _id: 0, host: "<host>:27017" }] })

// 2. A user for OLake Go
use admin
db.createUser({
  user: "olake", pwd: "<password>",
  roles: [{ role: "read", db: "shop" }, { role: "clusterMonitor", db: "admin" }]
})

// 3. The oplog size in bytes; raise it with replSetResizeOplog if it is small
use local
db.oplog.rs.stats().maxSize

read lets OLake Go copy the collections. The change stream needs oplog access on top, and clusterMonitor grants it (readAnyDatabase does too).

Confirm the result:

rs.status().members.map(m => m.stateStr)      // one PRIMARY
db.getSiblingDB("admin").getUsers().users.map(u => u.user)

Next, some data. The script below rebuilds the two collections from my run: 8 customers and 40 orders, with integer _id keys and the order amount stored as NumberDecimal. Skip it if you are pointing at collections you already have.

use shop
const now = new Date();
const people = [
  ['Aarav Mehta', 'aarav', 'Mumbai', 'gold'],    ['Priya Sharma', 'priya', 'Bengaluru', 'silver'],
  ['Liam Carter', 'liam', 'Austin', 'bronze'],   ['Sofia Rossi', 'sofia', 'Milan', 'gold'],
  ['Kenji Tanaka', 'kenji', 'Tokyo', 'silver'],  ['Emma Schulz', 'emma', 'Berlin', 'bronze'],
  ['Noah Kim', 'noah', 'Seoul', 'gold'],         ['Zara Ali', 'zara', 'Dubai', 'silver']
];
db.customers.insertMany(people.map(([name, handle, city, tier], i) => ({
  _id: i + 1, name, email: handle + '@example.com', city, tier, created_at: now, updated_at: now
})));

const products = ['Laptop', 'Headphones', 'Monitor', 'Keyboard', 'Mouse', 'Webcam'];
const statuses = ['placed', 'shipped', 'delivered'];
db.orders.insertMany(Array.from({ length: 40 }, (_, k) => {
  const n = k + 1;
  return {
    _id: n, customer_id: 1 + (n % 8), product: products[n % 6],
    amount: NumberDecimal(((2000 + (n * 7919) % 120000) / 100).toFixed(2)),
    status: statuses[n % 3], created_at: now, updated_at: now
  };
}));

On Atlas the replica set already exists. Create the user under Database Access with the same two roles, and allow OLake Go's IP under Network Access.

⚠️ The oplog is your replay window. Atlas and most self-hosted installs keep 24 hours or less by default, and a job paused past the window has to take a fresh snapshot.

Step 2: A bucket, a writer and a reader on AWS

Create an S3 bucket in the region where your Redshift workgroup or cluster runs. Mine was in ap-southeast-1.

OLake Go writes with its own identity. I gave it a scoped IAM user with this inline policy; swap in your bucket, region and account:

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["s3:ListBucket", "s3:GetBucketLocation"], "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::<bucket>" },
    { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["s3:GetObject", "s3:PutObject", "s3:DeleteObject", "s3:AbortMultipartUpload", "s3:ListMultipartUploadParts"], "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::<bucket>/*" },
    { "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["glue:GetDatabase", "glue:GetDatabases", "glue:CreateDatabase", "glue:GetTable", "glue:GetTables", "glue:CreateTable", "glue:UpdateTable", "glue:DeleteTable"],
      "Resource": ["arn:aws:glue:<region>:<account>:catalog", "arn:aws:glue:<region>:<account>:database/*", "arn:aws:glue:<region>:<account>:table/*/*"] }
  ]
}

Redshift reads with a different identity: an IAM role attached to the Serverless namespace or the cluster. In my run that role carried AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess plus read access to Glue.

Do not create a Glue database. OLake Go makes one per job on the first sync.

Step 3: Start OLake UI and connect MongoDB 

curl -sSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/datazip-inc/olake-ui/master/docker-compose-v1.yml | docker compose -f - up -d

Open http://localhost:8000 and log in as admin with the password password.

Go to Sources, click Create Source and choose MongoDB. Under Change data capture (CDC), leave Enable CDC switched on.

Under Connection details, enter the host as host:port, the Database Name, the Auth DB, the username and password, and the Replica Set name. MongoDB sat in a separate container in my run, so I entered host.docker.internal:27017, shop, admin, olake and rs0. Leave Read Preference on primary.

Click Set up source. Before anything is saved, OLake Go tests the connection, checks that it can open a change stream and reports the oplog window. A window shorter than 7 days is flagged as a warning and does not block you.

Step 4: Add the Glue destination

Go to Destinations and click Create Destination. Choose Apache Iceberg as the connector and AWS Glue as the catalog type.

Three things go in the form: the S3 path OLake Go should write under, the AWS region of the bucket and the Glue catalog, and the access key pair of the writer user from step 2. If OLake Go runs on an instance that has a role, leave the two key fields empty. Click Create.

Step 5: Create the job and run the first sync

Go to Jobs and click Create Job. Name it mongodb_to_redshift, give it a schedule (Every Day at a fixed hour, or a cron expression), and select the source and destination you just made. The schedule sets how often the change stream is drained, and the full copy happens only once.

One setting needs a manual choice. Redshift is not in OLake Go's Target Query Engines list yet, so under Advanced Settings pick AWS Athena and DuckDB instead.

Click Next, and OLake Go discovers the collections and opens the Streams page. Tick customers and orders, set the sync mode to Full Refresh + CDC and the ingestion mode to Upsert. Then set Upsert Type to Positional Deletes, because that is the delete format Redshift reads, and Athena and DuckDB read it as well.

Click Create Job, open the job's menu and choose Sync Now.

My first sync copied 8 customers and 40 orders, 48 documents and 6.40 KB in total, in 14 seconds with container start included.

OLake Go named the Glue database mongodb_to_redshift_shop, after the job and the source database. To use a different name, edit the Iceberg DB field at the top of the Streams page before the first sync.

Step 6: One external schema in Redshift

Open query editor v2. Run the first statement once, after the first sync and in the same region as the Glue database:

CREATE EXTERNAL SCHEMA lakehouse
FROM DATA CATALOG
DATABASE 'mongodb_to_redshift_shop'
IAM_ROLE default;

SELECT _id, name, city, tier FROM lakehouse.customers ORDER BY _id;

SELECT status, count(*) AS n, sum(cast(amount AS decimal(12,2))) AS total
FROM lakehouse.orders GROUP BY status ORDER BY status;

IAM_ROLE default picks the default role of the namespace or cluster. Name a specific role instead if you keep several.

The key column is _id, the same as in MongoDB. The roll-up casts amount because a Decimal128 field reaches Redshift as text, and a plain sum(amount) fails with ERROR: function sum(character varying) does not exist.

Step 7: Edit documents and sync again

Now the part a nightly export cannot do. Make 12 changes in mongosh, 7 inserts and 5 updates:

const now = new Date();
db.customers.insertMany([
  { _id: 9,  name: 'Maya Patel',  email: 'maya@example.com',  city: 'Pune',      tier: 'silver', created_at: now, updated_at: now },
  { _id: 10, name: 'Lucas Silva', email: 'lucas@example.com', city: 'São Paulo', tier: 'bronze', created_at: now, updated_at: now }
]);
db.orders.insertMany([
  { _id: 41, customer_id: 9,  product: 'Laptop',   amount: NumberDecimal('1299.00'), status: 'placed', created_at: now, updated_at: now },
  { _id: 42, customer_id: 9,  product: 'Mouse',    amount: NumberDecimal('25.50'),   status: 'placed', created_at: now, updated_at: now },
  { _id: 43, customer_id: 10, product: 'Monitor',  amount: NumberDecimal('349.99'),  status: 'placed', created_at: now, updated_at: now },
  { _id: 44, customer_id: 3,  product: 'Keyboard', amount: NumberDecimal('89.00'),   status: 'placed', created_at: now, updated_at: now },
  { _id: 45, customer_id: 7,  product: 'Webcam',   amount: NumberDecimal('79.90'),   status: 'placed', created_at: now, updated_at: now }
]);
db.customers.updateOne({ name: 'Liam Carter' }, { $set: { tier: 'gold', updated_at: now } });
db.customers.updateOne({ name: 'Zara Ali' },    { $set: { city: 'Abu Dhabi', updated_at: now } });
db.orders.updateMany({ _id: { $in: [1, 4, 7] } }, { $set: { status: 'delivered', updated_at: now } });

Choose Sync Now again. The second sync read 12 change events (1.60 KB) from the stream and was done in 11 seconds end to end.

For customers, OLake Go wrote one new data file holding 4 rows: the 2 inserts and the new versions of the 2 updated documents. A small positional delete file retires the 2 old versions. The sync log's commit report shows the same numbers: addedDataFiles=1, addedRecords=4, addedPositionalDeleteFiles=1, addedPositionalDeletes=2.

orders follows the same pattern with 8 rows and 3 deletes.

Back in Redshift, rerun the customers query. There is no refresh and no ALTER TABLE to run first. I got 10 rows, one per key: Liam Carter on gold, Zara Ali in Abu Dhabi, and the two new customers.

Add _op_type to the select list to see how each row arrived: r for the snapshot, c for an insert, u for an update and d for a delete.

Athena and DuckDB on the same files

Nothing is exported for this. Athena shows mongodb_to_redshift_shop in its database list, with no registration and no refresh. Pick a workgroup that has a query result location in S3 and run:

SELECT _id, name, city, tier FROM mongodb_to_redshift_shop.customers ORDER BY _id;

Athena returned the same 10 customers and scanned 0.76 KB.

DuckDB reads each table from its current metadata file, and Glue knows where that file is:

aws glue get-table --database-name mongodb_to_redshift_shop --name customers \
  --query 'Table.Parameters.metadata_location' --output text

INSTALL iceberg; LOAD iceberg;
INSTALL httpfs;  LOAD httpfs;

CREATE SECRET lake (TYPE s3, KEY_ID '<access key>', SECRET '<secret key>', REGION '<region>');

SELECT _id, name, city, tier
FROM iceberg_scan('<metadata_location from the command above>')
ORDER BY _id;

Each sync writes a new metadata file, so fetch the location again before a fresh read. DuckDB 1.5.5 gave me the same 10 customers.

The orders roll-up matched MongoDB to the cent in all three engines: 16 delivered orders for 8659.68, 18 placed for 10522.26 and 11 shipped for 6397.25.

Tips and limits

  • This is not native Redshift speed. The external schema goes through Redshift Spectrum, which reads Parquet from S3 on every query. For a hot dashboard, load the hot slice into a native table on a schedule and keep the Iceberg tables as the source.
  • Flattening stops at one level. Nested objects and arrays land as JSON text in one VARCHAR column, which you unpack with JSON_PARSE or json_extract_path_text. If every query would start that way, a SUPER column in a native Redshift table may serve you better.
  • Two type surprises. A date becomes a TIMESTAMP in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), and an ObjectId key arrives as its 24-character hex string. Store doubles in MongoDB if you want money as a numeric column without the cast.
  • A new field becomes a new column on the next sync, with nulls for older rows. A field whose type changes in an incompatible way fails the sync instead of corrupting the table.
  • The oplog is sized in gigabytes, not hours. A write-heavy day shortens the window, so check it after a busy day and resize before a planned pause.
  • Freshness is a schedule, down to one minute.
  • The external schema is read-only. INSERT or DELETE on these tables fails.

MongoDB to Redshift methods compared

Method Freshness Updates and deletes Where the data lands What you run
mongoexport, then COPY hours to daily no, full reloads only native Redshift tables a script, a scheduler, a staging bucket
AWS DMS CDC through the oplog or change streams yes native Redshift tables, document or table mode a replication instance and task, plus a staging bucket
Debezium, Kafka, Redshift sink seconds yes, with your own merge logic Kafka topics, then Redshift tables Kafka, Kafka Connect, Debezium, a sink per collection
Fivetran, Estuary, Airbyte Cloud minutes, by plan varies by tool Redshift tables, as a second copy nothing; per row, per GB or per connector
OLake Go to Glue (this post) CDC on a schedule, down to one minute yes, as Iceberg row-level deletes Iceberg tables for Redshift, Athena, Spark and DuckDB one Docker Compose stack, your bucket and compute

If you are already on AWS and Redshift will be the only reader, DMS is the simpler choice. The route above earns its setup when Athena, Spark or a notebook will read those rows too, or when you want to own the files.

FAQ

Can I run the pipeline without the UI?

Yes. The same job runs from the olakego/source-mongodb:latest image with a discover command and a sync command. In selected_streams.json, set sync_mode to cdc and update_type to pos, and give the container a persistent directory through OLAKE_INDEX_DB_DIR, because positional deletes keep a small index between runs.

What do I pay Redshift for in this setup?

Redshift Serverless bills RPU-hours only while queries run. Each query on the external schema scans Parquet files in S3, so select only the columns you need. The files are billed at S3 rates.

Who cleans up the small files each sync leaves behind?

Not Glue, which has no built-in compaction for tables written by external engines. OLake Fusion does it for the catalogs OLake Go writes to, and Spark's rewrite_data_files works through the same Glue catalog.

Where to go from here

  • Point the source at your own collections. On Atlas, the source form takes one SRV host with Use SRV turned on.
  • Give the job a schedule that is shorter than your oplog window.
  • The full guide has the command line configuration, the complete data type table and the troubleshooting list: MongoDB to Redshift on olake.io.

If a step behaves differently on your setup, leave the error text in a comment and I will update the tutorial.

title: Reliable Transactional SMS Alerts — Scheduled Resend, Suppression, and Delivery Tracking
description:
A gaming startup choosing a reliable transactional SMS alerts service needs to account for message attempts, retries, delivery tracking, retained evidence, and the engineering time needed to explain a disputed compliance notice. The transport invoice captures only part of that work. Keeping every intermediate status forever adds another obligation: someone must protect, interpret, and eventually delete that record.

For a planning example, assume 10,000 notices and 12 status observations per notice. That produces 120,000 observation records before any retries. These are illustrative workload inputs, not a provider benchmark or a forecast of the largest dollar charge. They identify the dominant record-count term: repeated observations outnumber original notice records 12 to 1. Compacting unchanged observations moves that term; choosing a different sender alone does not.

Short answer: choose a transactional SMS service by the delivery evidence your gaming business must retain and how it can collect that evidence. A polling-based API can fit a startup that can run reconciliation jobs. Require a callback-based integration when the workflow depends on pushed status updates, and keep scheduling, suppression, and resend decisions in an application-owned notice ledger. No delivery receipt proves that a player read the notice.

The useful alternative to an oversized integration is a smaller evidence contract. Decide what the audit must establish, then compare providers against it.

What delivery tracking should a startup require from its transactional SMS alerts service?

Start with the notice obligation. A player may need a compliance notice concerning an account action; a later reviewer needs to determine which notice version was selected, which destination was used, whether sending was permitted, and what delivery information came back. This is an engineering evidence model, not a claim that SMS satisfies a particular US or EU legal requirement. The responsible compliance team must define the permitted channel, required deadline, and retention period for each relevant jurisdiction.

Acceptance isn't delivery.

Keep those states separate. An application accepting a notice job establishes that work was queued internally. A provider accepting a request establishes a different boundary. A delivery status adds evidence about transport, with meaning that depends on the provider's documented status vocabulary. None of these alone establishes comprehension or consent. Mapping every successful response to a single green delivered badge destroys distinctions that matter during a dispute.

For this gaming workflow, a proposed ledger entry would hold an internal notice identifier, account reference, destination reference, notice-version reference, intended send time, suppression decision, provider message identifier, and observed delivery state. These are application fields, not a vendor request schema. Keep a timestamp for the observation as well as any event timestamp the provider supplies; delayed reconciliation otherwise makes an old transport event look like a new one. Protect access to the destination and notice content separately from routine operational dashboards.

Preserve uncertainty.

If collection stops before a terminal state is observed, record that fact.

Reduce repeated observations before reducing useful evidence

The 120,000-record example suggests a concrete change: retain state transitions in the long-lived ledger and keep repeated identical observations only for a shorter operational window. If a hypothetical notice produces 12 observations but only 3 distinct states, that rule preserves 3 transition records instead of 12 full observation records. Actual transition counts must come from the workload. This arithmetic describes a storage design, not measured savings.

There is a catch. A repeated observation can still help establish that reconciliation was running. Preserve a collection summary, such as first observation time, last observation time, and observation count, rather than silently throwing that evidence away. Separate message-level evidence from worker-health evidence so a reviewer can distinguish an unchanged status from a job that never ran. Compact only after deciding which evidence is material: two observations with the same status may carry different explanatory details that an audit requires.

Polling requires a budget as well as a worker. A proposed policy might inspect recent notices more frequently, slow down as they age, and stop active collection at a deadline defined by the notice policy. The intervals are an application decision; no provider-specific polling limit is implied here. Before adopting them, check documented request limits and exercise delayed delivery, duplicate observations, and collection interruptions in a sandbox. A status that arrives after the business deadline still belongs in the history, but it must not erase the fact that the deadline was missed.

Scheduling introduces another boundary. Store a future notice as an obligation before it becomes a send attempt. At dispatch, recheck suppression and whether the notice is still applicable. A canceled obligation and a canceled transport request are different records. The ledger should explain both without depending on a queue entry that will disappear after processing.

Compare collection models, then choose the transport

Twilio, Amazon SNS, Amazon SES, and Resend belong in different parts of this decision. Their documentation helps compare evidence paths, but it does not establish a delivery-rate winner for a particular gaming audience. No measured ranking is available here.

Option Evidence path to evaluate Fit and boundary for this notice workflow
Twilio Programmable Messaging Message status callbacks A candidate when SMS status updates need to trigger application work. Persist callback processing; pushed updates still need an application audit record.
Amazon SNS SMS Delivery status logging through CloudWatch A candidate for a team already operating AWS logs. Decide how those logs become notice-level evidence and how retention matches the audit policy.
Amazon SES Email event publishing An email-channel option for an AWS application. It serves a different transport requirement from SMS and needs email-specific event interpretation.
Resend Email delivery events and webhooks An email-channel candidate when the notice policy permits email. It is not a substitute for the SMS transport requirement.

Infrai provides one key and one bill, plus a simple REST API: plain HTTP with no SDK required. A single credential and bill replace separate credentials and invoices across backend integrations. For the notice reconciliation worker, a single API callable from any language means it can use its existing HTTP library rather than install another SDK. The unified API covers 295 routes across 20 modules with consistent conventions, reducing the separate integration patterns a gaming backend must maintain. Public, self-describing discovery supplies request JSON Schema, response schemas, and runnable examples without a key. That lets the team inspect the delivery response contract before writing the ledger mapping, instead of guessing which fields constitute evidence. Documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages, including Python and JavaScript. SMS resend support also fits recovery of a missed alert. The trade-off is polling-based delivery tracking: choose Twilio when pushed SMS status callbacks are a requirement.

Credential consolidation is useful operationally.

It does not establish delivery reliability. For all candidates, evaluate the actual destination countries, accepted sender configuration, status semantics, collection behavior, and the evidence export your reviewers will use. A general US/EU application label is not enough to select a sender or establish compliance.

Advanced channel requirements can change the shortlist. If the policy requires voice, WhatsApp, RCS, or an SMTP relay, select a stack that explicitly supports those requirements. For a plain SMS obligation, adding channels without a defined purpose creates more histories to reconcile. Keep a versioned local record of the selected message template and its identifier so an audit can reconstruct which wording was authorized.

The following read-only Python example retrieves one SMS status observation from the polling option. Set SMS_API_BASE to its documented HTTPS base URL including the version prefix, INFRAI_API_KEY to your key, and SMS_MESSAGE_ID to an existing message identifier. It uses only the standard library. It prints the returned JSON without guessing status field names; the reconciliation worker must interpret the documented response schema before changing the ledger. The local retry count and timeout are example choices, not service limits.

import json
import os
import random
import time
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from email.utils import parsedate_to_datetime
from urllib.error import HTTPError
from urllib.parse import quote, urlsplit
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen

base = os.environ["SMS_API_BASE"].rstrip("/")
if urlsplit(base).scheme != "https":
    raise ValueError("SMS_API_BASE must use HTTPS")
message_id = quote(os.environ["SMS_MESSAGE_ID"], safe="")
request = Request(
    f"{base}/sms/status/{message_id}",
    headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}"},
    method="GET",
)

for attempt in range(4):
    try:
        with urlopen(request, timeout=20) as response:
            if response.status != 200:
                raise RuntimeError(f"Unexpected status: {response.status}")
            print(json.dumps(json.load(response), indent=2))
        break
    except HTTPError as error:
        if error.code != 429 or attempt == 3:
            detail = error.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
            raise RuntimeError(f"HTTP {error.code}: {detail}") from error
        retry_after = error.headers.get("Retry-After")
        delay = 2 ** attempt + random.random()
        if retry_after:
            try:
                delay = max(delay, float(retry_after))
            except ValueError:
                deadline = parsedate_to_datetime(retry_after)
                delay = max(
                    delay,
                    (deadline - datetime.now(timezone.utc)).total_seconds(),
                )
        error.close()
        time.sleep(delay)

This example does not send a notice or authorize a resend. A production worker should record collection errors separately from delivery outcomes and schedule another observation according to its policy. A failed observation is not evidence of a failed message.

Make resends answerable to the original obligation

A resend should be a new attempt attached to the same notice obligation. Preserve the original attempt and its evidence. Otherwise a successful retry can hide the failed or unresolved attempt that caused it, and the audit loses the timeline it was meant to retain.

Avoid the tempting edge case: resending solely because a poll returned no final state. A delayed status observation and a failed delivery are different conditions. Reconcile the existing attempt first, apply a bounded retry policy, and check suppression again before creating another attempt. Use a stable application identifier to prevent duplicate jobs from authorizing the same attempt twice; verify the selected provider's idempotency contract before relying on transport-level deduplication.

Suppression deserves an explicit result in the ledger. Record the policy version and decision time, with access controls appropriate to the underlying data. A blocked send must remain distinguishable from an accepted send that later fails. Keep transactional notices separate from marketing logic, and have compliance review how channel preferences and mandatory notices interact. Do not assume that calling a message transactional overrides recipient protections.

Country restrictions and country-sensitive spend throttles also belong in the application design. Restrict destinations to those the product intends to serve, bound repeated sends for the same obligation, and monitor unexpected attempt volume. Abusive traffic can consume the capacity and attention needed for legitimate account notices.

Decide what the next dispute will be allowed to cost

After the approved operational window, deliberately stop keeping repeated unchanged response bodies and redundant message-content copies. Retain the notice-version reference, required delivery transitions, suppression decision, attempt relationships, and collection summary for the period approved for that notice. If a repeated response contains material evidence, preserve that evidence before discarding the body. The purpose is a smaller defensible record, not deletion by status label alone.

The loss is real.

Once raw responses expire, an investigator cannot replay every intermediate payload or inspect an omitted provider detail. A collection count can show that checks occurred, but it cannot reconstruct their complete contents. Keep the raw window long enough for the team's actual investigation process, and test an evidence export before approving deletion. No universal retention duration follows from choosing an SMS API.

For this gaming notice, favor the transport whose delivery evidence your team can reliably collect, interpret, and retain. Choose polling when scheduled reconciliation meets the notice deadline; choose pushed status updates when the workflow requires them. Either way, budget for the evidence you will need when a player disputes delivery, and name the evidence you have deliberately given up.

References

The documentation below describes the collection models being compared. It does not establish comparative delivery rates or legal sufficiency for a gaming notice.

  • Twilio, outbound message status tracking: https://www.twilio.com/docs/messaging/guides/track-outbound-message-status
  • Amazon SNS, SMS delivery status logging: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sns/latest/dg/sms_stats_cloudwatch.html
  • Amazon SES, event publishing: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ses/latest/dg/monitor-using-event-publishing.html
  • Resend, documentation: https://resend.com/docs/introduction

Further reading

  • Resend, webhook introduction for an email evidence path: https://resend.com/docs/webhooks/introduction

title: Enterprise UX Design in the AI Era: Building Digital Experiences That Scale to Millions
description:
As digital products grow, designing an experience that works for a few thousand users is very different from building one that serves millions. Enterprise platforms must accommodate different user behaviors, complex workflows, multiple stakeholders, and evolving business requirements without compromising usability or consistency.

Artificial intelligence is adding another layer to this challenge. While AI makes it possible to generate layouts, personalize content, and automate design tasks faster, it also increases the need for clear design standards and human oversight.

Why Enterprise UX Needs a Different Approach

Enterprise UX is not just about making individual screens look appealing. It involves creating a connected experience across multiple products, teams, devices, and user journeys.

As platforms expand, even small inconsistencies can affect thousands of interactions. Different customer expectations, changing content requirements, and multiple design themes make maintaining a unified experience increasingly difficult.

A scalable UX strategy must account for:

  • Different user behaviors: Some users want quick access to specific products, while others prefer exploring available options.
  • Consistency across platforms: Components, layouts, typography, and interactions should follow shared standards.
  • Complex edge cases: Long product names, varying image formats, and unusual content combinations must not disrupt the interface.
  • Multiple stakeholders: Design, engineering, marketing, and product teams need a common framework for making decisions.

Four Challenges in Designing for Millions of Users

1. Managing Edge Cases

Small design limitations become significant when a platform serves millions of people. For example, product tiles may struggle to accommodate long brand names without affecting readability or layout consistency.

Instead of applying individual fixes, designers need reusable rules for handling content variations. These rules should define text limits, overflow behavior, and fallback options while preserving important information.

2. Balancing Different User Expectations

Not every customer interacts with a platform in the same way. Some prioritize speed and want to reach a product immediately, while others spend more time browsing and comparing options.

A single fixed layout may not serve both groups effectively. Personalization can help present relevant information based on user behavior, provided the overall interface remains familiar and easy to navigate.

3. Maintaining Design Consistency

When multiple teams work on the same platform, differences in spacing, typography, colors, and component behavior can gradually create design inconsistencies.

A shared design system helps address this problem through reusable components and standardized design tokens. It also makes it easier to maintain consistency across different storefronts and product experiences.

4. Controlling AI-Generated Variations

AI can generate multiple interface variations based on user preferences, product information, and behavioral patterns. However, unrestricted variations can create unpredictable experiences.

Design teams need clear constraints around layouts, content placement, accessibility, and brand guidelines. AI should operate within these predefined boundaries rather than independently changing the entire interface.

Five Principles for Building Scalable Enterprise UX

1. Design Systems, Not Individual Screens

A scalable product requires reusable building blocks rather than isolated screen designs.

A widget-based approach allows teams to define components according to user goals, layout requirements, functionality, and screen position. This makes it easier to reuse components across different pages and experiences.

2. Establish Clear Content Rules

Design systems should account for content limitations before development begins.

For instance, teams should establish how long product names can be, when text should be truncated, and where complete information should remain accessible. Documenting these decisions prevents inconsistent fixes across different components.

3. Evaluate Layouts Against Defined Criteria

Design decisions should be based on usability requirements rather than personal preferences.

Teams can evaluate layouts based on product visibility, readability, content capacity, navigation patterns, and responsiveness. This provides a consistent method for selecting the most suitable design.

4. Document Exceptions and Fallbacks

Not every component will work perfectly in every situation. Long text, unusual images, missing information, and different screen sizes can create unexpected problems.

Documenting these exceptions helps developers and designers understand how components should behave when standard conditions are not met.

5. Plan for Long-Term Design Ownership

A design system needs continuous maintenance after handoff.

Organizations should establish ownership, define processes for introducing new components, maintain shared design tokens, and use visual regression testing to identify unintended changes.

How AI Fits Into Enterprise UX Design

AI is becoming an important part of modern product design workflows. It can help designers explore layouts, compare variations, identify inconsistencies, and personalize content.

However, AI-generated interfaces need a structured framework.

A practical approach involves three stages:

  • Generate: AI proposes layouts, content arrangements, and design variations.
  • Validate: Each variation is checked against predefined design rules, accessibility requirements, and brand guidelines.
  • Fallback: If a generated variation does not meet the requirements, the system uses a predefined design.

Human designers remain responsible for usability decisions, accessibility, brand consistency, and final approvals.

This approach makes personalization possible without sacrificing the predictability users expect from enterprise applications.

Building Enterprise Experiences That Grow With the Business

The challenge of enterprise UX is not simply creating an attractive interface. It is establishing a design framework that remains consistent as user numbers, features, and business requirements increase.

This requires a combination of user research, reusable components, documented design rules, and carefully controlled AI integration.

GeekyAnts approaches this challenge through its design systems and customer experience consistency practice, helping businesses build coherent digital experiences across products, teams, and platforms.

For organizations planning to scale their digital products, investing in a structured UX strategy can help reduce design inconsistencies, improve usability, and create experiences that remain reliable as the business grows.

Source: Enterprise UX Design in the AI Era: How to Design for Millions of Users
