title: Are you paying for backups of servers you deleted last year?
description:
Snapshot storage keeps growing when nothing is ever told to expire, and deleting a backup feels riskier than paying for it

A starting point for production

7 daily snapshots
4 weekly snapshots
Monthly only if the business or compliance needs them, with an end date

For non-production, a few days is usually enough, or none if both the environment and its data can be recreated

How to adjust the numbers

How much data you can afford to lose decides how often you back up

How late you could notice a problem decides how long you keep it. If bad data can go unnoticed for six weeks, four weeklies are not enough

Where the money hides

EBS snapshots stay after the volume is deleted, and GCP disk snapshots can stay after the disk is gone

Deregistering an AMI leaves its snapshots behind by default

Manual RDS snapshots outlive the database and bill until someone removes them

How to clean up

List snapshots older than your longest retention rule, then mark the ones whose source no longer exists

Treat those as candidates, not waste. Any of them may be the only copy left, so check the owner, image references and compliance holds before deleting

Keep it clean

Let AWS Backup, Data Lifecycle Manager or GCP snapshot schedules expire backups automatically, and give every manual snapshot an owner and an end date

Test your restores on a schedule. It is easier to trust a short retention when you know the recent backups work

A backup you have never restored is only an assumption

How old is your oldest snapshot, and does anyone know what it belongs to?

title: How to Debug Duplicate Search Chunks (While Preserving Listing Freshness)
description:
TL;DR: Duplicate chunks in vector search are usually an identity problem before they are a similarity problem. For a B2B SaaS listing aggregator, derive each vector ID from the source listing, a normalized content fingerprint, and a stable chunk ordinal; record the intended generation before bulk ingestion; upsert on retry; then expose a generation only after its complete manifest is durable. This does not create magical exactly-once delivery. It makes repeated delivery converge to one auditable state while preventing old and new listing chunks from appearing together.

A nearest-neighbor index is expected to return semantically similar records. Retrieval-augmented generation depends on that retrieval step, so duplicate evidence is not cosmetic: repeated listing text can crowd distinct evidence out of a small result set and make downstream answers look more certain than the corpus warrants. The useful debugging question is therefore not merely "why are two strings equal?" It is "which identity or publication invariant allowed both records to become eligible?"

How should you debug duplicate chunks in vector search results?

Start with one suspect result pair and compare four fields: source key, content fingerprint, chunk ordinal, and ingestion generation. Equal fingerprints with different vector IDs indicate nondeterministic identity, commonly caused by assigning a fresh identifier on each attempt. Equal source keys with different fingerprints and generations indicate stale publication. Different source keys with equal fingerprints may be legitimate syndication across listing sources, so deleting one blindly can erase provenance that reconciliation needs.

The distinction matters because bulk jobs are retried at inconvenient boundaries. A worker may send 500 records, lose the acknowledgement, and send the same 500 again. If IDs are random, the index has no basis for recognizing the second delivery as the same logical write. If IDs are deterministic and the storage operation is an upsert keyed by that ID, the retry targets the existing record. Idempotency is a property of the key and state transition, not of the queue's good intentions.

Retries happen.

Do not begin by tuning similarity thresholds. Two byte-identical chunks have the same semantic content regardless of the threshold, while two versions of a listing can remain close enough to compete after an address, price, or availability field changes. Threshold tuning can hide the symptom and retain the stale record.

Step 1: Make chunk identity reproducible

Choose a canonical source key from facts that survive retries, such as source_system plus the source's listing identifier. Normalize only representation noise: line endings, Unicode whitespace that your ingestion contract declares insignificant, and repeated horizontal spaces. Do not lowercase identifiers or remove punctuation merely to increase deduplication; those transformations can merge distinct suite numbers, product codes, or legal names.

Then chunk deterministically. The same normalized document and configuration must yield the same boundaries and ordinals. Store the chunking policy version because changing a 900-byte window to a 1,200-byte window creates a new interpretation of the document even when the source is unchanged. The following complete Go program produces a stable identifier and shows that a retry converges on the same key:

package main

import (
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "fmt"
    "regexp"
    "strings"
)

var horizontalSpace = regexp.MustCompile(`[\t ]+`)

func normalize(s string) string {
    s = strings.ReplaceAll(s, "\r\n", "\n")
    s = strings.ReplaceAll(s, "\r", "\n")
    return strings.TrimSpace(horizontalSpace.ReplaceAllString(s, " "))
}

func digest(s string) string {
    sum := sha256.Sum256([]byte(s))
    return hex.EncodeToString(sum[:])
}

func vectorID(source, listingID, policy string, ordinal int, chunk string) string {
    material := fmt.Sprintf("%s\x1f%s\x1f%s\x1f%d\x1f%s",
        source, listingID, policy, ordinal, digest(normalize(chunk)))
    return digest(material)
}

func main() {
    chunk := "ACME 42\r\nSuite 300"
    first := vectorID("partner-a", "L-1842", "chunk-v3", 0, chunk)
    retry := vectorID("partner-a", "L-1842", "chunk-v3", 0, chunk)
    fmt.Println(first == retry)
}

The SHA-256 digest here is an identifier construction, not a claim that hash equality proves business equivalence. Preserve the original source key, normalized-content digest, policy version, ordinal, and generation as metadata. A digest alone cannot explain why a record exists.

There is a deliberate trade-off in including the content fingerprint in the ID. An unchanged retry overwrites the same vector, while changed content obtains a new ID and can be staged beside the active version. That supports safe publication, but it also means cleanup is mandatory after the new generation becomes active. Omitting the fingerprint makes updates overwrite in place and reduces cleanup, yet readers can observe a partially replaced multi-chunk listing during a bulk run. For freshness-sensitive aggregation, staging is the more defensible choice.

Step 2: Publish generations, not individual vectors

A listing with eight chunks is one logical document, not eight independently publishable facts. Assign every ingestion attempt a generation, build an expected manifest of its deterministic vector IDs, and write those vectors in bounded batches. After all writes are acknowledged, read back or otherwise verify the manifest according to the index's consistency contract. Only then change the listing's active-generation pointer. Query filters must require that active generation.

This small state machine provides a clean recovery rule:

State Query eligible Retry action
Prepared No Reuse generation and IDs
Written, unverified No Verify or repeat upserts
Active Yes No-op if manifest matches
Superseded No Delete after retention policy permits

The activation record belongs in a transactional system of record with a uniqueness constraint on (source_key, generation) and an idempotency key for the ingestion request. The vector index remains a derived projection. This boundary is important: many indexes can upsert individual records, but a multi-record batch and a separate metadata write should not be assumed to commit atomically unless the chosen system explicitly guarantees it.

Exactly once is the wrong operational promise. The useful invariant is narrower: at most one complete generation per listing is query eligible, and replaying a committed request does not change its manifest. Delivery may occur more than once. Effects converge.

That boundary is testable.

Step 3: Reconcile evidence instead of counting requests

Request success is weak evidence. Reconciliation should compare the source-of-truth manifest with the indexed projection and emit counts for missing IDs, unexpected IDs, duplicate fingerprints within one source key, and multiple eligible generations. Keep cardinality labels bounded; place individual listing IDs in sampled logs or an audit table rather than metric labels.

Each transition should append an audit event containing the idempotency key, source key, generation, chunking policy, expected count, acknowledged count, manifest digest, actor or worker identity, and timestamp. Retention is a compliance and legal-policy decision, so do not hard-code a universal duration into the worker. The event needs to answer who requested the change, what set was intended, and which generation became visible.

A useful acceptance test injects failure after every external boundary: before the first upsert, midway through a batch, after the final upsert but before activation, and after activation but before acknowledgement. Run the same request again each time. The assertions are concrete: one active generation, an identical manifest digest, no duplicate vector IDs, and no search hit from a prepared or superseded generation. Then repeat with changed listing content and verify that readers see either the complete old generation or the complete new one, never a mixture.

Be careful with cross-source duplicates. If three partners carry the same listing description, a global content-only ID would collapse three provenance records into one and make takedown or correction ambiguous. Keep source identity in the vector ID, retrieve candidates, and perform an explicit business-level merge later using authoritative attributes. Search deduplication and entity resolution are separate controls.

Provenance wins.

Roll out without a flag day

Introduce the new metadata first and dual-write deterministic IDs into a shadow generation while existing reads continue. Reconcile source counts and manifest digests, then enable active-generation filtering for a small partition of source keys. Watch the four discrepancy classes rather than a single "duplicate rate," because a falling aggregate can conceal a rise in stale generations.

Once the new path is stable, backfill source by source, activate only verified manifests, and retire old IDs through the same audited workflow. Keep rollback simple: move the active pointer to the last complete generation; do not reconstruct it from whatever vectors happen to remain.

The durable fix is compact: deterministic identity makes retries idempotent, generation gating makes freshness atomic at the document boundary, and reconciliation demonstrates that the derived index still matches intent. A clean result set is the consequence of those invariants, not a post-query deduplication trick.

Sources

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://pkg.go.dev/crypto/sha256
  • https://pkg.go.dev/regexp
  • https://pkg.go.dev/strings

title: Windows VPS in BRL with Pix: license, FX fees and real cost
description:
Comparing the sticker price of a foreign USD/EUR Windows VPS against a Windows VPS billed domestically in Brazilian reais (BRL) with Pix is often misleading at first glance. Foreign pricing pages rarely surface four items that show up at checkout or on your monthly statement: the commercial Windows Server license, Brazil's 3.5% cross-border IOF tax, bank FX spreads and steep renewal jumps after an intro discount ends.

This guide walks through every piece of the real monthly cost, what is included on Nuvits Windows plans and which extra items still belong in your project budget.

Five components of the true Windows VPS cost

Put these five lines side by side before comparing any two Windows VPS offers:

Cost component Foreign host (USD / EUR on international card) Nuvits Windows VPS (billed in BRL)
1. Windows Server license Often added per core at checkout or shipped as a 180-day evaluation image Included in the monthly price (Windows Server 2022 or 2025, no trial)
2. Cross-border IOF tax 3.5% on the converted charge (Brazilian Decree 12,499/2025) Zero (domestic BRL billing)
3. Bank FX spread & rate swings Typically 3%–6% card markup plus monthly USD/EUR volatility Zero (fixed BRL price shown before paying)
4. Payment methods (PF & CNPJ) Requires an international credit card and FX accounting Pix, Brazilian boleto or local card
5. Lock-in & renewal rates Lowest headline prices often require 12–36 months prepaid Month-to-month with no lock-in (optional 12-month plan with 1st-year discount)

1. Windows Server license: included vs the 180-day evaluation trap

Unlike Linux distributions, Windows Server requires commercial licensing from Microsoft. Hosting providers typically handle it in one of three ways:

  • Included in the plan price: you pick Windows Server 2022 or 2025 when ordering, the server boots activated and there is no separate license fee or expiration countdown. That is how Nuvits Windows VPS plans work.
  • Checkout add-on per core: the landing page advertises the Linux base price and adds a per-vCPU Windows license fee only on the final checkout screen.
  • 180-day Evaluation image: the host gives you an unlicensed trial image. After 180 days, Windows begins shutting down every hour until you buy a standalone license or rebuild the server from scratch.

Always confirm that the commercial Windows Server license is already inside the quoted price for your chosen vCPU count.

2. The 3.5% IOF tax and bank FX spread

When Brazilian individuals or companies pay a foreign host on an international credit card, two extra charges sit on top of the headline price every month:

  1. 3.5% IOF tax: Brazil's Decree 12,499/2025 ended the previous gradual phase-out schedule and set the IOF rate on international card purchases at 3.5%.
  2. Issuer FX spread: most Brazilian card issuers add 3% to 6% above the central bank reference rate when converting USD or EUR into BRL.

Together, those fees make a foreign USD or EUR server 6.5% to nearly 10% more expensive than a naive spot-rate conversion, while leaving your monthly operating cost exposed to exchange-rate swings.

Watch out for estimated R$ display prices settled abroad. Some global hosts convert catalog prices to R$ on the marketing page while still processing the card internationally. Unless checkout runs domestically in BRL via Pix or boleto, your card statement can still carry IOF and FX spreads.

3. Renewals, lock-in and consumer protection

For an ERP or SQL Server host, the real metric is your predictable 12-month spend rather than a first-month teaser:

  • Month-to-month without lock-in: on Nuvits, the monthly table rate is not a teaser that doubles on month two. Card auto-renewal is optional; without it, you check your due date in the panel and renew via Pix, boleto or local card whenever you choose.
  • Optional 12-month cycle: if you prefer annual billing (including domestic card installments, with the full total displayed before confirming), the first year carries an initial discount and subsequent renewals use the regular current price.
  • No setup fee and statutory rights preserved: there is no hidden provisioning fee, and for consumer orders where Article 49 of Brazil's Consumer Protection Code (CDC) applies, the statutory 7-day right of withdrawal is preserved (see the cancellation and refund policy).
  • Company (CNPJ) procurement: you can enter a CPF or CNPJ at first payment and settle directly from corporate finance via Pix (confirmed in seconds) or boleto (up to 3 business days).

4. What is NOT included and stays in your budget

Keep three practical items in your budget on any unmanaged Windows VPS:

  • Third-party & extra Microsoft licenses: the included license covers Windows Server (2022 or 2025). Paid SQL Server editions (Standard), Microsoft Office and RDS CALs for more than two concurrent interactive RDP users are licensed separately by the customer. For databases under 10 GB, SQL Server Express is free.
  • Off-server backups: current Nuvits plans include 0 backup slots. Set aside a modest budget for encrypted off-server storage (S3-compatible bucket or another host) for daily ERP and database backups.
  • Server location: Nuvits Windows plans run in Germany. For ERPs, IIS, SQL Server and remote office desktops, RDP from Brazil works reliably; only workloads requiring single-digit millisecond latency inside São Paulo (such as exchange-colocated B3 trading bots) need a local São Paulo datacenter.

Picking the right Windows tier without overpaying

Because in-place resizing is not available on current plans, sizing accurately up front saves a migration later:

  • Windows 8 GB (4 vCPU, 100 GB SSD): 1–2 RDP users, light ERP, SQL Server Express or desktop automation.
  • Windows 12 GB (6 vCPU, 200 GB SSD): comfortable headroom for small teams and heavier Windows apps.
  • Windows 24 GB (8 vCPU, 300 GB SSD) and up: SQL Server Standard with meaningful RAM caching and concurrent multi-user setups.

Check live BRL pricing in the plan card alongside this article or in the full catalog table.

Next steps

  • Check live BRL plans with the Windows Server license included on Windows VPS and Windows RDP VPS.
  • Compare transparent month-to-month plans with no renewal surprises on Cheap VPS.
  • Deciding between 8 GB, 12 GB and 24 GB for ERP and SQL Server? Read How much RAM for a Windows VPS running ERP, SQL Server and RDP.

title: 在 Node.js 中使用代理：fetch(undici)、axios、got 的配置差异与常见坑
description:
作者：Leo Lin（林乐），FlashIP 产品经理，新加坡。利益披露：我在 FlashIP 工作，这是一家代理 IP 服务商。

在公司内网或只允许经代理出网的 CI 里写 Node.js，经常遇到这种情况：export HTTPS_PROXY=... 之后 curl 正常，axios 也正常，可是原生 fetch() 依然直连，got 也直连。原因很简单：这三类客户端各自用一套代理逻辑，读不读环境变量、怎么处理账号密码都不一样。

下面的结论来自 Node.js、undici、axios、got 和 hpagent 的官方文档（2026 年 11 月查阅），并在 Node 24.22.1 上配合本地日志代理逐个验证过。示例中的主机名和账号都是占位符。

1. 原生 fetch：默认不读 HTTP_PROXY

Node 18 起自带的全局 fetch() 基于 undici 实现，默认不读 HTTP_PROXY / HTTPS_PROXY。我只设置 HTTPS_PROXY 时，fetch('https://example.com') 直接返回 200，代理日志里一条 CONNECT 都没有。

想让它走代理，有三种做法。

做法一：打开 Node 内置代理支持（v24.5.0 / v22.21.0 起，文档标注为 Stability 1.1 "Active development"）

NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1 \
HTTPS_PROXY=http://user:pass@proxy.example.com:8080 \
NO_PROXY=localhost,127.0.0.1 \
node app.js

# 或者用命令行参数，两者同时存在时以参数为准
HTTPS_PROXY=http://proxy.example.com:8080 node --use-env-proxy app.js

打开后，全局 agent 会以 proxyEnv: process.env 创建，fetch() 和 http.request() / https.request() 都会走代理。v25.4.0 / v24.14.0 起还可以在代码里调用 http.setGlobalProxyFromEnv()，官方建议在发出任何请求之前调用。

做法二：undici 的 EnvHttpProxyAgent，适合还不能升级 Node 的项目：

import { fetch, EnvHttpProxyAgent, setGlobalDispatcher } from 'undici';

setGlobalDispatcher(new EnvHttpProxyAgent());
const res = await fetch('https://api.example.com/health');

注意它和 Node 内置支持有个差别：如果只设置了 http_proxy，undici 会把它同时用于 HTTP 和 HTTPS 请求。

做法三：undici 的 ProxyAgent，给单个请求指定固定代理：

import { fetch, ProxyAgent } from 'undici';

const dispatcher = new ProxyAgent('http://user:p%40ss@proxy.example.com:8080');
const res = await fetch('https://api.example.com/health', { dispatcher });

URI 里的账号密码会被 URL 解码，所以密码中的 @ 要写成 %40。也可以用 token 选项直接传 Proxy-Authorization 的值。

坑：npm 装的 undici 和 Node 内置的 undici 版本不一致。 Node 24 内置的是 undici 7.x，而 npm 上最新的是 8.x。我把 npm 版 undici 8 的 ProxyAgent 传给全局 fetch()，结果报 fetch failed，cause 是 invalid onRequestStart method。解决办法：fetch 和 ProxyAgent 都从同一个 undici 包里导入。

2. axios：自带代理逻辑，会读环境变量

axios 在 Node.js 环境下会读取 http_proxy / https_proxy，也会遵守 no_proxy。显式配置的写法：

import axios from 'axios';

const res = await axios.get('https://api.example.com/health', {
  proxy: {
    protocol: 'http',            // 代理本身是 HTTPS 时必须写 'https'
    host: 'proxy.example.com',
    port: 8080,
    auth: { username: 'user', password: 'p@ss' },
  },
});

如果你更想用 https-proxy-agent（比如需要给 CONNECT 请求加自定义头），记得同时设置 proxy: false。axios 文档的原话是，用自定义 httpAgent / httpsAgent 管理代理时，应当关闭 proxy：

import { HttpsProxyAgent } from 'https-proxy-agent';

const httpsAgent = new HttpsProxyAgent('http://user:pass@proxy.example.com:8080');
await axios.get('https://api.example.com/health', { httpsAgent, proxy: false });

几个容易踩的点：

  • 设置了 NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1 时，axios 会把基于环境变量的代理交给 Node 处理，但显式的 proxy 对象仍由 axios 自己处理。不要两套同时开，排查起来很痛苦。
  • 我在 axios 1.21.1 上实测：从 HTTPS_PROXY 读取的密码 p%40ss 会原样放进 Proxy-Authorization，没有解码，代理端自然返回 407。密码里有特殊字符时，建议改用 proxy.auth 显式传入。
  • axios 文档写明，HTTP/2 请求不能走代理。

3. got：完全不读环境变量，要自己传 agent

got 本身没有代理选项，只设置 HTTPS_PROXY 时请求照样直连。got 文档推荐的方案是 hpagent，它会复用 keep-alive 连接：

import got from 'got';
import { HttpProxyAgent, HttpsProxyAgent } from 'hpagent';

const proxy = 'http://user:pass@proxy.example.com:8080';

const res = await got('https://api.example.com/health', {
  agent: {
    http: new HttpProxyAgent({ keepAlive: true, proxy }),
    https: new HttpsProxyAgent({ keepAlive: true, proxy }),
  },
});

要点是按目标网站的协议选 agent：访问 https:// 网站用 HttpsProxyAgent，访问 http:// 网站用 HttpProxyAgent，与代理本身是 HTTP 还是 HTTPS 无关。另外，got 文档说明其内置的 HTTP/2 客户端不支持代理。

4. 快速排查清单

  • curl 走代理、fetch() 不走：内置代理没开，设置 NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1 或使用 undici dispatcher。
  • fetch failed + invalid onRequestStart method：undici 版本混用。
  • axios 返回 407：检查密码是否经过 URL 编码，改用 proxy.auth。
  • got 不走代理：它本来就不读环境变量，需要传 agent。
  • 内网地址也被代理了：检查 NO_PROXY。三者的写法支持程度不同，axios 支持 CIDR，Node 内置支持的文档里则没有列出 CIDR。

最后说一下凭据：不要把代理账号写死在代码里，应在运行时从密钥管理服务注入。如果服务器的出口 IP 是固定的，用 IP 白名单认证可以连密码都省掉，很多代理服务商都支持这种方式，我所在的 FlashIP 也支持账号密码和 IP 白名单两种认证。另外，Node 文档也特别提醒，内置代理支持不是匿名或隐藏流量的功能，只应连接你信任的代理。

参考资料

  • Node.js HTTP 文档（Built-in Proxy Support、http.setGlobalProxyFromEnv()）：https://nodejs.org/api/http.html
  • Node.js CLI 文档（--use-env-proxy）：https://nodejs.org/api/cli.html
  • undici 文档（ProxyAgent、EnvHttpProxyAgent）：https://undici.nodejs.org/
  • axios 请求配置：https://axios-http.com/docs/req_config
  • got 文档 Tips / Proxying：https://github.com/sindresorhus/got/blob/main/documentation/tips.md
  • hpagent：https://github.com/delvedor/hpagent
  • https-proxy-agent：https://github.com/TooTallNate/proxy-agents/tree/main/packages/https-proxy-agent

title: Permission prompts are a state machine, not a popup
description:
Every "Allow notifications?" dialog is a UI for state the operating system already tracks. When a team treats it as a one-off popup, the app ends up re-asking after a denial, hiding a feature with no explanation, or showing a dead screen where the camera feed should be.

A permission prompt is a gate the user has to pass through. Design Den Solutions plans Android, iOS and web apps so the gate opens when the person actually needs it. +91 98721 90965 | www.designdensolutions.com. AI-generated conceptual illustration.

The fix is not a nicer dialog. It is modelling the permission as state, and designing each state separately.

The four states you actually have

Every platform you will ship on has the same shape, even when the API names differ:

State What it means What you can do
Not asked The system has never shown a prompt You may prompt, once
Granted Access is live Run the feature
Denied The user said no this session Run the degraded path
Blocked The OS will not prompt again Send the user to Settings, with a reason

The fourth state is the one that gets skipped in planning, and it is the one users actually hit. "Denied" is recoverable in-app. "Blocked" is not: no API call will bring the prompt back. Your only move is to explain, and offer a route to the settings screen.

Design a visible outcome for each row. A table like the one above, filled in during scoping, prevents most first-run arguments later.

iOS: after the first "Don't Allow", the system stops asking

requestAccess and requestAuthorization only present UI when the status is not determined. Once the user has denied, the completion handler fires with false and no dialog appears. Calling it again does not help.

import AVFoundation

func ensureCameraAccess() async -> Bool {
    switch AVCaptureDevice.authorizationStatus(for: .video) {
    case .authorized:
        return true
    case .notDetermined:
        return await AVCaptureDevice.requestAccess(for: .video)
    case .denied, .restricted:
        // No prompt is possible. Explain, then offer Settings.
        return false
    @unknown default:
        return false
    }
}

Two details worth knowing:

  • .restricted is not the user's choice. Parental controls, device management or a policy can block the feature entirely, so the copy should not say "you denied this".
  • Notifications have a middle option. Requesting provisional authorisation delivers notifications quietly, without a prompt, and the user can promote them later. That is often a better first release than a hard ask on launch.

For the Settings route, UIApplication.openSettingsURLString opens your app's page directly. Say what to turn on before sending people there.

Android: rationale, a second denial, then silence

Android gives you the same four states with worse naming. shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale returns true when a rationale is warranted, and false both before the first ask and after the user has denied for good. The API cannot tell those two cases apart, so persist your own "we have asked before" flag.

private val cameraPermission =
    registerForActivityResult(ActivityResultContracts.RequestPermission()) { granted ->
        if (!granted && askedBefore) {
            // The system may never prompt again; show the Settings path.
        }
        askedBefore = true
    }

fun askForCamera() {
    when {
        ContextCompat.checkSelfPermission(this, Manifest.permission.CAMERA) ==
            PackageManager.PERMISSION_GRANTED -> openCamera()
        shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale(Manifest.permission.CAMERA) ->
            showRationale { cameraPermission.launch(Manifest.permission.CAMERA) }
        else -> cameraPermission.launch(Manifest.permission.CAMERA)
    }
}

On Android 11 and later, two denials are enough for the system to stop prompting. On Android 13 and later, notifications are a runtime permission (POST_NOTIFICATIONS) rather than something granted at install — which means every app built before that change needed a new first-run decision, not just a new manifest line.

Web: ask from a gesture, and check before you promise

The browser adds a wrinkle: some prompts are suppressed unless they follow a user action, and a blocked origin will not show anything at all. Query the state before you build a screen that depends on it.

async function currentGeoState(): Promise<PermissionState | 'unknown'> {
  if (!navigator.permissions?.query) return 'unknown';
  try {
    const status = await navigator.permissions.query({ name: 'geolocation' as PermissionName });
    return status.state; // 'granted' | 'denied' | 'prompt'
  } catch {
    return 'unknown';
  }
}

If the state is denied, do not call getCurrentPosition and wait for a timeout you have to handle anyway — show the manual fallback immediately. Notification permission behaves the same way: Chrome will not prompt without a user gesture, and after a block it stops showing the prompt altogether. Safari's support for permissions.query is partial, so treat unknown as a real branch rather than an edge case.

The pre-prompt is a state, not decoration

A screen that explains why you need the camera before the OS dialog appears is a genuine decision point: the user can say "not now" and stay in the app. Two rules keep it honest.

  1. Only ask for a permission the very next screen uses. A camera prompt on launch, before the user has seen a reason to take a photo, trains people to tap "Don't Allow".
  2. Every "no" needs somewhere to go. Upload from the photo library instead of the camera. Let the person type an address instead of using location. The degraded path is the product, not an error state.

The test matrix is six cases, not one

One device, freshly installed, tapping "Allow", proves almost nothing. The cases that break releases:

  1. Fresh install, allow.
  2. Fresh install, deny once.
  3. Deny until the OS stops prompting.
  4. Permission revoked in Settings while the app is backgrounded.
  5. Restricted state (parental controls, device management).
  6. Granted, but the hardware is unavailable — camera busy in another app, no GPS fix.

Cases 3 and 4 are where "it worked on my phone" turns into a support ticket.

Where the cost lands

A chain of permission dialogs on first launch is a trade: you spend first-run completion on access you may not need yet. Asking at the point of use, explaining in one sentence, and keeping a path for every refusal is cheaper to build than the re-engagement campaign you would run to win those users back.

If you are planning an Android, iOS or web app and want the first-run flow decided before the codebase is, we start with requirements, user journeys and interactive prototypes. title: 20 Rust Concepts You Need Before Merging Claude's Code
description:
Half of X is shipping Rust right now without knowing the "R" of Rust.

You open Claude Code or Codex, tell it to rewrite some slow Node or Python tool in Rust, grab coffee, come back to 1,500 lines of code, see cargo test go green, and hit merge.

Not gonna lie, it feels like magic. Right up until the day it blows up.

One stray .unwrap() panics and kills your whole process in prod. The agent sprays .clone() across a hot loop just to get the compiler to shut up. Or you sit there burning 40 turns watching the model fight a lifetime error coz you don't know enough Rust to tell it to stop digging and just return an owned String.

I rewrote Jot (my Mac capture and local dictation app) off Electron and into native Rust. AI wrote a ton of the boilerplate and glue code. The only reason the codebase didn't turn into an unmaintainable mess is that I review every diff before it lands.

Here's the thing: you don't need to be a Rust wizard writing lock-free allocators from scratch to review AI-generated Rust well. You just need solid mental models for 20 core concepts so when a PR lands in front of you, you can spot lazy agent shortcuts in 5 seconds.

Here are all 20, in plain English, with how they actually work under the hood and what to catch when your coding agent gets sloppy.

1. Cargo

If you're coming from JS/TS, think of Cargo as npm + tsc + vitest + vite rolled into one tool that actually agrees with itself. There is no "pick your bundler, pick your test runner, pray they work together." Cargo is the whole toolchain.

  • Cargo.toml is your package.json. It holds your project metadata and your dependencies (Rust calls packages "crates").
  • Cargo.lock pins exact versions so builds are reproducible across machines and CI.
  • cargo build, cargo test, cargo run, and cargo check handle compiling, testing, running, and fast type-checking without emitting a binary.

cargo check is the command you'll run the most. It runs the full compiler and borrow checker in a fraction of the time of a full build.

What to watch for in AI diffs: Agents love reaching for massive crates in Cargo.toml for tiny jobs, like pulling in a full async web stack or a giant utility crate just to make one HTTP call or parse one date. Every crate you add bloats compile times and your binary size. Check every new line in Cargo.toml like you're paying for it out of pocket.

2. Macros

Any time you see a name ending with ! in Rust, you're looking at a macro, not a normal function.

println!("loaded {} notes from {}", count, path);
let tags = vec!["rust", "ai", "jot"];

Why do they exist? Normal Rust functions have fixed argument counts and strict types. Macros run at compile time and expand into actual Rust code before the compiler type-checks anything. That's how println! can take 1 argument or 10, and still fail the build if your {} placeholders don't match the values you passed.

You'll also see attribute macros like #[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize)] sitting right above structs. Those auto-generate boilerplate trait implementations for you at compile time so you don't have to hand-write JSON serializers or debug printers.

What to watch for in AI diffs: Built-in and standard derive macros (vec!, format!, #[derive(...)]) are great. The red flag is when an agent invents a gnarly custom macro_rules! block just to avoid repeating 10 lines of code. Custom macros are painful to debug and produce awful compiler errors. Reject them and ask for plain functions.

3. Immutable by Default

In JS or Python, every variable can be reassigned unless you remember to lock it down. Rust flips that completely: every variable is immutable by default. If you want to change a value later, you have to explicitly opt in with mut.

let max_retries = 3;
// max_retries = 5; // compile error: cannot assign twice to immutable variable

let mut attempts = 0;
attempts += 1; // works coz we opted in with `mut`

Once you get used to it, reading code gets way faster. When you see let x = ... without mut, you know for a fact nothing 80 lines down is mutating x behind your back. That kills a whole category of "wait, where did this state change?" bugs.

What to watch for in AI diffs: If an agent slaps let mut on half the variables in a function when they're never even modified (or only mutated because the agent wrote an imperative loop instead of a clean expression), it's writing JavaScript in Rust syntax. Rust will even warn you about unused mut, so don't let those slip through.

4. Shadowing

Even though variables are immutable by default, Rust lets you declare a brand new variable with the exact same name using let again. That's called shadowing.

let port = " 8080 ";
let port = port.trim();                 // now &str
let port: u16 = port.parse().unwrap();  // now u16

Notice the difference between mut and shadowing: mut lets you change the value of a variable, but never its type. Shadowing creates a new binding, so you can cleanly transform data step by step (String -> &str -> u16) without inventing ugly names like raw_port_str, trimmed_port, parsed_port_num, and without leaving the variable mutable after you're done parsing it.

What to watch for in AI diffs: Shadowing is super clean over 3-4 lines of parsing or cleanup. It gets nasty inside a 100-line function where data starts as raw bytes, gets shadowed into a JSON struct, and then gets shadowed into a bool 50 lines later. If you have to scroll up to remember what type a variable is, ask for distinct names.

5. Stack and Heap

In garbage-collected languages (JS, Python, Go), you rarely have to think about where a value lives in memory. In Rust, stack vs heap is front and center coz it directly drives performance and ownership.

  • Stack: Fixed-size values whose size the compiler knows upfront (i32, u64, bool, small structs). Pushing and popping on the stack is basically just moving a pointer. Stupid fast, zero overhead, automatically cleaned up when the function returns.
  • Heap: Growable or dynamically-sized data (String, Vec, file contents, user input). The allocator has to find a block of memory, give you a pointer back (which lives on the stack), and later free that block.

The magic of Rust is that you get C-level control over stack vs heap without ever calling malloc or free by hand. The compiler inserts the cleanup code automatically at the exact point a heap value's owner goes out of scope.

What to watch for in AI diffs: Unnecessary heap allocations inside tight loops: calling .to_string(), Vec::new(), or Box::new() on every single iteration when a stack value or a reused buffer would do. That's the fastest way to make a Rust service run as slow as the script you replaced.

6. String vs &str

Every single person who touches Rust hits this wall on day one: why are there two string types?

  • String is an owned, growable UTF-8 string living on the heap. You can push characters to it, mutate it, and you're responsible for freeing it when it goes out of scope.
  • &str (pronounced "string slice") is a borrowed, read-only view into UTF-8 text that already lives somewhere else (either inside a String, or baked straight into your binary like "hello"). Zero allocation. 
// Good: accepts both &String and &"literal" with zero copies
fn log_event(name: &str) {
    println!("event: {}", name);
}

Rule of thumb: if a function only needs to read text, take &str. Only take String when the function genuinely needs to own the text (like storing it inside a struct or moving it to another thread).

What to watch for in AI diffs: Agents default to fn parse(input: String) all the time even when the function only reads input. That forces every caller to pass ownership or call .to_string() / .clone() just to call a helper. Flip read-only params to &str.

7. Ownership

Ownership is the whole game in Rust. Everything else (moves, borrows, lifetimes) flows from three simple rules:

  1. Every value in Rust has a single owner.
  2. There can only be one owner at a time.
  3. When that owner goes out of scope, Rust immediately drops the value and frees its memory. 
{
    let note = String::from("ship jot 2.3");
    // `note` owns the heap buffer here
} // scope ends -> Rust frees the memory right here. No GC pause.

That's how Rust gives you predictable, flat latency. There is no garbage collector waking up mid-request to pause your app and scan memory, and no manual free() calls you can forget or accidentally run twice.

What to watch for in AI diffs: When an agent gets confused about which struct should own a piece of data, it panics and wraps everything in Arc<Mutex<T>> (thread-safe shared mutable ownership). That compiles, sure, but now you've got lock contention, runtime overhead, and potential deadlocks for data that only ever belonged in one place.

8. Move

Because every value can only have one owner at a time, assigning a heap value (String, Vec, HashMap) to another variable or passing it into a function moves ownership. It doesn't silently copy the heap data, and it doesn't leave two variables pointing at the same memory.

let draft = String::from("hello");
let published = draft; // ownership moves from `draft` -> `published`

// println!("{}", draft); // compile error: value borrowed here after move

Once draft moves into published, the compiler treats draft as dead. You literally cannot touch it again, which makes use-after-free bugs impossible.

Simple stack-only types like i32, f64, or bool are tiny and cheap to duplicate, so they implement the Copy trait and just copy automatically instead of moving.

What to watch for in AI diffs: The second an agent sees error[E0382]: borrow of moved value, its knee-jerk reflex is to slap .clone() on the original variable and move on. Most of the time, the function shouldn't have taken ownership in the first place. It should have borrowed it.

9. Borrowing

If you want a function to inspect a value without taking ownership of it, you borrow it by passing a reference with &.

fn word_count(text: &str) -> usize {
    text.split_whitespace().count()
}

let body = String::from("plain markdown files beat databases");
let n = word_count(&body); // `body` is borrowed, not moved
println!("{} ({} words)", body, n); // `body` is still ours

Think of it like lending someone a book to read instead of giving it away. You still own it, and you can hand out as many read-only borrows (&T) at the same time as you want because readers can't step on each other.

What to watch for in AI diffs: Good Rust borrows by default and only takes ownership when it genuinely needs to store, transform, or consume the value. If a helper function takes Vec<Note> just to count or filter items and never stores the vector, change it to &[Note].

10. Mutable References

When a function actually needs to modify data you own without taking ownership, you pass a mutable reference (&mut).

fn add_tag(tags: &mut Vec<String>, tag: &str) {
    tags.push(tag.to_string());
}

Now here is the iron rule of Rust references, the one that prevents an entire universe of concurrency bugs:

At any given moment, for a single piece of data, you can have either:

  • any number of read-only references (&T), or
  • exactly one mutable reference (&mut T).

Never both at the same time. If someone is writing to a buffer, nobody else is allowed to read it or write to it concurrently. That single rule kills data races at compile time before your code ever runs.

What to watch for in AI diffs: Holding a &mut borrow alive across 40 lines of code, or across an .await point in async code. Keep mutable borrows tight and short-lived so you aren't locking out the rest of the function.

11. The Borrow Checker

The borrow checker is the compiler pass that enforces Ownership, Moves, and Borrowing before it lets you build a binary.

Everyone jokes about fighting the borrow checker when they start Rust. And yeah, it feels strict at first. That's because it refuses to let you ship bugs that other languages happily compile and leave for 3am production alerts: dangling pointers, use-after-free, iterator invalidation, and concurrent read/write races.

When the borrow checker rejects your code, it's usually not being pedantic. Nine times out of ten, it's telling you your data flow is tangled and two parts of your code are trying to mutate the same thing at once.

What to watch for in AI diffs: Never let an agent "solve" a borrow checker error by dropping into unsafe {} blocks, raw pointers, or static mut globals. If an agent reaches for unsafe in normal app code, reject the PR immediately. Simplify the data flow instead.

12. Clone

Calling .clone() makes a full deep copy of a value, including allocating fresh memory on the heap and copying every byte over.

let original = String::from("notes");
let copy = original.clone(); // two separate heap allocations, two owners

Let's be real: .clone() is NOT evil. If you're cloning a 20-byte config string on startup, or cloning a tiny struct on a UI button click, who cares. Clarity beats micro-optimization on cold paths every day of the week.

Where .clone() hurts is inside hot loops, request handlers, or on large vectors/buffers. Cloning a 50MB vector on every search keystroke will tank your app fast.

What to watch for in AI diffs: Five .clone() calls crammed into one 20-line function is the #1 tell that Claude or Codex lost a fight with the borrow checker and gave up. Check whether a simple & borrow fixes it cleanly.

13. Structs and impl

Rust has no classes and no inheritance trees. You put your data in a struct, and you attach methods to it in a separate impl block.

struct Note {
    title: String,
    pinned: bool,
}

impl Note {
    fn is_pinned(&self) -> bool {
        self.pinned
    }

    fn toggle_pin(&mut self) {
        self.pinned = !self.pinned;
    }
}

Look at &self vs &mut self right in the method signature. You can tell at a glance whether calling a method can mutate the struct or only read it. And without class inheritance, you naturally end up composing small, clean structs instead of five-layer BaseAbstractNoteManager hierarchies.

What to watch for in AI diffs: Agents love dumping everything into one giant "god struct" (AppState with 35 unrelated fields) and a 1,200-line impl AppState block. That also triggers borrow checker nightmares coz mutating one field borrows the whole struct. Split big structs by responsibility.

14. Enums and match

If you only know enums from TypeScript or Java, Rust enums are going to spoil you. Every variant of a Rust enum can carry its own typed payload.

enum JobState {
    Queued,
    Running { progress: u8 },
    Failed(String),
}

And when you branch on an enum with match, the compiler enforces exhaustiveness: you have to handle every single variant. If you add Cancelled to JobState three months from now, the compiler immediately points to every single match across your entire repo that forgot to handle Cancelled.

It turns "forgot to handle a new state in prod" into a compile error.

What to watch for in AI diffs: Watch like a hawk for _ => {} catch-all arms in match blocks. Agents love throwing _ => {} at the bottom to make the compiler happy, which completely destroys exhaustiveness checking and silently swallows new states you add next week.

15. Traits

Traits define shared behavior across different types, similar to interfaces in Go or TypeScript.

trait Searchable {
    fn matches(&self, query: &str) -> bool;
}

Any struct can implement Searchable, and you can even implement your own traits on types from external crates. Plus, Rust's standard library uses traits for everything: Display for formatting, Iterator for loops, From/Into for type conversions, Send/Sync for thread safety.

What to watch for in AI diffs: Premature generic soup. Agents love writing struct Store<T: Repo + Clone + Send + Sync + 'static> when your entire app only has one concrete struct and will never have a second one. Keep code concrete until you actually have two real implementations.

16. Option (No Null)

Rust does not have null or undefined. You will never see Cannot read properties of undefined in a Rust binary.

Instead, whenever a value might be absent, the type system forces you to say so explicitly with Option<T>, which is just an enum with two variants: Some(value) or None.

fn find_note(id: &str) -> Option<Note> {
    // returns Some(note) if found, or None if missing
}

Because Option<Note> is a completely different type from Note, the compiler won't let you access .title until you explicitly handle the None case (via match, if let Some(n) = ..., or combinators like .unwrap_or(...)).

What to watch for in AI diffs: Sentinel hacks from other languages, like returning an empty string "" or -1 to signal "not found" instead of Option<T>. If something can be missing, make the type Option<T> so the compiler forces every caller to deal with it.

17. Result and the ? Operator

Rust has no try/catch exceptions either. Anything that can fail (reading a file, parsing JSON, hitting a network socket) returns Result<T, E>: either Ok(value) or Err(error).

You might think checking every Result manually would be verbose like Go's if err != nil. That's what the ? operator is for:

fn read_config(path: &str) -> Result<String, std::io::Error> {
    let text = std::fs::read_to_string(path)?;
    Ok(text)
}

That little ? at the end says: "if this is Ok(val), unwrap val and keep going; if this is Err(e), return Err(e) from this function right now." Clean, readable, and every failure path is visible right in the function signature.

What to watch for in AI diffs: Silent error swallowing like let _ = save_file(&note); or .ok() that throws away an Err without logging or propagating it. When something fails in prod, you want to know why, not stare at a silent no-op.

18. unwrap and panic

Calling .unwrap() on an Option or Result is telling Rust: "I bet my whole process this is Some or Ok. If I'm wrong, crash immediately."

let port: u16 = std::env::var("PORT").unwrap().parse().unwrap();

If PORT isn't set, or someone puts "8080 " with a trailing space, the app panics and dies on the spot.

To be clear: .unwrap() is totally fine in unit tests and throwaway prototypes. In production code, handle the error properly with ?, match, unwrap_or_default, or at least .expect("PORT must be a valid u16") when crashing on startup is genuinely the only sensible behavior.

What to watch for in AI diffs: Cmd+F every AI-written Rust PR for .unwrap(). It takes 3 seconds and is the single highest-ROI check you can run before merging.

19. Clippy

Clippy (cargo clippy) is Rust's official linter, and it's way smarter than a typical style linter. It catches redundant clones, needless heap allocations, dead branches, sketchy casts, and hundreds of subtle non-idiomatic patterns that rustc technically allows.

Wire this straight into CI and into your coding agent's verification hook so the agent has to fix its own slop before handing you the PR:

cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings

The -D warnings flag turns every Clippy warning into a hard build error.

What to watch for in AI diffs: Agents will occasionally sneak #[allow(clippy::...)] at the top of a file or function just to shut Clippy up and get a green check without fixing the actual problem. Always check why an #[allow(...)] attribute was added.

20. Lifetimes

Lifetimes ('a) look scarier than they actually are. They are NOT about changing how long a value lives. They are just labels that tell the compiler how the lifetime of a returned reference relates to the inputs, so you can never return a reference to data that's already been freed.

90% of the time, Rust infers lifetimes automatically and you never type them. You only write them when a function takes multiple references and returns a reference, so the compiler needs to know which input the output is tied to:

fn longest<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str {
    if a.len() >= b.len() { a } else { b }
}

Read 'a in plain English as: "the reference I return is guaranteed to stay valid for at least as long as the shorter of a and b." That's it.

What to watch for in AI diffs: If you see an agent adding 'static bounds everywhere or wrestling with a 4-lifetime signature (<'a, 'b, 'c>) on a simple helper struct, step in and stop the loop. Nine times out of ten, returning an owned String or restructuring the struct is 10x simpler than threading lifetimes through three layers of code.

The 30-Second Rust PR Checklist (For AI Code)

Next time Claude Code or Codex hands you a Rust diff, don't just glance at green tests and hit merge. Run these five checks in 30 seconds:

  1. Search the diff for .unwrap() and unsafe.
  2. Audit every new crate added to Cargo.toml.
  3. Scan for .clone() spam or Arc<Mutex<T>> hiding borrow-checker fights.
  4. Check match blocks for lazy _ => {} catch-alls and let _ = swallowed errors.
  5. Run cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings (and watch for sneaky #[allow(clippy::...)]).

AI made writing Rust cheap. Knowing these 20 concepts is what keeps the codebase fast, safe, and readable six months from now.

First posted as an X Article.

Originally published on Medium.

title: Local Voice AI Characters on Windows 11: Node.js, Ollama, and WebSockets
description:
I am still pretty new to coding since I mostly come from the writing side, so building a local web app on Windows 11 where I can actually talk out loud to AI characters felt wild when it spoke back for the first time. The whole thing runs on Node.js on my boyfriend's PC, which packs 16 GB VRAM and 42 GB RAM. I am so glad he lets me hijack his machine becuause my own setup would have choked before the first model even loaded.

The annoying part is that I just wanted one clean app that opens and works. Instead I ended up juggling a Python venv and multiple local servers every single time I want to chat.

Local Speech to Text With Phonon-2 (and Windows venv Chaos)

For speech to text I went with phonon-2 from Fermion Research. It is a tiny English model around 158 MB to 164 MB built as a compressed derivative of NVIDIA's parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v3, averaging a 5.21% word error rate across the seven English Open ASR leaderboard test sets. It runs on CPU and exposes a local API compatible with standard dictation and audio clients.

Installing it on Windows 11 gave me massive headecks becuause I ran into so manny package incompabilities with my global Python install and PyTorch dependencies. Things kept breaking until I gave up fighting Windows and locked phonon-2 inside its own isolated venv.

Now every session starts by opening PowerShell and booting the STT server manually on port 8010:

& "C:\Users\elle\Documents\Python\phonon-2\venv\Scripts\phonon.exe" serve --port 8010

Once port 8010 is up, transcription comes back super fast at around 71ms on my tests. Pasting that giant file path every time still drives me crazy.

Adding Voices With Kyutai Pocket TTS (and Surviving the GPU Side)

To let my characters talk back, I wired up pocket-tts from Kyutai Labs, which supports Python 3.10 through 3.14 on PyTorch 2.5 or newer. Normally you launch its persistent local server in a second terminal tab like this:

python -m pocket_tts serve

Kyutai built pocket-tts to run on CPU out of the box and does not officially support GPU execution. There is not even a device flag on TTSModel.load_model(), so getting it onto CUDA means manually moving the nn.Module with tts_model.to("cuda") and pushing output tensors back to CPU via .detach().cpu().numpy() before encoding audio. Resolving the GPU side on Windows 11 was absolute hell with PyTorch CUDA builds and device mismatches. Once I finally got it working on GPU though, the audio generation speeds were blazing fast.

Real-Time Sentence Streaming Over WebSockets (Plus Real Latency Numbers)

Early on, waiting for the language model to finish an entire reply and then waiting for TTS to synthesize the whole paragraph killed the vibe of a real conversation. To fix that dead air, I built real-time sentence streaming straight off the first token (TTFT) coming out of the local SLM.

As Node.js receives streamed tokens from Ollama, it watches punctuation boundaries in real time. The instant a complete sentence lands, it drops that sentence into a queue bucket for TTS synthesis and pipes the generated audio straight back to the browser over WebSockets. You start hearing sentence one almost immediately while the model is still generating sentence two and three in the background.

Here is an actual latency readout from a live voice turn on my machine:

TTFT: 416ms [Anubis-Mini-8B-v1] | TTS #1: 652ms/1020ms | STT: 71ms

At 71ms for STT, 416ms to first token, and the first spoken sentence arriving in 652ms/1020ms, talking to a character finally feels snappy instead of like leaving voicemails.

Character Brains on Ollama: Gemma 4 12B vs Anubis-Mini-8B-v1

On the Ollama side I tested plenty of models on 16 GB VRAM and two really stuck with me.

gemma4:12b completely amazed me. Google released it on June 3, 2026 under Apache 2.0 with a 256K context window, a unified multimodal architecture handling images and audio natively, and roughly a 6.7 GB footprint in Q4 quantization on Ollama. My characters actually hold onto their personality quirks across long messy voice sessions without turning into stiff customer support bots.

I also had a great run with Anubis-Mini-8B-v1 by TheDrummer, an 8B model released in September 2026 tuned specifically for creativity, usability, and entertainment. At 4.92 GB in Q4_K_M GGUF format it flies on 16 GB VRAM, hits that 416ms TTFT easily, and brings way more attitude when a character needs weird humor.

Why I Am Sad About This Setup (and Watching WebLLM + Google Dev Drops)

Right now my Node.js web app stitches together phonon-2 on port 8010, Ollama on port 11434, and pocket-tts over local HTTP plus WebSockets to the frontend. It runs great once every terminal tab is alive, yet I still feel kinda sad staring at all those windows. I wanted this whole project to run cleanly without a fragile venv and without launching so manny external servers by hand.

That is why the browser AI releases dropping lately caught my attention so hard:

  • MLC WebLLM (@mlc-ai/web-llm) runs quantized models inside the browser via WebGPU and WebAssembly behind an OpenAI compatible API, caching weights locally. Its October 2026 release added Gemma 4 E2B instruction tuned models (q4f16_1 and q4f32_1) with text and audio input, followed by Gemma 4 prefill speedups in v0.2.87 and new MiniCPM5, SmolLM3, and LFM2.5 support in November 2026.
  • Google AI Edge LiteRT-LM (@litert-lm/core) and LiteRT.js have been moving fast too. Google launched LiteRT.js in July 2026 for WebGPU and WASM inference, and the LiteRT-LM Web SDK stream loads models directly on GPU with image and audio inputs while supporting Gemma 4 12B on web and speech models including Qwen3-ASR, Kokoro, and Qwen3-TTS.
  • Chrome Built-in Prompt API (LanguageModel) shipped on desktop in Chrome 148 back in May 2026 with text, image, and audio inputs plus promptStreaming(), needing 22 GB free disk space, 16 GB RAM, and at least 4 GB VRAM for audio input.

Combined with community browser ports of Pocket TTS like wasm-pocket-tts in Rust and WebAssembly or pocket-tts-onnx-export on ONNX Runtime Web, an entire local voice character app could eventually live inside a single browser tab with zero Python installs.

If anyone on here has already moved a multi server Node.js voice pipeline over to @litert-lm/core, WebLLM, or ONNX Runtime Web on Windows 11, drop your real TTFT and TTS numbers in the comments because I would love to ditch my terminal circus.

title: Building HAUL, a Desktop Download Manager in Rust and Tauri
description:
I just finished building HAUL, a desktop download manager written in Rust with Tauri.

What it does

  • Parallel downloads with live speed
  • Torrents, with a file picker so you choose what to download
  • Scheduling
  • Themes
  • 5 languages

Why Rust and Tauri

I wanted a download engine that is fast and safe with concurrency, and a small desktop app that does not ship a whole browser runtime of its own. Rust handles the engine. Tauri gives me a native window and a web UI on top.

The biggest lesson

The download engine was not the hardest part. Keeping a native-feeling UI fast on a modest laptop (8 GB RAM) took more work than the engine itself. Live speed updates, long download lists and torrent file trees all push the UI, so most of my time went into keeping updates cheap and the interface responsive.

What's next

HAUL is finished and working, and I'm now looking for a new owner for it. If you are interested, the details are here: https://www.sideprojectors.com/project/113486/haul-desktop-download-manager-rust-tauri

If you have questions about the Rust + Tauri side, ask in the comments.

title: Amazon Bedrock Pricing Explained with Examples
description:
Key takeaways

  • AWS Bedrock pricing is mostly per token: you pay for input tokens and output tokens separately, and output tokens usually cost several times more than input.
  • Batch inference costs roughly half of on-demand for supported models, if your job can wait for results.
  • Provisioned throughput is billed per hour per model unit and only makes sense for steady, high-volume traffic or custom models.
  • For RAG apps, embeddings are cheap (Titan Text Embeddings V2 is about $0.02 per million tokens), but the vector store can easily cost more than the model calls.

How AWS Bedrock pricing works

AWS Bedrock pricing has one core idea: you pay for what the model reads and writes, measured in tokens. Our AWS Bedrock consulting team can help you model the cost before you commit.

A token is a chunk of text, roughly three-quarters of an English word. Around that core sit extra charges for batch jobs, reserved capacity, Knowledge Bases, guardrails and agents.

Every model has its own rate, and rates change often. Everything below uses clearly labeled example rates. Always check the official Bedrock pricing page for the model and region you plan to use.

On-demand: pay per token

On-demand is the default. There is no commitment. You are billed per million input tokens and per million output tokens.

Input tokens include everything you send: the system prompt, conversation history, retrieved documents and the user message. Output tokens are what the model generates. Since output costs more, a chatty model with long answers adds up quickly.

Two features can cut on-demand costs:

  • Prompt caching (on supported models) lets you reuse a long, repeated prompt prefix at a discounted rate.
  • Cross-region inference routes requests across regions for better availability, usually at the same price as the source region.

Batch inference: roughly half price

Batch inference lets you submit a large set of prompts as a file in S3 and get results back later, usually within hours. For supported models, AWS prices batch at roughly 50% of on-demand as of late 2026.

Good fits: nightly document summarization, tagging a backlog of tickets, generating embeddings or descriptions for a product catalog. Bad fits: anything a user is waiting on.

Provisioned throughput

Provisioned throughput reserves model capacity, billed per hour per "model unit." Commitment options typically include no commitment, 1 month or 6 months, with longer terms costing less per hour.

It is required for some custom or fine-tuned models. For base models, it only makes sense when you have steady, high traffic that would hit on-demand rate limits, or when the math clearly beats paying per token. Most SaaS teams under Series B do not need it. Because you pay every hour whether you use it or not, an idle model unit is pure waste.

Knowledge Bases, guardrails and agents

Knowledge Bases do not have a large standalone fee. You pay for the embedding model to convert documents into vectors, the vector store that holds them, and the model calls at query time. The vector store is the trap. Some options, such as OpenSearch Serverless, have a minimum capacity that bills around the clock even with zero traffic. Our post on Bedrock Knowledge Bases setup, cost and limits covers the vector store choices in detail.

Guardrails filter harmful content, block topics and redact sensitive data. They are billed per unit of text processed, per policy type. Running several policies on every input and output can add a noticeable amount on high-volume apps.

Agents for Bedrock orchestrate multi-step tasks with tools. The main cost is not the agent feature itself but the extra model calls: an agent may call the model several times per user request to plan, call tools and summarize. Budget for 3-5x the tokens of a single call as a starting assumption, then measure.

Worked examples

These examples use made-up but realistic example rates. They are not real prices for any specific model.

  • Example large model: $3 per million input tokens, $15 per million output tokens.
  • Example small model: $0.25 per million input tokens, $1.25 per million output tokens.
Scenario Monthly volume Tokens Example cost
Support chatbot, large model, on-demand 50,000 conversations, 2,000 in / 400 out each 100M in, 20M out $300 + $300 = about $600
Nightly summaries, large model, on-demand 10,000 docs, 5,000 in / 500 out each 50M in, 5M out $150 + $75 = about $225
Same summaries, batch (about 50% off) Same Same About $112
RAG app, small model 30,000 queries, 3,000 in / 300 out each 90M in, 9M out $22.50 + $11.25 = about $34
Embedding 20,000 docs (one time) 2,000 tokens each, Titan V2 40M About $0.80

Three things stand out. First, the support chatbot spends as much on 20M output tokens as on 100M input tokens, so shorter answers matter. Second, batch halves a job that nobody is waiting on. Third, the RAG app's model calls cost about $34, while a vector store with a minimum capacity floor can cost far more than that every month. In small RAG apps, the infrastructure around the model often dominates the bill.

How to keep Bedrock costs under control

  • Pick the smallest model that passes your tests. Build an evaluation set of real prompts and compare models. Many tasks such as classification or extraction work fine on small models.
  • Trim input tokens. Shorten system prompts, cap conversation history, and retrieve fewer, better chunks in RAG.
  • Cap output length. Set max tokens and ask for concise answers.
  • Use batch for anything asynchronous. It is the simplest roughly 50% saving available.
  • Use prompt caching for long, repeated prefixes where the model supports it.
  • Choose the vector store carefully. Match it to your scale; do not pay a large always-on floor for a few thousand documents.
  • Tag and track. Use application inference profiles and cost allocation tags so you can see cost per feature or customer, and set AWS Budgets alerts.

FAQ

Is Amazon Bedrock free to start?

There is no upfront fee or minimum for on-demand model calls; you pay per token from the first request. Some related services, such as certain vector stores, do have minimum charges, so check those before you build.

Is Bedrock cheaper than calling model providers directly?

Per-token prices for the same model are often similar. The difference is usually in AWS integration: IAM, private VPC access, and consolidated AWS billing. Compare current official prices for your specific model.

When does provisioned throughput make sense?

When you run a custom or fine-tuned model that requires it, or have steady high traffic that hits on-demand limits. For spiky or modest usage, on-demand is almost always cheaper.

What usually surprises teams on their first Bedrock bill?

Long prompts that grow with conversation history, verbose output, agent loops making several model calls per request, and vector stores that bill around the clock.

Next step

If you want a cost model before you ship, or your Bedrock bill is growing faster than usage, we can help. See our AWS Bedrock consulting for RAG and Bedrock builds, or start with an AI Infrastructure Assessment to review your current setup.

title: Debounce or throttle, on a timeline
description:
The original has interactive demos you can play with: https://websgeek.com/debounce-vs-throttle

Debounce and throttle are two of the most used tools for taming noisy browser events, and two of the most mixed up. This post walks through what each one does, the edge cases that cause bugs, and when neither is the right answer.

The short version

Debounce waits until events stop for a set time, then runs your function once with the last value. Throttle runs your function at most once per interval for as long as events keep coming.

So: use debounce when only the final value matters, like a search box. Use throttle when you need steady updates during the activity, like tracking a scroll position.

Both are wrappers. You hand them a function and a wait, and they return a new function that decides when the original runs. The browser still fires every event. The wrapper only filters the calls you make in response.

Debounce waits for quiet

A debounce keeps restarting a single timer. Each new event cancels the waiting timer and starts a fresh one. Your function runs only if a timer survives the full wait, which happens only after the events stop.

function debounce(fn, wait) {
  let timer;
  return (...args) => {
    clearTimeout(timer);
    timer = setTimeout(() => fn(...args), wait);
  };
}

const search = debounce(query => fetchResults(query), 300);
input.addEventListener('input', () => search(input.value));

Typing "strawberry" at 150 ms per letter shows the difference. With no limit that is 10 requests. A 300 ms throttle sends 6: one on the first letter, then one at the end of each of five windows. Debounce sends 1, because a 150 ms gap never reaches 300 ms. Type slower than one letter per 300 ms, though, and debounce sends every letter too. It protects you from fast typists, not slow ones.

Two caveats. Debounce doesn't fix slow responses: a request for "straw" can still arrive after the one for "strawberry", so ignore stale responses or cancel them with an AbortController. And never delay the feedback itself. The key echo should stay instant. Only the expensive consequence is limited.

In React, calling debounce() in the component body creates a new wrapper with its own timer on every render, so nothing is debounced. Create it once, pass the value in, and cancel on unmount.

Throttle keeps a beat

A throttle opens a window each time it runs. Events arriving while the window is open are held back, and only the newest is kept. When the window closes, the throttle runs once more with that newest event and opens the next window. When events stop, the windows stop too.

Edges and deadlines

A burst of events has two edges: the first event and the moment the events stop. A wrapper can call your function at either edge, both, or neither.

  • Leading gives an instant response.
  • Trailing delivers the final value. For throttle, it is what keeps the last scroll or drag position from being lost.
  • With both on, a single event causes only one call, because the trailing call needs a second event.
  • With both off, nothing ever runs.

A leading-only debounce is a neat fix for double submits:

import { debounce } from 'lodash-es';

// Run on the first click, ignore repeats until 1 s of quiet
const submitOnce = debounce(sendOrder, 1000, {
  leading: true,
  trailing: false
});
button.addEventListener('click', submitOnce);

Debounce has another weakness: some activity never goes quiet, and a long paragraph typed without a pause can hold it off forever. maxWait adds a deadline. If the function hasn't run for that long, it runs anyway, then the debounce carries on. That is the right shape for autosave. Fittingly, lodash builds throttle as a debounce with both edges on and a maxWait equal to the wait.

Frames beat 16 milliseconds

For anything visual, the right update rate is the screen's refresh rate. throttle(fn, 16) is a common way to aim for about 60 updates a second, but many screens refresh faster, and a timer has no idea when the next frame is.

requestAnimationFrame runs your callback just before the browser draws the next frame. Store the newest position in the event handler and apply it once per frame:

let latestX = 0, queued = false;

pad.addEventListener('pointermove', event => {
  latestX = event.clientX;
  if (queued) return;
  queued = true;
  requestAnimationFrame(() => {
    queued = false;
    handle.style.transform = `translateX(${latestX}px)`;
  });
});

On a 120 Hz screen a frame lasts 8.3 ms, so a 16 ms throttle can update at most every second frame, and roughly half of the frames with movement show an old position.

A rule for each event

Ask what the person needs: the final value, a steady stream, or a value on every frame.

  • Search, filters, validation: trailing debounce of a few hundred milliseconds, and ignore or abort stale responses.
  • Autosave: debounce with maxWait.
  • Submit buttons: leading-only debounce, plus disabling the button while the request runs.
  • Resize: CSS first, then rAF for visual changes. Debounce expensive work like redrawing a chart. Use ResizeObserver for one element.
  • Scroll: rAF for visual effects, or IntersectionObserver if you only need what is visible. Throttle with the trailing edge for analytics or loading the next page.
  • Drag and hover effects: rAF, never debounce. A debounced drag handle doesn't move until the hand stops.

To detect that scrolling has stopped, the native scrollend event is a rival to debounce. It waits until the finger lifts, while a debounce can declare the scroll over when a finger is simply held still.

Sometimes you need none of this. If the work is cheap, such as setting one transform, a wrapper only adds delay, so measure first. Whichever you pick, create it once, cancel it on teardown, and give keyboard users the same edges as pointer users.

Try it live

Play with every demo on WebsGeek: https://websgeek.com/debounce-vs-throttle
