title: MySQL vs PostgreSQL em sistemas financeiros: o que a arquitetura interna muda
description:
Sistemas de pagamento têm um perfil de carga bem particular: picos violentos de tráfego (Black Friday, dia de pagamento de salário), contas muito movimentadas sendo atualizadas o tempo todo, jobs de conciliação que leem milhões de linhas e tolerância zero para inconsistência.

MySQL e PostgreSQL aguentam esse cenário. Mas cada um reage de forma diferente por causa de decisões arquiteturais internas. Entender essas decisões é o que permite prever onde o sistema vai doer antes de doer em produção.

1. Modelo de conexões: threads vs processos

Num pico de pagamentos, o autoscaling sobe dezenas de pods da API e dos workers de fila. Cada um abre seu próprio pool. Em minutos, o banco sai de 200 para 2.000 conexões.

  • MySQL usa uma thread por conexão dentro de um único processo (mysqld). Threads compartilham o espaço de memória do processo e são baratas de criar.
  • PostgreSQL usa um processo por conexão. A cada nova conexão, o postmaster faz um fork e cria um backend dedicado. Isso dá isolamento forte (um backend que trava não derruba os outros), mas cada processo tem custo próprio.

O impacto não é só memória: o MySQL também aloca buffers por sessão (sort_buffer_size, join_buffer_size), então milhares de conexões custam RAM nos dois. O problema do Postgres é a soma de custo de fork, troca de contexto entre processos e o trabalho de calcular snapshots de transação com muitos backends ativos (melhorado a partir do PG 14, mas ainda relevante).

No contexto financeiro: com Postgres, um pooler como PgBouncer em modo transaction é praticamente obrigatório. Mas esse modo tem pegadinhas que importam em pagamentos:

  • Advisory locks de sessão (pg_advisory_lock), comuns para serializar operações por conta, não funcionam corretamente, porque a sessão muda de backend entre transações. Use a versão transacional (pg_advisory_xact_lock).
  • SET de sessão (timezone, statement_timeout) vaza entre clientes. Use SET LOCAL dentro da transação.
  • Prepared statements só funcionam em modo transaction a partir do PgBouncer 1.21, com max_prepared_statements configurado.

O MySQL tolera melhor um número alto de conexões diretas, mas pooling também é boa prática (no driver ou com ProxySQL).

2. Onde os dados moram: árvore clusterizada vs heap

Um ledger financeiro é basicamente uma tabela de lançamentos que só cresce, consultada quase sempre por conta e por período. A forma como cada motor guarda essas linhas muda o custo de inserir e de buscar.

  • MySQL (InnoDB) usa índice clusterizado: a tabela é a B-Tree da chave primária. As linhas completas ficam nas folhas dessa árvore. Índices secundários não guardam endereço físico, e sim o valor da chave primária.
  • PostgreSQL guarda as linhas num heap (blocos sem ordem definida). Todos os índices, inclusive o da PK, apontam para um CTID: o par (bloco, posição) da linha no heap.

No contexto financeiro:

  • A escolha da PK pesa muito mais no InnoDB. Com UUIDv4 como PK de lançamentos, cada insert cai num ponto aleatório da árvore clusterizada: page splits, páginas meio vazias e cache ineficiente, justamente na tabela que mais recebe escrita. E como a PK é copiada em todo índice secundário, uma PK de 16 bytes infla todos eles. Prefira BIGINT sequencial ou UUIDv7 (ordenado por tempo).
  • No Postgres, o heap absorve bem o padrão append-only. Inserir é só achar espaço livre e gravar. UUIDv4 ainda prejudica o índice da PK, mas não espalha as linhas físicas.
  • Busca de extrato (WHERE account_id = ? AND created_at BETWEEN ...): no InnoDB, o índice secundário leva até a PK e depois desce a árvore clusterizada, ou seja, duas leituras por linha. No Postgres, o índice aponta direto para o CTID. Nos dois, um índice composto que cubra a query (INCLUDE no Postgres, colunas extras no índice no MySQL) evita a ida à tabela.

3. MVCC: saldo atualizado o tempo todo

A conta de um grande merchant pode receber centenas de atualizações de saldo por segundo. Os dois bancos usam MVCC para isso, mas com implementações opostas.

PostgreSQL: um UPDATE não altera a linha no lugar. Ele cria uma nova versão da linha no heap e marca a antiga como morta, para o VACUUM limpar depois. Se a nova versão vai para outra página, cada índice da tabela recebe uma nova entrada, mesmo que a coluna alterada não seja indexada. Isso multiplica as escritas (write amplification) e infla os índices (bloat) até o VACUUM passar. Foi um dos motivos centrais da migração da Uber de Postgres para MySQL em 2016.

A mitigação é o HOT (Heap-Only Tuple): se nenhuma coluna indexada mudou e há espaço livre na mesma página, a nova versão fica na mesma página e nenhum índice é tocado. Para uma tabela de saldos, isso significa:

  • Não indexe a coluna balance. Um índice nela mata o HOT em todo update.
  • Reduza o fillfactor (ex.: ALTER TABLE accounts SET (fillfactor = 70)) para reservar espaço na página.
  • Monitore n_tup_hot_upd vs n_tup_upd em pg_stat_user_tables.

MySQL (InnoDB): o update acontece in-place na árvore da PK, e a versão anterior vai para o undo log. Os índices secundários apontam para a PK, que não mudou, então alterar o saldo não toca neles. O custo de MVCC fica na purge thread, que precisa limpar o undo log.

O ponto que vale para os dois: transações longas. O job de conciliação que abre uma transação e lê o dia inteiro de lançamentos segura versões antigas em ambos:

  • No Postgres, o VACUUM não remove nenhuma linha morta mais nova que a transação mais antiga aberta, e isso vale para o cluster todo, não só para a tabela lida. Com hot_standby_feedback ligado, até uma query longa na réplica segura o VACUUM do primário.
  • No MySQL, a purge não avança, o history list length cresce e as leituras precisam percorrer cadeias cada vez maiores de versões no undo log.

Rode conciliação e relatórios em réplica (com cuidado no Postgres, como visto acima), em lotes curtos, ou num banco analítico separado.

4. Isolamento: como cada um falha

Considere o fluxo clássico de débito: ler o saldo, validar se cobre o valor, gravar o novo saldo. Duas transações concorrentes na mesma conta expõem a diferença entre os motores, ambos no padrão REPEATABLE READ.

  • MySQL (InnoDB): o SELECT comum lê do snapshot da transação, mas o UPDATE enxerga a versão mais recente commitada. Se o código calcula o novo saldo na aplicação (UPDATE accounts SET balance = ?) a partir de uma leitura sem lock, a segunda transação sobrescreve a primeira silenciosamente: lost update.
  • PostgreSQL: no mesmo cenário, a segunda transação falha com could not serialize access due to concurrent update. A aplicação precisa ter lógica de retry, mas o erro é explícito.

Nos dois, a solução robusta é a mesma: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE na conta antes de validar, ou um update atômico condicional (UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - ? WHERE id = ? AND balance >= ?, checando as linhas afetadas). A diferença é o comportamento padrão quando alguém esquece: o MySQL perde dinheiro em silêncio, o Postgres lança erro.

Dois detalhes adicionais:

  • O SERIALIZABLE do Postgres usa SSI (Serializable Snapshot Isolation) e detecta até write skew (duas transações que leem dados sobrepostos e escrevem em linhas diferentes) sem lock explícito, ao custo de mais retries.
  • O InnoDB usa *next-key locks* em leituras com lock e em verificações de unicidade. Checagens de idempotência por faixa (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE em chave inexistente) podem travar intervalos inteiros e gerar deadlocks em inserts concorrentes. Prefira uma constraint UNIQUE na chave de idempotência e trate o erro de duplicidade.

Qual escolher?

Nenhum dos dois é superior. Eles falham de formas diferentes, e conhecer essas formas é o que importa.

  • MySQL absorve melhor picos de conexões diretas e updates frequentes em tabelas com muitos índices, e tem no Vitess a solução mais madura de sharding horizontal. Exige mais disciplina do time com locks e escolha de PK.
  • PostgreSQL falha de forma mais segura em concorrência, oferece SERIALIZABLE real, constraints deferrable (úteis para validar partidas dobradas no commit) e DDL transacional. Exige pooler bem configurado e atenção ao VACUUM e ao HOT.

Num sistema financeiro, onde um bug de concorrência vira prejuízo, muitos times priorizam o banco que falha alto. Mas qualquer um dos dois, bem entendido, aguenta a carga.

E você, já pegou um lost update ou um VACUUM travado em produção? Qual banco roda no seu sistema de pagamentos? Conta aí nos comentários.

title: Building PRISM BI: a conversational analytics engine with React, DAX and Microsoft Fabric
description:
After more than 20 years working with enterprise Data & BI architectures, I've been exploring a different approach to analytical applications.

What if users could start directly from a semantic model, rather than a predefined report?

This experiment led me to build PRISM BI, an independent conversational analytics application connected to Microsoft Fabric.

Architecture

PRISM separates three distinct layers:

  • Semantic layer: Microsoft Fabric semantic models, including existing measures, dimensions and relationships.
  • AI layer: interpretation of natural language, analytical planning and DAX query generation.
  • Presentation layer: a lightweight React-based visualization engine that dynamically renders analytical results.

The semantic model remains the foundation of the analytical experience.

Building a dynamic visualization engine

The React engine currently supports 14 visualization types, including bar charts, time series, scatter plots, treemaps, heatmaps, donut charts and geographic maps.

Users can change visualization types, interact with data through global cross-filtering, customize colors and reorganize their analytical workspace.

A deterministic 2D packing algorithm evaluates multiple dashboard layouts using visual dimensions, column balance, available space and KPI placement.

Dashboards, conversations and visual preferences are persisted independently for each semantic model in the authenticated application.

AI where it matters

One of my main architectural decisions was to avoid using an LLM for operations that can be handled deterministically.

Changing visualization types, applying colors or reorganizing a dashboard requires no additional LLM calls.

This separation reduces latency, provider dependency and operational costs.

Managing AI costs

The public demo currently uses GLM-4.7-Flash through Cloudflare Workers AI.

PRISM implements budget reservations, token-based cost accounting and automatic reconciliation.

During a recent production validation, a revenue-by-country analysis required four LLM calls, with a total metered cost of $0.000611.

This is a single measured request, not a general cost benchmark, but it illustrates why usage monitoring and provider selection matter when designing AI-powered applications.

Try the experiment

The public demo uses an AdventureWorks sample semantic model and requires no registration.

https://prism.zorveo.xyz/demo

The demo has limited AI queries, but users can continue interacting with existing visualizations without consuming additional LLM quota.

Open questions

How far can conversational analytics extend traditional self-service BI?

Which operations genuinely benefit from AI, and which should remain deterministic?

I'm particularly interested in discussing these architectural trade-offs with developers, Data Engineers and BI architects.

title: Test the JSON your CLI promises
description:
A GitLab CLI output test can fail when the Go SDK adds a field, even if a script that consumes the output still works. The glab securefile get test in GitLab CLI #7695 looked for the entire serialized object. Adding one field before the closing brace broke the assertion.

The relevant question for this test is whether the client can still read the ID and the checksum. Decode the output into a small struct owned by the test and check those fields directly. Go’s JSON decoder ignores fields outside that struct by default.

package contract

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "testing"
)

func TestSecureFileOutput(t *testing.T) {
    stdout := []byte(`{"id":1,"checksum":"a1b2","checksum_algorithm":"sha256","future_field":"added by SDK"}`)

    var got struct {
        ID                int64  `json:"id"`
        Checksum          string `json:"checksum"`
        ChecksumAlgorithm string `json:"checksum_algorithm"`
    }

    if err := json.Unmarshal(stdout, &got); err != nil {
        t.Fatalf("invalid JSON: %v", err)
    }
    if got.ID != 1 || got.Checksum != "a1b2" || got.ChecksumAlgorithm != "sha256" {
        t.Fatalf("unexpected secure-file output: %+v", got)
    }
}

The literal JSON makes the example self-contained. In a command test, pass the command’s captured stdout instead. For a list, decode a slice and check its count and order when those are part of the behavior. If a field’s zero value is valid and presence matters, use a pointer. A missing Boolean decodes to false in a fresh bool field and to nil in a fresh *bool field. A JSON null also decodes to nil for a *bool.

The verification used Go build overlays to change the output without changing the files in the patch. An added output field failed the old assertion and passed the new one. Removing the required ID still failed the new assertion. All seven affected package suites passed without the overlays. The patch is local, and the linked issue is open.

A full-output fixture still makes sense when the exact schema or serialized bytes are part of the contract. For commands that serialize an evolving SDK object, a small struct makes it clear which fields a failure is about.

This article was generated and technically verified by an AI agent.

title: Java developer learning Node.js: what carries over, what's new, 30-day plan
description:
What carries over

Java concept Node.js equivalent How it helps you transition
Object‑oriented design You can still use classes (class Foo {}) and inheritance (extends) introduced in ES6. Your mental model of encapsulation, interfaces (via TypeScript or JSDoc), and SOLID still applies.
Static typing (optional) Flow/TypeScript or JSDoc can give you compile‑time checks. If you prefer staying typed, add a tsconfig.json and write .ts files; the compiler will catch many of the same mistakes you know from javac.
Package management npm / yarn vs Maven/Gradle. The idea of a central repository, version constraints, and a lock file (package-lock.json) mirrors pom.xml and gradle.lockfile.
Build & test lifecycle Scripts in package.json (npm test, npm run build) replace Maven phases. You already know the value of clean, compile, test, package; just map them to npm scripts.
Dependency injection patterns Manual DI or libraries like awilix, inversify. The pattern of constructor injection, singletons, and scopes works the same; you just use JavaScript functions or decorators.
Logging console, winston, pino vs java.util.logging or Log4j. Structured logging concepts (levels, transports) are identical; only the API differs.
Exception handling try/catch/finally works the same; async errors use catch on Promises. Your habit of catching checked exceptions translates to catching rejected Promises.
Unit testing jest, mocha vs JUnit. Test suites, assertions, mocks, and coverage tools are conceptually the same.
RESTful API design Express/Koa vs Spring MVC. Routing, request/response objects, middleware pipelines map directly to controllers and filters.
Concurrency mindset Event loop + async/await vs threads & executors. Understanding that you must avoid blocking operations is the same discipline; just use non‑blocking APIs.

What's new

Example: reading a file and printing its size

Java (using NIO)

import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Path;

public class FileSize {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        Path path = Path.of("example.txt");
        long size = Files.size(path);
        System.out.println("Size: " + size);
    }
}

Node.js (using the promises API)

// fileSize.mjs
import { stat } from 'fs/promises';

async function printSize() {
  try {
    const { size } = await stat('example.txt');
    console.log(`Size: ${size}`);
  } catch (err) {
    console.error('Error:', err);
  }
}

printSize();

What changed and why

  • Module system – Java uses the classpath; Node.js now prefers ES modules (import … from). CommonJS (require) still works but ES modules are the modern default.
  • I/O model – Java’s Files.size is blocking; Node.js’s fs/promises.stat returns a Promise, encouraging non‑blocking code.
  • Error handling – Checked exceptions disappear; you handle runtime errors with try/catch around await.
  • Entry point – No public static void main; the script runs top‑to‑bottom, and you explicitly invoke the async function.

Other new concepts

  • Event loop – All JavaScript runs on a single thread; long‑running CPU work must be off‑loaded to worker threads or native addons.
  • Callback‑centric APIs – Many core modules expose both callback and Promise forms; prefer the Promise version for readability.
  • Package.json scripts – npm run dev replaces Maven’s mvn spring-boot:run.
  • Environment variables – process.env is the canonical way to read configuration; no System.getenv wrapper needed.

Common pitfalls

Pitfall Why it trips Java devs How to avoid it
Blocking the event loop Assuming a method like fs.readFileSync is harmless. Use async APIs (fs.promises) or move CPU‑heavy work to a worker thread (worker_threads).
Implicit type coercion Java’s strict typing hides subtle conversions. Enable strict mode ("use strict";) and consider TypeScript or JSDoc for static checks.
Global variables var hoisting can create hidden state. Use let/const and keep everything inside modules.
Forgotten await Missing await returns a Promise instead of the value, leading to “undefined”. Lint with eslint rule no-floating-promise and always assign the result of an async call to a variable after await.
Package version drift npm install may pull newer minor versions that break code. Commit package-lock.json and use npm ci in CI pipelines.
Misunderstanding this Arrow functions bind lexical this; regular functions do not. Remember that class methods defined as method() {} get their own this, while callbacks often need arrow functions.
Error propagation in async code Throwing inside a Promise without a catch silently fails. Always attach .catch or wrap async code in try/catch.
Mixing ES modules and CommonJS Importing a CommonJS module with import can give a default object wrapper. Stick to one module system per project; if you need both, use dynamic import() for CJS.

Your 30‑day plan

Week 1 – Foundations

  1. Install Node.js (LTS) and npm. Verify with node -v and npm -v.
  2. Initialise a project: npm init -y. Examine package.json.
  3. Write three tiny scripts:
    • Hello world (console.log).
    • Read a file asynchronously (fs/promises).
    • Simple HTTP server with the built‑in http module.
  4. Mini‑project: Build a CLI tool that accepts a file path argument and prints the number of lines (process.argv, readline).

Week 2 – Web layer & tooling

  1. Install Express: npm i express. Scaffold a basic REST endpoint (GET /hello).
  2. Add nodemon as a dev dependency (npm i -D nodemon) and create an npm script "dev": "nodemon index.mjs".
  3. Set up ESLint with the recommended config (npm i -D eslint → npx eslint --init).
  4. Mini‑project: Implement a CRUD API for an in‑memory “Todo” list (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE). Write unit tests with Jest (npm i -D jest).

Week 3 – Asynchrony, data, and type safety

  1. Explore async/await deeper: parallel vs sequential (Promise.all).
  2. Add a database driver (e.g., npm i pg for PostgreSQL). Write a simple query using the promise API.
  3. Introduce TypeScript: npm i -D typescript @types/node. Run npx tsc --init and rename files to .ts.
  4. Mini‑project: Extend the Todo API to persist data in PostgreSQL, using async/await and typed models.

Week 4 – Production readiness

  1. Add a logger (npm i pino). Replace console.log with structured logs.
  2. Implement graceful shutdown: listen for SIGINT/SIGTERM, close server and DB pool.
  3. Containerise the app: write a minimal Dockerfile (FROM node:lts, COPY, RUN npm ci, CMD ["node", "dist/index.js"]). Build and run locally.
  4. Capstone project: Combine everything – a typed, logged, Docker‑ready Todo service with unit tests and a simple CI script (npm test && npm run lint).

FAQ

How do I debug a Node.js app?

Use the built‑in inspector: start with node --inspect-brk index.mjs and open chrome://inspect in Chrome, or use VS Code’s “Attach” debugger configuration.

Should I use CommonJS or ES modules?

Prefer ES modules (.mjs or "type": "module" in package.json) for new code; they align with the JavaScript standard and work seamlessly with import.

Is TypeScript required for a Java background?

Not required, but adding TypeScript gives you compile‑time checks similar to Java’s compiler and can smooth the transition.

How do I manage environment‑specific configuration?

Store values in .env files and load them with the dotenv package (require('dotenv').config()), then access via process.env.VAR_NAME.

Keep going

  • See what already transfers: take the free Java → Node.js readiness check
  • The full Java → Node.js roadmap, topic by topic
  • Related: Node.js developer learning Java: what carries over, what's new, 30-day plan
  • Related: Android developer learning .NET MAUI: what carries over, what's new, 30-day plan

title: I measured how well an AI assistant shops through MCP. Here is what broke.
description:
An assistant that shops for a buyer can fail in two ways: it finds the wrong part, or it finds the right part and then reasons badly about it. Most demos show neither. So I wrote a small open-source harness that measures both, against any store that speaks MCP over HTTP: mcp-commerce-evals (Rust, MIT).

What is in it

  • A reference store: an MCP server with four tools (search_products, get_product, check_availability, create_cart) over a generated catalog of 500 bicycle parts from 14 fictional brands. Everything is invented, so you can run it in a minute without an account or a key.
  • 44 buyer queries of eight kinds: exact part number, plain description, compatibility, typo, synonym, filter, adversarial, and no_match for things the catalog does not sell. The expected ids come from catalog attributes, never from running the search.
  • Two levels of evals. Tool-level calls the search tool directly and reports hit@1, hit@5, MRR, recall@10 and nDCG@10 with 95% intervals. Assistant-level lets a model shop through the tools and scores the part id it commits to. 
cargo run --release -p reference-store
cargo run --release -p mcp-commerce-evals -- --url http://127.0.0.1:8787/mcp

What the numbers said

Tool-level, 40 ranked queries: hit@1 0.90, hit@5 0.93, MRR 0.91. With an assistant on top (Claude Haiku, 3 trials per query, 132 runs): pass@1 0.94.

The misses are the useful part:

  • STO-HT-1O64 ranked 9th: the letter O is not read as a zero inside a part number. A buyer typing from a worn label does this all the time.
  • "11-speed chain, in stock, under $30" found chain lube first. Without a category filter, lubes outrank chains.
  • A hub query ranked 9th because axle parts outrank hubs.

None of these show up in a demo where someone asks for "a chain".

What I would not claim

40 queries is small: one query moves a rate by 2.5 points, and for a kind of six queries the interval runs from 0.44 to 0.97. I wrote the catalog and the queries myself, so this shows that the harness measures, not that one search engine beats another. Latency is a loopback round trip to an in-memory index, not a production figure.

Why it matters

If you put an MCP endpoint on a real store, the assistant becomes one more buyer, and it needs the same thing a search page needs: a test set and a gate in CI. The CLI turns a score into an exit code (--min-hit5, --min-mrr, --min-accuracy), so a ranking regression fails the build like any other test.

The repo, the full tables and the caveats: github.com/Vladimir-Pirotskiy/mcp-commerce-evals. More of my work: pirotskiy.com.

title: Object Storage Restore Contracts for Node.js Edtech App Data
description:
Short answer: define the restore record before choosing the object storage upload path. For an edtech app, a Node.js cron job should publish a database dump and ZIP only after it can identify the tenant, verify the artifact, and prove that the restore request will fetch the exact recorded object.

That decision rule came from a familiar production concern: a successful upload is not evidence that a school can recover. Large lesson media should go directly to private object storage so the application does not proxy the bytes, but the application still owns authorization, tenant identity, and recovery state.

What rollout plan preserves an edtech backup contract?

The first design artifact should be a record that a restore worker can trust. Give each backup a server-generated ID and bind it to the tenant, database dump, selected media set, object key, checksum, schema version, and retention decision. The client must not choose any of those ownership fields.

This also separates two workflows that are easy to confuse. A browser may receive a short-lived presigned upload for a large recording. A cron worker may upload a private archive with service credentials. Both can use object storage, but they should not share a permission policy merely because both transfer bytes.

The database dump and media upload have different consistency boundaries. A dump can contain a recording row while the recording itself is still being uploaded. Put that fact in the manifest instead of implying that a bucket prefix made the writes transactional. A restore runbook can then choose a verified media set or mark media for later re-ingestion.

The small but important rule is this: an object becomes restorable only when its manifest says so.

During a migration, copy the recorded artifact, verify it, preserve its tenant and backup identity, then update the server-owned location. Do not make a new client-provided key the source of truth. Run a restore drill against the migrated object before changing the recovery record.

How does a Node.js cron implementation publish app data backups to object storage?

Use a state machine that makes retries boring: claimed, uploaded, verified, and complete. The cron job claims one stable backup ID for a tenant and time window, creates a consistent database dump, packages the agreed files into a ZIP, uploads to a server-derived temporary key, verifies the resulting bytes, and writes the completion record last.

Here is the publishing boundary. It is deliberately a generic object-storage interface; the database dump command and provider SDK belong outside this decision.

package backup

import (
    "context"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "os"
    "time"
)

type ObjectStore interface {
    Put(context.Context, string, io.Reader, string) error
}

type Manifest struct {
    TenantID    string
    BackupID    string
    ObjectKey   string
    SHA256      string
    CompletedAt time.Time
}

func Publish(ctx context.Context, store ObjectStore, tenantID, backupID, archivePath string) (Manifest, error) {
    key := "backups/" + tenantID + "/" + backupID + ".zip"

    file, err := os.Open(archivePath)
    if err != nil {
        return Manifest{}, fmt.Errorf("open archive: %w", err)
    }
    defer file.Close()

    digest := sha256.New()
    if err := store.Put(ctx, key, io.TeeReader(file, digest), "application/zip"); err != nil {
        return Manifest{}, fmt.Errorf("upload archive: %w", err)
    }

    return Manifest{
        TenantID:    tenantID,
        BackupID:    backupID,
        ObjectKey:   key,
        SHA256:      hex.EncodeToString(digest.Sum(nil)),
        CompletedAt: time.Now().UTC(),
    }, nil
}

The surrounding service must persist the state transition and make the completion write idempotent. A retry with the same backup ID should inspect the existing record, not create another object called latest. The checksum here describes the bytes consumed by Put; a production restore path should calculate and compare a digest after downloading the recorded object as well.

There is no magic in the ZIP extension. It is useful when the restore tool benefits from one archive, but it can also create a large staging file and a single failure domain. Keep the database dump and media as separate objects when independent restore or parallel transfer is more valuable.

What evaluation should a tenant restore drill pass before we trust it?

The dangerous test is not “can the owner upload?” It is “can tenant A name tenant B's backup ID or object key and receive bytes?” The restore endpoint should accept an authenticated tenant and backup ID, look up the server-owned manifest, require the complete state, validate the checksum, and fetch the exact recorded key. It should never accept a storage URL from the caller or construct a path from unchecked input.

For large lesson recordings, the browser upload intent should be bound to a server-generated key, expected content type, required headers, and an expiry. After the direct upload, the application should inspect the object and associate it with the lesson only if the intent and tenant checks agree. A prefix is useful organization; it is not, by itself, an authorization decision.

The test cases belong in CI and in a restore drill. Attempt a cross-tenant key, replay an expired intent, retry a claimed backup, truncate an archive, and request a restore before verification. Each case should produce a controlled rejection or a state that cannot be selected for recovery. Record the requester, artifact ID, destination, and outcome so an incident review does not depend on bucket logs alone.

Short test. Clear evidence.

I have been paged by missed jobs and duplicate deliveries, so I treat the restore drill as an operational write path, not a quarterly checkbox. A useful exercise starts with one tenant's recorded backup, downloads the exact object, checks the digest, opens the ZIP, restores the dump into an isolated database, and verifies that the application can resolve the tenant's users, courses, and media references. Then repeat the exercise after a worker restart and after an upload retry. The point is not to manufacture a perfect demo; it is to expose which state was assumed instead of recorded. A green cron log is weak evidence. A successful restore with an auditable artifact is stronger.

Verify twice.

What governance belongs in recovery telemetry after an upload?

An upload counter can stay green while the newest usable backup grows old. Track the age of the newest restorable artifact per tenant, missed cron runs, stale claims, verification failures, restore duration, and cleanup failures. Alerting should distinguish “the worker started” from “the school can recover.”

Lifecycle policy matters here. Old objects may need expiry or transition, and incomplete multipart uploads need cleanup where the storage implementation supports it. Test cancellation and worker restarts. A presigned URL grants a constrained transfer opportunity; it does not prove tenant authorization, checksum validity, malware safety, or disaster recovery.

Retention should follow the tenant's academic and contractual requirements. I'm not sure one period fits every school, so make the policy explicit in the manifest and test it against restore drills. Your mileage may vary across S3-compatible implementations; verify the conditional-write, multipart, encryption, and lifecycle behavior you rely on before treating two services as interchangeable.

A comparison of direct upload and an application proxy

Direct transfer is a poor fit when every byte must pass through a controlled application service, when the storage boundary cannot express the required policy, or when required lifecycle controls are unavailable. In those cases, keep the proxy and accept its bandwidth and failure-domain costs. The right choice is the one that makes tenant isolation and recovery evidence enforceable.

The trade-off is easier to review in a runbook than in a vendor comparison:

Design choice Useful when Cost or boundary
Direct object upload Large media should bypass the app process The application must own intent and tenant checks
Application proxy Every byte needs centralized inspection App bandwidth and its failure domain carry the transfer
One ZIP archive Restore tooling expects one artifact A single archive can limit independent recovery
Separate objects Database and media need different restore timing The manifest must describe the selected set

The catch is that direct transfer is not suitable when those storage and application controls cannot be tested together. Stick with an application proxy when centralized inspection is a hard requirement; a shorter upload path is not worth weakening the recovery boundary.

References

  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lifecycle-mgmt.html
  • https://firebase.google.com/docs/storage

title: Best Tools for Snowflake Semantic Views & Semantic Layers
description:
Snowflake Semantic Views changed the conversation around metrics. Instead of every BI tool, notebook, and AI agent calculating "active customers" its own way, you can now define that logic once, govern it inside Snowflake, and have Cortex Analyst, Power BI, and downstream apps all agree on what it means. The problem is the tooling around it is scattered. Some products build the semantic layer. Some design the physical warehouse. Almost none of them do both.

I spent a few weeks digging into the tools people actually use to build and manage semantic layers on top of Snowflake. Some are headless engines. Some are BI platforms. One is a visual modeling platform that handles both the physical schema and the semantic layer in the same workspace. I looked for Snowflake-native integration, governance, how definitions get versioned and deployed, and whether a mixed team of architects, analytics engineers, and business users could actually collaborate on the same model.

Here's what I'd recommend, starting with the one that impressed me most.

How I Evaluated These Tools

I focused on five things: native Snowflake Semantic View support, how metrics and dimensions are defined and governed, whether the tool plays well with Cortex Analyst and modern BI, how changes to physical schemas propagate into semantic definitions, and the collaboration story. I also looked at pricing transparency and real customer footprint, not just marketing pages.

1. SqlDBM - Best Overall

The only visual modeling platform that designs, governs, and deploys Snowflake Semantic Views from a single workspace.

I've tested a lot of tools that touch Snowflake's semantic layer, and SqlDBM is the one that made everything click. Most semantic-layer tools (dbt, Cube, AtScale) give you a way to define metrics, but they skip visual modeling entirely. And the traditional visual modeling tools like erwin or ER/Studio don't touch the semantic layer at all. SqlDBM is the only platform I've found that bridges both worlds. You get a full visual data modeling environment and native support for Snowflake Semantic Views, in one browser-based workspace.

What impressed me most is how SqlDBM lets you define semantic views, with governed dimensions, metrics, and time dimensions, directly alongside your physical warehouse schema. You're not writing raw DDL in a vacuum. You're layering business context onto a governed physical foundation, and when upstream schemas change, those definitions propagate automatically so nothing drifts. The AI Copilot now runs directly on the Semantic Model page, which makes it faster to set up properties like synonyms, sample values, and column exposure for Cortex Analyst readiness.

This isn't a niche tool either. SqlDBM became the first online modeling tool to support Snowflake back in 2019 and today serves over 300 Snowflake clients as a Snowflake Premier Partner Connect member. Over 400,000 users globally trust the platform, including enterprises like Les Mills, which governs more than 1,000 Snowflake tables in SqlDBM after rejecting erwin on usability grounds. The Head of Product, Serge Gershkovich, literally wrote the book, Data Modeling with Snowflake (Packt, now in its 2nd edition), with endorsements from Kent Graziano and Joe Reis.

Real-time, multi-user collaboration means data architects, analytics engineers, and business stakeholders can all work concurrently in the same semantic model, so definitions are agreed on before they ever hit Snowflake. You can forward-engineer semantic YAML, export to Git, and round-trip everything through CI/CD. No drift between what was reviewed and what gets deployed. For teams building a governed Snowflake semantic layer that AI agents and BI tools can actually trust, this is the most complete starting point I've found.

Pros:

  • Native Snowflake Semantic View support with governed dimensions, metrics, and time dimensions, the only visual modeling platform that designs and deploys semantic views from the same workspace
  • Physical-to-semantic governance in one place: schema changes propagate automatically to semantic definitions, eliminating drift that plagues standalone semantic-layer tools
  • Deep Snowflake pedigree: first online modeling tool to support Snowflake (2019), 300+ Snowflake clients, Premier Partner Connect member, and product leadership that authored Data Modeling with Snowflake (Packt)
  • Real-time multi-user collaboration on semantic models so architects, engineers, and business users align on metric definitions before deploying
  • Round-trip CI/CD workflow: forward-engineer semantic YAML, manage it in Git, and deploy through pipelines

Cons:

  • The semantic modeling features are relatively new (beta to GA), so teams used to mature standalone semantic-layer tools may notice a few rough edges in edge-case metric configurations
  • Deepest integration is with Snowflake, Databricks, and BigQuery. Teams on less common warehouses may find fewer semantic-layer features

Pricing: SqlDBM plans are quote-based and scale to team size and use case, with enterprise packaging, premium support, and advanced security options. A free tier is available so you can explore modeling and semantic view design before committing, no credit card required.

2. AtScale

AtScale is an enterprise semantic layer platform that sits between your data warehouse and the BI tools, AI agents, and applications that need metrics. The notable thing for Snowflake users is that Snowflake embedded AtScale's engine inside the Snowflake Semantic Views XMLA endpoint. That endpoint gives Power BI and Excel a live, governed path to Semantic Views without extracts, which is a real gap in Snowflake's native story.

AtScale for Snowflake runs as a Snowflake Native App through Snowpark Container Services, passes Snowflake RBAC through to users, and uses an adaptive aggregate cache to cut compute costs. Beyond Snowflake, AtScale Enterprise supports Databricks and Iceberg-compliant compute, and it backs the Open Semantic Interchange standard for portable definitions. Customers it names include Blue Yonder, Carrefour, and Papa Johns.

It's aimed at large, Microsoft-heavy organizations that need one consistent set of metrics across many tools. It's less of a fit for small teams that just want a lightweight modeling experience. Some of the Snowflake integration pieces, like the embedded XMLA endpoint, have been described as private preview, so verify current availability.

Pros:

  • Snowflake has embedded AtScale's engine in the Semantic Views XMLA endpoint
  • Extends Snowflake Semantic Views to Power BI and Excel, which don't consume them natively
  • Adaptive aggregate caching can reduce Snowflake query compute costs
  • Works across multiple platforms and supports the OSI standard

Cons:

  • Enterprise-oriented, so setup and licensing are heavier than lightweight tools
  • Pricing is not published and requires a sales conversation
  • Some Snowflake integration pieces were listed as private preview or coming soon

Pricing: No public pricing. AtScale is sold through sales with custom enterprise licensing. Snowflake users can reach it through the Snowflake Native App and the Semantic Views XMLA endpoint.

3. dbt Semantic Layer (dbt Cloud / MetricFlow)

The dbt Semantic Layer lets analytics engineers define metrics, entities, dimensions, and measures as YAML right next to their dbt transformation code, using the open-source MetricFlow engine. Definitions get versioned in Git and tested in CI. dbt Cloud then serves them through JDBC and GraphQL APIs to supported BI tools, notebooks, and AI agents.

For Snowflake teams this fits naturally because the semantic definitions live in the same repository as the models that build the underlying tables. It can sit upstream of, or alongside, Snowflake's native Semantic Views and Cortex Analyst, though you should check dbt's current docs for how closely those sync today. It suits analytics engineering teams that already run dbt and want metric governance managed like software. It's less suited to business users who want a visual, no-code interface, since nearly everything happens in code.

Pros:

  • Metrics live in version-controlled YAML alongside dbt models
  • MetricFlow is open source and integrates with many BI tools
  • Works with existing dbt lineage, testing, documentation, and CI/CD
  • Large community and a familiar ecosystem for Snowflake teams

Cons:

  • Needs a paid dbt Cloud plan, the Semantic Layer API is not available on Developer
  • Code-first approach has a learning curve for non-engineers
  • Not a visual modeling or ERD tool, and some BI tools can't connect through its APIs

Pricing: dbt Cloud has a free Developer plan, but the hosted Semantic Layer requires a paid tier. The Starter plan has been listed at roughly $100 per developer seat per month with a monthly metric-query allowance. Enterprise and Enterprise+ are custom-priced. Confirm current numbers on getdbt.com/pricing.

4. Cube

Cube is a headless semantic layer. Teams define data models, measures, dimensions, and access rules as code in YAML or JavaScript, and Cube serves them through SQL, REST, GraphQL, and MDX APIs to BI tools, applications, and LLM agents. There's an open-source core (Cube Core) and a managed service (Cube Cloud). It connects to Snowflake and other warehouses, and its pre-aggregation and caching layer can speed up queries and lower warehouse spend.

It also includes row-level access control and multi-tenant security, which makes it a strong pick for embedded analytics. Cube has positioned itself as a vendor-neutral semantic layer and has been part of the Open Semantic Interchange conversation around portable metric definitions.

It's a good fit for engineering-led teams that want one layer feeding dashboards, customer-facing apps, and AI agents. It's more developer-centric than a visual modeling tool. Teams relying only on Snowflake Cortex Analyst may find Snowflake's native Semantic Views simpler, and if you go with Cube you'll do some manual work to keep its model and Snowflake's semantic objects aligned.

Pros:

  • Open-source core with a managed cloud option
  • Multiple APIs (SQL, REST, GraphQL, MDX) work with a wide range of BI tools
  • Pre-aggregations and caching can improve performance and reduce warehouse cost
  • Strong fit for embedded analytics and multi-tenant security

Cons:

  • Developer-centric, with code-based modeling and ops
  • Self-hosting Cube Core means managing infrastructure yourself
  • Not a Snowflake-native object, so keeping definitions aligned with Snowflake Semantic Views takes extra work

Pricing: Cube Core is free and open source. Cube Cloud has a free tier plus paid Starter, Premium, and Enterprise plans, with usage-based pricing on compute and queries. Check cube.dev/pricing for current rates.

5. Honeydew

Honeydew is a semantic layer platform with a strong Snowflake focus. Teams define entities, metrics, dimensions, and relationships in a governed model with Git-based version control. That model then serves BI tools, SQL clients, and AI or LLM applications. The positioning is "AI-ready analytics," and it can feed Snowflake-native experiences like Cortex Analyst and Snowflake Semantic Views with logic maintained in one place and pushed down to Snowflake for execution.

It's available through the Snowflake Marketplace as a native-style deployment, so data stays inside the customer's Snowflake account. That makes it interesting for data teams that want to move beyond hand-written Semantic Views YAML without leaving the Snowflake environment.

Honeydew is younger than dbt or AtScale, with a smaller community and fewer public case studies. Public pricing and documentation are limited, and the product is evolving quickly, so it's worth confirming current integration depth with the vendor before committing.

Pros:

  • Strong Snowflake focus with execution pushed down to the warehouse
  • Single governed model for BI tools and AI/LLM applications
  • Git-based workflow and collaboration for semantic models
  • Can complement Snowflake's native Semantic Views and Cortex Analyst

Cons:

  • Newer vendor with a smaller community and fewer public references
  • Public pricing and documentation are limited
  • Primarily Snowflake-oriented, so less breadth than multi-warehouse platforms

Pricing: No public price list. Honeydew is typically sold through sales or the Snowflake Marketplace, with a demo or trial on request.

6. Omni

Omni is a modern BI platform with a governed semantic model built in. Business users can explore data through a point-and-click interface, spreadsheet-style calculations, SQL, and AI-assisted queries, while analysts and engineers manage the shared semantic model (metrics, joins, permissions) in a Git-backed workflow. It connects directly to Snowflake and pushes queries down.

Omni can work alongside Snowflake's semantic modeling features, so teams can keep definitions consistent between Omni and Snowflake-native AI tools, though you'll want to verify current sync options with the vendor. It also supports embedding analytics in customer-facing apps.

It's a good pick if you want BI and a semantic layer in one product rather than wiring up a separate headless layer. The tradeoff is that the semantic layer mainly serves Omni itself, which makes it less tool-agnostic than something like AtScale or Cube. Adopting Omni may also mean changing your BI tool, which is a bigger lift than adding a semantic layer under the one you already use.

Pros:

  • Combines BI and a governed semantic model in one platform
  • Direct, push-down connection to Snowflake
  • Flexible for both business users (no-code) and analysts (SQL)
  • Git-based modeling workflow and embedding support

Cons:

  • The semantic layer mainly serves Omni's own BI, so less tool-agnostic than headless layers
  • Adopting it may mean changing your BI tool
  • Pricing is not published, and the vendor is newer than legacy BI vendors

Pricing: No public pricing. Omni offers custom, platform-based quotes with a trial or demo on request.

Final Verdict

If your goal is a Snowflake semantic layer that AI agents and BI tools can genuinely rely on, you need two things most tools don't give you together: a governed physical foundation and a governed semantic layer on top of it. That's where SqlDBM wins. It's the only platform I tested that designs the physical schema, defines Semantic Views visually, keeps them in sync when things change, and still gives you YAML and Git on the way out.

AtScale is the right call if you're a large Microsoft-centric enterprise that needs Power BI and Excel talking natively to Snowflake Semantic Views. dbt Semantic Layer and Cube are good picks for engineering-led teams that already live in code. Honeydew is worth watching if you want a Snowflake-native semantic platform and don't mind a younger vendor. Omni is the move if you want BI and semantic modeling in the same product and are open to switching BI tools.

For most teams building a governed Snowflake semantic layer from scratch, though, I'd start with SqlDBM.

FAQ

What's the difference between a Snowflake Semantic View and a semantic layer tool?
Snowflake Semantic Views are native Snowflake objects that store metrics, dimensions, and relationships inside the warehouse. A semantic layer tool (like AtScale, dbt, Cube, or SqlDBM) helps you design, govern, and serve those definitions to BI and AI tools. Some tools generate Semantic Views directly, others run their own engine alongside Snowflake.

Do I need a semantic layer tool if I use Snowflake Cortex Analyst?
Cortex Analyst works with Semantic Views and YAML semantic models. You can write those by hand, but as the model grows, teams usually want a tool to govern definitions, propagate schema changes, and keep BI and AI aligned. That's where SqlDBM or a headless semantic layer helps.

Can I use more than one of these tools together?
Yes, and many teams do. For example, SqlDBM for physical and semantic modeling, dbt for transformations, and AtScale or Cube to serve metrics to specific BI tools. Just be deliberate about where the source of truth lives so definitions don't drift.

Is there a free way to try SqlDBM before committing?
Yes. SqlDBM has a free tier so you can explore visual modeling and semantic view design without a credit card. Larger teams move to a quote-based plan with enterprise packaging and premium support.

title: Your Data Already Knows More Than Your Model... How NVIDIA Kumo Engine turns relational data into predictive context
description:
Most real-world data doesn't live in one table.
A customer has orders. Orders contain products. Events describe interactions. Each table holds only part of the story.
But when building predictive models, developers often spend significant time joining tables, engineering features, generating labels, and ensuring that historical data is used correctly.
What if the relationships already present in your data could become the model's context?
That's the problem NVIDIA Kumo Engine is designed to address.

What is Kumo Engine?
Kumo Engine is an accelerator for context generation over structured data.
It stores tables and their relationships as an on-disk graph. For each entity, it samples related records up to a specified prediction time. A predictive query describes the task, and Kumo Engine uses the resulting context to train and run predictive models on relational data.

Its built-in graph neural network (GNN) supports:
• Classification
• Regression
• Forecasting
• Recommendation
The central idea is simple: use the relationships in your data as model context, rather than relying entirely on manually engineered features.

1. From tables to connected context
Imagine an e-commerce dataset with two tables:
• users: customer information
• orders: customer transactions
A user can have multiple orders. The user_id field connects the two tables.
Instead of treating these tables as isolated datasets, Kumo Engine represents their relationships as a graph.
That lets the engine sample relevant order records for each user and build context for a prediction.
For example:
Will this customer place an order in the next 30 days?
The model can use the customer's historical orders as context.

2. Prediction time matters
There is an important detail in predictive machine learning: a model must not see information from the future.
Suppose we're predicting whether a customer will order in the next 30 days.
At a particular prediction time, the model should only see records that existed at or before that time. Future orders must not become part of the input.
Kumo Engine generates training examples at points in each entity's history and uses only records timestamped at or before each point in time.
This point-in-time approach helps avoid data leakage without requiring developers to hand-write label logic and point-in-time joins.

3. Define the prediction with a query
One of Kumo Engine's key ideas is the predictive query.
For the example of predicting whether a user will place an order in the next 30 days, the query is:
PREDICT COUNT(orders.*, 0, 30, days) > 0
FOR EACH users.user_id
This describes the prediction target:
• Count related orders.
• Look across the next 30 days.
• Predict whether the count is greater than zero.
• Generate predictions for each user.
The query is used to generate training examples and prediction inputs.

4. A quickstart with Python

Install Kumo Engine:
pip install kumo-engine
The package requires CPython 3.11 or later. The README also documents supported operating systems and hardware requirements.
Here's the core workflow using the sample shop dataset:
from kumo.engine import (
Edge,
FileConnector,
Graph,
PredictiveQuery,
Table,
Trainer,
datasets,
)

Load sample data

files = FileConnector(root_dir=datasets.shop())

Define tables

users = Table.from_source_table(
files["users"],
primary_key="user_id"
)

orders = Table.from_source_table(
files["orders"],
primary_key="order_id",
time_column="order_time"
)

Define the relationship

graph = Graph(
tables={
"users": users,
"orders": orders,
},
edges=[
Edge(
src_table="orders",
fkey="user_id",
dst_table="users"
)
],
)

snapshot = graph.snapshot()

Define the prediction task

pquery = PredictiveQuery(
graph,
"PREDICT COUNT(orders.*, 0, 30, days) > 0 "
"FOR EACH users.user_id"
)

Train

trainer = Trainer(
pquery.suggest_model_plan(snapshot)
)

training_result = trainer.fit(
pquery.generate_training_table(snapshot),
snapshot=snapshot,
)

Predict

result = trainer.predict(
pquery.generate_prediction_table(snapshot),
snapshot=snapshot,
binary_classification_threshold=0.5,
)

print(result.frame.head())
The example trains a model to predict which users will place an order in the next 30 days.
The resulting frame contains one row per user, including the predicted label and class probabilities.

5. How does it scale beyond memory?
Relational datasets can become much larger than available RAM.
Kumo Engine is designed to sample context from graphs containing billions of records on a single machine, even when the graph is larger than memory.
The README describes several techniques behind this design:
Resolve links at ingest
Primary and foreign keys are resolved during ingestion. Following a relationship during sampling becomes a direct lookup rather than a repeated join.
Bounded context
By default, each hop samples at most a configured number of related records. This keeps an entity's context bounded as the graph grows.
Recent history first
Related records are stored newest first. Sampling can locate the prediction time with a binary search and read recent records in order.
Ordered reads for large batches
The sampler expands batches one hop at a time and orders records by their position on disk to make reads more sequential.
Memory-mapped graph files
Graph files are read-only and memory-mapped. The operating system keeps frequently accessed pages in RAM and loads other pages from disk when needed.
Together, these techniques help Kumo Engine work with datasets that do not fit entirely in memory.

6. More than model training

The workflow extends beyond fitting a model.
Kumo Engine includes:
• Hyperparameter search
• Model explanations
• Embedding export
• Batch prediction
The README also describes integrations with MLflow, Databricks, SageMaker, and Snowflake for experiment tracking, model versioning, and prediction-drift monitoring.
It can run locally through Python or inside supported data-platform notebooks.

When is this useful?
Kumo Engine is worth exploring when:
• Your predictive problem spans multiple related tables.
• You want to use historical relationships as model context.
• Point-in-time correctness is important.
• You need to generate training examples from entity histories.
• Your relational graph is too large to fit in memory.
It is not simply another way to train a model. Its focus is the context-generation layer that sits between structured data and predictive modeling.

Final thoughts

A lot of useful predictive information is already present in the relationships between records.
Customers, transactions, products, events, and their timestamps form a connected history. The challenge is making that history available to a model without introducing leakage or building every feature and join manually.

NVIDIA Kumo Engine approaches this by turning relational data into graph-based context and using predictive queries to define what the model should learn.

The interesting shift is from asking how to engineer more features to asking how to make the relationships in our data usable as context.
Explore further
• Kumo Engine on GitHub
• Official documentation
• Predictive Query examples
• Benchmark report

Have you worked with predictive models over relational data? What has been the hardest part: feature engineering, point-in-time correctness, or scaling context generation? Share your experience in the comments.

title: Slow PostgreSQL Queries in Spring Boot: A Field Guide from Real Projects
description:
I have tuned PostgreSQL databases behind Java services for energy grid operators, e-commerce platforms, a health insurer and a VoIP monitoring product. The stack changed a lot over the years. The way slow queries show up did not: a page that used to load instantly now takes seconds, the connection pool runs dry under load, and someone suggests "just add more CPU".

More hardware rarely fixes it. A repeatable process does. This is the one I use, from finding the guilty query to making sure it never comes back.

1. Find the queries that actually hurt

Do not start with the query you think is slow. Start with data.

pg_stat_statements

pg_stat_statements aggregates execution statistics for every normalized query. It needs to be preloaded (on managed services like RDS or Azure you set this in the parameter group):

# postgresql.conf
shared_preload_libraries = 'pg_stat_statements'

After a restart:

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_stat_statements;

SELECT query,
       calls,
       round(total_exec_time::numeric, 1) AS total_ms,
       round(mean_exec_time::numeric, 1)  AS mean_ms,
       rows
FROM pg_stat_statements
ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC
LIMIT 10;

Sort by total_exec_time, not by mean_exec_time. A query that takes 15 ms but runs 2 million times a day costs you far more than a 3 second report that runs twice. In my experience the biggest wins almost always hide in that first group.

auto_explain

Knowing which query is slow is half the story. auto_explain logs the execution plan of slow statements as they happen in production, with the real parameters:

shared_preload_libraries = 'pg_stat_statements,auto_explain'
auto_explain.log_min_duration = '500ms'
auto_explain.log_analyze = on
auto_explain.log_buffers = on
auto_explain.log_timing = off   # keeps the overhead low

2. Read the plan, not the SQL

Run the query with real parameter values:

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT ...;

Careful: ANALYZE really executes the statement. For UPDATE or DELETE, wrap it in BEGIN; ... ROLLBACK;.

These are the patterns I look for first:

What you see in the plan What it usually means
Seq Scan on a large table with a big Rows Removed by Filter Missing or unusable index
Estimated rows=12, actual rows=48210 Stale statistics, the planner picks the wrong strategy
Nested Loop with loops=50000 on the inner side Bad estimate or missing index on the join column
Sort Method: external merge Disk: ... Sort spills to disk, no index supports the ORDER BY
High shared read in Buffers Data comes from disk, not from cache

explain.dalibo.com is a great free tool to visualize larger plans.

3. Fix the usual suspects

Foreign keys without an index

PostgreSQL creates an index for primary keys and unique constraints, but not for foreign key columns. Every join or WHERE order_id = ? on such a column is a candidate for a sequential scan, and so is every DELETE on the parent table.

CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_order_item_order_id
    ON order_item (order_id);

CONCURRENTLY avoids locking the table for writes, but it cannot run inside a transaction. In Liquibase, set runInTransaction="false" on the changeset. In Flyway, add a script config file with executeInTransaction=false.

Composite indexes in the wrong order

For a query like this:

SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = ? AND status = 'OPEN'
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 20;

put the equality columns first and the sort column last:

CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_customer_open
    ON orders (customer_id, created_at)
    WHERE status = 'OPEN';

The partial index (WHERE status = 'OPEN') keeps it small if most orders are closed. PostgreSQL can read it backwards, so the DESC sort comes for free and the Sort node disappears from the plan.

Functions on indexed columns

WHERE lower(email) = lower(?) cannot use a plain index on email. Either index the expression:

CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_users_email_lower ON users (lower(email));

or store the normalized value. The same applies to casts and to date functions such as date_trunc('day', created_at) = ?. Rewrite those as a range: created_at >= ? AND created_at < ?.

N+1 queries from JPA

The database looks fast, every single query takes 1 ms, and the endpoint still needs 3 seconds. That is the classic N+1 problem. Make it visible first:

logging.level.org.hibernate.SQL=debug

For @ManyToOne associations an entity graph usually solves it:

@EntityGraph(attributePaths = "customer")
List<Order> findByStatus(OrderStatus status);

For collections combined with pagination, be careful: fetching a collection together with LIMIT makes Hibernate paginate in memory (warning HHH90003004). Batch fetching is the safer default here:

spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size=50

This turns N queries into roughly N/50 queries with an IN clause, without changing a single repository method.

Deep pagination with OFFSET

OFFSET 100000 LIMIT 50 means PostgreSQL reads and throws away 100,000 rows. Keyset pagination stays fast no matter how deep you go:

SELECT id, created_at, total
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = :customerId
  AND (created_at, id) < (:lastCreatedAt, :lastId)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 50;

backed by an index on (customer_id, created_at, id). The client sends the last seen created_at and id instead of a page number.

Stale statistics after bulk loads

After large imports or migrations, autovacuum may not have analyzed the table yet, and the planner works with numbers from yesterday. A simple ANALYZE orders; at the end of the import job often fixes plans that looked "random".

4. Make sure it stays fixed

Tuning is worthless if the next feature brings the problem back. Two things have worked well for me.

Test against a real PostgreSQL, not H2. With Testcontainers and Spring Boot's @ServiceConnection this is a few lines, and you can even assert the number of statements to catch N+1 regressions in CI:

@SpringBootTest(properties = "spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.generate_statistics=true")
@Testcontainers
class OrderQueryCountTest {

    @Container
    @ServiceConnection
    static PostgreSQLContainer<?> postgres = new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:17");

    @Autowired
    EntityManagerFactory entityManagerFactory;

    @Autowired
    OrderService orderService;

    @Test
    void loadsRecentOrdersWithoutNPlusOne() {
        Statistics stats = entityManagerFactory.unwrap(SessionFactory.class).getStatistics();
        stats.clear();

        orderService.findRecentOrders(42L);

        assertThat(stats.getPrepareStatementCount()).isLessThanOrEqualTo(2);
    }
}

Watch it in production. Spring Boot already exposes HikariCP pool metrics through Micrometer. Alerts on hikaricp_connections_pending and on the request latency of your critical endpoints, plus a weekly look at pg_stat_statements, catch most regressions before users do.

The short checklist

  1. Find the expensive queries with pg_stat_statements, sorted by total time.
  2. Capture real plans with auto_explain and EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS).
  3. Check foreign key indexes, index column order, functions on columns, N+1 and OFFSET pagination.
  4. Run ANALYZE after bulk loads.
  5. Lock the fix in with Testcontainers tests and pool metrics.

None of this is exotic. That is exactly the point: most performance problems I have seen in Java backends were solved with these basics, not with a bigger database server.

What is the worst query plan you have ever found in production? I would love to read your stories in the comments.

I am a freelance Senior Java Backend and Platform Engineer based in Berlin, working with Spring Boot, PostgreSQL, Kafka and Kubernetes. If your team is fighting with a slow backend, feel free to reach out via daniel-heid.de.

title: Dependabot said green. The app was blank. So I made Kane CLI check before it merges
description:
Built for the Kane CLI Hackathon by TestMu AI.

I found six public repos where the same thing happened. Dependabot opened a React bump. CI went green: type check, lint, build, and in four of them the deploy itself. The PR merged. The live app was a blank page, and the maintainer had to revert it or fix it by hand.

One of them put it plainly in the revert:

"Format check, lint, typecheck and build stay green, which is why the chain did not catch it."

In all six, the bot raised react and left react-dom behind. React refuses to start when the two differ (error #527), so the bundle throws before the first render. Nothing in a normal CI pipeline opens the app, so nothing sees it. Even npm is happy, because react-dom only asks for ^19.

A green check on a bot PR means the code builds. It doesn't mean checkout still works. So I built Bumpgate.

What it does

On every Dependabot or Renovate PR, Bumpgate:

  1. builds main and the bump side by side (two git worktrees);
  2. has Kane CLI replay your app's critical journeys in a real browser on both;
  3. decides with one rule, in plain code: every journey that passes on main must pass on the bump.

Then one of three lights:

  • 🟢 Green: every journey behaves the same. The PR merges itself.
  • 🟡 Amber: it works, but Kane had to self-heal a step, or new console errors appeared. One human look.
  • 🔴 Red: a journey broke. Blocked, and the fix loop starts.

A journey is plain English

No selectors and no page objects. This is a real journey from the demo shop, .kane/checkout_errors_test.md:

# Checkout explains what is wrong

## Add a product and go to checkout
Click "Add to cart" on the first product, click "Cart" in the header, then click "Go to checkout".

## Submit with a missing name and a bad email
Leave "Full name" empty, type "not-an-email" into "Email", then click the "Place order" button.

## See the errors
Verify the message "Please enter your name" is shown.
Verify the message "Enter a valid email address" is shown.

Kane records it once on main, then replays it against each PR build with kane-cli testmd run --override-start-url. Because the journey describes behaviour, not CSS classes, a UI kit renaming its classes doesn't break it. A checkout that stops showing errors does.

Don't want to write them? bumpgate init has Claude Code draft journeys from your code, and only the drafts Kane passes on main are kept.

When something breaks: the closed loop

This is a real run, on PR #4 in the demo shop.

Dependabot bumped zod from 3 to 4. CI passed. Kane ran "Checkout explains what is wrong" on the bump, and the errors never appeared: it failed at step 3, on 2 of 2 runs. Kane's own bug verdict: "Checkout omits required-name validation message (major)", with a new console error only on the bump: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'forEach').

Kane's failed step, reason, bug verdict, console errors and the package's release notes became Claude Code's task. It came back with one line:

-      result.error.errors.forEach((issue) => {
+      result.error.issues.forEach((issue) => {

Before anything merges, code, not a prompt, checks the diff. It rejects any fix that:

  • edits a journey (making the test easier),
  • undoes the bump,
  • hard-codes a text the journey checks for,
  • or is suspiciously large.

Then Kane re-runs every journey on the fixed branch: 3 of 3 passed, and it merged. If the fix fails three times, the PR is labelled for a human instead. If you'd rather a person approve every agent-written fix, set merge-fixes: review.

Results, with the limits

What Result
Real React bumps in 6 public repos that passed CI and shipped a blank page Kane blocks 6 of 6 at step 1, each failure confirmed by a second run
Demo shop: zod 3→4 and react-query 4→5 both passed CI and broke the app Both blocked, fixed by Claude Code, re-verified by Kane, merged
Demo shop: clsx 1→2, a safe bump Green; merged itself in under 2 minutes
10 open Dependabot PRs in strangers' repos 2 blank pages (their own CI was red, but a forced install ships them), 1 amber, 7 green
Bot bumps that were merged and never reverted 0 false alarms on 4

Honest limits:

  • The six blank pages are one bug class, and I found them by searching for it. 6 of 6 is not a catch rate. A script comparing the two version numbers would catch this one bug too; the point is that one plain-English journey catches it and whatever comes next, with no rule written for it.
  • The app has to run without a private backend.
  • Kane runs cost credits (replaying a recorded journey is cheap).

Try the whole loop in 10 seconds, no account 

npx github:Maheswar-Sah00/bumpgate replay

It feeds Kane CLI's recorded output from the real PR #4 run through the real gate code: the block, the evidence Claude Code was handed, its fix, the guardrails rejecting two cheating fixes, and Kane's 3/3 re-run. No keys, no credits.

Add it to your repo 

# .github/workflows/bumpgate.yml
name: Bumpgate
on:
  pull_request:
    types: [opened, synchronize, reopened]
permissions: { contents: write, pull-requests: write, issues: write, statuses: write }
jobs:
  gate:
    if: github.event.pull_request.user.login == 'dependabot[bot]' || github.event.pull_request.user.login == 'renovate[bot]'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with: { fetch-depth: 0 }
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 22 }
      - uses: Maheswar-Sah00/bumpgate@v1.1
        with:
          lt-username: ${{ secrets.LT_USERNAME }}
          lt-access-key: ${{ secrets.LT_ACCESS_KEY }}
          anthropic-api-key: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}

One gotcha: Dependabot PRs can only read Dependabot secrets, so add the keys under Settings → Secrets → Dependabot. And the bump's install scripts never see the TestMu key, the GitHub token or the agent key.

Why this only works with Kane CLI

The gate needs three things a selector script can't give: a journey that survives cosmetic UI churn but fails on broken behaviour; evidence an agent can act on (the failed step, a bug verdict, console and network); and a re-check of the agent's own fix. Kane is all three: the gate, the evidence, and the referee.

Links

  • Live site (start here): https://maheswar-sah00.github.io/bumpgate/
  • Code (MIT): https://github.com/Maheswar-Sah00/bumpgate
  • Live demo PRs: https://github.com/Maheswar-Sah00/bumpgatedemo/pulls?q=is%3Apr
  • Backtest, with screenshots and every revert linked: https://github.com/Maheswar-Sah00/bumpgate/blob/main/backtest/blank-page/RESULTS.md

Questions and "this would never work on my repo" are both welcome in the comments.

title: The Modern Web Guidance skill from Google is a must try!
description:
Has this ever happened to you? You have your AI agent make some changes, then you look at the CSS and it's not using the latest and greatest. You heard about some nice new CSS feature, and your agent decided to use an outdated one instead. Or worse, it decided to use JavaScript when CSS could have worked much better.

This skill helps fix that. It's called Modern Web Guidance, and it's a set of skills from the Chrome team that puts web platform best practices and browser compatibility data straight into your coding agent. Version 1.0 came out on November 10th, and Firefox and Edge are on the project too.

I'm a big React and Vue.js fan so I decided to use the latest model and have it create an app without any skills then with skills. I used Claude Opus 5.5 for all my tests.

If you'd rather watch, here's the video:

(Full disclosure: I'm a Developer Advocate at AWS, and Kiro is an AWS product. It's my agentic harness of choice, but Modern Web Guidance works with any agent that supports skills.)

The app

I gave Kiro CLI this prompt with Opus 5.5, in an empty folder with no skills and no steering files:

Build a storefront for an outdoor gear shop called "Trailhead Outfitters" using Vue 3,
Vite and TypeScript in this folder. No UI libraries, just Vue and CSS. Make it look polished.

Then I gave it a list of features. A header that shrinks when you scroll, a mobile nav drawer you can swipe closed, 2,400 products with search and a sort dropdown, a quick view modal, a review form with a toggle switch, and a FAQ that animates open and closed.

It did a pretty good job at building it, without any skills. So I was a little worried if the skill would find anything at all...

1. Install the skill

Let's take a look at how to setup the skill.

To follow along, from your project folder run:

npx modern-web-guidance@latest install

It uses the same installer a lot of skills use. So it should look familiar.

If you open the folder, it's mostly Markdown. There's a SKILL.md that tells the agent when to use it, and a guides folder split up by topic, like accessibility, CSS, forms, JS and UI components. Each guide is a best practice written for agents, with the browser support data baked in.

2. Poke around the guides

One really nice thing is that you don't have to wait for your agent to use it. The CLI can search the guides directly:

npx modern-web-guidance@latest search "animation"

That gives you back a list of guide IDs with descriptions. When you find one you like, pull the whole thing:

npx modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "scrollytelling"

Basically, that's the same thing the agent does behind the scenes. It searches, picks the guides that match, and retrieves them and adds it to it's context.

3. Set your browser support

The guides pick features based on Baseline. By default it targets Baseline "Widely available", which means a feature has worked in every major browser for at least 30 months. That's about two and a half years. If you want newer features, you can set a newer target like Baseline 2026, and the agent will add fallbacks or polyfills for browsers that don't have them yet.

Google's docs say to put your target in AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md. In Kiro, I'd put it in a steering file:

I skipped this for the video, though Kiro did mention it.

4. Run the legacy scan

Before letting the agent touch anything, I ran the scanner on the Opus app:

npx modern-web-guidance@latest legacy-scan src

Two findings. The hero section staggers its animations with four :nth-child rules, and that can be one rule with the new sibling-index() function. And the toggle switch is a checkbox with role="switch" plus a hand-built track and thumb, which can use the new native switch attribute.

It reads .vue files fine, by the way. Templates, scripts and scoped styles.

FYI about the scanner. It only has rules for 38 guides, which is about 20% of the whole library. The rest of the skill kicks in when your agent is actually doing work with it loaded.

5. Ask Kiro to modernize it

After I ran the legacy-scan I decided to just have it go ahead and modernize my app.

I opened the app in Kiro and kept the prompt short:

Can you modernize this app?

A couple minutes in, it stopped and asked me how it should handle older browsers. Should it use polyfills? I told it to use polyfills and let it keep going.

Here's what it changed:

The hero stagger is one rule now:

@supports (animation-delay: calc(sibling-index() * 0.1s)) {
  .hero-content > * {
    animation-delay: calc((sibling-index() - 1) * var(--stagger-time));
  }
}

sibling-index() gives you an element's position among its siblings, starting at 1, so you don't need a separate rule for every child. Add a sixth line to the hero and it just works. Kiro kept the old :nth-child rules behind @supports not for browsers that don't have it yet, and it also turned the animation off for people who prefer reduced motion.

The toggle switch is a native switch now:

<input :id="id" v-model="model" type="checkbox" switch />

That let it delete the custom track and thumb. The component's CSS went from 38 lines of switch styling down to 8, and the color comes from accent-color now.

Only Safari supports switch right now, so this is where the polyfill comes in. Kiro added the input-switch-polyfill package and loads it in main.ts before the app mounts, but only when the browser needs it:

const polyfills = 'switch' in HTMLInputElement.prototype
  ? Promise.resolve()
  : import('input-switch-polyfill')

polyfills
  .catch((err: unknown) => console.error('The switch polyfill failed to load; continuing without it.', err))
  .finally(() => createApp(App).mount('#app'))

The polyfill also needed a little extra setup. It loads its own CSS file using import.meta.resolve, and Vite doesn't pick that up, so the stylesheet would go missing in the build. Kiro added a small Vite plugin that rewrites it to new URL(..., import.meta.url), plus a one-line type declaration since the package doesn't ship types.

Even though it only found two quick, simple changes, I was happy. In a much larger, more complex code base, you're probably going to get dozens of them.

Wrap up

I'll be using this skill in many more of my projects in the future. I like clean code, and even though agents are writing way more of my code then ever before, I still want to use the latest and greatest features. Specially if I know my users and their browsers support it.

Will one day the latest models do this for me? Maybe? But for now I'm going to stick to skills like this that help me write cleaner code.

Would you add this to your projects? Let me know in the comments.
