title: Load Testing Java Applications with Apache JMeter: A Practical Guide
description:
Performance problems rarely show up in unit tests. They show up on a Friday afternoon, when a checkout endpoint that responded in 120 ms at lunch starts taking eight seconds under real traffic. Apache JMeter is one of the most widely used open-source tools for catching those problems before users do. It is mature, scriptable, and it speaks HTTP, JDBC, JMS, and more out of the box. For Java teams, it also fits naturally into the build pipeline, because it runs on the JVM and can be driven from Maven, Gradle, Jenkins, or GitHub Actions.

This guide walks through a practical workflow: building a test plan, running it headless, adding assertions and correlation, writing a custom Java sampler, driving JMeter from Java code, reading the results, and wiring everything into CI. The examples target a Spring Boot service, but the ideas apply to any HTTP API.

What JMeter Actually Does

JMeter simulates many users sending requests to a system under test. Each simulated user runs through a sequence of steps, and JMeter records how long each request takes, whether it succeeded, and how many bytes came back. You then analyze those numbers to find bottlenecks, capacity limits, and regressions.

A test plan is a tree of elements. The most important ones are:

  • Thread Group: defines how many virtual users run, how fast they ramp up, and how long they keep going.
  • Samplers: send the actual requests. The HTTP Request sampler is the one you will use most.
  • Config Elements: set shared values such as base URL, headers, and cookies. HTTP Request Defaults and HTTP Header Manager are the usual choices.
  • Timers: add think time between requests so virtual users behave more like real people. Without timers you measure a flood, not a user journey.
  • Assertions: check that a response is correct. A fast 500 error is not a passing test.
  • Extractors: pull values out of one response, such as a token or an ID, and reuse them in the next request. This is called correlation.
  • Listeners: display or store results. Use them sparingly during real load runs, because they consume resources.

A minimal plan for a Spring Boot REST endpoint looks like this in JMeter's tree view:

Test Plan
 ├── Thread Group (50 users, 60s ramp-up, 5 min duration)
 │    ├── HTTP Request Defaults (host: orders.internal, port: 8080)
 │    ├── HTTP Header Manager (Content-Type: application/json)
 │    ├── HTTP Request: POST /api/orders
 │    │    ├── Response Assertion (status 201)
 │    │    └── JSON Extractor (orderId = $.id)
 │    ├── Constant Timer (500 ms)
 │    └── HTTP Request: GET /api/orders/${orderId}
 │         └── Response Assertion (status 200)
 └── Summary Report (listener, used only in GUI mode)

Notice the JSON Extractor. The second request uses the order ID created by the first one. That is the kind of dependency that real users create, and it is the part most teams skip the first time.

Never Run Load Tests in GUI Mode

The JMeter GUI is for building and debugging plans. It is not for load generation. Listeners that render graphs, and the GUI itself, consume memory and CPU on the machine running the test. If the load generator is the bottleneck, your results describe the load generator, not your application.

Save the plan as a .jmx file and run it headless:

jmeter -n \
  -t plans/orders-load.jmx \
  -l results/orders-run-01.jtl \
  -e -o reports/orders-run-01 \
  -Jhost=orders.staging.internal -Jthreads=50 -Jduration=300

The flags matter. -n runs without the GUI, -t names the test plan, -l writes raw results, and -e -o generates the HTML dashboard into a folder once the run finishes. The -J properties let you parameterize the plan. In the plan, reference them with ${__P(threads,10)}, where the second argument is a default.

Correlation and Dynamic Data

Most real applications return data that changes on every call: tokens, session cookies, generated IDs, CSRF values. If you hardcode one, the server rejects the request and your test measures error responses. Use extractors:

  • JSON Extractor for JSON bodies, using JSONPath expressions such as $.id or $.data[0].token.
  • Regular Expression Extractor for HTML pages or plain text.
  • CSV Data Set Config to feed realistic inputs, such as thousands of different customer IDs, from a file instead of reusing one value for every user.

Also remember that real clients send a login before doing anything else. A plan that skips authentication is testing a path that real users do not take.

Writing a Custom Java Sampler

Sometimes an HTTP request is not enough. You may need to call a gRPC service, publish to a queue through a proprietary client, or run a domain-specific calculation that must be measured. JMeter supports this through the Java Request sampler, which runs a class implementing JavaSamplerClient.

import org.apache.jmeter.protocol.java.sampler.AbstractJavaSamplerClient;
import org.apache.jmeter.protocol.java.sampler.JavaSamplerContext;
import org.apache.jmeter.samplers.SampleResult;
import org.apache.jmeter.config.Arguments;

public class PricingEngineSampler extends AbstractJavaSamplerClient {

    private PricingClient client;

    @Override
    public Arguments getDefaultParameters() {
        Arguments args = new Arguments();
        args.addArgument("endpoint", "http://pricing.internal:9000");
        args.addArgument("sku", "SKU-1001");
        return args;
    }

    @Override
    public void setupTest(JavaSamplerContext context) {
        // Called once per thread before the iterations start
        client = new PricingClient(context.getParameter("endpoint"));
    }

    @Override
    public SampleResult runTest(JavaSamplerContext context) {
        SampleResult result = new SampleResult();
        result.sampleStart();
        try {
            String sku = context.getParameter("sku");
            var price = client.quote(sku);
            result.setSuccessful(price != null && price.amount().signum() > 0);
            result.setResponseData(price.toString(), "UTF-8");
            result.setResponseCode("200");
        } catch (Exception e) {
            result.setSuccessful(false);
            result.setResponseCode("500");
            result.setResponseMessage(e.getMessage());
        } finally {
            result.sampleEnd();
        }
        return result;
    }

    @Override
    public void teardownTest(JavaSamplerContext context) {
        client.close();
    }
}

Two details to get right. Call sampleStart() and sampleEnd() yourself, so the timing covers only the operation you care about. And create expensive clients in setupTest, not in runTest, so you measure the service rather than your client's construction cost.

Driving JMeter from Java Code

Keeping test plans as XML in a repository is fine, but many Java teams prefer tests written in code, reviewed in pull requests, and refactored with the rest of the codebase. The jmeter-java-dsl library from Abstracta lets you build a plan with a fluent Java API and run it from a JUnit test.

import static us.abstracta.jmeter.javadsl.JmeterDsl.*;

import java.time.Duration;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import us.abstracta.jmeter.javadsl.core.TestPlanStats;

class OrdersLoadTest {

    @Test
    void ordersEndpointStaysUnderLatencyBudget() throws Exception {
        TestPlanStats stats = testPlan(
            threadGroup(50, 100,
                httpSampler("http://orders.staging.internal:8080/api/orders/42")
                    .method("GET")
                    .assertion(responseCode().is(200))
            ),
            jtlWriter("build/results/orders.jtl"),
            htmlReporter("build/reports/orders")
        ).run();

        // Fail the build if the 95th percentile exceeds 400 ms
        assertThat(stats.overall().sampleTimePercentile95()
            .toMillis()).isLessThan(400);
    }
}

Check the DSL version you use against its documentation, since method names evolve between releases. The principle stays the same: the test is code, it runs under JUnit, and a regression fails the build like any other test.

For teams that already use Maven, the jmeter-maven-plugin offers a similar path: it runs .jmx files during a build phase and can fail the build when thresholds are crossed. Pick one approach per project to keep things consistent.

Reading the Results

A load test produces a lot of numbers. Four of them matter most:

  • Throughput: requests per second the system actually handled. If throughput flattens while you add users, you have found a saturation point.
  • Response time percentiles: the average hides the problem. Track p90, p95, and p99. A healthy average with a terrible p99 means some users have a bad experience.
  • Error rate: any non-zero error rate under normal load deserves investigation. Look at the response codes first. A wave of 503s points to a different problem than a wave of timeouts.
  • Latency over time: a graph that slowly climbs during a 30-minute soak test usually means a memory leak, a connection pool that never drains, or a cache that never evicts.

Correlate JMeter's view with the server's view. In a Spring Boot service, expose Actuator metrics to Prometheus and watch JVM heap, GC pause time, thread pool saturation, and HikariCP connection wait time while the test runs. JMeter tells you that something is slow. The JVM and database metrics tell you why.

Running JMeter in CI

A load test that only runs on someone's laptop will be forgotten. Put it in the pipeline, but scope it carefully. Full-scale load tests belong in a dedicated environment on a schedule, while a smaller smoke-level test can run on every merge.

A GitHub Actions job that runs a headless plan and publishes the report might look like this:

name: orders-performance
on:
  schedule:
    - cron: "0 2 * * *"
  workflow_dispatch:

jobs:
  load-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-java@v4
        with:
          distribution: temurin
          java-version: "21"
      - name: Install JMeter
        run: |
          wget -q https://archive.apache.org/dist/jmeter/binaries/apache-jmeter-5.6.3.tgz
          tar -xzf apache-jmeter-5.6.3.tgz
          echo "$PWD/apache-jmeter-5.6.3/bin" >> "$GITHUB_PATH"
      - name: Run plan
        run: |
          jmeter -n -t plans/orders-load.jmx \
            -l results.jtl -e -o report \
            -Jhost=${{ secrets.STAGING_HOST }} -Jthreads=50 -Jduration=300
      - name: Fail on errors
        run: |
          errors=$(awk -F, 'NR>1 && $8=="false"' results.jtl | wc -l)
          if [ "$errors" -gt 0 ]; then echo "Found $errors failed samples"; exit 1; fi
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: jmeter-report
          path: report

Check the JMeter version on the Apache archive before you copy this, since older releases disappear from the mirror. The awk step reads the success column of the default CSV output, which is the eighth field, and fails the job if any sample did not pass.

Best Practices

  • Model real journeys, not isolated endpoints. Users log in, browse, add to cart, and pay. Test the sequence.
  • Add think time. A constant or Gaussian random timer between steps produces realistic concurrency.
  • Warm up before measuring. JVM services compile hot code paths during the first minutes. Discard the warm-up period from your results.
  • Use realistic data volumes. A test against an empty database tells you nothing about a table with fifty million rows.
  • Separate the load generator from the target. Run JMeter on its own machine, and watch its CPU. A saturated generator produces fake latency.
  • Set explicit thresholds. "The system should feel fast" is not a requirement. "p95 under 400 ms at 200 requests per second" is one you can test.
  • Keep test data and secrets out of the plan. Read credentials from properties or a vault, never from the .jmx file committed to Git.
  • Version the plans. Treat .jmx files like source code, and review changes to them.

A Practical Roadmap

If your team is starting from zero, a sensible sequence is:

  1. Record or script one critical user journey with the HTTP(S) Test Script Recorder or by hand.
  2. Add assertions, correlation, and realistic think times until the plan passes against a staging environment with one user.
  3. Run a headless baseline at moderate load and save the report as a reference.
  4. Add a nightly job in CI that compares the new run against the baseline and fails on a threshold breach.
  5. Expand to soak tests and stress tests, and connect the results to your application metrics dashboards.

Performance testing is not a one-time event. It is a habit that catches regressions early, when they are cheap to fix.

Key Takeaways

JMeter is a capable, free tool that fits well into Java delivery pipelines. Run it headless, correlate dynamic data, model real user journeys, and read percentiles instead of averages. Write custom samplers when HTTP is not enough, and consider a Java DSL when you want tests to live beside the code they measure. Above all, put a performance check in the pipeline so that slow code is caught by a build, not by a customer.

title: Control Flow Statements in Java
description:
1. What is Control Flow?

Control flow refers to the order in which statements are executed in a program.

Normally, Java executes statements one by one, from top to bottom. This is called sequential execution.

Example:

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Start");
        System.out.println("Learning Java");
        System.out.println("End");
    }
}

Output:

Start
Learning Java
End

But in real-world applications, we sometimes need to make decisions based on conditions. For example, an ATM should allow a withdrawal only when the account has sufficient balance.

This is where control flow statements are useful.

2. Types of Control Flow Statements

Java control flow statements are commonly divided into three categories:

  1. Decision-making statements
  2. Looping statements
  3. Jump statements

Decision-making statements

  • if
  • if-else
  • else-if
  • switch

Looping statements

  • for
  • while
  • do-while

Jump statements

  • break
  • continue
  • return

Decision-Making Statements

1. if Statement

The if statement executes a block of code only when the given condition is true.

Syntax:

if (condition) {
    // Code executes if condition is true
}

Example:

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int age = 20;

        if (age >= 18) {
            System.out.println("Eligible to vote");
        }
    }
}

Output:

Eligible to vote

Here, the condition age >= 18 is true, so Java executes the code inside the if block.

If the condition is false, Java skips the if block.

2. if-else Statement

The if-else statement is used when we want to execute one block of code if the condition is true and another block if the condition is false.

Syntax:

if (condition) {
    // Executes when condition is true
} else {
    // Executes when condition is false
}

Example:

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int balance = 2000;
        int withdrawAmount = 5000;

        if (balance >= withdrawAmount) {
            System.out.println("Withdrawal successful");
        } else {
            System.out.println("Insufficient balance");
        }
    }
}

Output:

Insufficient balance

Here, the account balance is less than the withdrawal amount. Therefore, the else block executes.

3. else-if Ladder

An else-if ladder is used when we have multiple conditions to check.

For example, in an examination result system, we may assign different grades based on students' marks.

Example:

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int marks = 82;

        if (marks < 0 || marks > 100) {
            System.out.println("Invalid marks");

        } else if (marks >= 90) {
            System.out.println("Grade A");

        } else if (marks >= 75) {
            System.out.println("Grade B");

        } else if (marks >= 50) {
            System.out.println("Grade C");

        } else {
            System.out.println("Fail");
        }
    }
}

Output:

Grade B

Here, Java checks the conditions from top to bottom. When it finds the first true condition, it executes that block and skips the remaining conditions.

The first condition validates the marks to ensure they are between 0 and 100.

4. switch Statement

A switch statement is another decision-making statement. It is useful when we need to execute different blocks of code based on the value of an expression.

For example, an ATM application can display different operations based on the customer's selection.

Syntax:

switch (expression) {
    case value1:
        // Code
        break;

    case value2:
        // Code
        break;

    default:
        // Default code
}

Example:

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int choice = 2;

        switch (choice) {
            case 1:
                System.out.println("Check Balance");
                break;

            case 2:
                System.out.println("Withdraw Money");
                break;

            case 3:
                System.out.println("Deposit Money");
                break;

            case 4:
                System.out.println("Exit");
                break;

            default:
                System.out.println("Invalid Choice");
        }
    }
}

Output:

Withdraw Money

Here, the value of choice is 2, so Java executes case 2.

What is break?

The break statement terminates the switch statement. After executing the matching case, Java exits the switch when it encounters break.

What is default?

The default block executes when none of the case values match the switch expression.

What is Fall-through?

If we remove break from a case, Java continues executing the statements in the following cases until it encounters a break or reaches the end of the switch.

Example:

int day = 2;

switch (day) {
    case 1:
        System.out.println("Monday");
        break;

    case 2:
        System.out.println("Tuesday");

    case 3:
        System.out.println("Wednesday");
        break;

    default:
        System.out.println("Invalid Day");
}

Output:

Tuesday
Wednesday

Here, case 2 does not contain a break. Therefore, Java continues executing case 3. This behaviour is called fall-through.

Difference Between if-else and switch

if-else switch
Checks conditions or expressions. Matches an expression against case values.
Supports complex Boolean conditions. Uses matching case labels.
Useful for ranges and multiple conditions. Useful for fixed choices and menu options.
Uses else as the final alternative. Uses default as the fallback.

Conclusion

Control flow statements are essential in Java because they help programs make decisions based on different conditions.

  • if executes code when a condition is true.
  • if-else chooses between two blocks.
  • else-if checks multiple conditions.
  • switch selects a matching case.
  • break exits a switch statement.
  • default handles unmatched switch values.

Understanding these statements provides a strong foundation for developing real-world Java applications such as ATM systems, employee management systems, banking applications, and student result management systems.

title: How to Make a Telegram Mini App: Step-by-Step Tutorial
description:
How to make a Telegram Mini App

To make a Telegram Mini App, create a bot with @botfather, build a web page that loads Telegram’s telegram-web-app.js script, host it on an HTTPS URL, and set that URL as the bot’s menu button or Main Mini App. The page reads the user’s theme and launch data from window.Telegram.WebApp, and your server checks that launch data (initData) with an HMAC-SHA256 signature derived from your bot token before it trusts who the user is. Everything else is ordinary web development.

This tutorial builds a working daily check-in app in plain HTML, JavaScript, and Node.js: the user opens it from the bot, sees their name and points, and taps the bottom button once a day for 10 points. It is small, but it has every part a real Mini App needs: theming, the main button, haptics, server-side validation, and server-side state. Every Telegram API name comes from Telegram’s own docs, mainly the Mini Apps documentation, checked on October 22, 2026 (the newest change listed there is Bot API 10.1 from June 11, 2026).

How a Mini App works: who does what

A Mini App is your own website that Telegram opens in a web view connected to your bot. Telegram adds two things: a JavaScript bridge to the Telegram app, and signed launch data about the user.

Part Where it runs Its job
Bot Telegram Owns the token, the menu button, and the Mini App settings you make in @botfather
Front end Telegram’s web view on the user’s device Your HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, in plain code or any framework
telegram-web-app.js Inside your page Exposes window.Telegram.WebApp: initData, themeParams, MainButton, HapticFeedback, openLink, openInvoice, and more
Your server Your HTTPS host Validates initData, stores users and balances, creates invoices
Bot token Your server only Talks to the Bot API and is the base of the validation key

One rule shapes everything else. Telegram’s docs warn that initDataUnsafe should not be trusted, and that you should use initData on your server only after validating it. Anyone can fake the browser object, so it is for showing a name, never for deciding who gets points.

Step 1: create the bot with BotFather

  1. Open @BotFather in Telegram and send /newbot. BotFather also has its own Mini App with the same functions, if you prefer buttons to commands.

  2. Choose a display name, then a username. Telegram’s bot features page says usernames are 5 to 32 characters, may only use Latin letters, numbers, and underscores, must end in “bot”, and cannot be changed later.

  3. Copy the token BotFather sends, in the form 110201543:AAHdqTcvCH1vGWJxfSeofSAs0K5PALDsaw (Telegram’s sample). Anyone with it can control your bot, and section 4.5 of Telegram’s Bot Platform Developer Terms prohibits making such credentials public. If it leaks, /token generates a new one.

Keep the token in an environment variable on your server, such as BOT_TOKEN, never in your HTML, JavaScript bundle, or Git repository. Make a second bot for testing, too, as Telegram suggests, so you never test on real users.

Step 2: build the front end with telegram-web-app.js

Create public/index.html. Telegram’s docs say to place telegram-web-app.js in the <head> before any other scripts; the ?64 suffix is the version shown in the docs on the day we checked.

<!doctype html>
<html>
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <script src="https://telegram.org/js/telegram-web-app.js?64"></script>
  <style>
    body {
      margin: 0;
      padding: 24px 16px;
      font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
      background: var(--tg-theme-bg-color, #ffffff);
      color: var(--tg-theme-text-color, #000000);
    }
    .hint { color: var(--tg-theme-hint-color, #707579); }
    .points { font-size: 48px; font-weight: 700; color: var(--tg-theme-accent-text-color, #2481cc); }
  </style>
</head>
<body>
  <h1 id="hello">Loading...</h1>
  <p class="points" id="points">0</p>
  <p class="hint" id="status">Claim 10 points once a day.</p>
  <script>
    const tg = window.Telegram.WebApp;
    tg.ready();
    tg.expand();

    async function api(path) {
      const res = await fetch(path, {
        method: 'POST',
        headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
        body: JSON.stringify({ initData: tg.initData }),
      });
      return { ok: res.ok, status: res.status, data: await res.json() };
    }

    function show(data) {
      document.getElementById('points').textContent = data.points;
    }

    api('/api/session').then(({ ok, data }) => {
      if (!ok) {
        document.getElementById('hello').textContent = 'Open this app from Telegram';
        return;
      }
      document.getElementById('hello').textContent = 'Hi, ' + data.name;
      show(data);
      tg.MainButton.setText('Claim daily points').show();
    });

    tg.MainButton.onClick(async () => {
      tg.MainButton.showProgress();
      const { ok, status, data } = await api('/api/claim');
      tg.MainButton.hideProgress();
      if (ok) {
        show(data);
        tg.HapticFeedback.notificationOccurred('success');
        document.getElementById('status').textContent = 'Claimed. Come back tomorrow.';
      } else if (status === 409) {
        tg.HapticFeedback.notificationOccurred('warning');
        tg.showAlert('You already claimed today.');
      } else {
        tg.HapticFeedback.notificationOccurred('error');
      }
    });
  </script>
</body>
</html>

What each part does:

  • tg.ready() tells Telegram the app can be shown and hides the loading placeholder. Telegram recommends calling it as early as possible, once the essential interface is loaded.

  • tg.expand() asks for the full available height when Telegram opens the app at part height. A Main Mini App and a direct link already open at full height by default.

  • Theme colors. Each themeParams color is also a CSS variable, such as --tg-theme-bg-color, so the page matches the user’s day or night theme; the value after the comma is the fallback in a normal browser. If you draw with JavaScript, read tg.themeParams and listen for themeChanged.

  • tg.MainButton is the native button at the bottom of the Telegram interface. Its methods return the button, so they chain, and Telegram recommends showProgress() when the action may take a while.

  • tg.HapticFeedback.notificationOccurred() takes success, warning, or error. For taps in games, use impactOccurred() with a style such as light or heavy.

  • tg.initData, the raw signed string, goes to the server on every call. The page never sends a user ID of its own.

Step 3: validate initData on the server in Node.js

Telegram documents the check in Validating data received via the Mini App. In short:

  1. Parse initData as a query string and take out hash.

  2. Sort the remaining fields alphabetically and join them as key=value lines separated by a line feed. This is the data-check-string.

  3. Compute the secret key: HMAC-SHA256 of the bot token, with the constant string WebAppData as the key.

  4. Compute HMAC-SHA256 of the data-check-string with that secret key, in hex, and compare it with hash.

  5. Check auth_date to reject old data.

In Node.js, with only the built-in crypto module, save this as validate-init-data.js:

const crypto = require('node:crypto');

function validateInitData(initData, botToken, maxAgeSeconds = 3600) {
  if (typeof initData !== 'string' || initData === '') return null;
  const params = new URLSearchParams(initData);
  const hash = params.get('hash');
  if (!hash || !/^[0-9a-f]{64}$/.test(hash)) return null;
  params.delete('hash');

  const dataCheckString = [...params.entries()]
    .sort(([a], [b]) => (a < b ? -1 : a > b ? 1 : 0))
    .map(([key, value]) => `${key}=${value}`)
    .join('\n');

  const secretKey = crypto.createHmac('sha256', 'WebAppData').update(botToken).digest();
  const expected = crypto.createHmac('sha256', secretKey).update(dataCheckString).digest();
  if (!crypto.timingSafeEqual(expected, Buffer.from(hash, 'hex'))) return null;

  const authDate = Number(params.get('auth_date'));
  const age = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) - authDate;
  if (!Number.isInteger(authDate) || age > maxAgeSeconds) return null;

  let user = null;
  try {
    user = JSON.parse(params.get('user'));
  } catch {
    return null;
  }
  if (!user || typeof user.id !== 'number') return null;
  return { user, authDate, startParam: params.get('start_param') };
}

module.exports = { validateInitData };

The details that trip people up:

  • Key order in the first HMAC. WebAppData is the key and the bot token is the message; swapping them is the most common bug. Use the result as raw bytes, not hex.

  • Only hash comes out. Every other field stays in the data-check-string, including signature. Telegram added that field with Bot API 8.0 so third parties can check the data with Telegram’s Ed25519 public key without knowing your token; your own HMAC check treats it like any other field.

  • Constant-time comparison. crypto.timingSafeEqual does not leak timing, and Node’s docs say it throws when the two inputs have different byte lengths. The regular expression makes sure hash is exactly 64 hex characters first. What is HMAC? explains why a plain === is not enough.

  • auth_date is the time the app was opened. One hour is the default above. If users keep your app open longer, validate once at launch and issue your own short-lived session token, rather than accepting days-old launch data.

  • Telegram user IDs are big. Telegram says user.id can have more than 32 significant bits (at most 52), so store it as a 64-bit integer, such as BIGINT, never a 32-bit INT.

Now the server. Install Express with npm install express and save this as server.js:

const express = require('express');
const { validateInitData } = require('./validate-init-data');

const BOT_TOKEN = process.env.BOT_TOKEN;
if (!BOT_TOKEN) throw new Error('Set BOT_TOKEN');

const app = express();
app.use(express.json({ limit: '10kb' }));
app.use(express.static('public'));

const points = new Map();
const lastClaim = new Map();

function telegramUser(req, res, next) {
  const result = validateInitData(req.body?.initData, BOT_TOKEN);
  if (!result) return res.status(401).json({ error: 'invalid init data' });
  req.tgUser = result.user;
  next();
}

app.post('/api/session', telegramUser, (req, res) => {
  const id = req.tgUser.id;
  res.json({ name: req.tgUser.first_name, points: points.get(id) ?? 0 });
});

app.post('/api/claim', telegramUser, (req, res) => {
  const id = req.tgUser.id;
  const today = new Date().toISOString().slice(0, 10);
  if (lastClaim.get(id) === today) {
    return res.status(409).json({ error: 'already claimed today', points: points.get(id) ?? 0 });
  }
  lastClaim.set(id, today);
  points.set(id, (points.get(id) ?? 0) + 10);
  res.json({ points: points.get(id) });
});

app.listen(process.env.PORT ?? 3000);

Every API route runs telegramUser first, so handlers only see validated users. The Map objects keep the example short; use a database in production. Start it with BOT_TOKEN=your-token node server.js.

Test the validation locally with a generated test vector

You do not need Telegram to test the check. This helper signs a launch string the way Telegram does, using a fake token. Save it as make-test-init-data.js:

const crypto = require('node:crypto');

function makeTestInitData(botToken, fields) {
  const params = new URLSearchParams(fields);
  const dataCheckString = [...params.entries()]
    .sort(([a], [b]) => (a < b ? -1 : a > b ? 1 : 0))
    .map(([key, value]) => `${key}=${value}`)
    .join('\n');
  const secretKey = crypto.createHmac('sha256', 'WebAppData').update(botToken).digest();
  params.set('hash', crypto.createHmac('sha256', secretKey).update(dataCheckString).digest('hex'));
  return params.toString();
}

module.exports = { makeTestInitData };

Then a short test, check-init-data.js: a valid string must pass, and a changed user ID or a different token must fail.

const assert = require('node:assert');
const { validateInitData } = require('./validate-init-data');
const { makeTestInitData } = require('./make-test-init-data');

const token = '123456789:TEST-token-for-local-checks-only';
const initData = makeTestInitData(token, {
  query_id: 'AAHtest',
  user: JSON.stringify({ id: 42, first_name: 'Ana' }),
  auth_date: String(Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000)),
});

assert.strictEqual(validateInitData(initData, token).user.id, 42);
assert.strictEqual(validateInitData(initData.replace('%22id%22%3A42', '%22id%22%3A43'), token), null);
assert.strictEqual(validateInitData(initData, '123456789:another-token'), null);
console.log('initData checks passed');

node check-init-data.js prints initData checks passed.

Why we also checked against an outside example

A helper that signs the same way as your validator can share its bugs, so we also ran the validator against the worked example in the community Telegram Mini Apps init data docs (age limit raised, since that sample is from 2022), and it passed. All code on this page ran on Node.js 22 with Express 5.3; tampered, expired, and missing launch data got a 401.

Step 4: host it on HTTPS and connect it to the bot

Telegram’s Bot API describes a Mini App URL as “an HTTPS URL”, so production needs a real certificate. You have three practical options:

  • Your own host. Any server that runs Node.js behind HTTPS works. Serve the page and the API from the same origin, as server.js does, and you avoid CORS.

  • A tunnel while you develop. Cloudflare’s Quick Tunnels give a local server a temporary trycloudflare.com URL with no account: run cloudflared tunnel --url http://localhost:3000. Cloudflare says they are for testing only, and the URL stops working when you stop the tunnel.

  • Telegram Serverless. Since October 6, 2026, Telegram Serverless can host a Mini App’s built front end at https://app<app_id>.tgcloud.ai/ and run endpoint functions that the page calls with Telegram.WebApp.Serverless.call. Telegram validates initData before it runs an endpoint. It is a different setup (JavaScript modules deployed with the tgcloud CLI), worth a look if you would rather not run a server.

Once the page is online, tell Telegram where it is. Telegram supports seven launch methods; these are the ones most apps use:

Launch method How to set it up Good to know
Main Mini App @botfather: /mybots, select the bot, Bot Settings, Configure Mini App, Enable Mini App Adds a Launch app button and media previews to the bot profile; opens from https://t.me/botusername?startapp; full height by default
Menu button /setmenubutton in BotFather, or setChatMenuButton in the Bot API for specific users Works the same way as a launch from an inline button
Inline button A web_app button under a bot message Gets the user and a query_id for answerWebAppQuery
Direct link https://t.me/botusername/appname Gets chat_type and chat_instance; add mode=compact to open at half height
Keyboard button A web_app keyboard button sendData sends up to 4096 bytes back to the bot and closes the app; launch data is empty
Attachment menu /setattach in BotFather Only for major advertisers on the Telegram Ad Platform, but every bot can use it in the test environment

For most apps, set a Main Mini App and a menu button with the same URL. Avoid the keyboard button for anything account-based: Telegram’s docs say the launch data is empty when the app opens from a keyboard button or inline mode, so there is no signed user to check. With ?startapp=summer in a link, the value arrives as start_param in initData; if it affects rewards, such as a referral code, read it on the server from validated data, as the validator above returns it.

Mistakes that break a Mini App’s security

Putting the bot token in front-end code, trusting initDataUnsafe or a user ID the page sends, skipping the auth_date check, comparing hashes with ===, and crediting points or goods from a client message instead of from your own server’s decision.

Step 5: test and debug your Mini App

Telegram offers a dedicated test environment, completely separate from the main one, where you create a new account and a new bot with BotFather. On iOS you reach it by tapping the Settings icon 10 times, then Accounts, Login to another account, Test; on Telegram Desktop, with Shift + Alt + right click on Add Account, then Test Server. There you may use plain HTTP links without TLS, and Bot API calls go to https://api.telegram.org/bot<token>/test/METHOD_NAME. Flood limits are not raised and may be stricter.

To inspect the page itself, turn on web view debugging:

  • Android: enable USB debugging, press and hold the version number at the bottom of Telegram Settings twice, choose Enable WebView Debug, and open chrome://inspect/#devices in Chrome.

  • iOS: tap Settings 10 times, toggle Allow Web View Inspection, connect the phone by USB, and use Safari’s Develop menu on your Mac.

  • Desktop: in the Beta version for Windows and Linux, enable webview inspection under Settings, Advanced, Experimental settings; in the macOS Beta, click Settings 5 times and enable Debug Mini Apps. Then right click and inspect.

Then run through the example: open it from the menu button, claim once and get 10 points, claim again and see the alert, switch between day and night themes, and open the URL in a normal browser, where the server must return 401.

Payments: sell digital goods only in Telegram Stars

Section 6.2 of the Bot Platform Developer Terms says all transactions for digital goods and services in a bot or Mini App must use Telegram Stars, because of the rules of the stores that host Telegram’s apps. Telegram’s Stars payments guide describes the flow, checked on October 22, 2026:

  1. Your server creates an invoice with sendInvoice or, for a Mini App, createInvoiceLink, with currency set to XTR, an empty provider_token, and exactly one price item.

  2. The page opens the link with tg.openInvoice(url, callback). The callback and the invoiceClosed event report paid, cancelled, failed, or pending.

  3. Your bot answers the pre_checkout_query update with answerPreCheckoutQuery within 10 seconds, or the transaction is canceled.

  4. You deliver only after the successful_payment update arrives, and store its telegram_payment_charge_id in case you need refundStarPayment.

The page’s paid status only updates the interface; delivery happens on the server. Your bot must also answer /paysupport, and section 6.2.1 says refunds come out of your balance. Physical goods use third-party payment providers instead. How to monetize a Telegram bot covers Stars subscriptions, paid media, and ad revenue, and Telegram Stars vs offerwall compares Stars with letting users earn. Once you sell for Stars, you can also start an affiliate program from the Mini App’s profile, as explained in affiliate marketing on Telegram.

Adding an offerwall to your Mini App

Once you have validated users and server-side balances, an offerwall is a small addition. Your server builds a signed offerwall link for the user’s own account ID, the page opens it with tg.openLink() in a tap handler (Telegram only allows openLink in response to a user interaction), and your server credits points when the offerwall sends a signed postback. If you also sell the same points, the Stars rule applies to those sales.

We cover the full integration, with code, in Add an offerwall to a Telegram Mini App, so we will not repeat it here. For the parts around it, see what to check before you choose an offerwall for a Mini App, the Node.js postback handler, postback security, and, if your Mini App is a game, how to build a Telegram tap-to-earn game. When the app works, how to grow a Telegram Mini App is the next step.

Where Moonetix fits in a Telegram Mini App

Moonetix is an affiliate network. A Mini App needs no SDK: your server signs one offerwall link per user, and Moonetix sends a signed server-to-server postback for every credit and every reversal, so points land in the same balance as the daily check-in above. Each app sets its own currency name and icon, conversion rate, user split, and wall design with a live preview. Offers depend on the user’s country and device, users on VPNs, proxies, Tor, or data center networks are blocked from the wall, and end users must be at least 16. Every publisher application is reviewed by hand, and once your account is approved, each app you add on a website we already checked is live right away. See how the wall works, or get in touch with questions.

Frequently asked questions

What language is a Telegram Mini App written in?

The front end is HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, in plain code or any framework such as React or Vue. The backend can be any language, because the initData check only needs HMAC-SHA256.

How do I validate Telegram Mini App initData?

Send Telegram.WebApp.initData to your server, remove hash, sort the other fields as key=value lines joined with a line feed, and compute HMAC-SHA256 of that string with a key that is the HMAC-SHA256 of your bot token under the key WebAppData. The hex result must equal hash, and auth_date must be recent.

What is the difference between initData and initDataUnsafe?

initData is the raw signed string meant for validation on your server. initDataUnsafe is the same data parsed into an object in the browser, and Telegram says it should not be trusted.

Do I need a server for a Telegram Mini App?

A purely static page needs only HTTPS hosting, but anything that must be trusted, such as accounts, points, or payments, needs a backend. That can be your own server or Telegram Serverless endpoints.

Can I test a Telegram Mini App without HTTPS?

Yes, in Telegram’s test environment, which allows plain HTTP links. In production, the Mini App URL must be HTTPS.

How do I open a Mini App from a link?

Set a Main Mini App in BotFather and share https://t.me/botusername?startapp. Add a value, such as ?startapp=summer, and it reaches your app as start_param.

This guide was first published in the Moonetix Academy.

title: Offerwall Postback in Node.js, Express and Next.js
description:
How do you handle an offerwall postback in Node.js?

Expose one GET route that reads the transaction ID, user ID, reward, status and hash as plain strings, recomputes the HMAC-SHA256 of tx:user:reward:status with your postback secret key, and compares it with crypto.timingSafeEqual after a length check. If it matches, apply the event inside a database transaction that locks one row per transaction ID: add the reward on status 1, take it back on status 2 only if you credited it, and skip repeats. Answer 200 for everything you accepted or ignored, 403 for a bad hash, and 500 when your own code fails, so the call is retried.

This guide gives you that as one small module you can share between an Express app and a Next.js App Router project, plus the signed offerwall link. It assumes you know why each check exists. If you do not, read Postback security first, and What is a postback URL? for the basics. The PHP version is in Offerwall PHP integration: Laravel and plain PHP.

Who does what

Part Does Never does
Browser or app Shows the signed link it got from your server Holds the link hash salt or the postback secret key, adds currency
Your Node.js server Signs the link, verifies postbacks, owns the wallet table Trusts a balance change that did not come from a verified postback
Moonetix Shows offers, tracks results, sends a signed postback for every credit and every reversal Pays your users directly

You need three values: the app ID in your offerwall link and the link hash salt from your offerwall’s settings page, and the postback secret key from the Postback page. The salt signs links and the key signs postbacks. They are different values, and mixing them up is the most common reason for a Link not valid page or a 403 on every postback.

Step 1: one shared module

Both frameworks call the same file, so the security logic exists once. It uses node:crypto and the pg client for PostgreSQL. Store the keys in environment variables (MOONETIX_APP_ID, MOONETIX_LINK_SALT, MOONETIX_POSTBACK_KEY, DATABASE_URL) and keep the .env file out of your repository.

First the table. One row per transaction ID, with the last status you applied:

CREATE TABLE moonetix_tx (
  transaction_id text PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id        text NOT NULL,
  reward         numeric NOT NULL,
  last_status    smallint,
  updated_at     timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

Then the module. The examples credit a coins column of type numeric on your users table:

// lib/moonetix.js (ES module)
import crypto from 'node:crypto';
import pg from 'pg';

const pool = new pg.Pool({ connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL });
const KEYS = ['tx', 'user', 'reward', 'status', 'hash'];

function env(name) {
  const value = process.env[name];
  if (!value) throw new Error(`${name} is not set`);
  return value;
}

export function wallUrl(userId) {
  const id = String(userId);
  const hash = crypto.createHmac('sha256', env('MOONETIX_LINK_SALT')).update(id).digest('hex');
  return `https://wall.moonetix.com/${env('MOONETIX_APP_ID')}?user_id=${encodeURIComponent(id)}&hash=${hash}`;
}

export function readParams(get) {
  const p = {};
  for (const key of KEYS) {
    const value = get(key);
    if (typeof value !== 'string') return null;
    p[key] = value;
  }
  return p;
}

function validHash(p) {
  const expected = Buffer.from(
    crypto.createHmac('sha256', env('MOONETIX_POSTBACK_KEY'))
      .update(`${p.tx}:${p.user}:${p.reward}:${p.status}`)
      .digest('hex')
  );
  const given = Buffer.from(p.hash);
  return given.length === expected.length && crypto.timingSafeEqual(given, expected);
}

async function applyEvent(p) {
  const status = Number(p.status);
  const client = await pool.connect();
  try {
    await client.query('BEGIN');
    await client.query(
      'INSERT INTO moonetix_tx (transaction_id, user_id, reward) VALUES ($1, $2, $3) ON CONFLICT (transaction_id) DO NOTHING',
      [p.tx, p.user, p.reward]
    );
    const { rows } = await client.query(
      'SELECT user_id, reward, last_status FROM moonetix_tx WHERE transaction_id = $1 FOR UPDATE',
      [p.tx]
    );
    const row = rows[0];

    if (status === 1 && row.last_status === null) {
      const r = await client.query('UPDATE users SET coins = coins + $1::numeric WHERE id = $2', [p.reward, p.user]);
      if (r.rowCount === 0) console.warn('moonetix: unknown user', p.user, p.tx);
      await client.query('UPDATE moonetix_tx SET last_status = 1, updated_at = now() WHERE transaction_id = $1', [p.tx]);
    } else if (status === 2 && row.last_status === 1) {
      await client.query('UPDATE users SET coins = coins - $1 WHERE id = $2', [row.reward, row.user_id]);
      await client.query('UPDATE moonetix_tx SET last_status = 2, updated_at = now() WHERE transaction_id = $1', [p.tx]);
    } else if (status === 2 && row.last_status === null) {
      await client.query('UPDATE moonetix_tx SET last_status = 2, updated_at = now() WHERE transaction_id = $1', [p.tx]);
    }

    await client.query('COMMIT');
  } catch (err) {
    await client.query('ROLLBACK');
    throw err;
  } finally {
    client.release();
  }
}

export async function handlePostback(p) {
  if (!p || !validHash(p)) return 403;
  if (p.tx.startsWith('test_')) {
    console.info('moonetix: test postback', p.tx, p.status);
    return 200;
  }
  await applyEvent(p);
  return 200;
}

Why it is written this way

  • One string per parameter. readParams takes a getter, so each framework decides how to read the query, and anything that is not exactly one string (missing, or an array from a repeated parameter) is rejected with 403 before hashing.

  • Byte length, not string length. The Node.js docs say timingSafeEqual throws if the two inputs have different byte lengths. A hash with non-ASCII characters can have the right number of characters and still a different number of bytes, so the check compares the two Buffers, and a forged hash gets a 403 instead of an exception.

  • Values hashed unchanged. The reward goes into the HMAC exactly as it arrived. Convert nothing before the check.

  • No floats. The reward goes from the query string to PostgreSQL as text and is added as numeric. Parsing it with Number() first would push a decimal reward through binary floating point for no reason.

  • One client for the whole transaction. The node-postgres docs say you must use the same client instance for every statement in a transaction and must not use pool.query for it. That is why the code calls pool.connect() and releases the client in finally.

  • The row lock does the idempotency. ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING creates the row on the first event, and FOR UPDATE makes a second copy of the same event wait until the first commits. It then sees last_status already set and changes nothing.

  • Reversals use the stored values. Status 2 takes back the reward saved with the credit, from the user it went to. A reversal for a transaction you never credited is recorded as 2, so a late copy of that credit, for example one you resend by hand, cannot pay afterwards.

  • Lazy key checks. env() throws when a key is missing, so a server without its key answers 500 and the event is retried, instead of hashing with an empty secret. Reading the keys inside the functions, not at import time, also keeps next build from failing on a build machine that has no secrets.

Test postbacks sent from the dashboard always have a transaction ID that starts with test_ and offer_id 0. The module checks their hash and logs them without crediting anyone. Remove that branch if you prefer to credit a test user and take the coins back by hand.

Step 2: the Express route

With the module in place, the Express side is two short routes: one that hands a signed link to your logged-in front end, and one that receives postbacks.

// server.js (Express 5, "type": "module" in package.json)
import express from 'express';
import { wallUrl, readParams, handlePostback } from './lib/moonetix.js';

const app = express();

app.get('/api/offerwall-link', requireLogin, (req, res) => {
  res.set('Cache-Control', 'private, no-store');
  res.json({ url: wallUrl(req.user.id) });
});

app.get('/moonetix/postback', async (req, res) => {
  const status = await handlePostback(readParams((key) => req.query[key]));
  res.sendStatus(status);
});

app.listen(3000);

  • requireLogin stands for your own session middleware. Your React, Vue or mobile front end calls /api/offerwall-link, gets the URL, and puts it in an iframe or a WebView. no-store stops any cache from handing one user’s signed link to another.

  • The Express 5 migration guide says rejected promises in handlers are now passed to the error handler as if you called next(err), and Express’s default error handler answers 500. So a database error during handlePostback becomes a 500, and Moonetix retries the event. On Express 4 you need a try/catch that sends 500 yourself.

  • The same guide says Express 5 changed the default query parser from “extended” to “simple”. With either one, ?tx=a&tx=b gives you an array, which is why readParams checks the type.

  • Keep the postback route outside anything built for browsers: login checks, CSRF middleware, per-IP rate limiters. Every postback comes from Moonetix’s servers, so a per-IP limit can block a busy day’s worth of genuine calls. The hash is what protects the route.

Set the postback URL on the Postback page of your dashboard with the macros the module reads, using the exact final address:

https://yoursite.com/moonetix/postback?tx={transaction_id}&user={user_id}&reward={reward}&status={status}&hash={hash}

You can add more macros for your logs, such as {event_id}, {offer_name}, {payout}, {sub1} or {integration}. Only the four signed values decide what you credit.

Step 3: the Next.js route handler

In the App Router, a route.ts file exports a function per HTTP method. The Next.js docs pass it a NextRequest and read query values with request.nextUrl.searchParams:

// app/api/moonetix/postback/route.ts
import type { NextRequest } from 'next/server';
import { readParams, handlePostback } from '@/lib/moonetix';

export const runtime = 'nodejs';

export async function GET(request: NextRequest) {
  const sp = request.nextUrl.searchParams;
  const params = readParams((key) => (sp.getAll(key).length === 1 ? sp.get(key) : undefined));
  try {
    return new Response(null, { status: await handlePostback(params) });
  } catch (err) {
    console.error('moonetix postback failed', err);
    return new Response(null, { status: 500 });
  }
}

Notes specific to Next.js:

  • searchParams.get() returns only the first value of a repeated parameter, so the handler counts values with getAll() and rejects anything that is not exactly one.

  • Pin the Node.js runtime. The module needs node:crypto and a TCP database connection. runtime = 'nodejs' is the default, and writing it down stops someone from switching the route to the Edge runtime later.

  • Caching. The Next.js version history says GET handlers changed from static to dynamic by default in version 15. If you are still on 14 or earlier, add export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic'.

  • No redirects. By default Next.js redirects /path/ to /path, and with trailingSlash: true it does the opposite. Moonetix does not follow redirects, so register the path in the form your config serves, with no redirect in between.

  • Proxy (formerly middleware). In Next.js 16 the middleware file was renamed proxy, and without a matcher it runs on every request. If it redirects signed-out visitors to a login page, exclude /api/moonetix/postback from its matcher, or every postback gets a redirect.

The signed link in a Server Component

Pages in the App Router are Server Components by default, so they can sign the link directly. Next.js only puts environment variables that start with NEXT_PUBLIC_ into the browser bundle, so never give the salt that prefix.

// app/earn/page.tsx
import { redirect } from 'next/navigation';
import { getCurrentUser } from '@/lib/auth';
import { wallUrl } from '@/lib/moonetix';

export default async function EarnPage() {
  const user = await getCurrentUser();
  if (!user) redirect('/login');

  return (
    <main>
      <h1>Earn coins</h1>
      <iframe
        title="Earn coins"
        src={wallUrl(user.id)}
        style={{ border: 0, width: '100%', height: 'calc(100vh - 64px)' }}
      />
    </main>
  );
}

getCurrentUser stands for your auth library’s session lookup. When it reads the session cookie, Next.js renders the page per request, so every user gets their own link. In a Next.js-only project, add import 'server-only' at the top of lib/moonetix.js, and the Next.js docs say importing it into a Client Component then fails at build time. Leave it out if Express shares the file: outside the Next.js server bundle, the package throws as soon as it is imported.

The iframe only loads on https pages of the website you registered for the app and its subdomains. If you send a Content Security Policy, allow https://wall.moonetix.com in frame-src. To open the wall in a pop-up from any page instead, see Add a floating Earn button to any website.

Express and Next.js side by side

Concern Express 5 Next.js App Router
Postback route app.get('/moonetix/postback', ...) app/api/moonetix/postback/route.ts exporting GET
Reading a value req.query.tx request.nextUrl.searchParams.get('tx')
Repeated parameter Becomes an array get() returns the first value
Uncaught error Default error handler answers 500 Catch it and return 500
Redirect traps Your own http to https or www rules, reverse proxy trailingSlash, proxy redirects
Where the link is signed A JSON endpoint behind your login A Server Component page

Credits, reversals and retries

Every event of one result carries the same {transaction_id}, and there are only two statuses:

Incoming status Last status in your table What the module does
1 (credited) none Adds the reward, stores 1
1 (credited) 1 or 2 Nothing, answers 200
2 (reversed) 1 Takes back the stored reward, stores 2
2 (reversed) none Stores 2 so a late credit cannot pay, answers 200
2 (reversed) 2 Nothing, answers 200

Amounts are never negative: a reversal carries the same positive {reward} as the credit, and the status tells you to subtract. An offer with several steps sends each step as its own result with its own transaction ID, so each step is simply another row. If the user has already spent the coins, the module lets the balance go below zero. You can instead hold withdrawals until it is recovered, as long as your terms allow it. Publisher earnings and reversals covers the business side.

Moonetix waits up to 6 seconds for any 2xx answer and does not read the body. On a failure or timeout it tries again up to 5 times, after about 1 minute, 5 minutes, 30 minutes, 2 hours and 6 hours, and events of one transaction arrive in order. Keep anything slow, such as emails or push notifications, out of the request: queue it after the commit. On a serverless host, a cold start plus a new database connection eats into those 6 seconds, so use your provider’s connection pooler. If the last retry fails too, you can send the postback again from your dashboard; see How to resend a failed postback.

Node.js mistakes that cost real coins

Comparing hashes with === instead of timingSafeEqual. Calling timingSafeEqual without a length check, so a short forged hash throws and your route answers 500 to an attacker. Running BEGIN through pool.query, so the lock and the update land on different connections. Answering 200 before the database commit, so a crash loses the credit with no retry. And crediting {payout} or another unsigned macro instead of the signed {reward}.

Step 4: test it before you go live

  1. In Integration status in the Integration section, use Check a link and its Test a link tool. Type the same user ID your code uses and compare the two links. They must be identical.

  2. Click Send a test postback in Integration status and check that your server answered 200 and logged a test_ transaction.

Test the crediting path locally with a hash you compute yourself, with MOONETIX_POSTBACK_KEY exported in your shell and a test user 42 in your database. Sample values only (use /moonetix/postback for the Express app):

TX=local_1 U=42 R=150 S=1
HASH=$(node -e "const c=require('node:crypto');console.log(c.createHmac('sha256',process.env.MOONETIX_POSTBACK_KEY).update(process.argv[1]).digest('hex'))" "$TX:$U:$R:$S")
curl -i "http://localhost:3000/api/moonetix/postback?tx=$TX&user=$U&reward=$R&status=$S&hash=$HASH"

  1. Run it twice: user 42 should gain 150 coins once. Change S to 2, recompute the hash, run it again, and the 150 coins come back off.

  2. Change one character of the hash and run it again. You must get 403. Then add &tx=x to the URL: also 403.

  3. After going live, every attempt and your server’s status code is in Reports, Postbacks. The Testing and troubleshooting docs list the common errors.

The full launch checklist is in How to test your app before it goes live. If a key leaks, replace it and redeploy the new environment variable right away, as described in How to rotate your keys and link salt.

Reference docs

The exact macros, statuses and hash format are in the Moonetix Postbacks, Credits and reversals and Offerwall link docs. For the platform APIs used above, see the Node.js crypto.timingSafeEqual and crypto.createHmac reference, the Express routing guide and Express 5 migration guide, the Next.js route.js reference and proxy.js reference, and the node-postgres page on transactions (all checked on October 21, 2026). Working in Python instead? See Offerwall postback in Python. For why rewards travel server to server at all, read What is server-to-server tracking? and Postback vs pixel tracking.

To check your handler, paste a postback it received into the postback hash checker: it shows the exact string that is signed and why a hash does not match.

One handler for every Moonetix integration

Moonetix is an affiliate network. Every app sends a signed server-to-server postback for every credit and every reversal, whether the user came through the offerwall link or iframe, the floating Earn button, the Offers API, or the Android, iOS, Unity, Flutter or React Native SDKs, so the module above serves all of them. Each app sets its own currency name, conversion rate, user split and rounding, and the {reward} arrives already converted. Every publisher application is reviewed by hand. See how the wall works, or get in touch.

Frequently asked questions

How do I verify a postback hash in Node.js?

Compute crypto.createHmac('sha256', key).update(${tx}:${user}:${reward}:${status}).digest('hex') with the values exactly as received. Turn both hashes into Buffers, check they have the same length, and compare them with crypto.timingSafeEqual.

Why does crypto.timingSafeEqual throw an error?

The two inputs have different byte lengths, which Node.js treats as an error rather than a mismatch. Compare the Buffer lengths first and return 403 when they differ.

Should the postback be an API route in Next.js?

Yes. Put it in a route.ts file under app/ that exports GET, keep it on the Node.js runtime, and make sure no proxy redirect or trailing slash redirect sits in front of it.

How do I stop a postback from crediting twice in Node.js?

Store the last status per transaction ID, and lock that row with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE inside a database transaction on a single client. A retry or a duplicate then finds the status already set and changes nothing.

What should a Node.js postback handler return?

Any 2xx within 6 seconds for events you applied or deliberately ignored, 403 for an invalid hash, and 500 when your own code or database fails, so the event is retried later.

Can I build the signed offerwall link in React?

Only on the server. Sign it in a Server Component or an API endpoint and send the finished URL to the browser, because anything in client JavaScript, including the salt, can be read by users.

This guide was first published in the Moonetix Academy.

title: Limitcast 0.20.10 fixes subagent caps under parallel starts
description:
Limitcast 0.20.10 is available on npm. The patch makes the per-session subagent cap hold when several starts arrive together. It also makes the scheduled-jobs report and Codex diagnostics more precise.

Subagent caps count starts, even in parallel

In 0.20.9, parallel hook processes could read the same count and each allow an agent to start. Limitcast now checks the count and reserves a slot together. It counts starts the guard admits, including any the host later rejects. Completion receipts still report usage, and a delayed receipt or long-running agent no longer reopens a slot.

With the guard installed, set a cap for one type in Claude Code, Codex, or Grok. Type names are case-insensitive. Resuming an existing subagent skips the count.

limitcast budget type Explore 1
limitcast budget type explore off

What the jobs report can tell you

limitcast report --jobs now labels connector activity as main-thread evidence. A connector with no recorded main-thread call can still be used by a child agent or a hook. Check those dependencies before testing a run with hooks disabled.

The report also describes how much of the prompt was served from cache. It leaves the cause of a cache miss open.

Codex doctor shows which hooks are disabled

limitcast doctor reports disabled Codex hooks separately from hooks that need approval. A trusted hook can still be disabled, so the distinction tells you what to check in /hooks.

Install the patch 

npm install -g limitcast@0.20.10
limitcast doctor

All 11 CI jobs passed on the release commit. In a fresh npm install, a cap of one admitted exactly one of six parallel test requests. The full list of changes is in the 0.20.10 changelog.

Originally published on limitcast.dev.

AI disclosure: This post was drafted with AI from the release changelog, source, and verified test results.

title: Snowflake Architecture
description:
Alright, let's dive deep into the world of Snowflake, shall we? Imagine a massive, crystal-clear glacier – that's kind of the vibe you get when you think about Snowflake. It's a cloud-based data warehousing platform that's totally changed the game for businesses looking to wrangle their data mountains. Forget the old-school, clunky systems; Snowflake is all about sleek, scalable, and, dare I say, fun data management.

So, What's the Big Deal with Snowflake? (Introduction)

In a nutshell, Snowflake is a Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) data warehouse built from the ground up for the cloud. It's not just another database; it's a revolutionary approach to storing, processing, and analyzing data that's fast, flexible, and surprisingly easy to use. Think of it as the Tesla of data warehousing – modern, powerful, and way ahead of the curve.

Before Snowflake, dealing with big data was like trying to herd cats through a maze. You had on-premises servers to manage, complex infrastructure to maintain, and scaling was a headache that involved buying more hardware and praying it worked. Snowflake swoops in and says, "Nah, we got this." It leverages the power of the cloud (think AWS, Azure, or GCP) to handle all the heavy lifting, so you can focus on what really matters: getting insights from your data.

This article is going to be your friendly guide to understanding Snowflake's architecture. We'll break down the "how" and the "why," so you can impress your colleagues and maybe even build some awesome data solutions yourself.

Before You Jump In: A Quick Checklist (Prerequisites)

While Snowflake is designed to be accessible, there are a few things that make the journey smoother. You don't need to be a distributed systems guru, but a basic understanding of a few concepts will definitely help:

  • Cloud Computing Fundamentals: You should have a general idea of what cloud platforms like AWS, Azure, or GCP are and how they work (e.g., virtual machines, storage, networking). Snowflake runs on these, so knowing the foundation is key.
  • SQL Savvy: Snowflake is all about SQL. If you know your SELECT from your JOIN, you're golden. Snowflake's SQL dialect is largely standard, with some powerful extensions.
  • Data Warehousing Concepts (Nice to Have): Understanding what a data warehouse is, why companies use them, and basic concepts like ETL/ELT will give you context for why Snowflake is so beneficial.
  • A Cloud Account (for Hands-On): If you want to play around with Snowflake yourself (highly recommended!), you'll need an account with one of the supported cloud providers. Snowflake offers a generous free trial, so don't be shy!

The Magic Behind the Curtain: Snowflake's Architecture Explained

This is where things get really interesting. Snowflake's architecture is its secret sauce. It's designed in a way that separates storage and compute, which is a big deal. Traditionally, these were tightly coupled, leading to all sorts of scaling problems. Snowflake breaks this mold with its three-layer architecture:

1. Database Storage: The Cold, Unchanging Glacier

This layer is where all your raw data, metadata, and query results live. It's built on top of your chosen cloud provider's object storage (like Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage, or Google Cloud Storage).

  • How it Works: Snowflake doesn't store your data in traditional database blocks. Instead, it breaks down your data into micro-partitions. These are small, columnar chunks of data, typically between 50MB and 500MB uncompressed.
  • Why it's Cool:
    • Cost-Effective: Object storage is incredibly cheap and durable.
    • Scalable: The cloud's storage is practically infinite.
    • Automatic Optimization: Snowflake automatically compresses, encrypts, and optimizes these micro-partitions. It also maintains metadata about these partitions, including statistics about the data within them. This metadata is crucial for query optimization later.
    • Immutability: Once data is written, it's not modified. This simplifies concurrency control and enables powerful features like Time Travel.

Code Snippet (Illustrative - Not actual storage commands):

While you don't directly interact with S3 buckets for storage, internally Snowflake manages it. Think of it conceptually like this:

-- Creating a table in Snowflake implicitly writes data to cloud storage
CREATE TABLE customers (
    customer_id INT,
    name VARCHAR,
    email VARCHAR
);

-- When you insert data, Snowflake breaks it into micro-partitions and stores them.
INSERT INTO customers (customer_id, name, email)
VALUES (1, 'Alice Smith', 'alice@example.com');

2. Query Processing (Compute): The Ever-Flowing Rivers

This is the "engine" of Snowflake. It's a distributed cluster of compute resources that execute your SQL queries. The brilliance here is that this layer is stateless and completely independent of the storage layer.

  • How it Works: When you run a query, Snowflake breaks it down into smaller tasks that are distributed across multiple compute nodes. These nodes fetch the necessary data from the storage layer (using the metadata we talked about to efficiently locate the relevant micro-partitions) and process it.
  • Why it's Cool:
    • Elastic Scalability: This is the game-changer. You can spin up or down compute resources (called "virtual warehouses") on demand, in seconds. Need to run a massive report? Scale up. Done? Scale down to save costs. You can even have multiple virtual warehouses of different sizes running concurrently without impacting each other.
    • Concurrency: Different virtual warehouses can access the same data simultaneously without contention. Imagine one warehouse running a heavy ETL process while another is used for interactive ad-hoc queries – no problem!
    • No Resource Contention: Because compute is separate, a heavy query won't slow down your users' interactive sessions.
    • Cost Control: You pay for compute only when it's actively running.

Code Snippet (Creating and using a Virtual Warehouse):

-- Create a virtual warehouse (think of it as a compute cluster)
CREATE WAREHOUSE analytics_wh
  WITH
    WAREHOUSE_SIZE = 'MEDIUM'
    AUTO_SUSPEND = 60 -- Suspend after 60 seconds of inactivity
    AUTO_RESUME = TRUE; -- Automatically resume when a query is submitted

-- Use the warehouse to run queries
USE WAREHOUSE analytics_wh;

-- Now your queries will run on this warehouse
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE order_date >= '2023-01-01';

-- You can easily scale up for demanding tasks
ALTER WAREHOUSE analytics_wh SET WAREHOUSE_SIZE = 'LARGE';

3. Cloud Services Layer: The Smart Ice-Floes

This is the "brain" of Snowflake. It's a collection of services that manage everything: authentication, access control, metadata management, query optimization, transaction management, and more. It's the orchestrator that makes the magic happen.

  • How it Works: This layer handles requests from users, coordinates with the compute layer, and manages the data in the storage layer. It's the maestro of the orchestra.
  • Why it's Cool:
    • Intelligent Query Optimization: This layer uses the metadata from the storage layer to create highly efficient query plans. It knows which micro-partitions to scan and which to skip, drastically reducing the amount of data that needs to be processed.
    • Metadata Management: It keeps track of all your data, schemas, users, and permissions.
    • Authentication and Security: Handles user logins and ensures data access is properly controlled.
    • Transaction Management: Ensures data consistency and integrity.
    • Caching: Implements various levels of caching (results cache, data cache) to speed up repeated queries.

Key Components within the Cloud Services Layer:

  • Authentication: Verifies user identities.
  • Access Control: Enforces permissions on data.
  • Metadata Management: Stores and manages information about data and its structure.
  • Query Optimization: Analyzes queries and generates efficient execution plans.
  • Transaction Management: Ensures ACID properties.
  • Cloud Controller: Manages the overall Snowflake environment.

The Awesome Perks: Why Businesses Love Snowflake (Advantages)

You're probably starting to see why Snowflake is so popular. Let's hammer home the benefits:

  • Scalability Without Pain: This is the headline. Scale compute up or down in seconds, independently of storage. No more provisioning servers months in advance.
  • Performance: Micro-partitioning, intelligent query optimization, and elastic compute deliver blazing-fast query performance.
  • Cost-Effectiveness: Pay-as-you-go for compute, and leverage cheap cloud object storage. Automatic suspension of warehouses further saves money.
  • Ease of Use: SQL interface means most data professionals can get started quickly. The SaaS model means no infrastructure to manage.
  • Concurrency: Handles many users and workloads simultaneously without performance degradation.
  • Data Sharing: Snowflake's Secure Data Sharing allows you to share live data with other Snowflake accounts (customers, partners, vendors) without copying or moving it. This is revolutionary for collaboration.
  • Time Travel: Go back in time up to 90 days to recover dropped tables, view historical data, or analyze changes over time. It's like a "Ctrl+Z" for your data.
  • Zero-Copy Cloning: Create instant, isolated copies of your databases, schemas, or tables for development, testing, or analytics without duplicating data or incurring extra storage costs.
  • Semi-structured Data Support: Handles JSON, Avro, ORC, Parquet, and XML natively, making it easy to query and analyze diverse data types.
  • Disaster Recovery: Built on robust cloud infrastructure with built-in redundancy and replication options.

Code Snippet (Time Travel):

-- Imagine you accidentally dropped a table
-- DROP TABLE sensitive_data;

-- No worries! You can restore it from yesterday
SELECT * FROM sensitive_data AT(TIMESTAMP => '2023-10-26 10:00:00'::TIMESTAMP_LTZ);

-- Or even better, restore it completely
UNDROP TABLE sensitive_data;

Code Snippet (Zero-Copy Cloning):

-- Create a clone of your production database for a development environment
CREATE DATABASE dev_db CLONE prod_db;

-- Now dev_db is an exact copy, but changes in prod_db won't affect it, and vice-versa.
-- And it took seconds and no extra storage cost (until you make changes).

Not All Sunshine and Rainbows: Potential Downsides (Disadvantages)

No technology is perfect, and Snowflake has its nuances:

  • Cost Can Be Unpredictable (If Not Managed): While cost-effective, if your users aren't mindful of query efficiency or if warehouses are left running unnecessarily, costs can escalate. Strong governance is key.
  • Vendor Lock-in (to an Extent): While Snowflake runs on major clouds, it is still a proprietary platform. Migrating away might require some effort.
  • Limited Control Over Infrastructure: As a SaaS product, you don't have low-level control over the underlying hardware or network. This is usually a good thing, but for niche requirements, it might be a limitation.
  • No Direct File System Access: You can't SSH into a Snowflake server and fiddle with files. All interaction is through SQL and its APIs.
  • Learning Curve for Optimization: While SQL is standard, truly mastering Snowflake's performance optimization techniques requires understanding its architecture and best practices.

The Feature Feast: What Makes Snowflake Shine (Features)

Beyond the core architecture, Snowflake packs a punch with features that empower users:

  • Multi-Cluster Shared Data Architecture: This is the foundation of its scalability and concurrency.
  • Virtual Warehouses: The elastic compute units.
  • Automatic Scaling: Warehouses can automatically scale up or down based on workload.
  • Data Sharing: Secure, real-time data sharing.
  • Time Travel: Recover and review historical data.
  • Zero-Copy Cloning: Instantaneous, cost-effective copies.
  • Snowpipe: Continuous, near real-time data ingestion from cloud storage.
  • Staging Areas: Temporary storage for data before loading.
  • User-Defined Functions (UDFs): Extend SQL with custom logic written in SQL, Java, Python, or Scala.
  • Stored Procedures: Automate complex tasks.
  • Data Marketplace: Discover and access third-party data directly within Snowflake.
  • Role-Based Access Control (RBAC): Granular security for data access.
  • Data Masking and Row Access Policies: Enhance data security and compliance.
  • Integration with BI Tools: Seamless connectivity with popular business intelligence and data visualization tools.

Code Snippet (Snowpipe for Continuous Ingestion):

Imagine you have files arriving in an S3 bucket. Snowpipe can automatically load them into Snowflake without you needing to manually trigger loads.

-- Create a stage pointing to your S3 bucket
CREATE STAGE my_s3_stage
  URL = 's3://my-data-bucket/incoming/'
  CREDENTIALS = (AWS_KEY_ID = '...' AWS_SECRET_KEY = '...');

-- Create a pipe that listens for new files on the stage
CREATE PIPE my_pipe AUTO_INGEST = TRUE AS
  COPY INTO my_target_table
  FROM @my_s3_stage
  FILE_FORMAT = (TYPE = 'CSV');

-- Now, whenever a new CSV file lands in s3://my-data-bucket/incoming/,
-- Snowpipe will automatically load it into my_target_table.

Wrapping It Up: The Snowflake Verdict (Conclusion)

Snowflake has fundamentally reshaped the data warehousing landscape. Its innovative architecture, separating storage and compute, unlocks unprecedented levels of scalability, performance, and flexibility. For businesses drowning in data or looking to gain deeper insights faster, Snowflake offers a compelling, cloud-native solution.

It's not just about faster queries; it's about enabling agility, fostering collaboration through data sharing, and simplifying data management so teams can focus on driving business value. While there are considerations around cost management and the nuances of optimization, the benefits overwhelmingly point towards Snowflake as a leader in modern data warehousing.

If you're looking to modernize your data strategy, take Snowflake for a spin. You might just find that wrangling your data can be surprisingly elegant and, dare I say, enjoyable. It’s a platform that truly lives up to its name – a crystal-clear, powerful, and scalable solution for your data needs.
