title: Fine-tuning on rented GPUs: how to lose a host without losing your steps
description:
GPU marketplaces like Vast.ai are a cheap way to fine-tune open models, as long as the data is not confidential: the host can see
the machine while your job runs. The harder problem is that training scripts assume the hardware under them stays alive.

When a host disappears, two things break:

  1. Checkpoints that only exist on the local disk are gone.
  2. If the machine hangs instead of dying, the rental keeps billing while nothing trains.

Here is what I ended up building, and what the measurements were.

1. Upload checkpoints outside the training loop. A small agent in the container watches the checkpoint directory and uploads
each finished checkpoint to Cloudflare R2. The training script writes a marker file when a checkpoint is complete, so half-written
ones are never uploaded. The agent uses a temporary key that only works for this job's folder.

2. Count traffic and start-up, not only the GPU price. One QLoRA 7B run was billed $0.81, most of it traffic for downloading
the model; after choosing hosts by the full hourly price including traffic, the next run was $0.19. In six later runs the first
training step came 4.5 to 8.5 minutes after renting, and those minutes are billed. My own rule of thumb, not a measurement:
checkpoint often enough that one lost interval costs less than one start-up.

3. Handle the dead host. A supervisor outside the GPU machine checks the instance and the agent's heartbeat. When the host
is gone it rents another machine, the agent restores the last checkpoint and the script resumes. In a test where I destroyed the
machine twice during one run, training continued after 3.5 and 13 minutes.

4. Handle the hung host. If the GPU stops responding for five minutes, or the job makes no progress for half an hour while the
GPU sits idle, the job is moved to another machine.

5. Handle the dead supervisor. If the supervisor itself goes away, nobody replaces failed machines or checks spending
limits. So the agent watches how long it has gone without a new storage key from the supervisor and, after a safety window, stops
the job and the machine from the inside. I tested this on Vast with the window shortened to a few minutes: the machine stopped,
and after that Vast billed only for disk. In normal settings the window is about 2.5–3.5 hours; I have not run a test of that
length.

Do it yourself or not. The hidden price of the free route is someone's time: setup, the recovery logic, a
watcher that runs around the clock and bill monitoring. If nobody on the team owns that, a service costs less
than the hours.

Disclosure: I run NomadGPU (nomadgpu.com), a small service that does the above on your own Vast.ai
account, with spending limits in dollars. Live numbers from our own test jobs:
status.nomadgpu.com/s/status.

title: What happens when a 40-second LLM call outlives Kafka's 30-second lock
description:
Kafka 4.2 made share groups production-ready: queue-style consumption where several consumers take records from the same partitions. Each record is locked to one consumer while it works on it. The default lock is 30 seconds.

Now put an AI agent behind that consumer. One event means a model call, maybe a tool call or two, maybe a retry. Forty seconds is not unusual.

So what happens when the agent is still thinking when the lock expires?

I measured it. Short version: the same event is processed again, up to five times, and every side effect it triggers can happen again. The fixes that work are not the ones I expected, and one framework's built-in fix did not hold.

Why this matters for agents

Classic Kafka consumers are fast: milliseconds per record. A 30-second lock is generous for them. Agents break that assumption:

  • Model latency varies a lot, and the tail is long.
  • Agents call tools, and tools have side effects: create a ticket, send an email, issue a refund.
  • An agent that runs twice on the same event does not just waste tokens. It can act twice.

In share groups, a record whose lock expires is delivered again to the next available consumer, with an increasing delivery count, up to a delivery limit (5 by default). That is correct queue behavior. It is just bad news when one delivery takes longer than the lock.

The experiment

I built this into Streamjack, an open-source harness I'm writing that tests AI agents consuming and producing Kafka events. The test runs on a disposable Kafka 4.2.1 broker with two simulated agent instances in one share group. Each record takes 3 seconds of "thinking" and then triggers one side effect. Timings are scaled down (a 2-second lock instead of 30) so the test runs in seconds; the ratio is the same.

Case Lock Deliveries Side effects
Processing blocks the consumer thread 2 s 5 5
Same, plus deduplication of the side effect 2 s 5 1
Lock longer than processing 6 s 1 1
Lock renewed from a free consumer thread while working 3 s (4.5 s of work) 1 1

It runs in CI on every commit, and each case also asserts that processing finished before the deadline and that exactly one acknowledgement succeeded where the record is delivered once.

Three things I learned

1. Deduplication fixes the side effects, not the work.
With an idempotency key on the side effect, the duplicate actions disappear. But the model still ran five times. For an LLM agent that is five times the cost and latency, and five chances for a non-deterministic model to decide something different.

2. A longer lock works, if you know your worst case.
The broker caps the lock (group.share.max.record.lock.duration.ms, 60 seconds by default). If your agent's p99.9 is above the cap, you cannot configure your way out.

3. Renewal works, but only from a thread that is free to renew.
Kafka 4.2 lets a consumer extend the lock with AcknowledgeType.RENEW. The catch: KafkaShareConsumer is not thread-safe, so the thread that talks to Kafka must stay free while another thread does the slow work:

CompletableFuture<Void> task = CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> slowWork(work));
while (!task.isDone()) {
    Thread.sleep(lock.toMillis() / 4);
    if (task.isDone()) break;
    consumer.acknowledge(current, AcknowledgeType.RENEW);
    consumer.commitSync();
    // The renewed record comes back through a later poll(); acknowledge that copy from now on.
    current = pollFor(consumer, current);
}
consumer.acknowledge(current, AcknowledgeType.ACCEPT);
consumer.commitSync();

A simple poll loop that does the work inline can never renew. That is exactly the "5 deliveries, 5 side effects" row.

What about frameworks?

You would expect your messaging framework to handle renewal. It depends.

  • Spring for Apache Kafka 4.2 has setShareAutoRenewLocks(true). It is off by default.
  • SmallRye Reactive Messaging (the Kafka connector behind Quarkus) renews automatically. In my experiments, with processing slower than the lock, the renewal did not keep the lock: the record was delivered again with an increasing delivery count, and a later record was acknowledged by the broker but never reached the handler. In the scaled-down runs, renewal also failed at every interval afterwards.

With SmallRye's default settings (30-second lock, renewal checked every 5 seconds) and a 40-second simulated model call, the first event was analyzed twice, and the next event still had not reached the agent 150 seconds later.

I reproduced this on Quarkus 3.40 and on a Quarkus 4 release candidate, built a minimal reproducer that also fails on GitHub Actions, and reported it upstream. The root cause is not confirmed yet, so treat this as "test it in your setup", not "this framework is broken".

One more detail from the reproducer: with a very short lock, even a fast handler was sometimes redelivered, apparently because renewal is timed from when the connector received the record. With default settings, renewal starts about 25 seconds in, so this mainly hits slow handlers. Like agents.

What I'd do

  1. Make side effects idempotent in application code. It was the only control that held in every case, including the framework issue. Not in the prompt: in code, keyed by the business id.
  2. Size the lock for your worst-case latency, within the broker's cap. Measure the tail, not the average.
  3. If you rely on renewal, test it with a handler that is slower than the lock. Check the delivery count, and check that the next record is still processed.

The general lesson is older than share groups: an at-least-once system will deliver twice, and an agent that acts must be safe to run twice. LLM latency just makes "twice" much more likely.

The tests, the opt-in framework experiments, and a longer write-up are in Streamjack. There is also a browser demo of the agent attacks Streamjack tests for.

title: From Fragile Spreadsheets to Rust in Days: How Agentic Development Kills Mundane Work
description:
How I replaced a flaky Google Apps Script and a 50,000-row spreadsheet with a high-speed Rust and PostgreSQL billing reconciliation tool in just a few days using agentic development.

Every business has a hidden operational tax, that recurring, soul-crushing workflow held together by manual downloads, duct-taped scripts, and a spreadsheet that takes thirty seconds just to scroll.

For a long time, ours was shipping reconciliation.

Shipping costs are among the hardest numbers in a business to pin down. Charges arrive after the fact, in pieces, and rarely line up neatly with the orders that triggered them. Worse, when you work with a courier that lacks a proper billing API, you are stuck with raw CSV and PDF dumps.

Our previous solution was a classic piece of operational triage: a Google Apps Script watching a Drive folder where CSVs were manually uploaded. It would parse the files and append new charges into a massive Google Sheet ledger.

It worked, until it didn’t:

  • Flaky execution: Silent failures and brittle parsing whenever formats slightly shifted.
  • Painful querying: Getting clean, aggregated data back out of the sheet was a chore.
  • crippling lag: As the ledger ballooned into the tens of thousands of rows, searching slowed to a crawl.
  • Zero intelligence: It had no anomaly detection to flag discrepancies before they cost us money.

In the past, fixing this properly meant spinning up a multi-month internal engineering project, debating architecture, and writing endless boilerplate. Instead, I leaned into agentic development to build a purpose-built replacement in Rust and shipped the core system in days.

The Shift: Moving at the Speed of Thought

Agentic development fundamentally changes the economics of internal tooling. When an AI collaborator can scaffold parsers, generate database migrations, write idiomatic Rust, and iterate on edge cases alongside you, the barrier between "I have an idea to fix this" and "It’s running in production" collapses.

Because the heavy lifting of boilerplate and syntax lookup was offloaded to agents, I could focus purely on system design and business logic, even while working in a language like Rust that I had only recently started exploring for side projects.

Instead of patching the spreadsheet, we replaced it with a high-performance ingestion and screening pipeline:

[ ZIP / Thousands of PDFs & CSVs ] 
               │
               ▼ (Seconds via Rust)
     [ Parallel Parser & Normalizer ]
               │
               ▼
        [ PostgreSQL DB ] ──► Automated Anomaly Screening ──► Exception Queue
  • Bulk Ingestion in Seconds: You drop a ZIP archive, or thousands of raw PDFs and CSVs directly into the tool. Rust’s concurrency and memory efficiency tear through the files, parsing and normalizing the messy courier formats in mere seconds.
  • Structured Storage: Everything lands cleanly in a PostgreSQL database, eliminating the lag, row limits, and fragility of a bloated spreadsheet.
  • Automated Screening: Instead of humans squinting at rows, the system automatically screens incoming charges against our shipment records, surfacing only the exceptions that actually require human judgment.

Four Ways This Changed Our Operation

1. Speed: Reconciliation That Keeps Up With the Business

What used to take hours of careful, repetitive checking every billing cycle now takes moments. High-volume file parsing happens almost instantaneously, freeing our team from routine data entry so they can focus exclusively on resolving flagged exceptions.

2. Accuracy: Clients Billed Right, Every Time

When carrier charges are reconciled against actual shipments quickly and consistently, revenue leakage stops. Clients are billed accurately and promptly, backed by automated screening that catches discrepancies far more reliably than tired human eyes ever could.

3. Insight: Real Visibility Into Spend

Speed was the first goal; visibility was the second. With every shipping cost accounted for in a proper relational database, we can finally report on our spend with confidence what we are paying, where it is going, and how margins shift over time. That gives us a clear picture of internal costs and a stronger footing for operational decisions.

4. Momentum: Days, Not Months

Perhaps the biggest win isn't the tool itself, but the pace it unlocked. Designed and delivered in days rather than months, the architecture is built to evolve. When the business needs a new anomaly check, a custom spend report, or an integration with another part of our stack, we can ship it rapidly without a heavyweight project cycle behind every tweak.

Stop Tolerating Fragile Workflows

The era of accepting flaky scripts and 50,000-row spreadsheets as "good enough for internal ops" is over. When you pair a modern systems language like Rust with agentic development workflows, small teams can build fast, resilient, bespoke software at a pace that used to be impossible.

We got faster billing, tighter reconciliation, and clear cost intelligence and more importantly, a foundation we can keep building on as fast as new needs emerge.

What’s the most fragile spreadsheet or manual script still surviving in your stack? Drop it in the comments, I'd love to hear what you're replacing next.

title: Compare Hetzner server sizes by price and availability
description:
Well, the AI boom has one casualty. Cheap servers. I remember getting a
server with 16 vCPUs and 32 GB of RAM for about $31 a month. When I looked
again, the option I could actually get at that size was over $100 a month.
It hurts your wallet.

Blossom uses Radar to watch Hetzner's stock and move eligible apps from
more expensive servers to cheaper ones when they come back in stock.

In a seven-day snapshot on November 21, 2026, the CX23 was available 24.9%
of the time we observed in Falkenstein and 29.5% in Helsinki. You get small
windows to snag an affordable server.

Here’s the approach Blossom uses now.

  • Compare prices for sizes that can actually run the workload.
  • Look at availability over a week or longer in the regions you can use.Stock at this moment tells you whether you can order today. The historyhelps you pick a size to depend on.
  • Keep a fallback that’s usually available. When a cheaper size returns,bring the replacement up, confirm it’s healthy, move traffic, then retirethe old capacity.

That last step is how we move eligible app capacity on Blossom. With stateful
services, check what happens to open connections before you move anything.

title: Público vs Privado em Go: como funciona a visibilidade (sem public nem private)
description:
Entenda como o Go controla o que é público e privado usando apenas a primeira letra do nome, com exemplos práticos de funções, structs, métodos e pacotes internal.

Se você vem de Java, C# ou TypeScript, provavelmente está acostumado a escrever public e private o tempo todo. Em Go, essas palavras-chave não existem. A visibilidade é definida de um jeito bem mais simples: pela primeira letra do nome.

Neste artigo vamos ver como isso funciona na prática, com exemplos de funções, structs e métodos, e também algumas boas práticas.

A regra de ouro

  • Letra maiúscula → exportado (público): pode ser usado por outros pacotes.
  • Letra minúscula → não exportado (privado): só pode ser usado dentro do mesmo pacote.

Isso vale para funções, variáveis, constantes, tipos, métodos e campos de struct.

package exemplo

var Versao = "1.0.0"   // público
var debug = false      // privado

const MaxItens = 100   // público
const timeout = 30     // privado

type Usuario struct{}  // público
type cache struct{}    // privado

Funções públicas e privadas

Vamos criar um projeto simples com a seguinte estrutura:

meuprojeto/
├── go.mod
├── main.go
└── calculadora/
    └── calculadora.go

calculadora/calculadora.go

package calculadora

// Soma é pública (começa com maiúscula): outros pacotes podem chamar.
func Soma(a, b int) int {
    return validar(a) + validar(b)
}

// validar é privada (começa com minúscula): só o pacote calculadora enxerga.
func validar(n int) int {
    if n < 0 {
        return 0
    }
    return n
}

main.go

package main

import (
    "fmt"

    "meuprojeto/calculadora"
)

func main() {
    fmt.Println(calculadora.Soma(2, 3)) // funciona: 5

    // calculadora.validar(5) // erro de compilação
}

Se você tentar chamar calculadora.validar(5), o compilador reclama:

cannot refer to unexported name calculadora.validar

Ou seja, o próprio compilador garante o encapsulamento. Não precisa de convenção ou de revisão de código para isso.

Structs, campos e métodos

A mesma regra vale para campos e métodos de uma struct. Um padrão muito comum é deixar o campo privado e expor o acesso por métodos públicos:

package conta

type Conta struct {
    Titular string  // público
    saldo   float64 // privado
}

// NovaConta é um "construtor": a forma idiomática de inicializar campos privados.
func NovaConta(titular string) *Conta {
    return &Conta{Titular: titular, saldo: 0}
}

// Depositar é um método público.
func (c *Conta) Depositar(valor float64) {
    if c.valorValido(valor) {
        c.saldo += valor
    }
}

// Saldo é um getter público para ler o campo privado.
func (c *Conta) Saldo() float64 {
    return c.saldo
}

// valorValido é um método privado.
func (c *Conta) valorValido(valor float64) bool {
    return valor > 0
}

Usando em outro pacote:

c := conta.NovaConta("Maria")
c.Depositar(100)

fmt.Println(c.Titular)  // ok
fmt.Println(c.Saldo())  // ok: 100

// c.saldo = 1000       // erro: campo não exportado
// c.valorValido(10)    // erro: método não exportado

Repare que não dá para alterar o saldo diretamente. Toda mudança passa por Depositar, que valida o valor. Isso protege a integridade dos dados da sua struct.

Pontos importantes (e pegadinhas)

1. A unidade de privacidade é o pacote

Em Go, "privado" significa "privado ao pacote", não ao arquivo nem à struct. Se dois arquivos estão na mesma pasta e declaram o mesmo package, eles enxergam as funções privadas um do outro.

Isso é diferente de Java, onde private restringe à classe.

2. Não existe protected

Go não tem herança de classes, então não existe o conceito de protected. Só há dois níveis: exportado e não exportado.

3. Getters não levam o prefixo Get

A convenção do Go é nomear o getter do campo saldo como Saldo(), e não GetSaldo(). Já o setter, se existir, costuma ser SetSaldo().

4. JSON só enxerga campos exportados

Esse é um erro clássico de quem está começando. Campos privados não são serializados pelo pacote encoding/json:

type Produto struct {
    Nome  string  `json:"nome"`
    preco float64 `json:"preco"` // NÃO vai aparecer no JSON!
}

Se o campo precisa aparecer na resposta de uma API, ele precisa começar com maiúscula:

type Produto struct {
    Nome  string  `json:"nome"`
    Preco float64 `json:"preco"` // ok
}

O mesmo vale para bibliotecas de ORM, como o GORM: campos não exportados são ignorados.

5. A pasta internal/

Quer restringir um pacote inteiro? Coloque-o dentro de uma pasta chamada internal/. O compilador só permite que o código do módulo pai (ou da pasta pai) importe esse pacote.

meuprojeto/
├── go.mod
├── cmd/
│   └── api/
│       └── main.go
└── internal/
    ├── handler/
    ├── service/
    └── repository/

Quem importar o seu módulo de fora não consegue acessar nada dentro de internal/. É ótimo para esconder detalhes de implementação sem precisar expor tudo como API pública.

6. Documente o que é público

Tudo que é exportado deve ter um comentário começando com o nome do identificador. O go doc e o pkg.go.dev usam isso para gerar a documentação:

// Soma retorna a soma de dois inteiros, ignorando valores negativos.
func Soma(a, b int) int {
    return validar(a) + validar(b)
}

Boas práticas

  • Comece privado. Exporte apenas o que realmente precisa ser usado por outros pacotes. É fácil tornar algo público depois, mas é difícil (e quebra compatibilidade) tornar público em privado.
  • Mantenha a API pública pequena. Quanto menos você expõe, menos precisa manter e documentar.
  • Use construtores (NovaX) quando a struct tem campos privados que precisam ser inicializados corretamente.
  • Use internal/ para organizar projetos maiores em camadas sem vazar detalhes.

Resumo

Característica Público (exportado) Privado (não exportado)
Nome começa com Maiúscula Minúscula
Acessível em Qualquer pacote Apenas no mesmo pacote
Aparece no JSON Sim Não
Aparece no go doc Sim Não

Conclusão

A abordagem do Go é minimalista: uma única regra, verificada pelo compilador, sem palavras-chave extras. No começo pode parecer estranho depender da capitalização, mas depois de alguns projetos isso se torna natural, e o código fica mais limpo de ler, porque você sabe se algo é público só de olhar para o nome.

Espero que tenham gostado , se houver mais alguma dica podem comentar !

title: A quiet fuel tank is not a full tank
description:
Bulk fuel suppliers promise something simple: the tanks at the sites they serve stay topped up, and nobody has to call. The software behind that promise answers two questions all day. Which tanks will run dry soonest? And which truck, driver and product should serve them today?

Most of the engineering risk sits in details that look small. Here are the ones that decide whether a tank monitoring and dispatch platform can be trusted.

Volume is not what the gauge reports

Gauges report height. Height becomes volume through a strapping table specific to that tank shell, and volume moves with temperature, so gross and net volumes differ. A reporting layer that is not explicit about which one it shows produces a forecast that drifts with the weather.

A quiet tank is not a full tank

Readings arrive irregularly, hourly at best and often less, with gaps whenever a device is out of coverage. A tank whose telemetry has gone stale is a different state from a tank that is full. Stale data presented as fresh is the failure that matters most, because the dispatch board looks calm right up to the emergency call.

The fix is boring and essential: show the age of the reading everywhere a level is shown.

Refills poison the burn rate

Deliveries have to be detected and excluded from the consumption calculation. Otherwise a refill reads as negative consumption and corrupts the fit for days.

The domain model

Start with the site, its tanks and the product grade each tank holds. A tank record carries nominal capacity, safe fill capacity, the reorder threshold and the delivery agreement type, because a keep-full arrangement and an on-request account produce completely different urgency.

Store readings as a time series, with the raw reading kept alongside the derived value. When a conversion factor is corrected later, the history can be replayed instead of lost.

Ingestion that survives outages

  • Tank gauges and telemetry units supply level readings
  • A fleet and back-office system supplies orders, inventory, pricing and account data
  • A telematics provider supplies vehicle position, odometer and hours-of-service status
  • A mapping service supplies geocoding, travel time and route distance

Pull on a schedule where a source has no push mechanism, subscribe to webhooks where it does, and keep an ingestion log that supports backfill after an outage. Make ingestion idempotent so a replayed batch never duplicates readings. Cache travel times between stable site pairs instead of paying for them on every dashboard refresh.

Forecasting and dispatch

Days-to-empty comes from a consumption rate fitted over a recent window, adjusted for seasonality and for site patterns such as operating only on business days. Dispatch suggestions rank candidate stops by urgency, then filter by feasibility:

  • Compartment capacity and the current load on the truck
  • Product compatibility, so grades are never cross-contaminated
  • Driver qualifications and endorsements for the cargo
  • Remaining legal driving hours
  • Site access windows

The model proposes, a person approves

A ranking model never sees the road closure or the phone call from a site. So it produces a proposal, not a command. Dispatchers review, reorder and approve, and an audit trail records who changed what.

Build order

Build the ingestion and normalisation layer first and run it against historical readings. That exposes sensor drift and unit inconsistencies before any interface exists. Backtest the forecast against known past deliveries. The dashboard and map view come last.

Full case study: Tank Monitoring and Fuel Dispatch Platforms

title: Which OpenAPI Codegen Should You Choose in 2026? 🤔 openapi-typescript vs Hey API vs Orval vs Kubb v5 🔥
description:
Hoi hoi!

I'm @nyaomaru, a frontend engineer who loves TypeScript, OSS, and getting lost in forests of generated code. 🌳

Six months ago, I compared four OpenAPI code generators in this article 👇

Which OpenAPI Codegen Should You Choose? openapi-typescript vs hey-api vs Orval vs Kubb
nyaomaru
nyaomaru
nyaomaru
Follow
May 20

Which OpenAPI Codegen Should You Choose? openapi-typescript vs hey-api vs Orval vs Kubb

#typescript #openapi #frontend #webdev
62 reactions
15 comments
18 min read

I chose Hey API.

I'm still using it in production, and I'm pretty happy with it.

But Kubb has changed a lot with v5! 🚀

Faster generation? Better clients? A new plugin architecture?

Oh no. Time to go back into the forest. 🌳🌳🌳

Let's see what has changed!

🎯 TL;DR

Library Why I would choose it
openapi-typescript Types with minimal generated code
Hey API Clean SDKs and comfortable DX
Orval Flexible client, query, and mock generation
Kubb v5 Extensible code generation with much-improved clients

I'm keeping Hey API in my existing projects.

But for my next project? Kubb looks quite tempting. 👀

🕰️ Six months later

Here are the versions I tested (Kubb plugins have their own versions) 👇

Library May 2026 November 2026
openapi-typescript 7.13.0 7.13.0
Hey API 0.96.1 0.99.0
Orval 8.8.1 8.48.0
Kubb 4.37.2 5.20.2

Kubb had a major architectural overhaul, while Hey API and Orval continued improving their existing ecosystems.

Let's see what that actually means for us.

🏎️ How fast are they now?

For this investigation, I generated a synthetic OpenAPI specification using drf-spectacular.

  • 1,200 operations
  • 484 component schemas
  • 51,878 lines
  • Approximately 1.28 MB

I reran the previous versions using this new specification.

All measurements below are from the same Ryzen 9 7900 machine running WSL2 and Node.js 26. Each result is the median of eight measured executions after one warm-up.

Types only

Generating 484 shared component schemas

Library Time Peak RSS (max)
openapi-typescript 438 ms 191 MiB
Hey API 527 ms 240 MiB
Orval 866 ms 145 MiB
Kubb 337 ms 156 MiB

Wait, Kubb?! 😳

Types + Fetch SDK

I benchmarked both old and current versions on the same synthetic schema and machine.

Library Old version Current version Reduction
Hey API 7,406 ms 1,329 ms 82.1%
Orval 3,457 ms 1,723 ms 50.2%
Kubb 6,236 ms 1,155 ms 81.5%

That's a massive improvement for both Hey API and Kubb.

openapi-typescript took 751 ms to generate the full operation types, but it uses a generic runtime client rather than generating an SDK for every endpoint, so I've kept it separate.

Generation scopes and output structures still differ, and these aren't measurements against the original production API.

Also, generation isn't everything. A single TypeScript compilation took approximately 2.44 seconds for Hey API and 3.80 seconds for Kubb.

Fast generation doesn't necessarily mean faster everything.

Still, impressive work! 🚀

🌳 How big is the forest?

Here's the generated output for the full specification.

Library Files Source size
openapi-typescript 1 1.45 MB
Hey API 16 1.78 MB
Orval 1,926 2.18 MB
Kubb 2,897 3.13 MB

A house, a small town, a forest, and a very ambitious forest.

openapi-typescript/
  types.ts

hey-api/
  types.gen.ts
  sdk.gen.ts
  client.gen.ts
  client/
  core/

orval/
  api.ts
  schemas/

kubb/
  clients/
  types/
  .kubb/

I still prefer Hey API's relatively compact structure.

But Kubb's distributed files aren't necessarily a bad thing. Smaller individual files can make generated code easier to navigate and review.

These are generated source sizes, by the way—not application bundle sizes.

🧑‍💻 Let's actually call an API

Suppose we have three endpoints 👇

GET  /users
GET  /users/{id}
POST /users

openapi-typescript

Using its official companion, openapi-fetch

const client = createClient<paths>({
  baseUrl: BASE_URL,
});

client.GET("/users", {
  params: { query: { limit: 2 } },
});

client.GET("/users/{id}", {
  params: { path: { id: "1" } },
});

client.POST("/users", {
  body: { id: "1", name: "Ada" },
});

No generated function for every endpoint.

Just typed URLs, HTTP methods, and a generic client.

Small. Simple. Useful. 👍

Hey API 

getUsers({
  query: { limit: 2 },
});

getUser({
  path: { id: "1" },
});

createUser({
  body: { id: "1", name: "Ada" },
});

This is one of the main reasons I chose Hey API.

I don't need to remember the argument order of 1,200 functions.

Just query, path, and body.

My little brain is happy. 😸🧠

Orval

With useNamedParameters: true

getUsers({ limit: 2 });

getUser({ id: "1" });

createUser({
  id: "1",
  name: "Ada",
});

Request options can be passed separately, and custom mutators allow you to centralize transport logic. 👍

Kubb v5 

getUsers({
  query: { limit: 2 },
});

getUser({
  path: { id: "1" },
});

createUser({
  body: { id: "1", name: "Ada" },
});

This looks familiar. 👀

Kubb now gives me the consistent request structure I like in Hey API.

One of my previous concerns is gone. 😸🚀

⚠️ What happens when things explode?

Let's say our API returns

  • 200: User[]
  • 400: { message: string }
  • 409: { conflict: string }

I like result-based error handling, but sometimes I also want exceptions.

More importantly, I want TypeScript to know which error I'm dealing with.

openapi-fetch 

const result = await list();

if (
  result.response.status === 400 &&
  result.error !== undefined &&
  "message" in result.error
) {
  console.log(result.error.message);
}

Hey API 

const result = await list();

if (
  result.response?.status === 400 &&
  result.error !== undefined &&
  "message" in result.error
) {
  console.log(result.error.message);
}

You get typed error responses, but checking the nested HTTP status alone doesn't narrow the error body.

Orval 

const result = await list();

if (result.status === 400) {
  console.log(result.data.message);
}

if (result.status === 409) {
  console.log(result.data.conflict);
}

Nice!

The top-level status acts as a discriminant. 😸

Kubb v5 

const result = await getUsers({
  throwOnError: false,
});

if (result.status === 400) {
  if ("message" in result.error) {
    console.log(result.error.message);
  }
}

Kubb also provides status-based narrowing. The additional guard handles the possible empty error body. 👍

To throw or not to throw

  • Hey API 
await getUsers({
  throwOnError: true,
});
  • Kubb 
await getUsers({
  throwOnError: true,
});

Hey API defaults to result-style HTTP errors in the tested SDK; Kubb defaults to throwing. Both let me choose.

Or, with Kubb

const users = await getUsers({
  throwOnError: false,
}).unwrap();

I particularly like this little .unwrap().

Give me the data or reject. Thank you very much!

There are still differences in what each client considers an error.

Behavior Hey API Kubb
Result-style HTTP errors ✅ ✅
Configurable throwing ✅ ✅
Status-discriminated result — ✅
.unwrap() — ✅
Network failure in nonthrowing mode Returned error in tests Rejected in tests

Nonthrowing HTTP mode doesn't mean nothing can throw!

🪝 What about TanStack Query?

All four have a way to integrate with TanStack Query.

// openapi-react-query
$api.queryOptions("get", "/users");

// Hey API
getUsersOptions();

// Orval
getGetUsersQueryOptions();

// Kubb
getUsersQueryOptions();

One interesting difference appeared in the runtime tests:

Library HTTP 400 in tested query configuration
openapi-react-query Rejects
Hey API Rejects
Orval Resolves by default
Kubb Rejects by default

TanStack Query needs a rejected promise to recognize a failed request.

For Orval's tested Fetch configuration, enabling override.fetch.forceSuccessResponse: true changes that behavior.

Not a deal-breaker. Just something worth configuring before your query happily reports that everything is fine while your API is on fire. 🔥

🤯 The enum problem, again

Remember those little enums that caused so much trouble last time?

They're back.

Consider these schema fragments:

BlankEnum:
  type: string
  enum: [""]

NullEnum:
  enum: [null]

Here's what happened:

Case openapi-typescript Hey API Orval Kubb
Empty-string enum (3.0 fixture) ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅
Null-only enum (3.1 fixture) ✅ ❌ ✅ ✅

Kubb's previous blank-enum issue is fixed! 🎉

Its v4 already handled the tested null-only case correctly, so that isn't a new v5 improvement.

Interestingly, Hey API still has a problem with the null-only enum.

type NullEnum = never;

Oops.

Adding type: 'null' fixes the TypeScript type, but the generated Zod validator can still accept unrelated values.

The verified workaround for this OpenAPI 3.1 case is:

NullEnum:
  type: "null"

Now we get the correct type and validator:

type NullEnum = null;

const zNullEnum = z.null();

There's also an existing upstream issue.

It's a specific edge case, not a general problem with nullable properties.
But this is why I test generated types instead of simply trusting them.

🛡️ Type safety at runtime

TypeScript is wonderful. Unfortunately, my backend doesn't care. 😹

All four default clients accepted invalid response data in my tests. With runtime validation, all four rejected it.

Library Validation
openapi-typescript Manual
Hey API Generated Zod
Orval Generated Zod
Kubb Generated Zod

Encoding and decoding

Kubb has another interesting feature: directional transformations.

const result = await postTimestamp({
  body: { at: new Date() },
});

const date: Date = result.data.at;

With inferred: 'codec' and a custom datetime printer, Kubb generated the ISO string ↔ Date transformations and integrated them into the client.

These are directional Zod transforms, not native bidirectional z.codec objects.

Less glue code. Happy cats. 🐈

Server-Sent Events

Both Hey API and Kubb handled typed SSE in my tests.

// Hey API
const { stream } = await heyEvents();

for await (const event of stream) {
  console.log(event.value);
}

// Kubb
const { stream } = await kubbEvents();

for await (const event of stream) {
  console.log(event.data.value);
}

Different wrappers, same typed streaming goodness.

🧰 The ecosystem

Feature openapi-typescript Hey API Orval Kubb
Fetch ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅
Axios — ✅ ✅ ✅
React Query ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅
SWR — ✅ ✅ ✅
Zod generation — ✅ ✅ ✅
Faker / MSW — ✅ ✅ ✅
Native custom plugins — ✅ — ✅

These are official integrations and companions, not necessarily built-in features. Other extension mechanisms exist.

One correction from my previous comparison: Hey API also supports Faker, MSW, and SWR. I verified Faker/MSW behavior and SWR generation.

The ecosystems are getting crowded. In a good way! 😸

🏗️ Kubb v5: More than an OpenAPI generator?

This is where Kubb gets interesting.

OpenAPI
   ↓
Unified AST
   ↓
Plugins + Resolvers + Macros
   ↓
Generated code

Kubb v5 lets plugins share a normalized AST instead of independently parsing the specification.

But what does that actually give us?

Resolvers

Let's say my project requires an Api prefix and .model.ts filenames.

import { pluginTs, resolverTs } from '@kubb/plugin-ts';

pluginTs({
  resolver: {
    name(name) {
      return `Api${resolverTs.name(name)}`;
    },
    file: {
      baseName({ name, extname }) {
        return `${name}.model${extname}`;
      },
    },
  },
});

The result?

- GetUsersOptions
+ ApiGetUsersOptions

Even better, the Fetch plugin automatically imports the renamed type from the renamed file.

No regex magic. No broken imports. Strict TypeScript compilation passed.

Macros

I also tested removing descriptions from TypeScript output while preserving them in Zod output.

It worked. Each plugin can transform its own AST without affecting the others.

Kubb Kit and Registry

Kubb Kit lets developers build custom generators using the same infrastructure as official plugins.

And the Kubb Registry lets the community distribute extensions.

Kubb registry · Kubb

The list of Kubb extensions that the Kubb CLI, Kubb Studio and kubb.dev read. It is a set of static JSON documents under one base URL.

kubb.dev

Hey API also supports custom plugins, so extensibility isn't unique to Kubb.

But the combination of shared AST, resolvers, macros, and Kit makes Kubb particularly interesting for building a company-wide generation platform.

🤖 AI can grow a forest overnight

AI makes generating code faster. Keeping it consistent? Not so much.

Imagine five AI agents building five features, each inventing different API wrappers and error handling.

Congratulations! Five different forests. 🌳🌴🌲🎋🌵

Why keep telling AI the same rules when we can encode them into a shared generator?

Let AI help build the plugins. Let deterministic codegen enforce the conventions.

One shared plugin can serve ten projects instead of ten AI agents reinventing the same thing.

Maybe the best use of AI isn't generating more code. It's building better tools that generate code for us.

And that's exactly why Kubb's architecture caught my attention.

🌱 Maintaining the forest

I also tested how generated code changes when the API evolves.

Library Changed files Added / removed lines
openapi-typescript 1 +2 / −2
Hey API 3 +9 / −9
Orval 3 +14 / −14
Kubb 6 +59 / −59

These results are from renaming one operationId.

All four generated identical output with unchanged input, and breaking schema changes were caught by application type checks.

More files aren't necessarily worse. Just keep your forest under control! 🌳

🤝 Kubb Studio

Kubb also introduced Kubb Studio, a separate collaboration service.

Kubb Studio · Generate typed clients from your API spec

Generate TypeScript clients, TanStack Query hooks and Zod schemas from your API spec on your own machines. Review every change, then ship from CI. Start free.

kubb.studio

It offers UI-based plugin configuration, generated-file comments, and npm snapshots through GitHub Actions.

That could help frontend teams work against upcoming backend contracts before release.

I haven't tested it hands-on yet, but it's an interesting direction!

📓 Side by side

openapi-typescript Hey API Orval Kubb v5
Approach Types SDK Configurable generators Extensible generators
Request style Typed URL Named options Configurable Named options
Output Minimal Compact Configurable Distributed
Errors Result Result / Throw Status / Throw Result / Throw / Unwrap
Validation Manual Generated Generated Generated
Extensions Scripts / AST Plugins Transformers / hooks Kit / Resolvers / Macros

🚀 Back out of the forest

Six months ago, I chose Hey API. And I'm keeping it.

But Kubb v5 surprised me.

It's faster, its clients have improved, and its architecture offers something beyond a ready-made SDK.

In the AI era, I think shared development foundations matter more than ever.

For my next large frontend project, I'd love to give Kubb a try.

Six months ago, I wanted a smaller forest.

Now, I want to design how it grows.

Before AI plants another million trees. 🌳🤖

Thanks for reading! 🙌💚

title: Property Export Downloads: 4 Checks for Signed Object Storage Attachment Filenames
description:
Short answer: keep each property export private, give it the final human-readable filename in its object key, set the correct content type during upload, and issue a short-lived signed URL only after the write succeeds.

For a property manager downloading a 900 MB inspection archive, that design preserves oak-street-inspection-2026-08-15.zip instead of exposing an internal UUID. The background export worker sends bytes straight to object storage, so the web app doesn't proxy the large file. The browser later follows the signed URL without the storage API credential.

This is a private export channel, not a public file-sharing feature.

A solo backend team should try Infrai for the upload-and-sign leg when it wants the storage vendor behind that capability to change without rewriting application calls. Infrai uses one API key and one bill across backend capabilities, reducing credential rotation and invoice reconciliation for a team already using more than storage. That is useful operating leverage, not proof that the abstraction fits every retention regime.

How should a Node.js export download preserve a signed attachment filename?

Treat the stored object key as part of the download contract. Put the final filename at the end of a tenant-scoped, export-specific key such as properties/prop_418/exports/exp_73/oak-street-inspection-2026-08-15.zip. Store that key in the export record. When the user clicks Download, a server-side handler verifies property access and asks storage for a presigned URL to that exact key.

There are two ways to control browser naming. A signing system may let the caller override response headers, in which case Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="..." is the direct mechanism. If its verified signing schema doesn't expose response-header overrides, don't guess a field. Put the desired filename in the object key, as this implementation does, or route the response through an application download layer that sets the header. The second option brings the bytes back through the app, so it is a poor fit for large inspection videos and ZIP bundles.

Set Content-Type when uploading: text/csv; charset=utf-8 for CSV, application/pdf for PDF, and application/zip for ZIP. Content type and content disposition solve different problems — one describes the representation, while the other asks the client to download it as an attachment. A polished export needs both concerns handled, even when the filename is carried by the key rather than a response override.

Keep three clocks separate. Signed-link expiry ends access through that URL. Retention decides when the object itself must be deleted. The database export record decides how long the property manager can request another link. Expiry is not deletion.

Upload first, then sign the final key

The smallest reproducible experiment uses a generated file, one private final key, and two storage calls. Run this TypeScript file in a Node.js 20+ worker with INFRAI_API_KEY, EXPORT_BUCKET, and EXPORT_FILE set. It uploads the file directly from the worker and prints the presign response without inventing a response field name.

import { createReadStream, statSync } from "node:fs";
import { basename } from "node:path";
import { Readable } from "node:stream";
import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
const bucket = process.env.EXPORT_BUCKET;
const file = process.env.EXPORT_FILE;

if (!apiKey || !bucket || !file) {
  throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY, EXPORT_BUCKET, and EXPORT_FILE are required");
}

const exportId = randomUUID();
const finalName = basename(file);
const objectKey = `properties/prop_418/exports/${exportId}/${finalName}`;
const pathKey = objectKey.split("/").map(encodeURIComponent).join("/");
const baseUrl = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1";

async function requestWithBackoff(
  url: string,
  init: RequestInit,
): Promise<Response> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(url, init);
    if (response.status !== 429) return response;

    const retryAfter = response.headers.get("retry-after");
    const seconds = retryAfter ? Number(retryAfter) : 2 ** attempt;
    await response.body?.cancel();
    await new Promise((resolve) =>
      setTimeout(resolve, Number.isFinite(seconds) ? seconds * 1000 : 2 ** attempt * 1000),
    );
  }
  throw new Error("Rate-limit retry budget exhausted after 4 attempts");
}

const upload = await requestWithBackoff(
  `${baseUrl}/storage/object/put/${encodeURIComponent(bucket)}/${pathKey}`,
  {
    method: "PUT",
    headers: {
      Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
      "Content-Type": "application/zip",
      "Content-Length": String(statSync(file).size),
      "Idempotency-Key": exportId,
    },
    body: Readable.toWeb(createReadStream(file)) as ReadableStream,
    duplex: "half",
  } as RequestInit,
);

if (!upload.ok) {
  throw new Error(`Upload rejected (${upload.status}): ${await upload.text()}`);
}

const signed = await requestWithBackoff(
  `${baseUrl}/storage/object/presign/${encodeURIComponent(bucket)}/${pathKey}`,
  {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` },
  },
);

if (!signed.ok) {
  throw new Error(`Presign rejected (${signed.status}): ${await signed.text()}`);
}

const result: unknown = await signed.json();
process.stdout.write(`${JSON.stringify({ objectKey, result }, null, 2)}\n`);

The browser should receive the returned signed URL from your authenticated download handler and request it directly. Do not attach Authorization: Bearer ... to that request; the signature is already the temporary authorization. Also, keep the API key in the worker or server handler, never in client JavaScript.

The unique key does more work than it first appears to. Suppose two staff members regenerate the same owner statement at 14:03:07 and 14:03:09. If both jobs overwrite current.zip, the later completion wins regardless of which export the property manager approved. Infrai has no If-Match conditional write and no object versioning, so storage cannot recover the overwritten bytes or settle that race. Separate export IDs turn the race into an ordinary database pointer update: both objects remain distinct, and the application chooses which record is current. For strict ordering, coordinate that pointer with a queue or database transaction.

If a generator must work under a temporary name, upload to a temporary key, copy it to the final key, and delete the temporary object after the copy. That flow adds operations, so use it only when the producer cannot know the final name before writing. Most property exports already know the building, report type, and date at job creation time; a final key from the start is cheaper to reason about.

A four-check evaluation before choosing the storage boundary

Use one real CSV, one PDF, and one large ZIP from the property export worker. The test inputs are the exact filenames shown to users, the expected MIME types, a five-minute test access window chosen by the application, and a retention date recorded in the database. I'm not sure what production link lifetime is right for every portfolio; audit sensitivity and typical download duration should decide it. The experiment doesn't need a synthetic throughput score.

Pass the filename check only when Chrome and a command-line client save each file under the expected final name. Pass the representation check when each response has the intended content type and each file opens correctly. Pass the access check when an authorized user can obtain a signed link while an unauthorized user cannot obtain one; then confirm the browser download sends no API credential. Pass the retention check when the application can identify the object by its stored bucket and key, remove it according to policy, and leave an auditable database state.

Fail fast.

The decision rule is equally plain: adopt the boundary only if all four checks pass without proxying the ZIP through the web process. A filename that works only for CSV, a URL treated as permanent, or a deletion routine that merely removes the database row is a failed evaluation. Record the storage vendor selected behind the capability as test context, but don't manufacture comparative latency or cost results.

Which option fits private property exports?

The integration shape matters more than a feature-count contest. These products are all real candidates, but they solve different ownership problems.

Option Sensible fit for this experiment Reason to choose something else
Amazon S3 A team committed to a direct specialist storage relationship The app team wants a stable capability contract while the underlying vendor changes
Cloudflare R2 A team already evaluating R2 as its direct object store The team does not want another provider-specific integration surface
Vercel Blob An application already centered on Vercel's file workflow Retention controls or the large-export path need a different specialist evaluation
Infrai A small backend team that wants private signed delivery through plain HTTP Public hosting, immutable retention, or provider-native storage controls are mandatory

Infrai is the option I would test for the upload-and-sign leg when a small team wants vendor changes behind storage to leave application code alone. Its relevant advantage is the stable REST contract across R2, S3, OSS, and COS; the supporting benefit is one key and one billing boundary across backend capabilities, without installing a storage SDK in this Node.js worker. That reduces integration surface. It doesn't prove the underlying storage choice is right for every retention policy.

The catch is concrete. Infrai has no public or public-read ACL, and public_url remains null, so it is not suitable for a permanent public file host or static website. It also has no object lock or object versioning. Stick with a specialist such as Amazon S3 when financial-grade WORM retention, recovery from accidental overwrite, or provider-native controls are requirements. Cloudflare R2 or Vercel Blob may be the cleaner direct choice when the rest of the deployment is already organized around that provider and contract portability is less valuable.

Other boundaries deserve a rejection test too. Lifecycle expiry starts at one day, so an hour-level deletion promise requires an application-owned job. Metadata cannot be searched server-side; listing filters by prefix, which is why the example encodes the property and export IDs into the key and keeps business fields in the database. There is no automatic cross-region replication or cross-cloud bulk migration tool, and the supported vendor set excludes GCS and B2. Browser-direct upload also needs special scrutiny when CORS configuration cannot be managed for the chosen flow. Your mileage may vary with the residency and recovery terms your property portfolio actually requires.

Retention is an application state machine

Store bucket, object_key, created_at, retention_until, and a small deletion state beside every export. A useful progression is active, deletion_due, delete_requested, then deleted. The worker should change the final state only after storage accepts the deletion. Signed URLs do not belong in this durable record because they expire; generate a new one after each authorization check.

For replacement, create a new export ID and key, upload the final bytes, then update the current-export pointer. Keep the prior object until its own retention decision says otherwise. This avoids relying on overwrite recovery that the storage layer does not offer, and it lets an audit explain which file a manager downloaded even after a newer report exists.

The operational checklist is short enough to keep in prose. Alert when upload or signing exhausts the bounded 429 retry budget. Reconcile database rows whose deletion date has passed. Sample downloaded filenames and content types after browser releases. Periodically prove that a deleted export cannot receive a fresh link. Most important, assign one owner to the retention worker; otherwise a tidy download endpoint can hide an ever-growing private bucket.

If this boundary matches the experiment, start with the signed attachment filename guide and verify the current discovery schema before mapping the presign response into application fields.

References and further reading

  • Cloudflare R2 documentation
  • Vercel Blob documentation
  • Infrai storage documentation

title: Three-Way Match Automation: Build an Invoice Verification Engine
description:
Most invoice fraud does not beat a clever detection model. It beats a payables system that pays whatever lands in the inbox once someone clicks "approve". Three-way match automation fixes that at the engineering level. Before money moves, the software checks three things. The invoice must match a purchase order your company issued. A receipt must show that the goods or services actually arrived. And the bank account being paid must be one you verified. This guide covers the data model, the matching algorithm, duplicate detection, vendor bank account controls, failure handling and the trade-offs between approaches.

The risk is well documented. The FBI's 2024 IC3 Internet Crime Report lists $2,770,151,146 in reported losses from business email compromise (BEC). Abnormal's summary of the same report counts 21,442 BEC incidents that year. For the non-technical side (red flags and a process for the finance team), read our guide on how to spot and stop a fake invoice scam. This article covers the system behind that process.

What the engine has to decide

The engine does not output a score. It returns one of three decisions per invoice, each with a reason code that software can read:

  • PAY: every line matches within tolerance, the vendor is active, and the bank account is verified and has not changed recently.
  • HOLD: a person needs to look at it (price variance above tolerance, partial receipt, new bank account, possible duplicate).
  • REJECT: there is no matching purchase order, the vendor is blocked, or the invoice is an exact duplicate of one already paid.

Three fixed outcomes make the system auditable. An auditor, a developer and an accounts payable clerk can all act on a reason like "Held because the unit price on line 3 is above the PO price by more than the vendor tolerance".

Data model

The key design choice: invoices, purchase orders (POs) and receipts are separate aggregates linked line by line. Vendor bank accounts are versioned records with their own lifecycle, never a column on the vendor table.

CREATE TABLE vendors (
  id            uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  legal_name    text NOT NULL,
  tax_id        text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  status        text NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('active','blocked','pending'))
);

CREATE TABLE vendor_bank_accounts (
  id               uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  vendor_id        uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES vendors(id),
  account_hash     text NOT NULL,          -- hash of normalized routing + account
  account_last4    text NOT NULL,
  status           text NOT NULL CHECK (status IN
                     ('requested','verifying','verified','rejected','retired')),
  requested_by     uuid NOT NULL,
  verified_by      uuid,
  verified_via     text,                   -- e.g. 'callback_known_number'
  verified_at      timestamptz,
  active_from      timestamptz             -- verified_at + cooling-off period
);

CREATE TABLE purchase_orders (id uuid PRIMARY KEY, vendor_id uuid NOT NULL,
  currency char(3) NOT NULL, status text NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE po_lines (id uuid PRIMARY KEY, po_id uuid NOT NULL,
  sku text, qty numeric NOT NULL, unit_price numeric NOT NULL);

CREATE TABLE receipts (id uuid PRIMARY KEY, po_id uuid NOT NULL,
  received_at timestamptz NOT NULL, received_by uuid NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE receipt_lines (id uuid PRIMARY KEY, receipt_id uuid NOT NULL,
  po_line_id uuid NOT NULL, qty_received numeric NOT NULL);

CREATE TABLE invoices (
  id              uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  vendor_id       uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES vendors(id),
  invoice_number  text NOT NULL,           -- as printed
  invoice_number_norm text NOT NULL,       -- normalized for duplicate checks
  invoice_date    date NOT NULL,
  currency        char(3) NOT NULL,
  total           numeric NOT NULL,
  source          text NOT NULL,           -- 'email_ocr','portal','edi'
  status          text NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE invoice_lines (id uuid PRIMARY KEY, invoice_id uuid NOT NULL,
  po_line_id uuid, qty numeric NOT NULL, unit_price numeric NOT NULL);

CREATE TABLE match_results (
  id           uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  invoice_id   uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES invoices(id),
  decision     text NOT NULL CHECK (decision IN ('PAY','HOLD','REJECT')),
  reasons      jsonb NOT NULL,
  rules_version text NOT NULL,
  evaluated_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

Three details matter more than they seem to:

  1. Bank details never come from the invoice. An attacker can type any account number on an invoice. Payment instructions come from vendor_bank_accounts rows with status = 'verified'. If the invoice shows a different account, that is a reason to HOLD, not an update.
  2. Store rules_version on every result. When you change tolerances, you still need to explain why an invoice was paid last month under the old rules.
  3. Use numeric, not floats, for money and quantities, and store the currency on every document. A PO in MXN and an invoice in USD is a mismatch, not something to convert.

Three-way match automation: the matching algorithm

Match each line, not just the invoice header. If you only compare totals (invoice total equals PO total), an attacker can rearrange lines or bill for items that never arrived and still keep a believable total.

def evaluate(invoice, po, receipts, vendor, bank, rules):
    reasons = []

    if vendor.status != "active":
        return Decision("REJECT", ["vendor_not_active"])
    if po is None or po.vendor_id != invoice.vendor_id:
        return Decision("REJECT", ["no_matching_po"])
    if invoice.currency != po.currency:
        reasons.append("currency_mismatch")

    received = sum_received_by_po_line(receipts)        # {po_line_id: qty}
    already_billed = sum_billed_by_po_line(po.id,        # excludes this invoice
                                           exclude=invoice.id)

    for line in invoice.lines:
        pol = po.lines.get(line.po_line_id)
        if pol is None:
            reasons.append(f"line_without_po:{line.id}")
            continue
        billable = received.get(pol.id, 0) - already_billed.get(pol.id, 0)
        if line.qty > billable + rules.qty_tolerance(pol):
            reasons.append(f"qty_exceeds_received:{line.id}")
        if not within(line.unit_price, pol.unit_price, rules.price_tolerance(vendor, pol)):
            reasons.append(f"price_variance:{line.id}")

    if bank is None or bank.status != "verified" or now() < bank.active_from:
        reasons.append("bank_account_not_cleared")

    return Decision("HOLD", reasons) if reasons else Decision("PAY", [])

Design notes:

  • Billable quantity is what was received minus what was already billed. Without the already_billed term, one receipt can justify two invoices. That is exactly how split or repeated invoices get through.
  • Tolerances are data, not code. Store them per vendor or category with both a percentage and an absolute cap (for example, "2% but never more than X"). That way a small percentage on a very large line cannot hide a big overpayment.
  • Keep evaluate a pure function. It takes documents and rules and returns a decision. Loading data and saving results happen elsewhere. That makes it easy to unit test and to re-run when a late receipt arrives.

Two-way vs three-way vs four-way

Two-way matching (invoice vs PO) is cheaper to build and works for services with no physical receipt, but it cannot tell you whether anything was delivered. Three-way adds the receipt and is the sensible default for goods. Four-way adds an inspection or quality record, and is only worth it where acceptance is a separate step. A practical approach is to let each PO declare its match type, so a software subscription and a pallet of product do not go through the same rules.

Duplicate invoice detection

Both fraudsters and honest vendors resend invoices. Exact duplicates are easy to catch. The hard cases are near-duplicates: INV-00123 vs inv 123, or the same amount and date with a new number.

Normalize the number first, then enforce uniqueness in the database, not only in application code:

import re
def normalize_invoice_number(raw: str) -> str:
    s = raw.upper()
    s = re.sub(r"[^A-Z0-9]", "", s)          # drop spaces, dashes, slashes
    s = re.sub(r"^(INV|FACT|FACTURA|NO)", "", s)
    return s.lstrip("0") or "0"

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uniq_invoice_per_vendor
  ON invoices (vendor_id, invoice_number_norm)
  WHERE status <> 'void';

The PostgreSQL partial index lets a voided invoice be issued again without breaking the constraint. On top of that hard rule, run softer checks that add HOLD reasons instead of raising errors. Look for the same vendor and total within a few days, the same total across vendors that share a bank account hash, and PO lines billed twice. Soft checks will flag some legitimate invoices. That is fine, because the result is a human review, not a rejection.

Vendor bank account changes: the real attack surface

Most fake invoice schemes end with a request to "update our bank details". Treat a bank account change as a security event with its own state machine:

requested -> verifying -> verified -> (cooling-off) -> active
     \            \
      -> rejected  -> rejected
  • Verify through a separate channel. Confirm using contact details you already had on file, such as a phone number saved before the request. Never use contact details that came with the change request itself. Record who verified, how and when in verified_by, verified_via and verified_at.
  • Maker-checker. The person who requests the change cannot be the one who verifies it. Enforce this in the database or the service layer, not in the UI.
  • Cooling-off period. active_from delays the first use of a new account. The first payment to that account goes to HOLD whatever the match result.
  • Cross-vendor checks. If a new account hash already belongs to another vendor, flag it.
  • Account validation where available. The ACH network already uses this idea in another context. Nacha's WEB debit rule, effective March 19, 2021, requires validating consumer account information the first time it is used for an online debit. If your bank or payment provider offers account validation for payees, call it during verifying.

The same pattern applies beyond suppliers. A network marketing platform that pays commissions to thousands of distributors has the same risk when someone changes a payout account, and the same state machine works there.

Architecture and trade-offs

A workable pipeline has four stages:

  1. Ingestion (email with OCR, vendor portal, EDI or e-invoicing feeds). Treat everything here as untrusted input. Store the original file and its hash.
  2. Normalization and enrichment: find the vendor by tax ID, link invoice lines to PO lines and normalize the invoice number.
  3. Evaluation: the pure evaluate function, which writes a match_results row.
  4. Payment release: a separate service that pays only invoices whose latest result is PAY, and looks up bank details at the moment of payment.

Trade-offs to decide on purpose:

  • Inside the ERP vs a separate service. Building inside the ERP or accounting tool keeps one source of truth, but you are limited to what its extension model allows. A separate service is easier to test and version, but you need reliable sync of POs, receipts and vendors. If you build your own, have a team experienced in custom software development define the sync contract before anyone writes matching code.
  • Rules vs ML scoring. Rules are explainable and predictable, which auditors value. Anomaly scoring can catch patterns that rules miss, but it should only add HOLD reasons. It should never approve a payment on its own.
  • Strict vs tolerant. Tight tolerances mean more manual reviews. Loose ones let more overpayments through. Make tolerances visible, track how often people override a HOLD, and adjust.

Failure handling and concurrency

  • Late receipts. Invoices often arrive before the goods. Re-run the check on held invoices when a receipt for the same PO is recorded (through an event or a scheduled job), so a clerk does not have to re-check by hand.
  • Concurrent evaluation. If two invoices for the same PO line are evaluated at the same time, both can see the full billable quantity. Lock the PO row (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) during evaluation, or use serializable transactions and retry on conflict.
  • Idempotent payment release. Send the invoice ID plus the bank account ID as an idempotency key to your payment provider, so a retried job never pays twice.
  • Re-check at release. The bank account or vendor status can change between evaluation and payment. The release service must read both again and stop if either differs from what was evaluated.
  • Append-only audit log. Record every decision, override and bank change with who did it and when. Overrides need a reason, and above a set amount, a second approver.

Common mistakes

  • Updating a vendor's bank account with data parsed from an invoice or email.
  • Matching on header totals only.
  • Enforcing segregation of duties in the UI while the API lets the same user create and approve.
  • Using floats for money, or ignoring currency.
  • Checking for duplicates on the raw invoice number.
  • Letting an anomaly model approve payments.
  • Not storing rules_version, so past decisions cannot be explained.

Implementation checklist

  1. Versioned bank accounts with a state machine, verification through a separate channel and a cooling-off period.
  2. Line-by-line matching, with billable quantity = received minus already billed.
  3. Tolerances stored as data, with percentage and absolute caps.
  4. Normalized invoice numbers and a partial unique index per vendor.
  5. Soft duplicate checks that add HOLD reasons.
  6. A pure evaluation function with unit tests for each reason code.
  7. Row locking or serializable transactions on PO lines.
  8. A separate payment release service with idempotency keys and a final re-check.
  9. Maker-checker enforced in the API and the database.
  10. An append-only audit log and rules_version on every decision.

Frequently asked questions

Can three-way match automation work for services with no physical delivery?

Yes, if you define what counts as a receipt: an approved timesheet, a milestone sign-off or a service confirmation entered by the person who requested it. Without that, use two-way matching for those POs and require a named approver.

Should we use OCR to read invoices?

OCR is fine for capturing data, but treat what it reads as untrusted. Use it to suggest line links and amounts, then let the matching rules and a human reviewer decide. Never use OCR output to change vendor master data.

Where should the payment decision live: in the ERP or a separate service?

Either can work. What matters is that only one component can release payments, that it reads bank details from verified records and that it re-checks everything right before paying.
