title: Style queries let the parent set the variant, not the class
description:
You have a sidebar full of cards, and every one of them carries card--compact. The template loop adds the class, so nobody types it by hand. Fine. Then design looks at the page and says the compact cards further down shouldn't be compact, because the tight padding there isn't separating anything. It just looks inconsistent.

The class sits on the card. The reason for the class comes from where the card is on the page. Wrong place.

Kevin Powell's new CSS-Tricks article fixes this with container style queries, which the article says are now Baseline Newly Available. The move: stop putting the variant on the component. Put a setting on an ancestor, and let the component decide what to do with it.

Same at-rule, different question

A size query asks how wide the container is. A style query uses the same @container at-rule and asks what a custom property is set to:

@container style(--theme: high-contrast) {
  .card {
    background: white;
    color: black;
    border-color: black;
  }
}

Read it as: if the nearest container has --theme: high-contrast, style .card like this.

No setup required. Every element is a style container by default, so there's no container-type to declare. With size queries, a missing container-type is the usual reason nothing happens. Here that failure mode is gone.

Custom properties only, for now. The spec also covers regular properties, like style(display: flex), but the article says that isn't supported anywhere yet.

The rule that catches people is that an element can't query itself:

.card {
  --card-layout: alternative;
}

@container style(--card-layout: alternative) {
  .card {
    grid-template-columns: 1fr 2fr; /* doesn't work */
  }
}

Same as size queries. The query looks at an ancestor, so the property has to be set somewhere above .card. Powell notes that if() is on the way and can read custom properties on the element it's used on. The trade-off is that if() covers a single property, while a style query block holds as many declarations as you need.

From modifier to setting

Here's a density modifier the familiar way, as an attribute:

[data-card-density="compact"] {
  padding: .5rem;
  gap: .5rem;
}

And the style query version from the article:

[data-card-layout="alternative"] {
  --card-layout: alternative;
}

.card {
  @container style(--card-layout: alternative) {
    padding: .5rem;
    gap: .5rem;
  }
}

More code. Yes. Powell admits that if you think in modifiers, it looks like extra work for nothing. The payoff is upstream. The alternative styles are written once, inside .card, and anything that can set --card-layout can switch them on: a media query, a container query, a :has() selector, a parent section. A CMS option that writes one custom property onto a section of the page works too.

That's the sidebar fix. In the article's version, a @media (width > 700px) block sets up the two-column layout and gives .sidebar its compact density through a custom property. The card markup doesn't change. The decision moves to the part of the page that actually has the context.

The overflow grid that should scroll down

The better demo is the overflow grid. Powell's base pattern:

.overflow-grid {
  display: grid;
  gap: 1rem;
  grid-auto-flow: column;
  grid-auto-columns: max(40%, 25ch);
  padding-block-end: 1rem;
  overflow: auto;
}

It scrolls sideways. Drop it into a hero that splits into two columns on larger screens and sideways scrolling in that narrow column gets awkward. He wants it to scroll vertically there instead.

First, make the flow direction a setting with a default of column:

.overflow-grid {
  grid-auto-flow: var(--overflow-grid-direction, column);
}

Then the split flips the setting when it goes to two columns:

.split {
  @container main (width > 40rem) {
    --overflow-grid-direction: row;

    grid-template-columns: repeat(2, 1fr);
  }
}

On its own, that looks bad. The grid is still sized for horizontal scrolling, so you get a tall column and no overflow at all. Flipping grid-auto-flow changed the direction. None of the sizing came along.

So the grid listens for its own setting:

.overflow-grid {
  @container style(--overflow-grid-direction: row) {
    grid-template-columns: 1fr; /* a single, full-width column */
    max-block-size: 50vb; /* keep the overflow, but vertically */
  }
}

Look at who knows what. .split never selects .overflow-grid. It sets one custom property. The grid owns every rule about how it looks in each direction. Custom properties inherit, so the same value feeds the var() in grid-auto-flow and the style query, and because it's set on .split, an ancestor, the self-query rule never gets in the way.

Styling a child from its layout works. Powell calls it awkward and says it leads to fragile code bases. I agree, and this example makes the case better than any argument about selector coupling I've read.

Modifier classes stay

Powell is clear that this doesn't retire modifier classes or data attributes. If a button just needs to be the accent version or a pill, a modifier is the right tool. It also styles the element it sits on, which a style query can't. And sometimes a plain media query, a container query or an intrinsic layout does the job without either.

His test for when style queries pay off: the condition and the styles live in different places, or one condition has to change several things at once.

Try it on your next layout

Find a component you style from its parent. A selector like .split .overflow-grid gives it away. Turn whatever the parent is changing into a custom property with a default. Move the rules into a @container style() block inside the component. Have the parent set the property. Keep it on an ancestor.

The missing piece is querying real properties. style(display: flex) is in the spec, and no browser supports it yet. Until then, custom properties are the switch.

title: Python Passes JavaScript in JetBrains' 2026 Survey While Rust Leads Plans
description:
JavaScript held the top spot in JetBrains' annual developer survey every single year since the study launched in 2017, outlasting framework churn and backend runtime wars. In the tenth edition of the State of Developer Ecosystem 2026 report (covered by TechRepublic on November 19–20), that nine-year streak finally snapped: Python took first place at 65% usage, ahead of JavaScript at 59%.

Drawing on cleaned responses from 28,945 developers across 198 countries and regions surveyed between May and July 2026, the report documents a wider shift across the software stack. It shows TypeScript tripling its footprint since 2017 to dominate growth potential, Rust and Go leading what engineers plan to learn next, PostgreSQL widening its lead over MySQL, and a sharp gap between how junior and senior engineers judge AI coding agents.

We have not run our own independent developer poll; all percentages, index scores, and methodology adjustments below come from JetBrains Research's published 2026 report and TechRepublic's November 2026 coverage.

Python overtakes JavaScript while TypeScript leads growth potential

Looking at single-year usage alone misses the ten-year arc JetBrains highlighted in its 2026 data. Usage of JavaScript (59%), HTML/CSS (52%), SQL (47%), and Java (42%) all peaked around 2019–2020 and have drifted downward gradually since then. Over the same stretch, Python climbed to 65% on the back of AI tooling, data pipelines, and backend automation, matching its lead in November's TIOBE and PYPL rankings.

Meanwhile, TypeScript reached 43% usage (more than triple its 2017 share) and topped JetBrains' third annual Language Promise Index with a score of 212, ahead of Rust (179) and Python (146). That index blends five-year growth, adoption intent, and user loyalty to estimate which languages carry the strongest momentum heading into 2027.

On the adoption-intent side, Rust ranks first among languages developers plan to pick up within the next six months (10% of respondents), followed by Go (8%) and Python (5%). Both Rust and Go also sit among the highest-paid language skills in the 2026 dataset.

This table compares the top languages in JetBrains' 2026 State of Developer Ecosystem report across current usage, Language Promise Index standing, and 6-month adoption intent.

Language 2026 Reported Usage Language Promise Index 6-Month Adoption Plan Primary Momentum Driver
Python 65% (1st overall) 146 (3rd) 5% (3rd) AI engineering, data processing, automation
JavaScript 59% (2nd overall) Not in top 3 Not in top 3 Core web interactivity and legacy frontend
HTML / CSS 52% Not ranked in top 3 Not ranked in top 3 Web markup and styling baseline
SQL 47% Not ranked in top 3 Not ranked in top 3 Relational analytics (PostgreSQL hit 59% DB share)
TypeScript 43% (3x since 2017) 212 (1st) Gradual JS migration Type safety across frontend and Node/Deno stacks
Java 42% Not in top 3 Not in top 3 Enterprise backend maintenance
Rust High-pay tier 179 (2nd) 10% (1st) Memory-safe systems, compilers, and security tooling
Go High-pay tier Not in top 3 8% (2nd) Cloud infrastructure, CLIs, and concurrent APIs

If your team maintains a large Python codebase, pairing this momentum with upcoming runtime upgrades like Python 3.15's lazy imports and Tachyon profiler is becoming standard practice rather than niche optimization.

Expand

Laptop screen showing programming code alongside data analysis charts

PostgreSQL pulls ahead and AI agents split junior vs. senior devs

Outside programming languages, two operational findings in the 2026 survey stand out for engineering managers:

  • PostgreSQL widens its database lead: PostgreSQL jumped nine percentage points to reach 59% usage, pulling further ahead of MySQL at 54%.
  • AI agents are routine, yet seniority splits trust: More than half of employed developers now use AI agents across over 60% of their work tasks, and only 23% say they have no plans to try new AI tools in the coming year. However, experience changes how much engineers trust agent output: 60% of developers with 1–2 years of experience say AI-generated solutions are better than their own, compared with 47% of veterans with 16+ years of experience, who tend to wrap agents in explicit specs, guidelines, and verification checks.

JetBrains also uncovered a sharp measurement mismatch inside engineering leadership. While 51% of tech managers track token usage to evaluate AI spending, only 30% find token counts genuinely insightful. By contrast, 39% consider net time gain insightful, yet only 28% actually measure it. Meanwhile, more than half of managers at small companies report satisfaction with AI ROI, compared with just 34% at large enterprises.

What changed in JetBrains' 2026 methodology (and job sentiment)

Every annual survey comes with sampling caveats, and JetBrains disclosed several methodology changes in 2026 that explain why some numbers shifted faster than usual. Researchers ran 535 randomized questions across nine languages, applied 91 anti-fraud filters (nearly double 2025's count), advertised with unbranded creatives to reduce JetBrains-user bias, and still weighted down JetBrains IDE users' share by 10% alongside region and language weights.

Even in a tough hiring climate where only 18% of global developers rate local job market conditions as favorable (with Japan standing out as an outlier at 43%), 75% of respondents say they would still choose the same career if starting over, led by architects, team leads, and DevOps engineers. And on the lighter side of the data, 47% of respondents still code for fun as a hobby, while dogs narrowly beat cats at 39% to 36%.

Expand

Programming code displayed on a dark laptop screen

Why Python's lead and Stack Overflow's numbers diverge

Comparing JetBrains' 2026 findings with other November benchmarks shows how survey methodology shapes language rankings. In Stack Overflow's 2026 developer survey, JavaScript still holds the top spot in reported usage while Rust overtakes PHP and Go, and Python tops developer wish lists. On JetBrains' sample of 28,945 respondents, Python's 65% share puts it six points clear of JavaScript's 59%, echoing Python's first-place standing in November's TIOBE and PYPL indexes.

For engineering teams, the exact rank order between Python and JavaScript matters less than the shared direction across all four datasets: AI and data-engineering workloads are pulling Python deeper into production backends, TypeScript has become the default safety layer for web codebases, and Rust plus Go remain the primary targets when teams build new performance-critical or cloud-native services.

Practical takeaways for engineering leaders planning 2027

Survey rankings should inform hiring and tooling roadmaps without triggering unnecessary rewrites of stable production apps. Three pragmatic moves fit the 2026 data:

  1. Adopt TypeScript incrementally over rewriting: If you run plain JavaScript services, adding TypeScript strictness module by module captures type-safety benefits without halting feature delivery.
  2. Reserve Rust and Go for new boundaries: Use Rust where memory safety or low-level throughput matters, and Go for cloud services or CLIs, rather than porting working Java or Python monoliths purely to chase survey momentum.
  3. Fix AI ROI metrics before expanding seat budgets: Stop treating raw token consumption as a proxy for engineering velocity, and start tracking net cycle-time reductions and code-review bottlenecks instead.

Frequently asked questions

Why did Python pass JavaScript in JetBrains' 2026 survey?

Python reached 65% reported usage compared with JavaScript's 59% as AI engineering, data processing, and backend scripting kept expanding while JavaScript, HTML/CSS, and Java gradually declined from their 2019–2020 peaks.

Which language leads JetBrains' 2026 Language Promise Index?

TypeScript leads the Language Promise Index at 212 (with 43% overall usage), ahead of Rust at 179 and Python at 146.

How many developers participated in the 2026 State of Developer Ecosystem survey?

JetBrains based the 2026 report on cleaned responses from 28,945 developers across 198 countries and regions, surveyed between May and July 2026 using 91 anti-fraud validation criteria.

title: Day 31 of My React learning journey - Custom Hooks and Children Props.
description:
1.What are Custom Hooks in React?

They are Javascript functions that allows us to reuse stateful logic between multiple React components.

React provides built-in-hooks such as:

  • useState
  • useEffect
  • useContext
  • useReducer

we can create our own Hooks based on our requriements.

Important rules:

  • A Custom Hook name should start with use.
  • Custom Hooks can use other React Hooks.
  • They help us reuse logic across components.

Example of a Custom Hook

i

import { useState } from "react";

function useCounter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

  const increment = () => {
    setCount(count + 1);
  };

  const decrement = () => {
    setCount(count - 1);
  };

  return { count, increment, decrement };
}

export default useCounter;

Here:

  • useCounter is our Custom Hook.
  • useState manages the counter value.
  • increment increases the count.
  • decrement decreases the count.
  • We return the count and functions so components can use them. 
import { useState } from "react";

function useCounter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

  const increment = () => {
    setCount(count + 1);
  };

  const decrement = () => {
    setCount(count - 1);
  };

  return { count, increment, decrement };
}

export default useCounter;

Here:

  • useCounter is our Custom Hook.
  • useState manages the counter value.
  • increment increases the count.
  • decrement decreases the count.
  • We return the count and functions so components can use them.

Using the Custom Hook in a Component

import useCounter from "./useCounter";

function App() {
  const { count, increment, decrement } = useCounter();

  return (
    <div>
      <h2>Count: {count}</h2>

      <button onClick={increment}>Increment</button>
      <button onClick={decrement}>Decrement</button>
    </div>
  );
}

export default App;

We can use the useCounter Hook in other components too.

2.What are Children Props in React?
props.children is a special prop in React that allows a component to receive content placed between its opening and closing tags.

Example:

function Card(props) {
  return (
    <div>
      {props.children}
    </div>
  );
}

function App() {
  return (
    <Card>
      <h2>Welcome to React</h2>
      <p>Learning React step by step!</p>
    </Card>
  );
}

export default App;

Output:

Welcome to React
Learning React step by step!

3.Why do we use Custom Hooks and Children Props?

**
Custom Hooks:**

  • Reuse logic between components.
  • Reduce repeated code.
  • Keep components cleaner and easier to maintain,

Children props:

  • Make components more reusable.
  • Allow flexible content inside components.
  • Help create reusable layouts,card and containers.

I learnt how Custom hooks help us reuse logic across React components and props.children allows us to pass content inside components.

title: Weak randomness that protects nothing — and the one that only looks harmless
description:
"Weak randomness" sounds like a verdict. In a scanner report it is only a pointer — and this teardown is about the two times that pointer landed in a real run, and why neither one meant what the label suggested.

This is from a run we publish so builders can see what a check actually looks like before they buy one. No client code was involved. Two public Java codebases, scanned as-is with a frozen OWASP rule set (Semgrep 1.140.0):

  • MyBatis JPetStore-6 — an online-store web app: 46 Java files, 7,628 lines
  • Spark (perwendel/spark) — a Java web framework: 184 Java files, 21,272 lines

Total: 230 files, 28,900 lines, about 46 seconds. 16 findings issued, every one read in context and dispositioned: 1 real fix (low), 1 informational, 14 not-a-defect.

An earlier teardown in this series covered the one real fix (a deletion cookie missing its Secure flag). This one is about CWE-330 — weak randomness — the smallest category in the report: exactly two hits.

What was checked

The rule set covers, among others, weak randomness (CWE-330), SQL injection (CWE-89), and insecure cookies (CWE-614). It reads Java source only. Code or logic living in XML mappers, configuration, or another language is outside its sight, and the report says so out loud — "not checked" is never dressed up as "checked and clean."

Hit one: a random number that guards nothing

JPetStore-6, .mvn/wrapper/MavenWrapperDownloader.java:97 — CWE-330, ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextLong().

Read in context, the value does one job: it helps name a temporary file while the Maven wrapper downloads itself during a build. It is not a session token. It is not a reset code, an ID anyone can guess their way into, or a key. Nothing an attacker wants depends on whether that number is predictable.

Disposition: not a defect. A random value only matters to security when something trusts it — when guessing it gets you in, resets something, or reveals something. Here, guessing it gets you the name of a temp file.

Hit two: harmless here, hazardous as a habit

Spark, src/test/java/spark/examples/books/Books.java:48 — CWE-330, new Random() minting an ID in the bundled example app.

This one is the mirror image. In its actual home — a demo app inside a test tree — predictable IDs hurt nobody; it is example code showing how the framework works. So it is not a defect either.

Disposition: informational — and that word is doing real work. Example code is the most-copied code in any ecosystem. The day that new Random() ID pattern gets pasted into production — into order IDs, invite links, password-reset tokens, anything sequential-or-guessable that an outsider can enumerate — it becomes a genuine vulnerability with a quiet origin: "it came from the framework's own example."

Same rule, same label, two different reasons to stand down — and a third case, the production copy, where the correct answer would have been "fix this first."

The question that separates them

For any weak-randomness hit, one question does most of the adjudication:

What breaks if someone can predict this number?

  • Nothing depends on it (a temp-file name) → not a defect, with the reason written down.
  • Something demo-only depends on it (an example app's IDs) → informational; flag the pattern, not the file.
  • Access, money, identity, or recovery depends on it (tokens, reset codes, production IDs) → real finding, fix before launch, with a cryptographically secure generator.

A scanner cannot ask that question. It does not know what your number protects. That is not a scanner failure — it is the boundary of what pattern matching is, and the reason the human read is part of the service rather than an apology for the tool.

The numbers underneath

This rule set was not tuned for this sample. On its labeled calibration corpus (OWASP Benchmark v1.2, scored blind — the detector never saw the answer file), it measured precision 0.7169 and Youden J 0.4100.

In plain terms: hits that do not survive reading are expected, budgeted behavior. In this run the full tally was 1 real fix (Spark's deletion cookie, Response.java:314, missing the Secure flag), 1 informational (the example-code randomness above), and 14 not-a-defect — each with its reason printed beside it, including the four "SQL injection" warnings in a routing file that contains no SQL at all.

What a builder can use from this

  1. Ask what the number protects before you touch the code. Severity lives in the dependency, not in the generator's name.
  2. Treat example code as future production code. Audit the patterns your examples teach, because your users will copy them verbatim.
  3. Write the disposition down. "Not a defect — value names a temp file, protects nothing" can be re-checked in seconds a year from now. An unexplained dismissal has to be re-argued from scratch.

If you want this kind of check on your own app before launch, the intake is at verify.novitasnexus.com — verify@novitasnexus.com if you prefer email.

title: Godot HUD tutorial 2D: hearts, a stamina bar that holds a grudge, and icons that gray out when locked
description:
A label that says "HP: 1 / 5" is technically a HUD. So is a sticky note on your monitor. Both work. Neither one makes a player sweat.

This is a step by step Godot HUD tutorial for 2D: a row of hearts driven by HP, a stamina bar with a "ghost" drain that holds a grudge for a moment so the hit reads, a pulse on the last heart, and a skill bar where the fireball goes muted during its cooldown, sweeps back to color, and counts down. One slot stays locked, because every RPG needs a thing you can see and not have.

The HUD never touches the player. The player emits signals. The HUD listens. Everything in the GIF above is a real Godot 4.3 run, recorded with Movie Maker, and every script below is the file that ran.

1. Set up the project

I used Godot 4.3 with the Compatibility renderer and a 1280x720 viewport. That is the setup everything below was tested on.

Copy in only the icons you need. This demo uses three state folders from Cozy RPG HUD Icons:

res://icons/normal/01_heart.png
res://icons/normal/02_heart_empty.png
res://icons/normal/04_stamina.png
res://icons/normal/14_sword.png
res://icons/normal/20_fireball.png
res://icons/muted/14_sword.png
res://icons/muted/20_fireball.png
res://icons/locked/21_ice_shard.png

The icons are smooth vector-style art at 128x128, so leave texture filtering on (the pack README says the same). They get scaled down to 40, 56 and 104 px here, and filtering keeps the outlines smooth.

The muted and locked files have the same names as the normal ones. That matters later: a state change is a folder change. (An earlier devlog walks through all six states. Here we just put three of them to work.)

2. The player only emits signals

The player owns the numbers. It has no idea a HUD exists. Save this as res://player.gd:

extends Node
# player.gd: owns the numbers. It never touches the HUD. It only emits signals.

signal health_changed(current: int, max_hp: int)
signal stamina_changed(current: float, max_stamina: float)
signal skill_used(skill_id: StringName, cooldown: float)

const SKILLS := {&"sword": 0.8, &"fireball": 3.0}

@export var max_hp := 5
@export var max_stamina := 100.0
@export var sprint_cost := 40.0     # per second
@export var stamina_regen := 30.0   # per second
@export var regen_delay := 0.6      # seconds after the last spend

var hp := max_hp
var stamina := max_stamina
var sprinting := false
var _regen_wait := 0.0
var _cooldowns := {}  # skill_id -> seconds left


func take_hit(amount: int) -> void:
    hp = clampi(hp - amount, 0, max_hp)
    health_changed.emit(hp, max_hp)


func heal(amount: int) -> void:
    hp = clampi(hp + amount, 0, max_hp)
    health_changed.emit(hp, max_hp)


func spend_stamina(amount: float) -> bool:
    if stamina < amount:
        return false
    stamina -= amount
    _regen_wait = regen_delay
    stamina_changed.emit(stamina, max_stamina)
    return true


func try_cast(skill_id: StringName) -> bool:
    if _cooldowns.get(skill_id, 0.0) > 0.0:
        return false
    _cooldowns[skill_id] = SKILLS[skill_id]
    skill_used.emit(skill_id, SKILLS[skill_id])
    return true


func _process(delta: float) -> void:
    for id in _cooldowns.keys():
        _cooldowns[id] = maxf(_cooldowns[id] - delta, 0.0)

    var old := stamina
    if sprinting and stamina > 0.0:
        stamina = maxf(stamina - sprint_cost * delta, 0.0)
        _regen_wait = regen_delay
        if stamina == 0.0:
            sprinting = false
    elif _regen_wait > 0.0:
        _regen_wait -= delta
    else:
        stamina = minf(stamina + stamina_regen * delta, max_stamina)
    if stamina != old:
        stamina_changed.emit(stamina, max_stamina)

Three signals carry everything the HUD needs: health_changed, stamina_changed and skill_used. The player also refuses a cast while that skill is still cooling down, so the HUD never has to be the one that says no.

The regen_delay is small but important. Without it, stamina starts refilling the frame you stop spending, and the ghost bar in step 5 never gets its moment.

3. Build the HUD scene

Make a new scene, res://hud.tscn, with this tree:

HUD (CanvasLayer)                  hud.gd
  Top (PanelContainer)             top-left, offset 24, 24
    VBox (VBoxContainer)
      %Hearts (HBoxContainer)      heart_row.gd
      StaminaRow (HBoxContainer)
        StaminaIcon (TextureRect)  04_stamina.png, 40x40
        %StaminaBar (Control)      stamina_bar.gd, min size 260x26
          Ghost (ProgressBar)      Full Rect
          Bar (ProgressBar)        Full Rect
  Skills (PanelContainer)          anchored bottom center
    Row (HBoxContainer)
      %Sword (skill_slot.tscn)     icon_file = 14_sword.png
      %Fireball (skill_slot.tscn)  icon_file = 20_fireball.png
      %IceShard (skill_slot.tscn)  icon_file = 21_ice_shard.png, locked = on

The % means Access as Unique Name (right click the node). Then scripts can say %Hearts and you can rearrange the tree without fixing paths.

Styling is plain StyleBoxFlat overrides:

  • Both panels: dark cocoa background, a 3 px brown border, 16 px corner radius.
  • Ghost: a dark background style and a pale cream fill.
  • Bar: a green fill and a StyleBoxEmpty background, so the ghost shows through behind it.
  • Turn off Show Percentage on both bars. Nobody in a boss fight wants to read "70%".

Order matters. Bar comes after Ghost in the tree, so it draws on top.

4. A heart row with a low-health pulse

One TextureRect per heart. Full or empty. Save as res://heart_row.gd:

extends HBoxContainer
# heart_row.gd: one TextureRect per heart. Full or empty. Pulses on the last heart.

const FULL := preload("res://icons/normal/01_heart.png")
const EMPTY := preload("res://icons/normal/02_heart_empty.png")

@export var heart_size := 56
@export var low_hp := 1

var _pulse: Tween


func set_hearts(current: int, max_hp: int) -> void:
    while get_child_count() < max_hp:
        var rect := TextureRect.new()
        rect.expand_mode = TextureRect.EXPAND_IGNORE_SIZE
        rect.stretch_mode = TextureRect.STRETCH_KEEP_ASPECT_CENTERED
        rect.custom_minimum_size = Vector2(heart_size, heart_size)
        rect.pivot_offset = rect.custom_minimum_size / 2
        add_child(rect)
    for i in get_child_count():
        var rect: TextureRect = get_child(i)
        rect.visible = i < max_hp
        rect.texture = FULL if i < current else EMPTY
    _set_pulse(current > 0 and current <= low_hp, current - 1)


func _set_pulse(on: bool, index: int) -> void:
    if _pulse:
        _pulse.kill()
        _pulse = null
    for rect in get_children():
        rect.scale = Vector2.ONE
        rect.modulate = Color.WHITE
    if not on:
        return
    var heart: TextureRect = get_child(index)
    _pulse = create_tween().set_loops()
    _pulse.set_trans(Tween.TRANS_SINE)
    _pulse.tween_property(heart, "scale", Vector2(1.2, 1.2), 0.25)
    _pulse.parallel().tween_property(heart, "modulate", Color(1.35, 0.85, 0.85), 0.25)
    _pulse.tween_property(heart, "scale", Vector2.ONE, 0.35)
    _pulse.parallel().tween_property(heart, "modulate", Color.WHITE, 0.35)

The row builds its own hearts the first time set_hearts runs, so max_hp can change without editing the scene.

The pulse is a looping Tween on the last full heart: scale up a little, tint it warmer, then come back. Two details worth knowing:

  • Set pivot_offset to the center. The default pivot is the top left corner, and a heart that pulses from its corner looks like it is trying to leave.
  • Kill the old Tween before you make a new one. An infinite loop you forgot about will keep pulsing a heart you already healed.

5. A stamina bar with a ghost drain

The trick is two ProgressBars stacked on top of each other. The front one drops at once. The ghost behind it waits, then drains. The pale gap between them is the damage, and it stays on screen long enough to read. The ghost holds a grudge, but only for 0.35 seconds.

Save as res://stamina_bar.gd:

extends Control
# stamina_bar.gd: the front bar drops at once. A ghost bar behind it waits, then drains.

@export var ghost_delay := 0.35
@export var ghost_time := 0.45

@onready var bar: ProgressBar = get_node("Bar")
@onready var ghost: ProgressBar = get_node("Ghost")

var _ghost_tween: Tween


func set_value(current: float, max_value: float) -> void:
    bar.max_value = max_value
    ghost.max_value = max_value
    if current >= bar.value:
        # Refill: no ghost needed. Only lift the ghost if the bar passed it.
        bar.value = current
        ghost.value = maxf(ghost.value, current)
        return
    # A drop: park the ghost where the bar was, then let it catch up later.
    ghost.value = maxf(ghost.value, bar.value)
    bar.value = current
    if _ghost_tween:
        _ghost_tween.kill()
    _ghost_tween = create_tween()
    _ghost_tween.tween_interval(ghost_delay)
    _ghost_tween.tween_property(ghost, "value", current, ghost_time) \
        .set_trans(Tween.TRANS_QUAD).set_ease(Tween.EASE_OUT)

Each drop restarts the ghost Tween. During a sprint, stamina_changed fires every frame, so the ghost keeps getting told to wait. It stays parked at the starting value until you stop running, then drains in one smooth slide. That is the "how much did that sprint cost me" moment, and it took zero extra code.

Refills skip the ghost. Nobody needs a dramatic reveal of stamina coming back.

If you have bar art, TextureProgressBar works the same way. Both are Range nodes, so value and max_value behave the same. Change the two type hints in the script. (I only ran the ProgressBar version for this post.)

6. A skill slot that goes muted on cooldown

A TextureProgressBar already has everything a cooldown needs: a texture under, a texture on top, and a radial fill mode. Put the muted icon under and the normal icon on top, set the fill to clockwise, and value becomes "how recharged is this".

Make res://skill_slot.tscn with a TextureProgressBar root (custom minimum size 104x104, Nine Patch Stretch on) and one child Label called Countdown set to Full Rect, centered, size 34, with a dark outline. Attach res://skill_slot.gd:

extends TextureProgressBar
# skill_slot.gd: color icon when ready. Muted icon plus a clockwise sweep while cooling down.

@export var icon_file := "20_fireball.png"
@export var locked := false

@onready var countdown: Label = get_node("Countdown")

var cooling := false


func _ready() -> void:
    fill_mode = FILL_CLOCKWISE
    min_value = 0.0
    max_value = 1.0
    step = 0.0
    countdown.text = ""
    if locked:
        texture_under = load("res://icons/locked/" + icon_file)
        texture_progress = null
        value = 0.0
    else:
        texture_under = load("res://icons/muted/" + icon_file)
        texture_progress = load("res://icons/normal/" + icon_file)
        tint_under = Color(0.7, 0.7, 0.7)  # darken the muted part so the sweep reads
        value = 1.0


func start_cooldown(seconds: float) -> void:
    if locked or cooling:
        return
    cooling = true
    value = 0.0
    var tween := create_tween()
    tween.tween_method(_tick.bind(seconds), 0.0, 1.0, seconds)
    await tween.finished
    cooling = false
    countdown.text = ""
    # A quick flash so "ready" is noticed
    modulate = Color(1.6, 1.6, 1.6)
    create_tween().tween_property(self, "modulate", Color.WHITE, 0.25)


func _tick(t: float, seconds: float) -> void:
    value = t
    countdown.text = "%.1f" % (seconds * (1.0 - t))

What happens on a cast:

  1. value jumps to 0, so the whole slot shows the muted icon.
  2. tween_method runs _tick from 0 to 1 over the cooldown. The color icon sweeps back in clockwise and the label counts down.
  3. When the Tween finishes, the label clears and the slot flashes once so the player notices it is ready.

tint_under darkens the muted part a little. Muted is designed to keep some color, which is nice in a menu and a bit too polite for a cooldown sweep. The darker under texture makes the edge of the sweep easy to see at a glance.

The locked slot uses the locked icon as its under texture, has no progress texture, and ignores start_cooldown. It just sits there with its little padlock, being aspirational.

With Nine Patch Stretch on, the 128 px icons drew at the 104 px slot size in this 4.3 run, clockwise fill included.

7. Wire the HUD to the player

res://hud.gd connects the signals and pulls the starting values once:

extends CanvasLayer
# hud.gd: listens to a player. It knows nothing about damage, sprinting or spells.

@onready var hearts: HBoxContainer = %Hearts
@onready var stamina_bar: Control = %StaminaBar
@onready var slots := {
    &"sword": %Sword,
    &"fireball": %Fireball,
}


func watch(player: Node) -> void:
    player.health_changed.connect(hearts.set_hearts)
    player.stamina_changed.connect(stamina_bar.set_value)
    player.skill_used.connect(_on_skill_used)
    # Pull the starting values once, so the HUD is right on frame one.
    hearts.set_hearts(player.hp, player.max_hp)
    stamina_bar.set_value(player.stamina, player.max_stamina)


func _on_skill_used(skill_id: StringName, cooldown: float) -> void:
    if slots.has(skill_id):
        slots[skill_id].start_cooldown(cooldown)

From whatever scene owns both, it is three lines. This is from the demo's main.gd:

var hud = load("res://hud.tscn").instantiate()
add_child(hud)
hud.watch(player)

The HUD never asks the player for anything after that. You can delete the HUD and the player keeps working. You can test the HUD with a fake player that only emits signals. You can swap the hearts for a bar next month and nobody else has to know.

For the demo I drove the player from a script: one hit, a 1.2 second sprint, a sword swing, a fireball, two more hits, a 30 stamina dodge, a recast attempt while the fireball was still cooling down, then a heal. The calls are the public ones above, for example:

player.spend_stamina(30.0)

What I checked

All of this ran in Godot 4.3.stable (Compatibility renderer, xvfb, Movie Maker at 30 FPS). Both runs exited with code 0 and no script errors.

  • The HUD found 2 cooldown slots (sword, fireball) and built 5 hearts on frame one.
  • Signals in order: health_changed(4, 5), skill_used(sword, 0.8), skill_used(fireball, 3), health_changed(2, 5), health_changed(1, 5), health_changed(3, 5).
  • Stamina after the 1.2 second sprint: 52 of 100. In the frames, the ghost stayed at the pre-sprint value until the sprint stopped, then drained.
  • A second fireball cast during its cooldown returned false, and the slot kept counting down.
  • The last heart pulsed at 1 HP and stopped when healed to 3.
  • The locked slot never changed.
  • Run length: 330 frames, 11 seconds. The GIF and both stills come from those runs.

Tuning notes

  • Ghost timing: 0.3 to 0.4 seconds of delay reads well. Much longer and players think the bar is broken.
  • Low HP threshold: low_hp is an export. With 10 hearts you probably want it at 2 or 3.
  • Countdown format: %.1f is good for short cooldowns. For anything over 10 seconds, whole numbers look calmer.
  • Keyboard hints, tooltips and a "not enough stamina" shake are easy to add on top. Each one is another listener, not another reference to the player.

Skip the icon homework

The code here is short. The slow part of a HUD like this is the art: a full and an empty heart that match, plus a muted and a locked version of every skill, all lined up so a swap is just a path change.

That is what Cozy RPG HUD Icons is. You get 64 icon designs in six states (normal, muted, grayscale, locked, muted locked, grayscale locked), all as 128x128 PNGs, plus six matching 1024x1024 atlases with JSON coordinates for each state. Same file names in every state folder, same atlas cells in every sheet. The hearts, stamina, sword, fireball and ice shard above are five of the 64.

Get them here: Cozy RPG HUD Icons

title: Building a restart-safe Minecraft death chest plugin without losing items
description:
Death chests look simple until you test the edge cases. A player dies with a full inventory and armor, the server restarts before they return, another player tries to open the grave, an explosion chain starts nearby, and suddenly the "simple" chest plugin is deleting items or duplicating XP.

While building GraveGuard 1.1.0 for Paper 1.21.x, I ended up with four rules that made the implementation much more reliable.

1. Treat the grave as data, not as a chest

A chest is only the world representation. If the player's inventory cannot fit into the chest inventory, do not silently overflow onto the ground and definitely do not drop the excess into the void.

The durable record should be serialized plugin data:

  • owner UUID
  • world and exact block position
  • item stacks, including overflow
  • stored XP value/progress
  • protection expiry
  • creation time

The chest can be rebuilt from that state after restart. If the chest inventory is full, remaining items stay in the serialized grave record instead of spawning as loose entities.

2. Persist before you need persistence

Do not wait for a graceful shutdown. Write grave state when the grave is created and update it whenever the contents meaningfully change.

That means the death flow is roughly:

  1. capture inventory and XP
  2. create the serialized grave record
  3. save it
  4. place the world chest/hologram/compass state

If step 4 fails after step 3, you can repair the world object. If the server dies before step 3, the player loses everything — exactly the bug the plugin exists to prevent.

3. XP is not just "levels"

A naive implementation stores player.getLevel() and later calls setLevel(). That loses partial progress toward the next level.

If you promise exact XP recovery, store total XP progress carefully and restore both level and progress through Bukkit's XP methods. Then test weird values, not only round levels: level 0 with partial progress, high levels, and deaths after enchantment/table use.

4. Protection needs server-operational semantics

Owner protection is more than cancelling inventory clicks.

Also consider:

  • block break attempts
  • explosions
  • hoppers and other inventory movement
  • server restarts extending or pausing timers
  • what happens when the owner respawns far away
  • admins needing a cleanup path

For GraveGuard, the owner receives the return compass after respawn rather than while still in the death screen. That tiny timing choice avoids a surprising edge case where the item never enters the new inventory.

Validation matters more than the feature list

The final test was not "does a chest appear?" It was a bot-driven Paper test covering death, restart, intruder access, explosion protection, owner recovery, XP restoration, and overflow behavior.

That is the difference between a death-chest demo and a plugin a server owner can trust during a weekend PvP event.

GraveGuard 1.1.0 is public here:

  • Hangar: https://hangar.papermc.io/SecondWindMC/GraveGuard/versions/1.1.0
  • GitHub: https://github.com/SecondWindMC/GraveGuard/releases/tag/v1.1.0
  • Project site: https://secondwindmc.github.io/

I am interested in feedback from other Paper developers: what is the nastiest inventory-loss edge case you have seen in production?

title: Kil-C 0.29.24: less memory, faster business jobs, same answers
description:
Kil-C 0.29.24 is out. There's no new syntax, and every program gives the same answers as before, checked byte for byte. This update is about doing the same work with less: big files now take far less memory, and three business jobs got faster.

What changed

  • Large files use much less memory
  • JSON reading is faster
  • Date and quote handling is faster
  • Log analysis is faster and lighter

Business jobs, 0.29.23 → 0.29.24

  • Bank statements: 135 → 112 ms, 238 → 103 MB
  • Event processing: 434 → 379 ms, 409 → 43 MB
  • Log analysis: 289 → 244 ms, 441 → 151 MB
  • Sales report: same speed, 22 → 16 MB
  • Invoices: unchanged

Event processing now uses a tenth of the memory it did last week.

Against other languages

We ran the same five jobs in Rust, Go and Python, and every language produced identical output. Kil-C finished first in all five.

  • Bank: Kil-C 112 ms, Rust 151 ms, Go 1.14 s, Python 3.68 s (33× faster than Python)
  • Events: Kil-C 379 ms, Rust 511 ms, Go 2.00 s, Python 6.39 s
  • Logs: Kil-C 244 ms, Rust 325 ms, Go 1.39 s, Python 7.14 s
  • Sales: Kil-C 384 ms, Rust 445 ms, Go 416 ms, Python 2.19 s
  • Invoices: Kil-C 60 ms, Rust 84 ms, Go 100 ms, Python 630 ms

Memory: better, not a clean sweep

Kil-C now uses less memory than Rust on every business job. On event processing, for example, it's 43 MB against Rust's 498 MB. Go still uses less memory than Kil-C on three of the five jobs, and we're working on it.

Energy

We measure energy in joules per run instead of assuming that faster means less power. Kil-C used less energy than Rust, or the same, on all 16 programs we test. A few examples:

  • Event processing: 11% less (in the last version it used more)
  • Log analysis: 16% less
  • Invoices: 26% less
  • Counting: 53% less

On the business jobs, Kil-C uses 81–91% less energy than Python.

How we measured

Measured November 25, 2026. Each number is the middle of repeated runs, with the languages taking turns.

See more

There's more data than fits in one post:

  • The website: kilc.dev has the head-to-head races against Python, pandas, JavaScript, Java and Go, plus Kil-C Studio and the business packages.
  • The test page: kilc.dev/#tests has every test in full: all 16 programs against Rust, Go and Python, energy, memory, start-up, and Gridline, our spreadsheet. It includes the tests where we don't win.

Check both, and tell us in the comments what you'd like us to test next.

title: Introducing Pano View: An Open-Source 360 Panorama Development Toolkit for React and Three.js
description:
Introduction

I've been working with panoramic imagery, virtual tours, 360° video, and immersive web applications for many years.

While there are several established panorama viewers and development tools available, I wanted a solution that integrates naturally into modern React applications, provides greater flexibility, and gives developers more control over their application architecture.

That's why I started building Pano View, an open-source panorama development toolkit built with React, Three.js, React Three Fiber, and TypeScript.

What initially started as a panorama viewer has gradually evolved into a broader development toolkit covering panorama rendering, image processing, and visual content authoring.

The project is released under the MIT license.

More Than a Panorama Viewer

Pano View currently consists of three complementary packages, each addressing a different part of the panorama development workflow.

  1. Pano View — Panorama Rendering

Pano View is a React component library designed for building interactive panoramic experiences.

Its key features include:

Equirectangular and cubemap panorama rendering

Multi-resolution tiled panoramas with dynamic LOD

360° panoramic video playback

Interactive and customizable hotspots

Multi-scene navigation and transitions

WebGL and WebGPU rendering

WebXR and mobile VR support

Compatibility with existing krpano tile formats

TypeScript APIs and component-based architecture

Although the rendering layer is built on React Three Fiber, developers can integrate the viewer directly into React applications without having to manage the underlying Three.js rendering environment themselves.

npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/@ericchen1990/pano-view

  1. Pano Converter — Panorama Processing for Node.js

Rendering is only one part of building a panorama-based application. Preparing and processing panoramic assets is equally important, particularly when dealing with high-resolution imagery.

Pano Converter provides a standalone Node.js toolkit for panorama processing, including:

Panorama conversion

Cubemap generation

Multi-resolution tile generation

Panorama reconstruction

Programmatic APIs and CLI tools

It can be integrated into server-side processing pipelines, automated workflows, and content management systems.

Pano Converter can also be used independently of the viewer and does not require React.

npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/@ericchen1990/pano-converter

  1. Pano Editor — Embeddable Visual Authoring

Pano Editor provides visual content authoring capabilities for panoramic experiences and virtual tours.

Rather than requiring developers to build an entire panorama editor from scratch, it is designed to help them integrate visual editing capabilities into their own React applications.

This is particularly useful for SaaS platforms and content management systems where users need to create and manage their own immersive experiences.

npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/@ericchen1990/pano-editor

Why React and Three.js?

One of the fundamental design decisions behind Pano View is to build on an existing ecosystem rather than introduce another standalone rendering framework.

React provides a familiar component-based development model, while Three.js and React Three Fiber provide a flexible foundation for graphics rendering.

This approach allows developers to:

Integrate panoramas into existing React applications.

Build custom interfaces using familiar React components.

Connect panoramic experiences with application state and business logic.

Leverage the broader Three.js ecosystem.

Customize interactions without being restricted to a predefined application structure.

The intention is not to replace Three.js or React Three Fiber, but to provide specialized panorama capabilities on top of them.

WebGL, WebGPU, and WebXR

Modern browser graphics technologies are opening up new possibilities for immersive web experiences.

Pano View supports both WebGL and WebGPU rendering, as well as WebXR for immersive experiences on compatible devices.

Supporting these technologies within the same development toolkit allows developers to explore modern rendering capabilities while continuing to build applications for conventional desktop and mobile browsers.

Potential Use Cases

Pano View is designed as a development toolkit rather than a fixed-purpose virtual tour application.

It can be used to build:

Virtual tours and interactive exhibitions

Real estate and architectural visualization

Immersive educational platforms

Interactive tourism experiences

360° video applications

Cultural heritage and digital museums

Panorama-based SaaS products

Custom content authoring platforms

The project is already being used in a real-world immersive education platform, where it supports interactive panoramic learning experiences.

Try It Out

The interactive playground provides demonstrations of the project's rendering capabilities, interactions, and development tools.

Interactive Playground

https://pano-view-playground.vercel.app/

GitHub Repository

https://github.com/Eric-Chen1990/pano-view

npm Packages

Pano View

Pano Converter

Pano Editor

Final Thoughts

Pano View is my attempt to make panorama development more accessible, flexible, and better integrated with modern web development practices.

Instead of building a closed ecosystem or an all-in-one application, the project focuses on providing reusable components and specialized tools that developers can integrate into their own products.

I'd love to hear feedback from developers working with React, Three.js, WebGPU, WebXR, panoramic imagery, or immersive web applications.

What challenges have you encountered when building panorama-based applications? Are there particular capabilities or development workflows that you find difficult with existing solutions?

Feedback, discussions, and contributions are always welcome.

title: Write the validator once: Rust on the desktop, WebAssembly in the browser
description:
When the same rules run in two languages, they drift. A date the browser accepts, the desktop tool rejects. A money amount looks fine in a form, then fails later because JavaScript rounded it. I ran into this while sharing formatters and validators between a desktop app and a standalone page that has no install.

The fix is not a second implementation, and it is not "we will be careful." It is one implementation, compiled twice: Rust on the native side, and the same crate compiled to WebAssembly for the page. This is a short, working walk through that split, using a ledger line as the example, because amounts and dates are where a TypeScript-only check quietly goes wrong.

You will end up with a pure Rust crate, a handful of cargo test cases, a thin WebAssembly wrapper, and a JavaScript call that returns the same violations as the tests.

What we are validating

A ledger line is a debit, a credit, an amount in minor units (cents, or the equivalent), a currency, a booked-on date, and a short reference. The checks are ordinary, which is the point:

  • the amount is a whole number, not zero, and not larger than a stated limit
  • the currency is a three-letter uppercase code from a list the caller supplies
  • the booked-on date is a real calendar day in YYYY-MM-DD form, and is not after "today"
  • the reference and account ids match simple character rules, and the two accounts are different

"Today" is not read from a clock inside the crate. The caller passes it in. That is what makes the same function testable, and what makes the native build and the WebAssembly build comparable.

1. Keep the core crate pure

Use a small workspace with two crates: ledger_rules holds every rule and has no knowledge of JavaScript; ledger_rules_wasm is a door that parses JSON and calls the first crate.

The amount is a string, not an i64 or a JavaScript number. Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER is 2^53 − 1. Above that, a JSON number is no longer an exact integer. A string such as "2500" or "-199" crosses the boundary without being rounded.

pub struct LedgerLine {
    pub amount_minor: String,
    pub currency: String,
    pub booked_on: String,
    pub reference: String,
    pub debit: String,
    pub credit: String,
}

pub struct Context<'a> {
    pub today: &'a str,
    pub currencies: &'a [&'a str],
}

pub struct Violation {
    pub field: &'static str,
    pub code: &'static str,
    pub message: String,
}

pub fn validate(line: &LedgerLine, ctx: &Context<'_>) -> Vec<Violation> { /* ... */ }

validate collects every problem and returns them all. It does not panic on bad input, and it does not stop at the first error. A form can highlight several fields at once, and a desktop tool can show the same list.

The amount parser is intentionally strict. It rejects a decimal point, a leading plus, and scientific notation, all of which a JavaScript toString() on a number can produce.

fn parse_amount(raw: &str) -> AmountError {
    let s = raw.trim();
    if s.is_empty() {
        return AmountError::Empty;
    }
    if s.contains('.') || s.contains('e') || s.contains('E') || s.contains('+') {
        return AmountError::NotInteger;
    }
    match s.parse::<i64>() {
        Ok(0) => AmountError::Zero,
        Ok(n) if n.unsigned_abs() > AMOUNT_ABS_MAX as u64 => AmountError::OutOfRange,
        Ok(_) => AmountError::Ok,
        Err(_) => AmountError::NotInteger,
    }
}

Dates need the same attitude. YYYY-MM-DD is compared as a calendar date, including leap years. The crate does not call Date, and it does not accept a timestamp with a time or a zone. If you need those, parse them in the wrapper and pass a calendar day in.

fn parse_iso_date(s: &str) -> Result<(i32, u8, u8), ()> {
    let bytes = s.as_bytes();
    if bytes.len() != 10 || bytes[4] != b'-' || bytes[7] != b'-' {
        return Err(());
    }
    let year: i32 = std::str::from_utf8(&bytes[0..4]).unwrap().parse().map_err(|_| ())?;
    let month: u8 = std::str::from_utf8(&bytes[5..7]).unwrap().parse().map_err(|_| ())?;
    let day: u8 = std::str::from_utf8(&bytes[8..10]).unwrap().parse().map_err(|_| ())?;
    if !(1..=12).contains(&month) || day == 0 || day > days_in_month(year, month) {
        return Err(());
    }
    Ok((year, month, day))
}

fn is_leap(year: i32) -> bool {
    year % 4 == 0 && (year % 100 != 0 || year % 400 == 0)
}

fn days_in_month(year: i32, month: u8) -> u8 {
    match month {
        1 | 3 | 5 | 7 | 8 | 10 | 12 => 31,
        4 | 6 | 9 | 11 => 30,
        2 if is_leap(year) => 29,
        2 => 28,
        _ => 0,
    }
}

The from_utf8(...).unwrap() calls are on fixed slices of an existing &str, so they cannot fail. The date itself is still validated. 2025-02-29 is rejected; 2024-02-29 is accepted; 2026-11-26 is rejected when today is 2026-11-25.

2. Test the rules natively first

Do not start with the browser. If a rule is wrong, you want cargo test to say so in a fraction of a second, on the same crate the desktop app will link.

#[test]
fn rejects_a_javascript_style_decimal_amount() {
    let mut line = valid();
    line.amount_minor = "25.00".into();
    assert_eq!(codes(&line), vec![("amount_minor", "not_integer")]);
}

#[test]
fn rejects_impossible_and_future_dates() {
    let mut line = valid();
    line.booked_on = "2025-02-29".into();
    assert_eq!(codes(&line), vec![("booked_on", "format")]);
    line.booked_on = "2024-02-29".into();
    assert!(codes(&line).is_empty());
    line.booked_on = "2026-11-26".into();
    assert_eq!(codes(&line), vec![("booked_on", "in_future")]);
}

valid() is a well-formed line, and codes maps each violation to (field, code) so the tests stay short. Add cases for an empty amount, a zero amount, a lowercase currency, a missing account, and two accounts that match. I also keep one test that feeds several problems at once, so a later change cannot silently start returning only the first error.

3. Add a thin WebAssembly door

The second crate depends on ledger_rules, serde_json, and wasm-bindgen. Pin wasm-bindgen to the same version as the wasm-bindgen command you will run. The crate's only job is to turn two JSON strings into a LedgerLine and a Context, call validate, and turn the result back into JSON. LineJson and ContextJson are Serde types with the same fields. If the JSON itself is invalid, the function still returns a JSON array, with field set to _, and it does not panic.

#[wasm_bindgen]
pub fn validate_ledger_line(line_json: &str, ctx_json: &str) -> String {
    let line: LineJson = match serde_json::from_str(line_json) {
        Ok(v) => v,
        Err(err) => return error("_", "bad_json", &format!("Invalid line JSON: {err}")),
    };
    let ctx: ContextJson = match serde_json::from_str(ctx_json) {
        Ok(v) => v,
        Err(err) => return error("_", "bad_json", &format!("Invalid context JSON: {err}")),
    };

    let currencies: Vec<&str> = ctx.currencies.iter().map(String::as_str).collect();
    let context = Context {
        today: &ctx.today,
        currencies: &currencies,
    };
    let line = LedgerLine {
        amount_minor: line.amount_minor,
        currency: line.currency,
        booked_on: line.booked_on,
        reference: line.reference,
        debit: line.debit,
        credit: line.credit,
    };

    let violations: Vec<serde_json::Value> = ledger_rules::validate(&line, &context)
        .into_iter()
        .map(|v| {
            serde_json::json!({
                "field": v.field,
                "code": v.code,
                "message": v.message,
            })
        })
        .collect();
    serde_json::to_string(&violations)
        .unwrap_or_else(|_| error("_", "encode", "Could not encode the result."))
}

Build it, then generate the JavaScript glue. --target nodejs is convenient for a check script; use --target web when the caller is a page.

rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown

cargo test -p ledger_rules
cargo build --target wasm32-unknown-unknown --release -p ledger_rules_wasm

wasm-bindgen target/wasm32-unknown-unknown/release/ledger_rules_wasm.wasm \
  --out-dir js/pkg --target nodejs --out-name ledger_rules

From JavaScript, or TypeScript, the door is one function that takes two JSON strings and returns a JSON array:

import { validate_ledger_line } from "./pkg/ledger_rules.js";

type Violation = { field: string; code: string; message: string };

const ctx = {
  today: "2026-11-25",
  currencies: ["EUR", "USD", "GBP", "IRR"],
};

const line = {
  amount_minor: "2500",
  currency: "EUR",
  booked_on: "2026-11-20",
  reference: "INV-1092",
  debit: "CASH1001",
  credit: "REV2002",
};

const violations: Violation[] = JSON.parse(
  validate_ledger_line(JSON.stringify(line), JSON.stringify(ctx)),
);

For a well-formed line, violations is empty. Change amount_minor to "25.00" and you get { field: "amount_minor", code: "not_integer" }, which is the same pair the Rust test asserts.

I compiled this crate, ran eight native tests with cargo test, generated the Node module with wasm-bindgen 0.2.130, and ran the same cases from Node. They agreed.

Pitfalls

Pass amounts as strings. If the page holds the amount in a number and then JSON.stringifys the object, values above Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER will already have been rounded before Rust sees them. Keep the value as text from the input field to the crate.

Do not panic in the wrapper. A panic in WebAssembly is a poor debugging experience and a blank form. Parse errors should come back as data, in the same shape as rule violations.

Do not read a clock, the filesystem, or the network in the shared crate. The moment a rule calls the current time, the tests need stubs and the two runtimes can disagree. Pass "today", currency lists, and limits in as Context.

Keep the wrapper thin. If a new rule lands only in the TypeScript that calls the module, you are back to two implementations. New rules go in ledger_rules first, with a test, and the wrapper only learns a new field if the JSON shape changes.

Pin the tools together. The wasm-bindgen crate and the wasm-bindgen CLI must be the same version. A mismatch often fails at generate time with a version error, which is easy to misread as a target problem.

Be precise about dates. A JavaScript Date will accept values this crate rejects, and it will also surprise you with time zones. If the user typed a calendar day, validate that day.

When this is worth it

For a required-field check on a marketing form, a second implementation is cheaper than a toolchain. This split starts to pay when the rules have a shape you do not want to write twice: calendar dates, integer money, checksums, formatters, or OpenAPI-style constraints that also need to run in a desktop app.

I use it in Alita when a desktop window and a standalone page have to agree. The core stays a normal Rust library. WebAssembly is only the way a browser is allowed to call it.

I'm Aran Shayan, a frontend developer at SOHA who builds data-heavy interfaces and the APIs behind them. More at aranshayan.com.

title: XPS to PDF Conversion in Java
description:
XPS to PDF conversion in Java is essential for many enterprise workflows that need reliable, print‑ready documents. Conholdate.Total for Java is a powerful SDK that simplifies this task for Java developers. In this guide you will learn how to set up the library, run a complete conversion example, explore key options, and apply performance best practices.

How to Perform XPS to PDF Conversion in Java - Step by Step

  1. Add Maven or Gradle Dependency: Include Conholdate.Total in your build file so the SDK classes are available. 
   <repositories>
       <repository>
           <id>conholdate-repo</id>
           <name>Conholdate Maven Repository</name>
           <url>https://repository.conholdate.com/repo/</url>
       </repository>
   </repositories>
   <dependency>
       <groupId>com.conholdate</groupId>
       <artifactId>conholdate-total</artifactId>
       <version>24.9</version>
       <type>pom</type>
   </dependency>
  1. Initialize the Converter: Load the XPS source using XpsLoadOptions. 
   LoadOptions loadOptions = new XpsLoadOptions();
   try (Converter converter = new Converter("sample.xps", loadOptions)) {
       // conversion will be performed in the next step
   }
  1. Configure PDF Output: Set compliance, page size, orientation, and render mode via PdfConvertOptions. 
   PdfConvertOptions pdfOptions = new PdfConvertOptions();
   pdfOptions.setCompliance(PdfConvertOptions.PdfCompliance.PDF_A_1B);
   pdfOptions.setPageSize(PdfPageSize.A4);
   pdfOptions.setPageOrientation(PdfPageOrientation.PORTRAIT);
   pdfOptions.setRenderMode(PdfRenderMode.FAST);
  1. Execute the Conversion: Call converter.convert with the output path and options. 
   converter.convert("sample_converted.pdf", pdfOptions);
  1. Benchmark the Process: Record start and end times with Instant to evaluate performance. 
   Instant start = Instant.now();
   // conversion code here
   Instant end = Instant.now();
   System.out.println("Conversion completed in " + 
       Duration.between(start, end).toMillis() + " ms");

For more details on each class, refer to the API reference.

XPS to PDF Sample - Complete Code Example

The following code demonstrates the core functionality of XPS to PDF conversion in Java using Conholdate.Total.

import com.groupdocs.conversion.Converter;
import com.groupdocs.conversion.options.load.LoadOptions;
import com.groupdocs.conversion.options.load.XpsLoadOptions;
import com.groupdocs.conversion.options.convert.PdfConvertOptions;
import com.groupdocs.conversion.options.convert.PdfConvertOptions.PdfCompliance;
import com.groupdocs.conversion.options.PdfPageSize;
import com.groupdocs.conversion.options.PdfPageOrientation;
import com.groupdocs.conversion.options.PdfRenderMode;

import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Paths;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.time.Instant;

public class XpsToPdfDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // Input XPS file and desired PDF output
        String inputPath = "sample.xps";
        String outputPath = "sample_converted.pdf";

        // Start timing for benchmarking
        Instant start = Instant.now();

        // Load options (can be extended with password, etc.)
        LoadOptions loadOptions = new XpsLoadOptions();

        // Conversion options with PDF-specific settings
        PdfConvertOptions pdfOptions = new PdfConvertOptions();
        pdfOptions.setCompliance(PdfCompliance.PDF_A_1B);               // PDF/A-1b compliance
        pdfOptions.setPageSize(PdfPageSize.A4);                         // A4 page size
        pdfOptions.setPageOrientation(PdfPageOrientation.PORTRAIT);    // Portrait orientation
        pdfOptions.setRenderMode(PdfRenderMode.FAST);                  // Faster rendering, lower memory

        // Perform conversion inside try‑with‑resources to ensure proper cleanup
        try (Converter converter = new Converter(inputPath, loadOptions)) {
            converter.convert(outputPath, pdfOptions);
        } catch (Exception e) {
            System.err.println("XPS to PDF conversion failed: " + e.getMessage());
            e.printStackTrace();
            return;
        }

        // End timing and report duration
        Instant end = Instant.now();
        Duration elapsed = Duration.between(start, end);
        System.out.println("Conversion completed in " + elapsed.toMillis() + " ms");

        // Verify that the PDF file was created
        if (Files.exists(Paths.get(outputPath))) {
            System.out.println("PDF file successfully created at: " + outputPath);
        } else {
            System.err.println("PDF file was not created.");
        }
    }
}

Note: This code example demonstrates the core functionality. Before using it in your project, make sure to update any file paths and configuration values to match your actual environment, verify that all required dependencies are properly installed, and test thoroughly in your development environment. If you encounter any issues, please refer to the official documentation or reach out to the support team for assistance.

Conholdate.Total for Java - Prerequisites and Setup

To start converting XPS to PDF, you need Java 8 or higher and a valid Conholdate.Total license. Download the SDK from the download page. After adding the Maven dependency shown earlier, you can also use Gradle:

repositories {
    maven {
        url "https://repository.conholdate.com/repo/"
    }
}
implementation 'com.conholdate:conholdate-total:24.9'

Make sure to place your license file in the application directory or set the license programmatically as described in the documentation.

Key Features of Conholdate.Total for Java for XPS to PDF

  • PDF/A‑1b Compliance - Guarantees long‑term archiving compatibility.
  • Fast Rendering Mode - Optimizes memory usage for large XPS files.
  • Page Size and Orientation Control - Adjust output to A4, Letter, portrait, or landscape.
  • Extensible Load Options - Future‑proof handling of password‑protected XPS files.
  • Comprehensive API - Full access to conversion settings via the Java SDK.

For a deeper dive, see the official documentation.

Conversion Options: Tuning PDF Output

The PdfConvertOptions class offers several properties you can tweak:

  • Compliance - Choose between PDF/A‑1b, PDF/A‑2b, etc. (already set in the sample).
  • PageSize - Options include A4, LETTER, LEGAL.
  • PageOrientation - PORTRAIT or LANDSCAPE.
  • RenderMode - FAST for speed, HIGH_QUALITY for better visual fidelity.

You can modify any of these directly in the code snippet shown in the steps section.

Performance Considerations for XPS to PDF Conversion

  1. Render Mode - Using PdfRenderMode.FAST reduces CPU load and speeds up conversion, which is useful for batch processing.
  2. Stream vs File - For large documents, consider using streams instead of file paths to lower I/O overhead.
  3. Benchmarking - The sample measures elapsed time with Instant. Run the conversion multiple times and calculate average duration to get a reliable benchmark.
  4. Thread Safety - Create a separate Converter instance per thread; the SDK is not thread‑safe for shared instances.

Applying these tips helps you achieve consistent conversion times, especially when integrating the SDK into a servlet or a Spring Boot service.

Conclusion

XPS to PDF conversion in Java becomes straightforward with Conholdate.Total for Java. By following the steps, configuring the options, and applying performance best practices, you can generate PDF/A‑1b compliant documents efficiently. Remember to obtain a proper license for production use; you can explore pricing details on the pricing page or request a temporary license to evaluate the SDK.

Common Questions

How do I perform XPS to PDF conversion in Java using Conholdate.Total?
Use the Converter class with XpsLoadOptions and PdfConvertOptions. The sample code in this article shows the exact sequence of calls.

What Maven dependency is required for XPS to PDF conversion in Java?
Add the Conholdate Maven repository and the conholdate-total artifact as demonstrated in the setup section. The same coordinates work for Gradle.

Can I run the conversion from the command line without writing Java code?

Wrap the conversion call with Instant.now() before and after execution, then calculate the duration. For more accurate results, run the conversion multiple times and average the timings.

title: CSS Modules in react?
description:
In React, CSS Modules are CSS files where class names are scoped locally by default.
The CSS file have to have the .module.css extension and can be used by importing it into your React file(s).

Creating a CSS Module

Let's create a CSS module called Button.module.css, where we style some buttons.

Create a file named Button.module.css, and insert some styles in it:

Button.module.css

.mybutton {
  padding: 10px 20px;
  border: none;
  border-radius: 4px;
  cursor: pointer;
}

Using a CSS Module 

import styles from './Button.module.css';

function App() {
  return (
    <div>
      <button className={styles.mybutton}>
        My Button
      </button>
    </div>
  );
}

We import the styles object from the CSS Module
We use styles.mybutton to access the mybutton class
The actual class name of the button will be unique (e.g., _mybutton_q1obu_1)

I just published GraveGuard 1.1.0, a Paper 1.21.x death-grave plugin, and packaged it with SecondWind as a tested SMP mechanics bundle.

title: Windows Kiosks and Command Line Tools, Built From Java
description:
The two kinds of software people least expect to write in Java are the app that owns a panel PC in a shop and the tool you type into a terminal. Both used to be bad fits for the same reason: a JVM to install, seconds of startup, and a runtime that doesn't own the machine. Codename One compiles your Java ahead of time to C and then to one native executable, so both problems go away. This week that covers locked down Windows kiosks and command line tools.

What is Codename One? Codename One is an open-source framework for building native iOS, Android, desktop, and web apps from a single Java or Kotlin codebase. Learn more at codenameone.com.

Two weeks ago we added embedded Linux. Plenty of devices in shops, factories and lobbies run Windows on a panel PC instead, because that's what the hardware vendor shipped and what IT knows how to manage.

Kiosks on Windows IoT Enterprise

A kiosk is an app that owns the device. The customer at a self-checkout shouldn't be able to reach the desktop, open a browser or press Alt+F4. On Windows, getting there usually means a native app plus a day of fighting Shell Launcher and Group Policy.

One build hint turns your app into one:

codename1.arg.windows.embedded=true
codename1.arg.windows.embedded.board=imx8
codename1.arg.windows.embedded.rotation=90

The result is the same native .exe the native Windows port builds, with no JVM, configured for a device:

  • A frameless window that covers the monitor and stays on top.
  • The Windows key, Alt+Tab, Alt+F4 and Ctrl+Esc are blocked.
  • Codename One's own on-screen keyboard instead of the Windows one, so it matches your UI.
  • Rotation, density, the target monitor and the cursor set by build hints or environment variables, so one build serves a portrait totem and a landscape counter.

Board profiles cover generic x64 with or without a mouse, generic arm64, i.MX 8 and Qualcomm IoT boards. Windows 10 and 11 IoT Enterprise are supported. Windows 10 IoT Core isn't.

Deploy over SSH 

mvn cn1:deploy-device -Dcn1.device.host=kiosk.local -Dcn1.device.user=Administrator \
    -Dcn1.device.kioskUser=kiosk -Dcn1.device.keyboardFilter=true

That copies the app to the device, configures Shell Launcher so the app replaces the desktop for the kiosk user, and with keyboardFilter=true also blocks Ctrl+Alt+Del. If the app crashes, Shell Launcher restarts it. mvn cn1:device-logs follows the log from your machine.

Talking to the hardware

The same com.codename1.hardware API from the Linux port works on Windows. Every COM port is available, which covers most receipt printers, scales and card readers:

Hardware hw = Hardware.getInstance();
SerialPort printer = hw.openSerial("COM3", 9600, 8, SerialPort.PARITY_NONE, 1);
byte[] receipt = "Thank you!\n".getBytes("UTF-8");
printer.write(receipt, 0, receipt.length);

hw.setBacklightBrightness(hw.getMaxBacklightBrightness() / 2);   // night mode

GPIO, I2C, SPI and PWM go through the Windows.Devices APIs, which need a board whose vendor ships the bus drivers. IoT boards do. Most x64 panel PCs don't, and on those the API reports that the feature isn't available rather than failing at run time. The backlight works over DDC/CI or WMI. CAN and a hardware watchdog aren't available, because Windows has no standard interface for either.

The app on the kiosk shares its entity classes with your backend and your phone app, which is the point of building all of them from one project.

Command line tools with real terminal UIs

Most internal tooling is a command line tool: deploy scripts, data migrations, admin utilities. Java has always been an awkward fit for those because of JVM startup and because you need to ship a JVM. Codename One's backend now builds a CLI as one native executable with nothing to install beside it.

The command line is declared with annotations in the picocli style, and bound at build time with no reflection:

@Command(name = "deploy", description = "Deploys a service.",
        mixinStandardHelpOptions = true)
public class Deploy implements Callable<Integer> {
    @Option(names = {"-s", "--service"}, description = "Service to deploy")
    String service = "api";

    @Override
    public Integer call() throws Exception {
        // ...
        return 0;
    }
}

The new console API draws the output:

Console.print(new Table("Service", "Status", "Replicas")
        .align(2, Table.Align.RIGHT)
        .addRow("api", Console.style("running", Console.Style.GREEN), 3)
        .addRow("worker", Console.style("degraded", Console.Style.YELLOW), 2)
        .render());

try (ProgressBar bar = new ProgressBar("upload", 40).unit("files")) {
    for (int i = 0; i < 40; i++) {
        upload(i);
        bar.step();
    }
}

Spinner spinner = Spinner.start("waiting for health checks");
waitForHealthy();
spinner.succeed("healthy");

Interactive prompts handle the questions a deployment tool asks:

String env = Prompt.select("Environment", Arrays.asList("staging", "production"));
List<String> regions = Prompt.multiSelect("Regions", Arrays.asList("us-east", "eu-west"));
if (!Prompt.confirm("Deploy to " + env + "?", false)) {
    return 1;
}

Select with the arrow keys.
Confirm, password and number prompts.
Parallel progress.
Multiple selection.

There's also a Tree, MultiProgress for parallel work, LiveRegion for output that redraws in place, password and number prompts, and raw key reading. Console knows the terminal's width, whether output is a terminal at all, and how many colors it supports, and it honors NO_COLOR and CLICOLOR_FORCE. Pipe the tool into a file and the colors and spinners step aside by themselves.

It isn't a windowing toolkit with panes. It's the set of pieces that make up nearly every CLI people like to use.

Build the executable with ./mvnw cn1:backend-package. It compiles to C and then to a native binary for the host machine, which can be Linux or macOS. During development it runs on the JVM like any other backend code, and the Initializr has a "Command-line tool" project type for Maven and Gradle.

Learn more

The embedded Windows chapter covers board profiles, deployment options and hardware access. The command line chapter covers commands, options, the console API and packaging. If you're running kiosks on Windows today, I'd like to know what you're using to build them.

Security

Feature

Custom organization policies for Agent Platform Workbench instances

You can now use custom organization policies to allow or deny the creation and update of Agent Platform Workbench instances based on their configuration. Custom constraints for the notebooks.googleapis.com/Instance resource are enforced when you create or update an instance, and support dry-run mode. This feature is now generally available (GA). For more information, see Create custom organization policy constraints.

Apigee X

Feature

Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool arguments are sent to the location their OpenAPI parameter declares

This change applies to Apigee X in all supported regions.

An MCP tool argument whose OpenAPI parameter declares in: header is now sent to your backend as a request header, and one that declares in: cookie is sent in the Cookie header. Previously both were appended to the query string. in: query and in: path parameters are unchanged, and every parameter still appears in the tool's inputSchema, so MCP clients supply arguments exactly as before. If a backend reads one of these values from the query string, declare the parameter in: query or read it from its declared location.

On a tool call that supplies at least one cookie argument, the Cookie header is replaced with only the declared cookie parameters, omitting any others. Any cookie your backend relies on must be declared as an in: cookie parameter.

An MCP proxy that was already deployed continues to use the previous query-string behavior until its configuration is next regenerated. To adopt the new routing on an existing MCP proxy, deploy a new revision of it.

For the full mapping, see Tool argument placement on the backend request.

Security

On October 24, 2026, we published a security bulletin for Apigee.

Two vulnerabilities in PHP core (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, "PHP2Shell") allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code remotely on a server running a vulnerable PHP version. The impact is limited to Drupal-based Apigee developer portals, which customers deploy and operate. Apigee, Apigee Hybrid, and the Apigee integrated portal don't use PHP and aren't affected.

Security bulletin published: GCP-2026-072
