title: How to choose a web data API for product and monitoring workflows
description:
Disclosure: I work at Flowda.

This page is published by Flowda, one of the products compared.

How to choose a web data API for product and monitoring workflows

Choosing a web data API is not a single decision. Different teams need different outputs: a search result, page content, a structured record, or a signal that a page has changed. If you start by comparing providers without defining your workflow, you will end up with a tool that works in a demo but fails in production.

This guide walks through a practical way to choose and test a web data API for real product workflows.

Start with the output your application needs

Before comparing providers, write down the exact output your application needs.

For example:

  • a search request that returns relevant URLs;
  • page content from a known URL;
  • structured records from a supported page type;
  • a list of URLs from a domain;
  • a change signal when a page changes.

These are not interchangeable. A search result is not the same as a usable page. A page URL is not the same as the content behind it. A change event is not the same as a new record.

If you define this early, you can test the API against the actual workload instead of a sample request.

Separate discovery from extraction

Many workflows combine two jobs:

  1. Find a URL or set of URLs.
  2. Read the content behind those URLs.

Some APIs handle both in one call. Others separate them. The important thing is to understand whether discovery and extraction are distinct in your workflow.

If you already know the URL, you probably need extraction. If you do not, you may need search or site mapping first.

For example, a product-price monitor usually needs:

  1. A known product URL.
  2. The current title and price.
  3. A repeat check on a schedule.
  4. A comparison with the previous version.
  5. A notification when the value changes.

That workflow is different from a one-time export.

Test the response shape, not just the request

A successful HTTP response does not mean you received useful data. Your application needs a particular response shape.

When you test a request, record:

  • the endpoint;
  • the input URL;
  • the response status;
  • whether the API reports success inside the payload;
  • whether the fields you need exist;
  • whether the values are usable without extra parsing;
  • whether failed fetches are distinguishable from successful ones.

For example, a product record should include a title, price, currency and availability. A page that returns navigation text or a login screen is not usable product data, even if the request technically succeeded.

This is why validation should happen before storage. Treat partial or invalid records as failed, not as successful fetches.

Use the same authentication in tests and production

A common mistake is testing without the same permissions you will use in production.

In Flowda, you create an API key in the console and choose which endpoints it can access. In production, the key is sent as a bearer token:

Authorization: Bearer <API_KEY>

When you test, use the same endpoint scope and headers you plan to deploy. Otherwise, a request can behave differently after release.

A good test log includes:

  • endpoint;
  • input URL;
  • response status;
  • API-reported success;
  • fields used;
  • elapsed time;
  • retry count.

That makes later debugging much easier.

Test both success and failure paths

Most integrations are tested only with good pages. But production reliability depends more on how the system handles failures.

Test what happens when:

  • the page is unavailable;
  • the page redirects elsewhere;
  • the page returns a login screen;
  • the layout changes;
  • a required field disappears;
  • the response is slow;
  • the API reports an extraction failure.

Then decide how your application should respond:

  • retry immediately;
  • retry later;
  • mark the record stale;
  • alert an operator;
  • pause the monitoring job;
  • keep the last valid record.

Flowda, for example, can return HTTP 200 with data.success: false when the target cannot be fetched. Your application should treat that as a failed extraction rather than as usable content.

This distinction is one of the most important parts of the integration.

Decide whether every check needs to be live

Some workflows need the page exactly as it exists at request time. Others can tolerate a recent snapshot.

Flowda lets you control this with max_age_ms. If your application must observe the page now, request a live fetch:

{
  "max_age_ms": 0
}

But not every check needs that. For pages that rarely change, snapshot reuse may be fine. For high-impact pages, live fetching may be necessary.

A useful pattern is:

  • allow snapshot reuse for low-frequency checks;
  • request a live fetch for pages with high business impact;
  • request a live fetch after a validation warning;
  • reduce the check frequency for stable pages.

This helps you balance freshness, reliability and cost.

Monitor changes, not just pages

A page monitor should not simply say “the page changed.” It should say whether the change matters.

Start by identifying the section or fields you care about. For a pricing page, you may care about price, currency and availability. For a documentation page, you may care about headings and body text.

Then test the monitoring path deliberately:

  1. Create a watch job.
  2. Capture a baseline snapshot.
  3. Edit a visible line on the target page.
  4. Wait for the next check.
  5. Confirm that the diff contains the expected line.
  6. Confirm that your webhook receives the event.

Flowda Watch, for example, can check a page on a schedule and send a line-level diff by webhook when content changes.

But the event is only the beginning. Your handler should validate whether the changed line is meaningful, deduplicate repeated events and route the alert to the correct owner.

Deduplicate before you alert

If a page oscillates or changes multiple times in a short window, a raw change stream can become noisy.

Use a stable deduplication key:

  • page identifier;
  • field or section;
  • previous value;
  • new value;
  • time window.

Then decide what to do with repeated events:

  • drop exact duplicates;
  • merge repeated changes into one incident;
  • escalate if the change repeats;
  • reset the alert once the page stabilizes.

This makes the alerting system useful rather than noisy.

Measure cost per validated record

Raw request count is not enough. You should measure the work your application actually produces.

For a monitoring workflow, track:

  • pages monitored;
  • checks per day;
  • live fetches versus snapshot reuse;
  • requests that returned usable records;
  • requests that failed validation;
  • change events received;
  • change events that required downstream action.

Two useful metrics are:

  • cost per validated record;
  • cost per useful change event.

These are more meaningful than cost per raw request, because a raw request can return content your application cannot use.

Validate schema before storage

If your application depends on structured data, validate the response schema before storing anything.

For a product record, you may need:

  • title as a non-empty string;
  • price as a numeric value;
  • currency as an ISO code;
  • availability as a known enum;
  • url as a canonical product URL;
  • updated_at as a timestamp you control.

If a field is missing, do not treat the record as complete. Store it as partial only if your system can handle partials safely. Otherwise, mark it failed and keep the last valid version.

This prevents downstream systems from consuming incomplete data as authoritative.

Run a small pilot before scaling

Do not jump from local testing to full production.

Run a pilot with a limited set of pages:

  • your most important page type;
  • one slow or dynamic page;
  • one page that changes often;
  • one page that rarely changes;
  • one edge case where fields might disappear.

Track every request and response. Compare successful records against raw requests. If the pilot shows stable records and reliable alerts, you can scale gradually.

Keep the integration simple

A web data API integration should be easy to reason about.

A minimal structure is:

request -> validation -> storage -> downstream action

For monitoring:

monitor -> webhook -> validation -> deduplication -> alerting

Each step should have one purpose. If you mix validation, storage, alerting and business logic in one place, debugging becomes harder.

What to check before production

Before you launch, make sure you have tested:

  • the exact output your application needs;
  • discovery versus extraction;
  • authentication and endpoint permissions;
  • response shape;
  • fetch success versus business success;
  • failure handling;
  • live fetch versus snapshot reuse;
  • monitoring and change events;
  • deduplication;
  • cost per validated record.

A web data API should fit the job, not just demonstrate that it can return a page. Define the workflow first, test the real workload second, and only then compare providers.

title: AI text detectors should never be used to accuse anyone (Wednesday AI Opinion)
description:
Wednesday AI Opinion. Today's take: an "AI-written" score from a text detector is not evidence. It should never be the reason someone gets accused, rejected, failed or fired.

I build with LLMs every day, and I get why people want a detector. Schools, hiring teams and content platforms are flooded with generated text. But a tool that is wrong in predictable, unfair ways is worse than no tool, because it gives a guess the look of proof.

Here's why I think that, with sources.

1. The company that built ChatGPT shut down its own detector

In January 2023 OpenAI released a classifier to flag AI-written text. On its own "challenge set" it correctly identified only 26% of AI-written text as "likely AI-written," and wrongly labeled human-written text as AI-written 9% of the time. OpenAI said plainly that it "is not fully reliable."

As of July 20, 2023, OpenAI withdrew it "due to its low rate of accuracy" (OpenAI).

If the team with the most access to the model couldn't make detection reliable, a third-party score deserves a lot of skepticism.

2. False positives are not random. They hit non-native writers

Stanford researchers (Liang, Yuksekgonul, Mao, Wu, Zou, published in Patterns, 2023) tested seven widely used GPT detectors on 91 human-written TOEFL essays and 88 US 8th-grade essays:

  • The detectors were near-perfect on the US 8th-grade essays.
  • They misclassified more than half of the TOEFL essays as AI-generated, with an average false positive rate of 61.22%.
  • 89 of the 91 TOEFL essays (97.80%) were flagged as AI by at least one detector.
  • The essays all seven detectors flagged had significantly lower perplexity. In plain words: simpler, more constrained English looks "AI-like" to these tools.

The authors also showed simple prompting could bypass the detectors, and they caution against using them in evaluative or educational settings (arXiv:2304.02819).

So the people most likely to be wrongly accused are the ones writing in their second language.

3. The people you actually want to catch can evade them

Sadasivan et al. (University of Maryland, "Can AI-Generated Text be Reliably Detected?") stress-tested watermarking, neural-network, zero-shot and retrieval-based detectors with a recursive paraphrasing attack. Paraphrasing significantly reduced detection rates while only slightly degrading text quality in many cases. They also showed watermarked models can be spoofed so that human text gets misclassified (arXiv:2303.11156).

That's the worst combination: honest people get flagged, and motivated people paraphrase their way through.

4. Do the base-rate math before you trust a flag

This part is my own illustration, using OpenAI's published rates (26% true positive, 9% false positive). Say you check 1,000 documents and 100 of them are actually AI-written:

  • Flagged correctly: 26% of 100 = 26
  • Flagged wrongly: 9% of 900 = 81

That's 107 flags, and about 3 out of 4 are innocent people. The rarer real AI use is in your pile, the worse this gets. A "flagged" result alone tells you very little.

What I'd do instead

  1. Never act on a detector score alone. Treat it, at most, as a weak hint to look closer, and tell people when a tool is in use.
  2. Change the process, not the policing. Ask for drafts, version history, or a short conversation about the work. In hiring, test skills live instead of scoring cover letters.
  3. Say what AI use is allowed. "Use AI to brainstorm, cite it, write the final yourself" beats a secret ban you can't enforce.
  4. If you build the product, prefer provenance over guessing. Record where content came from when it's created, instead of trying to guess afterwards from style.
  5. Audit for bias. If you must use a detector, measure its false positives on your real population, especially non-native writers, before it touches a decision.

Detection is a guess dressed up as a number. Don't let it make decisions about people.

Where do you stand: should AI detectors be allowed in grading or hiring at all?

References

  • OpenAI, "New AI classifier for indicating AI-written text" (Jan 31, 2023; withdrawn July 20, 2023): https://openai.com/index/new-ai-classifier-for-indicating-ai-written-text/
  • Liang et al., "GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers," Patterns (2023): https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.02819
  • Sadasivan et al., "Can AI-Generated Text be Reliably Detected?": https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.11156

title: How to Test a Delta-Hedge Backtest With Two Trades and a Cash Ledger
description:
A hedge simulator gets two stock fills. It sells 80 shares at $108 and buys them back at $100. The options cost $600 and expire worthless. Charge five cents per share on both stock trades and the simulator should return +$32. Change just the sell fill to $107.60 and the answer becomes exactly zero. Those two runs can expose a surprising number of bookkeeping errors.

This article was drafted with AI assistance. All prices, fills and probabilities below belong to a constructed example. The Python program uses only the standard library.

Give the simulator something it can get wrong

Buy one call and one put with the same $100 strike and expiry. Each contract has a multiplier of 100. Both settle in cash at expiry, so the pair pays 100 times the absolute distance between the final stock price and $100. Its opening price is $6 per share for the pair, or $600 in total. The stock starts at $100. There is one scheduled hedge decision between entry and expiry. At expiry we close any stock position. Set interest, dividends, borrow fees and option execution costs to zero for this test. The stock is available to borrow. Options Industry Council on the long straddle

We can generate the price and hedge size from the same model. At the hedge decision, the stock is $92, $100 or $108 with respective pricing weights of 5/32, 22/32 and 5/32. The remaining move to expiry is independent and uniformly distributed over −$10 to +$10. Writing x for the mid-period stock price minus the strike, in dollars, averaging the absolute terminal payoff gives a per-share option value of 5 + x²/20 for |x| ≤ 10. Its slope is x/10. The three mid-period marks are $8.20, $5 and $8.20. Their weighted average gives the $6 opening price. The symmetry gives an opening delta of zero, so we begin with no stock.

At $108 the model delta is +0.80 per share of the underlying. The option position therefore has the local directional exposure of 80 shares, and the hedge order sells 80. At $92 the sign reverses and the hedge buys 80. These quantities are available before the expiry price is known. Keep the fill price in a separate field so you can change execution without retroactively changing the order size. Options Industry Council on delta

Keep two independent accounts of the same path

The cash ledger starts at minus the premium. For each stock fill, subtract the signed quantity times its fill price and subtract the fee. A sale has a negative quantity and therefore adds cash. At expiry add the option settlement. With the stock flattened, the final cash balance equals net profit or loss measured from immediately before entry.

The second account starts at zero and tracks gains since entry. For each interval, use the stock position held at its start times the change in the reference stock price. Add the change in the option mark. At the end of the interval, execution contributes the signed trade quantity times (reference price minus fill price), less fees. The fill adjustment makes the second account work even if the stock sale receives a worse price than the hedge signal saw. The same fee enters each independent calculation once.

Save the following as hedge_replay.py and run python3 hedge_replay.py. Prices passed to the replay are integers or exact decimal values. The model schedules full fills and uses whole-share targets at each of its three decision prices.

from decimal import Decimal as D
from typing import NamedTuple

STRIKE = D("100")
MULTIPLIER = D("100")
WIDTH = D("10")
FEE = D("0.05")
NODES = [(D("92"), D(5) / 32), (D("100"), D(22) / 32),
         (D("108"), D(5) / 32)]


def quote(spot):
    offset = spot - STRIKE
    if abs(offset) > WIDTH:
        return abs(offset), D(1) if offset > 0 else D(-1)
    value = WIDTH / 2 + offset**2 / (2 * WIDTH)
    return value, offset / WIDTH


PREMIUM = MULTIPLIER * sum(quote(spot)[0] * weight for spot, weight in NODES)


class Result(NamedTuple):
    cash: D
    marked: D
    shares_traded: D
    fees: D


def replay(mid, close, *, mid_fill=None, hedge=True, fee=FEE):
    mid_value, delta = quote(mid)
    target = -MULTIPLIER * delta if hedge else D(0)
    settlement = MULTIPLIER * abs(close - STRIKE)
    events = [
        (mid, mid_value * MULTIPLIER, target, mid if mid_fill is None else mid_fill),
        (close, settlement, D(0), close),
    ]
    stock, shares_traded, fees = D(0), D(0), D(0)
    cash, marked = -PREMIUM, D(0)
    last_spot, last_option = STRIKE, PREMIUM

    for spot, option_value, next_stock, fill in events:
        marked += stock * (spot - last_spot) + (option_value - last_option)
        change = next_stock - stock
        cost = abs(change) * fee
        cash -= change * fill + cost
        marked += change * (spot - fill) - cost
        shares_traded += abs(change)
        fees += cost
        stock, last_spot, last_option = next_stock, spot, option_value

    cash += settlement
    assert stock == 0 and cash == marked
    return Result(cash, marked, shares_traded, fees)


def conditional_mean(mid):
    # The terminal P&L is linear on either side of the strike.
    lo, hi = mid - WIDTH, mid + WIDTH
    knots = [lo] + ([STRIKE] if lo < STRIKE < hi else []) + [hi]
    integral = D(0)
    for left, right in zip(knots, knots[1:]):
        endpoints = replay(mid, left).cash + replay(mid, right).cash
        integral += (right - left) * endpoints / 2
    return integral / (hi - lo)


up, flat, down = (replay(mid, STRIKE) for mid in (108, 100, 92))
assert PREMIUM == 600
assert up == down == Result(D(32), D(32), D(160), D(8))
assert flat == Result(D(-600), D(-600), D(0), D(0))
assert replay(108, 100, hedge=False) == flat
assert replay(108, 100, fee=D("0.25")).cash == 0
assert replay(108, 100, mid_fill=D("107.60")).cash == 0
assert replay(108, 100, mid_fill=D("107.59")).cash == D("-0.80")
assert replay(108, 108).cash == 192  # $800 option settlement, zero stock gain

mean = sum(weight * conditional_mean(mid) for mid, weight in NODES)
assert mean == D("-2.50")
print(f"up and back {up.cash:+.2f} | flat {flat.cash:+.2f} | "
      f"down and back {down.cash:+.2f} | model mean {mean:+.2f}")

The output is up and back +32.00 | flat -600.00 | down and back +32.00 | model mean -2.50.

Catch the right error for the right reason

On the move from $100 to $108, the account has zero stock. The option mark rises from $600 to $820. On the way back, the account is short 80 shares and earns $640 on stock while the option gives up $820. Interval gains are +$220 and −$180 before fees. A spreadsheet that uses the newly computed short position on the first interval invents a $640 loss on shares it had yet to sell. At $92, a sign error that always sells stock fails the mirror-path test. The separate $108 expiry test exercises a positive option settlement, which the two headline examples cannot test.

The up-and-back path earns $40 before costs and trades 160 shares counting both sides. Its break-even fee is $40/160, or $0.25 per share per side. At five cents per share in fees, a 40-cent deterioration in the sale price consumes the remaining $32. We hold the original 80-share order fixed for that exercise. A model that recomputes delta from the worse fill is testing a different decision rule. In a KAEL AI review of this example, I would ask for the decision quote and the execution report side by side. With both records in hand, another researcher can vary either price and explain the difference.

Give the winning path its proper weight

To calculate the last number in the output, assume the simulated paths follow the same probabilities used to price the option. At fixed midpoint, the expiry cash result is piecewise linear in the closing price, with a kink at the strike. The integral in the program splits there and takes one trapezoid per linear segment. That gives an exact average over the continuous terminal distribution and removes random sampling error.

There is a short independent check. The expected option settlement equals the initial premium. The stock's conditional expected move after the hedge is zero. Trading occurs at the $92 and $108 nodes, with a combined probability of 10/32, and each round trip costs $8. Expected net P&L is therefore −$2.50 per pair. That number belongs to these pricing and path assumptions. With live data, the first things an engineer needs to reproduce an observed result are the original hedge timestamp, the pre-trade position, the fills, and the two option marks bounding each interval.

title: The Illusion of the 200 OK: Why Core Banking QA Lives and Dies in the Database
description:
The UI said "Transfer Successful," but the ledger is out of balance. A practical guide to database testing for QA engineers in fintech.

The Silent Bleed

(A hypothetical scenario, built from common failure patterns in payment systems.)

On a Monday morning, a digital bank's settlement job throws a critical exception. The platform is short by millions.

No alarms fired over the weekend. The app showed near-perfect uptime. Every automated transfer test in CI was green, and every API call had returned HTTP 200 with a clean response: {"status": "SUCCESS"}.

Yet inside the database, hundreds of senders had been debited while the receivers got nothing.

In banking, an HTTP status code is a transport-layer illusion. It tells you the web server received a request and didn't crash. It tells you nothing about whether the money moved or the ledger balanced.

If you sign off money-movement tickets based only on API responses and green UI checkmarks, you are flying blind.

Application State vs. Database State

A transfer usually runs in several steps:

  1. Verify the sender's balance
  2. Insert a debit record
  3. Insert a credit record
  4. Update the balances
  5. Return a response

Here is the flaw. If step 2 succeeds and step 3 fails (a network blip, a lock timeout, a null constraint), what happens next depends on how developers set the transaction boundary.

If auto-commit was on, or a try/catch swallowed the database error to return a "graceful" response, the server still sends 200 OK. The client believes the transfer worked.

Meanwhile the database holds a debit with no matching credit. The money has vanished.

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client / UI
    participant API as API Server
    participant DB as Database

    C->>API: POST /transfer ($200)
    API->>DB: Verify sender balance
    DB-->>API: OK
    API->>DB: Insert DEBIT (sender)
    DB-->>API: Committed
    API->>DB: Insert CREDIT (receiver)
    DB--xAPI: Lock timeout / constraint error
    Note over API: try/catch swallows the error
    API-->>C: 200 OK {"status": "SUCCESS"}
    Note over DB: Debit exists, credit does not.<br/>Ledger is out of balance.

Why Real Banks Don't Store a Single Balance Column

Real core banking systems do not keep one mutable balance field. If an account went from $1,000 to $800, who deducted the $200? A card swipe, an ATM, or a rogue script?

Banks use double-entry bookkeeping. Balances are calculated from immutable ledger rows. Every movement needs equal, offsetting debits and credits.

Two details every QA should know:

  • Money is stored as NUMERIC or Decimal, never FLOAT. Floating-point numbers use binary approximations that cause fraction-of-a-cent drift.
  • A unique reference ID (an idempotency key) on every journal entry lets the database reject duplicates.

4 Database Checks to Run Before Signing Off

Before marking any money-movement ticket "QA Passed," close the browser, open your database tool, and run these.

Note: the queries below are illustrative and PostgreSQL-flavored. They assume a simple schema: journal_entries(id, reference_id) and ledger_lines(journal_entry_id, account_id, direction, amount, currency, created_at), where direction is 'DEBIT' or 'CREDIT'. Adapt table and column names to your own system.

1. The orphan check

Group ledger lines by journal entry and look for any entry where debits don't equal credits.

SELECT journal_entry_id,
       SUM(CASE WHEN direction = 'DEBIT'  THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS total_debits,
       SUM(CASE WHEN direction = 'CREDIT' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS total_credits
FROM ledger_lines
GROUP BY journal_entry_id
HAVING SUM(CASE WHEN direction = 'DEBIT'  THEN amount ELSE 0 END)
    <> SUM(CASE WHEN direction = 'CREDIT' THEN amount ELSE 0 END);

What to look for: even one row means stop testing. Money entered or left the ledger without an offset.

2. The negative-balance check

Compute each account's balance from its ledger lines and flag anything below zero (unless an overdraft limit exists).

SELECT account_id,
       SUM(CASE WHEN direction = 'CREDIT' THEN amount ELSE -amount END) AS balance
FROM ledger_lines
GROUP BY account_id
HAVING SUM(CASE WHEN direction = 'CREDIT' THEN amount ELSE -amount END) < 0;

What to look for: a negative balance usually means a concurrent withdrawal or race condition got past the application's checks.

3. The duplicate-transfer check

Count journal entries per reference ID and flag any ID that appears more than once.

SELECT reference_id, COUNT(*) AS entry_count
FROM journal_entries
GROUP BY reference_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

What to look for: a count above 1 means the app doesn't enforce a unique constraint on the idempotency key. A double-tap on "Send Money" on a slow connection can create two transfers.

4. The zombie-transaction check

Query the database's activity view for transactions stuck "idle in transaction" for more than about 10 seconds.

SELECT pid, state, now() - xact_start AS transaction_age, query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state = 'idle in transaction'
  AND now() - xact_start > interval '10 seconds';

What to look for: these hold row locks and drain the connection pool, which can lead to wider outages.

The Zero-Sum Reconciliation Test

Add one more check to your regression pipeline: a reconciliation query that proves the ledger equation holds.

Total debits − total credits = 0

Run it per currency over the day's entries:

SELECT currency,
       SUM(CASE WHEN direction = 'DEBIT'  THEN amount ELSE 0 END)
     - SUM(CASE WHEN direction = 'CREDIT' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS drift
FROM ledger_lines
WHERE created_at >= CURRENT_DATE
GROUP BY currency
HAVING SUM(CASE WHEN direction = 'DEBIT'  THEN amount ELSE 0 END)
     <> SUM(CASE WHEN direction = 'CREDIT' THEN amount ELSE 0 END);

If the drift is anything other than zero, the ledger is out of balance, and the status should read something like CRITICAL_LEDGER_OUT_OF_BALANCE.

Chaos-Testing Atomicity

To catch silent rollback failures, deliberately break a transfer halfway and check what the database does. Here is the test design:

  1. Insert a journal entry and debit Account A
  2. Raise a simulated failure before the credit step
  3. Assert that the transaction rolled back completely

Then verify in the database, not in the API response:

  • Account A's balance is unchanged
  • No orphan journal entry exists for that reference ID

A Pytest script with a database driver can automate this, wrapping the steps in a single transaction and asserting on the final ledger state.

5 Traps That Cost Junior QAs Credibility

# The trap The senior approach
1 Trusting the green UI toast Query the journal and ledger lines to confirm both legs committed.
2 Testing one request at a time Fire 20 simultaneous withdrawals against a $100 account to expose race conditions and double-spending.
3 Checking only the sender's balance Check the sender, the receiver, the fee account, and the reconciliation view together.
4 Ignoring fee and tax ledgers A $100 transfer with a $2 fee should reduce the sender by $102, credit the receiver $100, and credit $2 to the bank's fee ledger.
5 Asserting on floats Use exact Decimal assertions (Decimal('10.1000')) to catch silent floating-point corruption.

Naive Updates vs. Immutable Ledgers

Area The flaw The fix
Mutating a balance column Destroys history, invites race conditions under load, and makes audits impossible. Append-only ledger lines, with balances computed from history and protected by constraints.
Isolation and locking Running at default READ COMMITTED without row locks lets concurrent requests read stale balances and approve overdrafts. Pessimistic row locking (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) or SERIALIZABLE isolation with retry logic. The right choice depends on your database and workload.
Error handling Catching database exceptions and returning HTTP 200 with an error message in the body. Abort the transaction explicitly and return accurate 4xx or 5xx codes.

A Hypothetical Case: The Midnight Cashback Drift

(A composite scenario with illustrative numbers, not a specific real incident.)

A neobank adds an "Instant Cashback" feature. For purchases over $50, an async microservice credits $5 to the customer's wallet.

It passes staging: the UI shows the cashback badge and the API returns 200.

In production, under load, the cashback service runs out of database connections. The service catches the timeout, logs a warning, and returns 200 so checkout isn't interrupted.

The purchase debit succeeds, but the cashback credit silently fails. The internal ledger drifts out of balance, and nobody notices until the nightly reconciliation job runs.

The lesson: QA had validated the status code and the UI toast. Nobody checked the database under load.

How to Explain This in a Senior QA Interview

A common question: "A payment gateway returns 200 OK, but the recipient never gets the money. How do you debug it at the database level?"

A strong answer works through four steps:

  1. Transaction boundary: were the debit and credit in a single transaction, or split across calls?
  2. Orphan journal check: did a partial debit commit without a matching credit?
  3. Outbox or event check: if the system is event-driven, was the downstream message written and processed?
  4. Lock and rollback logs: were there serialization failures or lock timeouts that aborted the transaction silently?

The principle: verify state at the storage layer, not the transport layer.

3 Takeaways for Your Team

  • Never sign off on HTTP status codes alone. Write automated assertions against the ledger before approving a release.
  • Make zero-sum reconciliation a blocking check in CI. A non-zero drift should fail the pipeline.
  • Inject failures mid-transaction. Kill connections halfway through multi-step operations and confirm rollbacks leave no orphan records.

In banking QA, the API response is a claim. The database is the proof.

What is the most terrifying silent data corruption or ledger drift bug you've found in production? Share your war stories in the comments.

title: Google Images thought our name was an eye condition
description:
ARLTS is a free, non-profit English-learning app for learners in Vietnam and beyond. The name is an abbreviation of Academic Resources for Language Learners and Teachers.

It turns out "Arlt's line" is a medical term: a line of tiny marks on the inner eyelid. When people looked up "arlts" on Google Images, they got close-up photos of eyelids. Not the first look we hoped people would get.

Here is what we did about it.

1. Give Google a picture for every page

Our app is one web page with many views: Learn, Play, Test, and 10 learning activities, 15 little games, 6 tests, and more. Before, Google had almost nothing to look at but our logo.

Now there's one picture per main page, 51 in all. A headless Chrome opens each page and takes a 1280-pixel-wide picture of it, the way a learner would view it.

2. Tell Google where they are

Each page now points to its own picture in its link-preview tags (og:image and twitter:image). Our page map file lists every picture under the page it belongs to, with an <image:image> entry. And the page facts block (the machine-readable facts on the home page) names our logo and links to our other profiles, which helps Google tie the name ARLTS to us.

3. Keep the pictures from going out of date

Pictures of a page drift as the page changes. Our deploy runs a check first: if the page file changed after the last pictures were taken, it retakes all 51 (about a minute) before the upload. Nobody has to remember to do it.

What we learned

  • If your name looks like a word that already means something, Google will go with the older meaning until you give it a reason not to.
  • Pictures help. A page with real pictures of the product gives Google Images something to work with.
  • Automate the boring part, or it won't happen.

It can take weeks for Google Images to catch up, and we don't know yet how well it works. We'll report back.

If you're curious, the app is at https://arlts.org. It's free, with no account needed.

title: How I Built a 16,000-Page Browser Game Portal & AI Tools Directory on Cloudflare
description:
Over the past few months, I built and deployed two very different content-heavy web projects on the exact same stack—Astro + Cloudflare (Pages, Workers, D1, and R2)—with the goal of keeping infrastructure dead simple, fast globally, and cheap to maintain.

Here is a quick breakdown of what worked well, what broke along the way, and the architecture behind both sites.

Project 1: DashJoy Studio — A 16,000+ Page Browser Game Portal

DashJoy Studio is a lightweight browser game portal built for instant play on desktop, Chromebook, and mobile without downloads or forced sign-ups.

The stack & key lessons

  1. Static generation + R2 for 69,000+ WebP thumbnails
    Bundling tens of thousands of cover images directly inside the build output quickly hits deployment file limits. Moving all resized WebP covers and thumbnails (512px, 192px, 160px, 96px) to Cloudflare R2 behind a custom image domain kept the Astro Pages deployment lean while delivering instant edge-cached images.

  2. Migrating votes, reports, and player comments to Workers + D1
    Originally, broken-game reporting and voting ran in a small Docker container backed by SQLite on a VPS. Moving that entire API to Cloudflare Workers + D1 eliminated server maintenance, dropped cold-start latency globally, and made it easy to add a lightweight Player Comments system with rate limiting, spam-link filtering, and a built-in moderation dashboard.

  3. Dedicated "Ad-Free Originals" via Workers Static Assets
    One common frustration on casual game portals is waiting through third-party pre-roll ads. To fix that, I created a separate static Workers project hosting ad-free HTML5 classics—like 2048, Tower Building, OutRun JS Racer, Classic Block Tetris, and Chess vs AI—adapted for dark backgrounds and consistent aspect ratios. You can try them directly in the Ad-Free Originals section.

Project 2: Dorameow — A Bilingual AI & Developer Tools Directory

Alongside the gaming portal, I also built Dorameow, a clean English/Chinese directory for curated AI products, open-source developer tools, and concise daily AI news digests.

Why Astro works so well for directories

  • Zero client-side JavaScript by default: Category grids, tool comparison pages, and daily news posts render as pure HTML/CSS and load almost instantly.
  • Simple bilingual routing: Keeping English and Chinese routes in a single Astro project makes it easy to publish daily updates without maintaining two separate codebases.
  • No bloat: Minimal scripts, fast search/filtering, and clear categories so developers can actually find a useful tool in 10 seconds instead of scrolling through sponsored banners.

Takeaways for Indie Builders

  • Split heavy media from your app deploy early (Cloudflare R2 saves a ton of pain once you pass a few thousand assets).
  • Cloudflare D1 is more than enough for small community features like voting, reporting, comments, and leaderboards—no need to babysit a VPS database.
  • Keep self-hosted sub-apps in separate deployments so updating one interactive feature never forces a full rebuild of a 16,000-page static site.

If you're building with Astro or Cloudflare Workers—or just want to test a quick ad-free game break—feel free to check out DashJoy Studio or Dorameow. Always happy to hear feedback!

title: Ein Termin im eigenen Kalender ist eine Notiz. Ein Termin, den ein Assistent an
description:
Ein Termin im eigenen Kalender ist eine Notiz. Ein Termin, den ein Assistent an sieben Leute verschickt, ist eine Entscheidung.

Genau an dieser Grenze entscheidet sich, ob ein Werkzeug dir Arbeit abnimmt oder neue macht.

FOX WIZ trennt deshalb zwei Klassen von Aktionen. Lesen, zusammenfassen, Entwurf bauen läuft im Hintergrund. Senden, einladen, Datei teilen wartet auf deinen Tap.

Wer so etwas einrichtet oder selbst baut, kommt mit einer Liste weiter. Schreib vor dem ersten Start auf, welche Aktionen Außenwirkung haben:

  • E-Mail senden (nicht: Entwurf anlegen)
  • Einladung an andere verschicken (nicht: Block im eigenen Kalender)
  • Datei oder Link freigeben
  • Kontaktdaten ändern, die andere sehen

Alles auf dieser Liste bekommt eine Bestätigung. Alles andere darf sofort laufen. Diese Trennung ist der eigentliche Aufwand – nicht das Modell dahinter.

Der zweite Teil ist unbequemer: Eine Freigabe, die man nach drei Tagen blind wegklickt, ist keine Freigabe, sondern Theater. Deshalb gehört zu jeder Bestätigung ein Satz, der sagt, was konkret rausgeht – Empfänger, Betreff, Anhang. Nicht „Aktion bestätigen“, sondern „Diese Mail geht an sieben Personen“.

Welche Aktion darf bei dir niemals ohne Rückfrage rausgehen – und bei welcher würdest du die Rückfrage sofort abschalten?

title: Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B Ships 5.9 GB Local Agentic Coding — Overlay Suggestions Still Hit the WASAPI Floor
description:
On 24 November 2026 PrismML released Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B, an upgrade to its ternary-compressed Qwen3.8 27B derivative. It keeps the 5.9 GB footprint while improving multi-turn tool use and agentic coding. SWE-bench Verified rises from 60.8 to 75.6; AppWorld from 51.2 to 90.5. On an RTX 4090 it hits roughly 204 tokens/s with multi-token prediction; on H100 about 291. Weights are Apache 2.0, runnable via PrismML's llama.cpp fork or MLX.

That is a practical unlock for on-device agents that touch private repos or files. It is not a free pass for the audio path if you are shipping a live overlay that needs short suggestions or translations during a technical interview or sales call in another language.

Why local models still wait on capture

A usable real-time overlay needs clean dual-track PCM before any model sees the audio:

  1. Microphone: what you say.
  2. Loopback of the render endpoint: what the remote party says through the call client.

Both must stay in shared-mode WASAPI so the call client keeps the device. Exclusive mode would break the call. The audio engine (audiodg.exe + audioeng.dll) mixes and applies any APOs. Typical shared period is 10 ms. You can request less via IAudioClient3; the engine often ignores it under load.

Rough budget once samples leave the callback (modern laptop, enhancements off):

Stage Typical cost
WASAPI shared period 10 ms
Callback → lock-free ring + convert 1–3 ms
Resample to 16 kHz mono + light VAD 2–5 ms
Local STT first partial 40–120 ms
Small local polish / suggestion model 20–80 ms
Overlay paint <16 ms

A 200 tok/s local LLM is fast for text. The first usable partial still waits on the buffer period plus framing. Drop enhancements, pin the capture thread, and keep a lock-free SPSC ring or the floor moves up.

Minimal dual-track sketch 

// Shared-mode loopback + mic (error handling omitted)
IMMDeviceEnumerator* enumerator = nullptr;
CoCreateInstance(__uuidof(MMDeviceEnumerator), nullptr, CLSCTX_ALL,
                 __uuidof(IMMDeviceEnumerator), (void**)&enumerator);

IMMDevice* defaultRender = nullptr;
enumerator->GetDefaultAudioEndpoint(eRender, eConsole, &defaultRender);

IAudioClient* loopbackClient = nullptr;
defaultRender->Activate(__uuidof(IAudioClient), CLSCTX_ALL, nullptr, (void**)&loopbackClient);

WAVEFORMATEX* format = nullptr;
loopbackClient->GetMixFormat(&format);
loopbackClient->Initialize(AUDCLNT_SHAREMODE_SHARED,
                           AUDCLNT_STREAMFLAGS_LOOPBACK | AUDCLNT_STREAMFLAGS_EVENTCALLBACK,
                           100000, 0, format, nullptr);  // request ~10 ms

// Mirror for capture endpoint without LOOPBACK.
// Callback copies to SPSC ring only. Consumer thread resamples, VAD, feeds STT or local model.

From the ring you can feed a local STT (faster-whisper, Whisper.cpp, Windows ML Speech Recognition Task, or a small GGUF) then a short polish pass with something like Bonsai 2.5 or a smaller sibling. The model never sees the samples until the capture side is correct.

Running the local model

PrismML ships GGUF packs that need their llama.cpp fork (rotated Hadamard basis). A typical command for a short suggestion after a transcript chunk:

./llama-cli -m Ternary-Bonsai-2.5-27B-PTQ1_0.gguf \
  -p "Polish this interview reply to be concise and technical: [transcript]" \
  -c 8192 --temp 0.7 -n 128

On a loaded 4090 the decode is fast enough that the dominant delay is still the audio framing, not the token generation. Keep the context short for the polish step; full agent loops belong in a separate process.

Architecture notes and tradeoffs

  • Shared mode is non-negotiable for call clients. Exclusive would require the call to release the device.
  • Local models remove network RTT and keep transcripts on-machine, but they still consume the same WASAPI period.
  • Ternary packing makes a 27B-class model fit in 6 GB, so a dedicated polish process can stay resident without thrashing. Throughput numbers assume the model is already loaded; cold start and KV cache still matter for interactive use.
  • Overlay lifetime is independent. A Win32 layered window or DirectComposition surface can paint suggestions while the coding-agent UI is closed.
  • Disable audio enhancements (Communications tab or IAudioClient properties) or the period and APO chain add tens of milliseconds.

PrismML's numbers show local agentic coding is now practical on consumer GPUs. The audio capture path has not changed. If your product needs sub-200 ms end-to-end from speech to overlay text, the buffer period and callback discipline still set the floor.

Shared-mode WASAPI periods dominate before any local model runs.

I'm building Talkaside, a Windows app for job interviews and calls in another language.
Drafted with AI assistance from this project's code and logs.

title: The cache read ratio decides your agent bill, not the list price
description:
If you compare models by list price per 1M tokens, you are comparing the wrong number for anything agent-shaped. Here is a measurement that makes the case, from a thread I followed on r/LLMDevs where three people posted their own numbers.

The measurement

One practitioner instrumented a real long-running coding session: 233 requests, median input ~148,000 tokens, median output ~500 tokens — roughly 230:1 input to output.

Of that input, 91% was cache reads, 9% cache writes, and fresh input was close to zero.

That single ratio changes what a bill is made of. Fresh input is the expensive part; cache reads are typically a small fraction of it. When 91% of your input is cache reads, your effective input price is set by the cache read ratio, not by the headline input price.

The ratio is not a constant across providers

This is the part that breaks comparisons. Two vendors can have the same list input price and very different cache behaviour. In the same thread, one person noted that one model's cache read is priced at 19% of its input price, while for a major Western provider it is around 5%.

A 4x difference in the multiplier applied to 91% of your input is not a rounding error. It can invert the ranking.

Concretely, in that thread the person who built a cost calculator reported that a model with a higher list price came out cheaper for an agent workload than two cheaper-listed alternatives — purely because of the cache read ratio. Same list price table, opposite conclusion, once the cache column was filled in.

And a second crossover: the ranking flips at about 40% output share on one comparison, and at about 24% on another once hosting was added as a variable. Those are wide margins, not knife-edge ties. If your workload sits anywhere between 24% and 40% output share, "which model is cheaper" has no answer that does not first settle the cache and hosting questions.

Why a synthetic preset can hide this entirely

The most useful correction in that thread came from someone reporting a 2.4x saving from caching, where another had claimed 10x.

Both were right, and the difference was the workload shape:

agent preset real long session
input 12k 148k
output 1.5k 500
what dominates the bill output input
caching impact modest (~2.4x) very large

In a preset with 12k in and 1.5k out, output dominates, so caching input cannot help much — 2.4x is the honest number. In a real agent session where context has grown to 148k and each turn emits ~500 tokens, input dominates, and the cache read ratio is the single biggest lever in the bill.

So a preset that looks reasonable can invert the conclusion. The preset said "caching is a 2.4x thing". The real workload says it is the main thing.

What to add to a calculator

Two fields, both measured per request rather than assumed:

  1. Repeated-prefix share — what fraction of the input is a stable prefix that can be cached.
  2. Cache read price ratio — the cache read price as a fraction of the fresh input price, per provider.

Then a third field that is optional but useful for agents: fresh input per turn. Not total context — the uncached part. That is the portion you actually pay full price for, and it can be an order of magnitude smaller than the context size.

A reconciliation worth keeping in mind: a preset of "12k in / 1.5k out" and a measured session of "148k in / 500 out" can both be true, because one measures raw context and the other effectively measures billable input. With 91% cache reads, 148k raw leaves about 13k of fresh input — which is almost exactly the 12k the preset assumed. The preset was not wrong; it was denominated differently.

The honest limits

  • These are three practitioners' numbers, not a benchmark. One long session, one calculator, one thread.
  • Cache behaviour is provider-specific and changes. Read prices, write prices, and cache lifetimes all move. A cache read ratio measured last month may not hold.
  • The 40% and 24% crossovers are specific to particular model pairs on particular dates. Read them as evidence that the flip is real and wide, not as constants.
  • I did not verify these numbers independently. They are reported measurements from people running the workload, which is more than a list price table gives you, but less than a controlled test.
  • Cache writes are not free. A 5-minute cache write tier can cost more than fresh input, so short-lived caches can lose money. The break-even depends on how many reads you get per write — and that is another field a calculator should ask for.

The pattern across all of this: a per-token price is a property of a model, but a bill is a property of a workload. The fields that decide the bill — prefix share, cache read ratio, fresh input per turn — are workload properties, and almost no price table asks for them.

title: Signal #142: Claude Code's Leaky Approval Files, Claude Ship, GPT-6.2 Pricing, and More
description:
This week's most important item is a defect, not a launch: Claude Code's "Yes, and don't ask again" option can persist credentials typed into approved commands into a local file that may end up in a public repository. Alongside that, Anthropic's Claude Ship pushes PR review and approval toward agent-speed, OpenAI cut API prices on GPT-6.2 for agentic workloads, and a handful of smaller releases are worth a look. Here's what to do about each.

Claude Code leaks secrets through local approval-rule files

When you select "Yes, and don't ask again" in Claude Code, the approved shell command is written to .claude/settings.local.json, including any credentials embedded in it. If your global gitignore doesn't cover that path, a later git add . or a repo initialized from that directory can publish the secret.

This is a defect in existing behavior, and the default protections cannot be trusted today. Treat it as an incident-level item for any machine where you've used the feature.

Verdict: Act now. Run git rm --cached .claude/settings.local.json, add the file to the repo's .gitignore, audit its contents, and rotate every credential it has ever held. Delete rules containing secrets, and reference credentials through environment variables instead of inlining them in commands. Check your global gitignore while you're at it.

Claude Ship automates PR review, fixes, and approvals on GitHub

Claude Ship runs three agents: one for review, one for CI repair, and one for approval, with merge decisions governed by a natural-language policy file. Its /ship command also watches a PR for up to seven days and pushes fixes, which changes the attention model for a PR after it's opened. The approval path is the piece that matters most, since it replaces a human checkpoint.

Only Code Review is generally available. PR Steward and Claude Approvals are beta. Requirements are a Claude Team or Enterprise plan, GitHub-only repositories, Claude Code v2.1.330+, GitHub CLI 2.63+, and git 2.38+.

Verdict: Evaluate. Try it on one non-critical repository in observe-only mode, with a spend limit configured. Don't mark Claude Approvals as a required check until you've validated the policy against real PRs. A natural-language merge policy is only as good as the cases you've tested it on.

GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol ship at lower API prices

Astra 6.2 is priced at $8/$40 per MTok, with cached input dropping to $0.40/MTok. Sol 6.2 is $2/$10, matching the prior Sol price. The model IDs are gpt-6.2-astra and gpt-6.2-sol. The cached-input discount is aimed squarely at long agentic sessions, where repeated context dominates the bill.

The author reports weaker benchmark results than Claude Fable 5.2 and frequent, confusing clarification requests during long tasks. Those are the kinds of issues that only show up in your own traces.

Verdict: Evaluate. For subagent-heavy loops, the cache discount is worth measuring immediately. Requires LLM 0.38 or a direct API call. Validate on your workloads, especially for clarification behavior, before migrating production agents.

RF-DETR Atto detects objects in 1 ms

RF-DETR's Atto, Femto, and Pico are small detectors selected by latency budget. The fine-tuning and TensorRT export workflow matches what you'd expect from YOLO-class tooling, which is the point: it's a drop-in alternative where you previously defaulted to YOLO. Latency is reported per image at batch size one, so you can map the table directly onto a deployment budget.

Verdict: Evaluate, with a licensing caveat. It's a credible replacement for YOLO26-N or DEIMv2 on latency-bound NVIDIA deployments. You'll need a CUDA build of PyTorch, TensorRT for FP16 export, and a labeled dataset. Research and evaluation are fine now, but commercial self-hosting requires the Enterprise add-on under the Roboflow Platform Model License 1.0. Read that license before you build on it.

Vercel AI Gateway adds GPT-Live 1.1 full-duplex voice

If you already have a GPT-Live integration, upgrading is a model ID change to openai/gpt-live-1.1. The endpoint and protocol stay the same. Client delegation lets the app answer model-requested tasks with any text model on AI Gateway while the voice session continues, which is the architecturally interesting part.

The snippets omit connection handling, parsing, and shutdown, so "just a model swap" undersells the work.

Verdict: Evaluate. Try it in the model playground. For production, you still own delegation permissions, confirmation flows, cancellation, WebSocket management, and audio streaming. Budget real integration time.

Vercel AI Gateway adds Decision-1.1 structured-output model

Decision-1.1 returns boolean, choice, or score answers rather than free text, and its probabilities are calibrated enough to set explicit thresholds for acting, flagging, or escalating. The migration from Decision-1 is a model ID change to microsoft/decision-1.1, and requests show up in your gateway logs and budgets.

The article gives no benchmark numbers, so the calibration claims are unverified for your domain.

Verdict: Evaluate. For classification and routing, typed outputs beat parsing free-form text, and this is a low-risk swap. Requires AI SDK 7.0.128+ or OpenAI Python SDK 3.26.0+. Measure accuracy on your own labeled data before you commit to any threshold.

If you want this kind of triage every week without wading through release notes, subscribe to Signal at https://repowrapped.com/signal. We'll keep flagging the defects and the migrations that actually change your code.

title: From Sales to Software Engineer: How I Learned to Code, and What I'd Do Differently with AI
description:
What this post is about
How I taught myself to be an engineer after leaving sales with zero experience: what still holds up, and what I'd do differently now that we have AI. If you're on the same path, I hope it helps.

Who it's for
Anyone trying to break into software engineering with no experience.

The short version

  1. Put in the hours and the reps first. AI doesn't change that.
  2. Focus on how to think, not just which tools to use. Build something close to a real production setup, and understand the concepts behind it.
  3. Learn the design and concepts first, then learn by building with AI. That knowledge is what lets you judge what AI gives you.

I went from sales to software engineering with no background in it. Six years later, I build AI agents at a major Japanese IT company. Most of the learning I describe here happened about six years ago, so some tools have changed since then.

I've written about the whole career switch before. This post zooms in on the learning part.

From Sales to Software Engineer: How I Got to a Leading Japanese IT Company in 5 Years

What's inside

  1. Hours and reps first (three months of full-time study)
  2. After bootcamp: building as if it were a real job
  3. A tech lead who changed how I learn
  4. Nail down the design, then learn by building with AI

1. Hours and reps first

I stopped worrying about doing it well and focused on putting in the time. After leaving sales, I joined a coding bootcamp (DMM WebCamp) and spent 10 hours a day on it for three months, including the time I spent building apps.

My goal was simply to invest the hours. I aimed for about 1,000 hours, counting those three months plus the studying that came after. Once you commit to a number of hours, the goal stops being "until I'm good enough" and becomes "how many hours are left".

I borrowed a habit from my sales days. Back then I logged my calls and appointments in a notebook every day and looked back at what worked and what didn't. I did the same with studying: I tracked the numbers and reviewed them. Seeing my progress made it much easier to stick with it.

I picked a bootcamp because I knew I needed an environment that would keep me going.

I moved through the curriculum fast, and used the rest of my time to work backward from the job I wanted: learning the tech I'd need and building a portfolio.

What still holds up: Going all in for a short stretch and putting in the reps.
Now: AI makes your hours go much further. You can ask the moment you get stuck, and building takes less time.

2. After bootcamp: building as if it were a real job

Even after bootcamp, I kept studying while job hunting.

A lot of interviewers asked about fundamentals beyond the framework: databases, object-oriented programming, algorithms. In one interview, a question about database transactions stumped me. So I went after my weak spots, built them into my portfolio, and practiced explaining them in my own words.

My portfolio, The-View, is a site for sharing scenic photos tagged with their location. I deliberately picked an ordinary idea and let the engineering do the talking. I didn't want to stop at a working app. I wanted a setup close to what a real development team uses.

  • Infrastructure: Set up your own production environment in the cloud (AWS)
  • Dev environment: Make it run the same everywhere (Docker)
  • Testing: Be able to verify nothing's broken
  • CI/CD (automating tests and releases): Let the pipeline test and deploy for you

I believe that mindset of recreating a real working environment still matters, even with AI.

The code is on GitHub: https://github.com/sora-uzu/The-View
I also wrote a guide on writing a README (in Japanese):

How to write a README that helps beginners get hired (Japanese)

Building it all from scratch still pays off today. I can now spot gaps and odd choices in the designs and setups AI suggests.

Picking your tech

  • Go with the languages employers are asking for right now. If I were starting today, I'd probably pick TypeScript or Python.
  • Learn the concepts, not just the services. What you learn on AWS carries over to Azure and friends. Build a CI/CD pipeline once, and the next tool will feel familiar.

What still holds up: Interviewers want to hear how you made your decisions. Be ready to explain them.
Now: When AI writes your AWS setup, Dockerfile or CI config, ask about the underlying concepts too. Asking why it made that choice is where the real learning happens. Still, without the fundamentals, you can't tell whether the answer is any good.

3. A tech lead who changed how I learn

I flipped the order: learn first, then build.

As a beginner I did study, but mostly I built first and looked things up when I got stuck.

At my second company, almost everyone had a science background, and the gaps in my fundamentals became painfully obvious. That's where I met a brilliant tech lead who showed me how to study.

Get the language, framework and design knowledge in first. Then start typing.

Once I switched, I was writing code already knowing why it should look that way.

The biggest change: I could finally read the intent behind code. For example, we were carving a job-listing service's API out of a monolith (one big application) into microservices (small, separate services). First I had to understand the existing service and its source code. Because I'd studied design beforehand, I could follow why things were structured the way they were, and moving features over to the new API went smoothly.

What went in

  • Frameworks, design patterns and architecture. I read books and dug deep.
  • Computer science. I used Recursion, a service for learning computer science. It made a real difference.
  • Algorithms. If you come from a non-science background, algorithmic thinking can feel foreign. It did for me. I ran through easy LeetCode problems (a coding practice site) several times until that way of thinking became second nature.

What still holds up: What you put in matters.
Now: AI can churn out the detailed code. So the thing to invest in is the higher-level stuff, design and concepts, so you can judge what AI hands back.

4. Nail down the design, then learn by building with AI

If I were starting from zero today, I'd get the design and concepts down first, then have AI build lots of things and learn from them. Instead of cramming every detail from books before writing anything, I'd learn by reading what gets built.

My loop has four steps:

  1. Give small, focused instructions. Know what you want and why before you ask
  2. Read the AI's explanation
  3. Ask about anything that doesn't click
  4. Update your mental model

Because I read the output and ask questions instead of handing everything off, my understanding grows a bit at a time. The point isn't to understand everything before moving on; it's to understand enough for the task, then keep going. My check is simple: I have the AI explain it and see if I'm convinced.

What works well

  • You see the big picture fast. Something is running before you know all the details. Even in a language I'd never used, I got a feel for the overall shape quickly.
  • You learn as you build. Once it works, you ask why, and your understanding catches up.

The catch, and what to do about it

The catch: in a language you don't know, it's hard to tell whether the AI got it right.

  • It runs, but is the design sound? Working code isn't necessarily well-written code.
  • You don't know the conventions. Without a sense of what's idiomatic, you can't push back.

The fix is to learn architecture and design well enough to explain them in your own words before you lean on AI. You don't need every detail memorized. If you know the thinking behind it, you can judge the output. In short, build your own yardstick before you ask AI to build.

If you're just starting out

  • Put in the hours and the reps. Set a target, track it, and review it. (I went full-time for three months. Your mileage may vary.)
  • Learn how to think, not just the tools. Pick the languages employers want, and learn infrastructure and CI/CD through their concepts.
  • Learn design and concepts first, then build with AI. That's what lets you judge the output.

Wrapping up

If you found this useful, a reaction or a comment would make my day.

If something's unclear, you're curious about anything, or you're unsure how to approach your studies, ask away in the comments.
