title: AI Agent Memory: Who Owns Your Stored Data?
description:
Privacy in AI agents depends on who can access, manage, store, and delete the information an agent remembers. While memory can help an AI agent work across different sessions, it also raises important questions about data ownership and user control. We need to understand what gets saved, why it stays available, and who has permission to use it. Keep reading to explore how AI memory works and what privacy controls should matter.

Why AI Agent Memory Raises Privacy Concerns

AI agents can collect useful information during everyday tasks. They may remember project details, writing preferences, previous instructions, work processes, and other information that helps them respond more accurately.

However, not every detail shared during a conversation should become a permanent memory. Some information is useful for future tasks, while other details may be temporary or private.

This creates an important difference between remembering information and having permission to retain it.

For example, an AI agent helping with content planning may need to remember a preferred writing style or an ongoing project topic. However, it may not need to retain private conversations, login details, or sensitive business information.

Without clear rules, stored information can create unnecessary privacy risks. A memory system should have a clear purpose and should not treat every conversation as information worth keeping.

Who Owns the Information an AI Agent Remembers?

Ownership and control are not necessarily the same thing. Users may provide the information an AI agent remembers, but the platform may determine how that information is stored, processed, and retained. The agent itself uses the information to perform tasks, while the service provider establishes the technical and policy boundaries around its use.

Understanding these responsibilities helps us identify who can access stored information, who can manage it, and who is accountable when something goes wrong.

The User Who Provides the Information

Users provide the original information through conversations, documents, instructions, and other inputs. They should understand what the AI agent stores and how that information supports future tasks.
Control should include the ability to review saved information, correct inaccurate details, and remove memories that are no longer useful.

The AI Agent That Processes the Information

The AI agent uses stored information to support its tasks. It may retrieve previous instructions, identify relevant details, or apply saved preferences when responding.
However, processing information does not automatically give an agent unlimited permission to retain or reuse everything it encounters.

The Platform That Stores the Memory

The platform or service responsible for storing memory also plays an important role. Its policies and technical controls determine how information is protected, accessed, retained, and deleted.

We should not assume that users have complete control over every stored record. Different platforms may follow different data policies, so clear documentation is necessary to understand these responsibilities.

What Information Should an AI Agent Remember?

A useful memory system needs to separate information based on its purpose and sensitivity. Not every detail has the same value, and not every detail deserves long-term storage.

For example, information that supports ongoing work may be useful for future sessions, while temporary details may only be relevant to a single task.

A practical approach is to organize information into several categories:

  • User preferences: Preferred writing styles, response formats, and communication preferences that help personalize repeated tasks.
  • Project information: Current goals, deadlines, requirements, and decisions that help an agent maintain continuity.
  • Work history: Previous instructions, completed tasks, and relevant decisions that provide context for future activities.
  • Temporary details: One-time instructions or short-term plans that may no longer be useful after a task is completed.
  • Sensitive information: Passwords, financial details, and private records that require strict protection and should generally stay out of ordinary long-term memory.

This separation helps prevent unnecessary data collection and makes stored information easier to review. The goal is not to make an AI agent remember everything. It is to retain information that has a clear purpose while limiting unnecessary exposure of private details.

How Can We Control What an AI Agent Remembers?

Privacy controls should be part of the memory system rather than an afterthought. Users need practical ways to understand what an agent remembers and decide how that information can be used.

Two capabilities make memory management easier: reviewing stored information and controlling how long it remains available.

1. Memory Review and Editing

Users should be able to inspect stored information and understand why it exists. If an agent remembers an outdated preference or an incorrect project detail, there should be a way to correct it.
Regular reviews also help identify information that is no longer relevant. This prevents old instructions or unnecessary details from influencing future responses.

2. Data Retention and Deletion

Stored information should not remain available indefinitely without a clear reason. Memory systems should explain how long information stays stored and what happens when users request its deletion.
Users should also understand whether deleting a memory removes only the active memory entry or affects related records, backups, and other stored copies. These details depend on the platform's data policies and technical design.

Important Privacy Controls to Consider

Before relying on an AI agent for ongoing tasks, we should examine the privacy features available and understand how they protect stored information.

Several controls can make memory management more transparent and reliable:

  • Memory visibility: Users should be able to see which information has been saved and understand what the agent retains.
  • User permissions: Access settings should define which information, documents, and resources the agent can use. This helps prevent unnecessary data exposure.
  • Memory editing: Users should have a way to correct inaccurate details or update outdated information so the agent can work with relevant context.
  • Deletion controls: A clear deletion process allows users to remove memories they no longer need and understand what happens afterward.
  • Retention settings: Platforms should explain how long information remains stored and whether memories are removed automatically or require manual action.
  • Access protection: Security measures should restrict unauthorized access to stored information, particularly when an agent handles private or business data.
  • Activity records: Relevant records of memory access and management activities can help users and organizations understand how information is being handled.

Having these controls available does not automatically make a system private. Their value depends on whether they work reliably, protect stored information, and give users a clear understanding of how to apply them.

The Role of Long-Term Memory in Responsible AI Development

Long-term memory can make AI agents more useful when they need to continue work across multiple sessions. It allows an agent to retain relevant context instead of rebuilding its understanding from the beginning every time.

However, memory quality should not be measured only by how much information an agent can retain. Privacy, accuracy, and user control are equally important.

For a closer look at this concept, long-term memory for AI agents provides a useful reference for understanding how persistent context supports AI agents beyond individual conversations.

The important consideration is how memory is designed and managed. A responsible system should distinguish useful information from unnecessary personal details and provide clear rules for accessing stored context.

We should also consider how memory changes over time. An old project requirement may no longer apply, and a previous preference may become outdated. Without regular review, an agent could rely on information that no longer reflects the current situation.
This is why memory management should remain an ongoing process rather than a one-time setup.

Common Privacy Mistakes When Using AI Agent Memory

Even when a memory system offers useful features, poor information management can create avoidable risks. Some problems come from unclear permissions, while others happen because users do not understand what an agent retains.

Here are four common mistakes worth avoiding:

  • Saving too much information: Keeping unnecessary conversations or document details increases the amount of information an agent retains. We should prioritize relevant context instead of saving everything by default.
  • Ignoring outdated memories: Old instructions, incorrect details, and completed project information can affect future responses. Regular reviews help keep stored context accurate and relevant.
  • Overlooking access permissions: Giving an agent access to more documents, accounts, or systems than necessary can expose information unnecessarily. Access should match the agent's actual responsibilities.
  • Assuming deletion removes every copy: Removing an active memory entry does not necessarily remove related records, backups, or other stored data. Users should understand the platform's deletion policies before relying on them.

These mistakes show why privacy requires more than secure storage. Responsible memory management also depends on sensible information-sharing habits, appropriate permissions, and regular reviews.

Questions to Ask Before Trusting an AI Agent With Long-Term Memory

Understanding an AI agent's memory features is only part of the process. We should also examine how the system handles information throughout its lifecycle.

Before using an agent for ongoing personal or professional tasks,
consider these questions:

Can We See Everything the Agent Remembers?

A clear memory interface helps us understand which details are retained. Without visibility, it becomes difficult to identify unnecessary or inaccurate information.

Can We Decide What Gets Saved?

A good memory system should provide clear options for controlling what information becomes part of its persistent context. Users should not have to assume that every conversation will be saved.

Can We Delete Information Permanently?

Deletion policies should explain what happens after a memory is removed. We should understand whether the information disappears from active memory, related storage, or other records.

Who Can Access the Stored Information?

Access rules should explain whether information is available only to the user and agent or whether other parties may access it under specific conditions.

How Is Sensitive Information Protected?

We should look for clear explanations of data protection, access restrictions, and retention practices. Sensitive information requires additional care and should not be treated like ordinary task context.

How to Manage Privacy in AI Agent Memory

Responsible AI use starts with understanding the information we share. Even when a system provides memory controls, our own information management habits still matter.

We can reduce unnecessary exposure by sharing only the details needed for a task, reviewing stored information regularly, and avoiding sensitive data unless there is a clear and secure reason to use it.

Organizations should also establish rules for employee access, project information, and document handling. These rules help prevent private information from becoming part of an agent's persistent context without proper approval.

Most importantly, privacy expectations should be clear before an AI agent becomes part of an everyday workflow. This gives everyone a better understanding of what information can be retained and who is responsible for managing it.

Making Long-Term Memory More Accountable

AI agent memory should help systems retain useful context without creating unnecessary privacy risks. That requires more than secure storage. Users need clear information about what gets saved, who can access it, and how stored data can be managed.

As AI agents become part of everyday workflows, memory management should include clear permissions, regular reviews, and transparent retention policies. These practices help prevent outdated or unnecessary information from influencing future tasks.

Ultimately, building trust in AI memory starts with giving users meaningful control over the information their agents retain.

Visit: https://evermind.ai/features/long-term-memory-for-ai-agents

title: I gave my AI coding agent one rule file. Here's the before and after.
description:
Every AI coding agent builds the same landing page. You know the one: purple-to-blue gradient, "Revolutionize your
workflow", a row of grey LOGO boxes, three cards with 🚀 🔒 ⚡.

I wanted to know how much of that comes from the model and how much comes from us never telling it what good looks
like. So I ran the same prompt twice:

build a landing page for my meeting-notes app

Run 1: no rules. I got exactly the page above.

Run 2: same agent, same prompt, plus one file in the project root: an AGENTS.md with design rules. The hero
showed the actual product (a call transcript with decisions filling in as people speak), the headline said
"Your notes are written before the meeting ends.", there was one accent colour and one animation, and the proof
line had real-looking numbers instead of fake logos.

The rules that did most of the work

  1. The hero shows the product working. No abstract illustration. This alone kills the gradient blob.
  2. Banned phrases. "Unlock the power of", "Supercharge", "Seamless", "Revolutionize", "Next-generation". The agent has to find the specific thing to say.
  3. One accent colour. And an explicit ban on purple-to-blue gradients, neon glows and gradient text.
  4. Motion with a job. Before any animation the agent fills in: "When ___ happens, ___ moves, so the visitor understands ___." No sentence, no animation.
  5. A checklist before "done". The first question: could this page belong to any other company?

Reduced motion is part of the rule too, so the animation always has a complete still state:

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .step { animation: none; opacity: 1; transform: none; }
}

Try it

The whole playbook is open source, in the rule-file formats the major agents read:

npx @deliverwebsite/unslop init

Repo: https://github.com/deliverwebsite/unslop (made by us at DeliverWebsite UI).

What's the clearest sign of AI slop you keep seeing? I'm collecting them for the next version of the rules.

title: Test your prompt once and you'll overrate it
description:
If you test an LLM prompt by running each case once and counting the passes, you're measuring something closer to a best-case number than what you'll see in production.

Here's a concrete example from a benchmark we run, CatalogBench, where models turn a sparse product feed and some photos into a product listing that could go live without inventing anything. Every model gets the same 56 products, three times each. A listing only counts as publish-ready if every blocking check passes. All figures below are from the live CatalogBench page (results dated up to 21 November 2026): the "Publish-ready, run to run" column shows the lowest and highest single-run score, and the headline column counts products that passed in all three runs.

Claude Haiku 5.5: 41% to 55% per run, 27% every time

Run Claude Haiku 5.5 once and, depending on which run you happened to get, it passes 41.1% or 55.4% of the products, or somewhere in between. That's a big swing on its own: pick the lucky run and it looks like a decent cheap option.

But only 26.8% of products passed in all three runs. Its mean pass rate across the runs is 47.0%, so over 40% of the passes in a typical run are products it fails in at least one other run.

Those are the cases that hurt you. A product that passes on Tuesday and fails on Wednesday with the same prompt, same input and same model will get past a one-shot test and then break for real users.

It's not just small models

Model Single run (lowest to highest of 3) Passed all 3 runs
Claude Haiku 5.5 41.1% to 55.4% 26.8%
Claude Opus 5.5 66.1% to 76.8% 55.4%
GPT-6 Sol 75.0% to 75.0% 66.1%
GPT-6.1 Sol 75.0% to 80.4% 75.0%

A few things stand out:

  • Claude Opus 5.5 loses more than 10 points between its worst single run and its every-run score, and more than 20 from its best.
  • GPT-6 Sol is the sneaky one. It scored exactly 75.0% on all three runs, so if you only tracked the headline pass rate you'd call it perfectly stable. But only 66.1% of products passed every time. The total stayed the same while which products passed changed between runs.
  • GPT-6.1 Sol is the reverse: its every-run score equals its worst single run, so nearly everything it passes, it passes every time. That kind of consistency is worth something even when the peak number isn't the highest.

The order of models can change too. Claude Sonnet 5.5 scores 44.6% to 48.2% per run, below Haiku 5.5's best run, but 32.1% every time, above Haiku's 26.8%. Test each once on a lucky day for Haiku and you'd pick the less reliable model.

Why this happens

Even at the same settings, model outputs vary from call to call. On a borderline case, small differences decide the result: one run reads an attribute off the photo, the next guesses it; one run leaves out an unsupported claim, the next repeats it from the supplier copy. A single pass tells you the model can get that case right, not that it will.

What to do about it

  • Run every case several times. Three is a reasonable minimum. It costs three times as much, but a test suite is usually small next to production traffic.
  • Track "passes every time" as the main number. A mean pass rate across runs is better than one run, but it still blends flaky and solid cases together. The share of cases that pass in all runs is closer to what users will see.
  • Look at the flaky cases individually. Cases that pass in some runs and fail in others are where your prompt is underspecified, or where the task is right at the edge of what the model can do. They're often the most useful ones to fix: tighten the instruction, add the missing context, or add a check.
  • Compare models on the same measure. If you're choosing between two models, a one-run comparison can easily flip. Compare their every-run scores on the same cases.
  • Re-run when anything changes. A new model version, a prompt edit or a provider change can move which cases are flaky, even when the headline number barely moves. GPT-6 Sol above shows how a steady headline can hide that.

Takeaway

One clean run tells you a prompt can work. Several runs tell you whether it does. The gap between the two is where the production bugs live.

The data behind this, including the per-product view of which listings passed in all, some or none of the runs, is on the CatalogBench page. We run it as part of Spring Prompt, which also does this kind of repeated testing on your own prompts.

title: Start with the job you can check by hand
description:
Before I build an agent for a job, I do the job by hand once and write down what a good result looks like.

Not a feeling. A check. The names match. The total adds up. The date is the date that was asked for. If I cannot write that check in plain words, I am not ready to hand the job over, because I will have no way to tell a good run from a bad one.

That is the order I work in at Mira Vale Agents: hand run first, check written down, then the agent runs it and the check decides if the work stands.

The service page is here: https://mira-vale-agents.lovable.app

title: No benchmark ranked this month's AI models the way reviewers did. Ours included.
description:
The day after Gemini 4 Neon came out, Theo, who runs his own coding test suite, posted that he didn't care about the numbers any more: "Neon is super pleasant to work with" (X, 19 November). The same day, our own run put Neon first of 35 models on the factual brief of CatalogBench, our product-listing benchmark. A reviewer and a benchmark agreed.

I wanted to know how often that happens, so we checked every model launched in the past month.

It doesn't happen often. No leaderboard ranked the month's models the way reviewers did, and ours are no exception. On direct "A beat B" calls the picture is better: agent benchmarks agreed with 83% to 88% of reviewer votes, the Artificial Analysis index with 80%, and most of our own business-task benchmarks with 63% to 71%.

What we did

  • Models released 20 October to 19 November 2026.
  • 250 hands-on quotes from 27 reviewers on YouTube, blogs, newsletters and X, including Theo, Simon Willison, Matt Shumer, Every and Ethan Mollick.
  • Each quote scored from -2 (strongly negative) to +2 (strongly positive) by two raters, both Claude Opus 5.5, the second blind to the first. 79% of scores were identical and none flipped sign.
  • Compared against 28 benchmark measures, ours and third parties'.

A model's "vibe score" is the average of those scores. We average within each reviewer first, so someone who posted ten times about one model counts once, and we only rank models that at least three reviewers used.

One month and 11 models is a small sample. Keep that in mind for everything below.

Rank correlation: no detectable relationship

We measured how closely each benchmark's order follows the reviewers' with a Spearman rank correlation (+1 is the same order, 0 is no relation). Across the benchmarks the values ran from -0.55 to +0.17. Ours sit in the lower half of that range: the Spring Prompt Score at -0.35 and DeckBench at -0.55.

Model Vibe score Reviewers
Gemini 4 Neon +1.38 4
Muse Ember +1.25 4
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 +1.00 3
Claude Fable 5.2 +0.88 21
Gemini 4 Carbon +0.85 14
GPT-6.1 Terra +0.73 5
Gemini 4 Hydrogen +0.15 6
Kimi K3.1 Pro +0.08 7
Qwen4-Max +0.04 3
GPT-6.2 Astra -0.01 17
GPT-6.2 Sol -0.06 9

Three things explain most of the gap.

GPT-6.2 tops the charts and the complaints. Astra and Sol score 62 and 57 on the Artificial Analysis index and come 2nd and 3rd of the month's models on our Score. With reviewers they are last. The complaints were about use rather than capability: hard to steer, stops early, hard to read. Matt Shumer: "They were essentially unusable." (X, 17 November). Theo's video shows the split inside one person: his own benches had Astra winning across the board, and half an hour later he said he wouldn't choose it over Opus 5.5 for any of his work.

Cheap models are judged against their price. Muse Ember and DeepSeek Flash 1017 are in the reviewers' top three and score 36 and 33 on the Artificial Analysis index, against 65 for Claude Fable 5.2. A capability leaderboard doesn't ask whether a model is good for what it costs. Reviewers often do.

The top of the ranking is thin. Neon leads on four reviewers and one day of posts. Fable 5.2 and GPT-6.2 Astra rest on 21 and 17.

Head-to-head: agent benchmarks agree most

A narrower test: when a reviewer says from their own use that model A beat model B, does the benchmark also put A above B? We found 149 such statements and counted each reviewer once per pair.

Agent benchmarks came out on top (LiveBench long agentic 88%, Terminal-Bench 4.1 86%, Arena Agent 83%) because they test the work these reviewers actually do. 67 of the 250 quotes were about coding or agents, and another 59 were front-end, 3D and game demos. The fit is not automatic though: LiveBench's coding category agreed with only 33% of votes.

These percentages are not a league table. Four match-ups carry most of the votes, led by Fable 5.2 over GPT-6.2 Astra (8 reviewers to 1). Any benchmark that puts Fable first and Astra below Carbon scores well almost by default.

Reviewers don't agree with each other either

Gemini 4 Carbon was the top or joint-top model of the month for Bijan Bowen and Ethan Mollick, and near the bottom for Theo, who found it too slow. They test different things: Bijan builds 3D scenes from one prompt, Theo runs coding agents all day.

We looked at the seven reviewers who rated at least five models and found the benchmark each one's ranking follows most closely. Simon Willison lines up with Artificial Analysis's Terminal-Bench run (+0.67) and DesignArena (+0.63). Bijan Bowen with LiveBench coding (+0.69). Ethan Mollick with Vals, Terminal-Bench 4.1 and Arena Agent (+0.60).

It's tempting to read that as "Willison is a DesignArena person". The data doesn't support it. With five to ten models per reviewer and about 25 benchmarks tried against each, a high best match turns up by luck. When we shuffled each reviewer's scores at random across the same models, the best match was typically +0.63 to +0.76, and 30% to 88% of shuffles matched or beat the real one.

Where our own benchmarks sit

Mid-table on head-to-heads, lower half on the monthly ranking. The furthest from reviewers is the sales brief of CatalogBench, which asks for persuasive product copy. In our 19 November run, GPT-6.2 Sol and Astra were publish-ready on it 80% and 75% of the time, against 66% for Fable and 31% for Carbon, close to the reverse of the month's most common reviewer calls. It agreed with 40% of votes.

That's mostly because the two measure different work. Our benchmarks cover product listings, slide decks, survey analysis and ad budgets. Of the 250 hands-on quotes, 20 were about writing and 3 about research. The reviews hold almost nothing for a business-task benchmark to agree or disagree with.

Limits

One month, 11 rankable models, four of them on only three or four reviewers. Neon and GPT-6.2 had one or two days of takes when we collected; Fable had ten. With so few models, one or two can move a correlation a lot: using the second rater's scores alone shifts some benchmarks by 0.3 to 0.5. We make no claim of statistical significance. Effort settings also differ: our runs use provider defaults, Artificial Analysis and Arena mostly the top setting.

What I'd take from it

  • Use a benchmark that measures your kind of task to make a shortlist.
  • Read reviewers for what a model is like to work with day to day, and notice what they actually build.
  • Then run your own prompt on your own cases. Neither a leaderboard nor a reviewer has tested your prompt.

The full write-up, with every quote, link and rating plus the correlation and head-to-head tables as a JSON file, is on the Spring Prompt blog. We'll run it again once Neon and GPT-6.2 have two weeks of reactions.

title: Test a Support Runbook With a Restricted Receiving Account
description:
A support runbook can be accurate for its author and unusable for the receiving team. The commands may be correct. The missing assumption is often the account: the author inspected a resource with privileges that the receiving analyst will not have. A document review alone can miss that difference.

Rehearse the documented task with the intended receiving account before accepting the handover. Record each step's required capability, target resource and result. If a step cannot run, stop at that boundary and identify the missing prerequisite. An administrator's successful demonstration answers a different question from a restricted analyst's ability to follow the instructions.

The example below is an executable, in-memory capability model. Its controlled defect failed four of nine tests; the corrected path passed all nine. These observations concern the small Python model only. No cloud account, production permission, customer environment or real support action was used. The model helps make a runbook's assumptions explicit; it does not validate an organization's IAM configuration.

An AI agent prepared this tutorial and synthetic code and ran the local checks. Human manuscript review has not been performed. The reported observations concern the included in-memory fixture.

Give the receiving account a specific task

The fictional receiving analyst needs to inspect a diagnostic report and decide which authorized owner should handle a held job. The analyst can read the report. The analyst cannot retry the job. That boundary makes a useful rehearsal: the runbook must provide a complete diagnostic path without requiring the analyst to perform the restricted recovery action.

Name the account in the rehearsal material. In this example it is receiving-readonly. Its declared capabilities are read:report and read:absent. The second capability exists solely to exercise the distinction between permission to inspect a resource and the resource actually being present. These strings are local model values, not cloud permission names or credentials.

The synthetic resource map contains report and job. A report inspection has no modeled side effect. A retry appends an entry to an in-memory effects list. That list gives the tests something concrete to inspect when a step should have been denied. It is deliberately separate from the evidence list, which records attempted steps whether they complete or stop.

A useful runbook states what the analyst is expected to conclude from the report. If the next action requires a different owner, the diagnostic path should end with a handover to that owner. Silently assuming that the analyst can obtain broader privileges turns the instructions into a different operating procedure.

Controlled local execution: four failing checks, followed by nine passing checks.

Treat prerequisites as data the runner checks

Each step has a name, an action, a resource and a declared required capability. The model supports two actions: inspect requires a read capability, while retry requires a write capability. The runner derives the expected capability from the action and resource. It then checks that the declared capability matches the derived value.

That extra check matters. A step named retry must not acquire permission merely by declaring read:report as its prerequisite. Trusting the supplied capability label would allow the worksheet to authorize its own operation. The operation mapping is therefore part of the runner's fixed model, while the step declaration is input to validate.

The same principle appears in OWASP's authorization guidance under "Validate the Permissions on Every Request". In this example, each modeled step receives a fresh capability check. The quote supports the general authorization principle; it does not make this local runner a production security boundary.

After validating the declaration, the corrected runner checks the account's capability before checking whether the resource exists. A denied request therefore stops as DENIED. An authorized request for an absent resource stops as MISSING_RESOURCE. This ordering also prevents the example from using a resource lookup to reveal existence before permission has been established.

Read the small runner before running it

The implementation uses Python's standard library. Account and Step are immutable data records. The resource map is supplied explicitly. The runner returns an evidence record and the list of modeled effects; it does not open files, contact a service or execute a shell command. Copy the code into runbook.py to reproduce the example.

The broken parameter is a controlled teaching defect. With broken=True, the runner skips the account capability check. It still validates action declarations and resource presence. Keeping the defect narrow makes the failed observations interpretable: the exercise concerns a missing permission check, rather than an arbitrary collection of unrelated bugs.

The corrected path is the default. The test module uses an environment setting only to choose the deliberately defective path for the negative control. That switch is not a recommended runtime feature for a real access-control component. It exists so readers can reproduce both the failure and the correction using the same fixture.

Notice where the effects list changes. The append occurs only after the action declaration, capability check and resource lookup have succeeded. A failed prerequisite produces an evidence entry and stops the sequence before the modeled retry. The tests inspect this state directly instead of treating an exception message as proof that no action occurred.

"""Synthetic in-memory rehearsal. This is not an IAM enforcement component."""
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Account:
    name: str
    capabilities: frozenset[str]

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Step:
    name: str
    action: str
    resource: str
    required_capability: str

OPS = {"inspect": "read", "retry": "write"}

def run(account, steps, resources, *, broken=False):
    evidence, effects = [], []
    for step in steps:
        expected = f"{OPS.get(step.action, 'unknown')}:{step.resource}"
        if step.action not in OPS or step.required_capability != expected:
            status = "INVALID_DECLARATION"
        elif not broken and expected not in account.capabilities:
            status = "DENIED"
        elif step.resource not in resources:
            status = "MISSING_RESOURCE"
        else:
            status = "COMPLETED"
            if step.action == "retry":
                effects.append(f"retry:{step.resource}")
        evidence.append({"step": step.name, "account": account.name,
                         "required": expected, "status": status})
        if status != "COMPLETED":
            break
    return {"account": account.name, "evidence": evidence, "effects": effects}

Preserve the first blocked step

A runbook sequence may begin with a permitted inspection and then request a restricted action. The runner keeps the completed inspection in its evidence list, records the blocked retry and stops. It does not continue to a later step that might make the overall sequence appear successful.

For the receiving analyst, that sequence is useful even though it cannot complete the retry. The evidence identifies what the analyst did inspect, which step was blocked and which capability that step required. The handover can carry those observations to the authorized recovery owner without asking the analyst to pretend the entire runbook was completed.

Stopping also prevents a later read from disguising the blocked action. A simplistic runner might execute all steps, collect a final successful read and report overall success. The fixture instead returns the ordered evidence list. A receiving reviewer can see the boundary rather than infer it from the last visible status.

The model does not infer a production incident's business outcome from these statuses. COMPLETED means the local modeled step passed its checks. DENIED means the declared account lacked the modeled capability. Neither status says whether a real customer transaction succeeded, whether a job is safe to retry or whether a production recovery action has been approved.

Reproduce the controlled failure

Save the accompanying tests as test_runbook.py beside runbook.py. The tests use synthetic account and resource values. Run them first with RUNNER_MODE=broken, then without that setting. The first execution is expected to fail. Retaining that failure is part of the demonstration rather than an error to hide in the published result.

In the actual controlled run, four tests failed. They concerned denial of an unavailable write, absence of effects for that write, denial before a resource lookup and stopping at the blocked step. The other five tests passed because the defect did not change their tested conditions. Those passing tests did not establish that the defective runner was safe.

With the capability check restored, the same nine tests passed. The correction was the permission guard before the resource lookup and effect. No account capability was added to make the test pass. The receiving account remained receiving-readonly in both executions. The result shows the intended local behavior under the declared synthetic inputs.

The test suite is small enough to inspect. It covers the permitted read, the denied write, the unchanged identity, an authorized missing resource, a denied lookup, sequence stopping, a false capability declaration and an unsupported action. Several tests examine the same denied-write boundary from different angles. Nine passing tests are nine test methods, not nine independent security guarantees.

import os
import unittest
from runbook import Account, Step, run

class RehearsalTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        self.account = Account("receiving-readonly", frozenset({"read:report", "read:absent"}))
        self.resources = {"report": {"status": "queued"}, "job": {"status": "held"}}
    def execute(self, steps):
        return run(self.account, steps, self.resources, broken=os.getenv("RUNNER_MODE") == "broken")
    def test_permitted_read_completes(self):
        r = self.execute([Step("inspect", "inspect", "report", "read:report")])
        self.assertEqual(r["evidence"][0]["status"], "COMPLETED")
        self.assertEqual(r["effects"], [])
    def test_unavailable_write_is_denied(self):
        r = self.execute([Step("retry", "retry", "job", "write:job")])
        self.assertEqual(r["evidence"][0]["status"], "DENIED")
    def test_denied_write_has_no_effect(self):
        r = self.execute([Step("retry", "retry", "job", "write:job")])
        self.assertEqual(r["effects"], [])
    def test_authorized_missing_resource_is_distinct(self):
        r = self.execute([Step("lookup", "inspect", "absent", "read:absent")])
        self.assertEqual(r["evidence"][0]["status"], "MISSING_RESOURCE")
    def test_denial_precedes_resource_lookup(self):
        r = self.execute([Step("lookup", "inspect", "secret", "read:secret")])
        self.assertEqual(r["evidence"][0]["status"], "DENIED")
    def test_identity_never_changes(self):
        r = self.execute([Step("retry", "retry", "job", "write:job")])
        self.assertEqual({x["account"] for x in r["evidence"]}, {"receiving-readonly"})
    def test_stop_at_blocked_step(self):
        r = self.execute([Step("inspect", "inspect", "report", "read:report"), Step("retry", "retry", "job", "write:job"), Step("later", "inspect", "report", "read:report")])
        self.assertEqual([x["step"] for x in r["evidence"]], ["inspect", "retry"])
        self.assertEqual(r["effects"], [])
    def test_forged_read_declaration_cannot_allow_write(self):
        r = self.execute([Step("retry", "retry", "job", "read:report")])
        self.assertEqual(r["evidence"][0]["status"], "INVALID_DECLARATION")
        self.assertEqual(r["effects"], [])
    def test_unknown_operation_rejected(self):
        r = self.execute([Step("other", "delete", "job", "unknown:job")])
        self.assertEqual(r["evidence"][0]["status"], "INVALID_DECLARATION")
if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main(verbosity=2)

RUNNER_MODE=broken python3 -m unittest -v
python3 -m unittest -v

Distinguish a missing resource from denied access

Suppose the analyst can inspect absent, but absent is not in the synthetic map. The result is MISSING_RESOURCE. The receiving instructions should identify the missing prerequisite and the owner who can supply or explain it. Granting additional permissions would not create the resource or establish that its absence is expected.

Now consider secret, for which the analyst has no declared capability. The result is DENIED before the model asks whether secret exists. That observation concerns the account boundary. The operator should resolve the appropriate access or escalation arrangement through its own process, without treating the rehearsal as authorization to broaden the account.

A production system may intentionally expose less detail than this model, or return a common response for several conditions. Adapt the receiving instructions to the actual interface and permitted observability. The important comparison is between what the runbook assumes and what the receiving role can obtain. The model's status vocabulary is an example, not an API contract for every platform.

Keep the owner of each prerequisite visible. A resource availability question may belong to a platform team. An access request may belong to a separate authorization owner. A business decision about retrying work may belong elsewhere again. Combining all three under a generic contact-support instruction makes it harder for the receiving analyst to request the right next action.

Use the evidence manifest as a handover object

For each rehearsed step, retain the step name, receiving account, expected capability and status. Add the environment description and resource reference at the rehearsal level. Keep the proposed next owner beside any blocked step. The runner returns the first four fields; the surrounding handover material supplies the operating context and ownership decision.

Do not describe the evidence as a complete authorization audit. The fixture does not record policy inheritance, session restrictions, network conditions or identity-provider configuration. It records the supplied local account and the path that the local model took. That narrow observation is enough to challenge a runbook assumption without pretending to inspect a real deployment.

The receiving reviewer should be able to distinguish an observed result from a proposed next step. For example, the local retry was denied is an observation from this execution. A recovery owner should decide whether retrying is appropriate is a proposed responsibility. The manifest should not turn the second statement into evidence that the action has been approved.

Use synthetic resource references in shared examples. A real handover may need controlled links to logs or diagnostic reports, but those links should remain within the organization's existing access arrangements. The published fixture contains no production records. Reproducing the code does not require a cloud subscription, privileged token or access to a customer's support environment.

Correct the procedure before widening the account

A blocked step can reveal that the runbook assigned the wrong task to the receiving role. If the analyst's job is diagnosis and escalation, the appropriate correction may be to end the permitted path with an evidence packet for the recovery owner. Adding write access would change the role rather than repair the instructions.

Alternatively, the operator may decide that a receiving role genuinely requires an additional capability. That is a separate authorization decision. The rehearsal can identify the required capability and the affected step, but it cannot grant the permission or determine who should receive it. Keep that boundary explicit when translating the example into operational work.

A third possibility is that the runbook targets the wrong resource. The analyst may have the correct intended permissions while the instructions point to an obsolete diagnostic location. In that case, revising the resource reference and repeating the authorized review addresses the actual problem. An administrator's successful lookup at another location would not establish that the original instructions were usable.

Record the correction and repeat the relevant path with the intended restrictions intact. Keep the earlier blocked result so another reviewer can understand why the procedure changed. A clean final screenshot is less useful than a small history connecting the original assumption, the observed boundary and the accepted revision.

Review the model's limits before applying the idea

The supplied Account object is trusted fixture input. Anyone editing the Python file can change its capabilities. The example does not authenticate a person or protect a resource against an attacker controlling the process. The capability check is a local decision model used to rehearse a declared procedure.

The effects list is equally limited. It records an intended retry marker in memory. It does not simulate a distributed transaction, a remote timeout or the possibility of a side effect occurring before a response is lost. Those concerns require separate integration tests against the actual system behavior and its permitted test environment.

There is no concurrent policy change in the fixture. A real account's effective access can change during a session, and a resource can disappear between checks and use. The example cannot prove that a production authorization check is atomic with an action. Treat the runner's deterministic ordering as an explanation of the exercise, not a substitute for the receiving platform's security design.

The model also does not verify that the runbook describes the right business recovery. A permitted write can still be an incorrect operational decision. The receiving team needs the relevant acceptance rule, evidence and approval owner for that decision. Permission to perform an action and authority to choose that action are related but separate parts of the handover.

Make a restricted rehearsal part of acceptance

Choose one documented receiving task and name the actual intended role. List the expected resources and prerequisites before the rehearsal. Establish which observations can be collected in an authorized test environment and which questions need another owner. Keep the exercise small enough that the receiving reviewer can inspect every required step.

Then compare the documented route with the observed route. A permitted diagnostic path should produce the evidence the instructions promise. A blocked action should retain the missing prerequisite and stop before the modeled effect. An absent resource should remain distinguishable from an authorization conclusion only where the interface and the reviewer's permissions support that distinction.

Ask the receiving reviewer to explain the next step using the retained evidence. Can the reviewer identify the blocked operation and the owner who should resolve it? Can another analyst resume without borrowing the author's account? Those are proposed handover questions to examine in the real environment; the local fixture has not answered them for a customer deployment.

Retain the account boundary in later revisions

A runbook is likely to change after the first handover. New diagnostic sources, renamed resources and revised recovery procedures can introduce a prerequisite that the receiving role does not have. Keep the account declaration and the affected step evidence with the reviewed version so those changes remain visible.

When a new step is proposed, ask what action it performs before accepting its capability label. The false-declaration test illustrates this point: a read label cannot justify a retry operation. In a real implementation, the authoritative permission mapping belongs to the actual platform and its authorization owner. The worksheet should refer to that mapping rather than invent a replacement policy.

Review the required output as well as the permission. An account may be able to open a report while the report omits the field needed for the documented decision. This model treats resource contents as available data and does not evaluate their adequacy. A later authorized rehearsal should inspect whether the receiving role can obtain the evidence the procedure requires.

Keep that content question separate from the fixture's passing result. The nine tests establish local branching and absence of the modeled effect under the tested restrictions. They do not establish that a diagnostic report is complete, that a receiving person understands it or that an escalation owner is available. Recording those limits makes the small test reusable without inflating its meaning.

Read one completed rehearsal record

Consider the fixed runner's two-step sequence: inspect the synthetic report, then request a retry of the synthetic job. The first evidence entry identifies receiving-readonly, read:report and COMPLETED. The second identifies the same account, write:job and DENIED. The effects list remains empty. These values can be reproduced with the code and declared resource map below.

The first entry supports a narrow conclusion: the local account satisfied the modeled prerequisite for inspection and the supplied report resource existed. It does not say that a real report would contain enough information to diagnose a held job. Preserve the original task question beside the result so the receiving reviewer can evaluate that separate requirement later.

The second entry gives the handover a specific missing prerequisite. It does not tell the analyst to acquire write:job. The next owner may choose an authorized recovery, request more evidence or revise the runbook so the receiving role stops after diagnosis. Record that decision outside the runner's observation rather than encoding a proposed resolution as though it had already happened.

If the analyst submits only a screenshot of the first successful inspection, the receiving record loses the blocked step. If the analyst submits only the final denial, it loses the permitted work already completed. The ordered evidence list carries both. That is why the runner records a status for the blocked step before it stops.

Make the next owner's request specific

A useful escalation can identify the runbook version, receiving role, blocked step and required capability, then ask for a defined decision. For the synthetic case, the request is whether the documented task should end with diagnosis or include an authorized retry by another role. The evidence supports asking that question; it does not settle the answer.

Attach the relevant resource reference and its access conditions through the organization's established channel. A receiving owner should know whether a link points to an actual retained observation, a changing dashboard or an example. This fixture supplies only synthetic data, so its public output can be reproduced without exposing an operational record.

Ask the next owner to preserve the disposition with the reviewed runbook. If the task remains diagnostic, revise the instructions to name the receiving evidence and escalation destination. If an additional action is accepted, state who performs it and which review or approval applies. Neither route requires the article's fixture to become a production authorization service.

Finally, define what would trigger another rehearsal. A changed operation, a different resource or a new receiving role can invalidate an earlier observation. Repeat the affected review rather than copying the previous passing result onto the revised procedure. Keeping that scope attached to the evidence makes a modest local exercise useful during later handovers.

Leave a reproducible receiving record

The practical deliverable is the reviewed runbook, the intended account boundary and the ordered evidence for the rehearsed steps. Retain the failed control alongside the passing correction when sharing this example. A reader can then reproduce why skipping the capability guard changes the outcome instead of relying on an unsupported assertion that access was checked.

For a real handover, keep the environment, applicable runbook version and unresolved prerequisites with that record. Repeat the relevant review when one of those assumptions changes. The procedure becomes reviewable when the receiving team can show what it could inspect, where it had to stop and who owns the next authorized decision.

More insights to read

Integration Acceptance Tests for Retries and Duplicate Requests

Architecture Decision Records: A Receipt-Worker Review

How to Specify a Blockchain Ledger Integration Contract

Queue Migration Acceptance: Residual Work and Final Ownership

Batch Recovery Trace: Checkpoints, Row States and Resume Decisions

title: How to enable RLS in Supabase, and what every request returns after
description:
TL;DR. Enable RLS in Supabase with one statement per table, alter table public.todos enable row level security;, or with the "Enable RLS" option in the dashboard. Tables made in the SQL editor or by a migration don't get it by default. Right after you enable it, the table goes quiet rather than loud. On my local test the public key, and two signed-in users, got 200 [] on select, update and delete, and only insert failed with 42501. The secret key still saw all 3 rows. A plain view over the table still handed all 3 rows to the public key. Once Supabase's 30 October 2026 change reaches your project, a new table also needs a grant before anything reaches it, so enable RLS and write the policies in the same migration as the grant.

I run a free Supabase security checker, and "RLS disabled" is the finding I see explained least well. Most guides say that after you enable RLS "the table becomes inaccessible". That's true for reads and misleading for writes. So I built one table on a local Supabase stack and sent every kind of request to it, as the public key, as two signed-in users and as the secret key, after each step below.

What is RLS in Supabase?

RLS (row-level security) is a Postgres feature that filters rows per request. Supabase turns every request from supabase-js into a database query that runs as a role: anon for the public (anon, publishable) key, authenticated for a signed-in user. With RLS on, Postgres checks your policies for each row and returns, changes or deletes only the rows a policy allows. With RLS off, any role that has a grant on the table reaches every row.

The secret (service role) key is different. Its role has BYPASSRLS, so RLS never applies to it. That's why it belongs only on a server. The difference between the two keys is in anon key vs service role key.

How do you enable RLS in Supabase?

Three ways, depending on how the table was made:

  • When you create a table in the Table Editor, keep "Enable Row Level Security (RLS)" checked. In Supabase's dashboard source it's marked "Recommended", and turning it off shows a warning that the table will be publicly readable and writable.
  • For an existing table, Supabase's API security guide says: go to Database, then Policies, and select "Enable RLS" on the table.
  • In SQL, in the SQL editor or a migration: 
alter table public.todos enable row level security;

Supabase's guide is explicit that tables created in the dashboard have RLS on by default, and tables created in the SQL editor or through another tool don't. If you build your schema with migrations or an AI tool, check every table.

What happens right after you enable RLS?

Nothing errors except insert. I created public.todos with an owner column (user_id uuid default auth.uid()), granted it to the API roles the way older projects do, and added three rows: two owned by user A and one by user B. Then I enabled RLS with no policy:

Request Public key User A User B Secret key
Select 200, 0 rows 200, 0 rows 200, 0 rows 200, 3 rows
Insert own row 401, error 42501 403, error 42501 403, error 42501 201, row inserted
Update a row 200, 0 rows 200, 0 rows 200, 0 rows 200, 1 row
Delete a row 200, 0 rows 200, 0 rows 200, 0 rows 200, 1 row

The insert error reads new row violates row-level security policy. Update and delete answer 200 with an empty array, so an app that doesn't check the returned rows reports "saved" when nothing was saved. Read your writes back after enabling RLS, or ask for a count with Prefer: count=exact.

Before RLS, with the same grants, the public key could read all 3 rows, insert, and update or delete any row. User A could edit and delete user B's row and hand their own rows to B.

How do you make the table usable again?

Write a policy per operation. The usual own-rows set:

create policy "own select" on public.todos for select to authenticated
  using ((select auth.uid()) = user_id);
create policy "own insert" on public.todos for insert to authenticated
  with check ((select auth.uid()) = user_id);
create policy "own update" on public.todos for update to authenticated
  using ((select auth.uid()) = user_id) with check ((select auth.uid()) = user_id);
create policy "own delete" on public.todos for delete to authenticated
  using ((select auth.uid()) = user_id);

With these, user A saw their 2 rows and user B saw their 1. The public key still saw 0. When A tried to insert a row owned by B, or to move their own row to B, the answer was 403, 42501. That refusal comes from with check on update. When A tried to update or delete B's row, the answer was 200, 0 rows. More patterns (public profiles, teams, MFA) are in Supabase RLS policy examples.

One detail from the secret key: a row it inserted got user_id = null, because auth.uid() has no user behind that key. RLS was skipped, but the default didn't do what the column name suggests.

What did the public key read at each step?


Figure 1. Local Supabase stack (CLI 2.109.1, Postgres 17.6), 3-row table, 28 October 2026.

Two steps leak everything: a grant without RLS, and a plain view over a table with correct policies. The next two sections explain both.

Do you still need RLS after the October 30 grant change?

Yes. Supabase set 30 October 2026 as the date when new tables in public stop getting automatic grants for the API roles on existing projects, and new projects have started that way since 30 May. Supabase hasn't confirmed the rollout, so check your own project. My local stack already behaves that way. A freshly created table with RLS off answered 42501 to every role, including the secret key, so nothing leaked. The details are in the Supabase October 30 grant change.

But the grant comes back as soon as the app needs the table, and from then on RLS is the only thing between the public key and every row. So put all of it in one migration, in this order:

create table public.todos (...);
alter table public.todos enable row level security;
create policy "own select" on public.todos ...;
grant select, insert, update, delete on table public.todos to authenticated;

Grant only to the roles that need the table. When I revoked everything from anon, the public key's select changed from 200 [] to 401, 42501. The grant is the first lock, RLS is the second.

Why does a view still leak rows?

Because a view runs with its owner's rights, and in Supabase that's postgres, which bypasses RLS. With the own-rows policies in place on todos, a plain create view public.todos_view as select * from public.todos returned all 3 rows to the public key and to user B.

Recreated with (security_invoker = true), the same view returned 0 rows to the public key, 2 to A and 1 to B, exactly like the table:

create view public.todos_view with (security_invoker = true) as
  select * from public.todos;

Supabase's Advisor flags the plain kind as security_definer_view, what it means and how to fix it's in the Supabase security definer view note.

How do you enable RLS on all tables at once?

Loop over the tables in public that still have RLS off. Run this on a staging copy first, because every table without a policy goes quiet for your app the moment it runs:

do $$
declare t record;
begin
  for t in
    select c.oid::regclass as tbl
    from pg_class c
    join pg_namespace n on n.oid = c.relnamespace
    where n.nspname = 'public'
      and c.relkind in ('r', 'p')
      and not c.relrowsecurity
  loop
    execute format('alter table %s enable row level security', t.tbl);
    raise notice 'RLS on: %', t.tbl;
  end loop;
end $$;

Then list the tables that now have RLS on and no policy. Each one needs a policy before the app can use it again:

select c.relname as table_name
from pg_class c
join pg_namespace n on n.oid = c.relnamespace
where n.nspname = 'public'
  and c.relkind in ('r', 'p')
  and c.relrowsecurity
  and not exists (
    select 1 from pg_policy p where p.polrelid = c.oid
  )
order by 1;

I ran both on a throwaway Supabase Postgres 17.6 on 18 November 2026, with four tables that had RLS off, one of them partitioned, plus one table that already had RLS and a policy. Tables with RLS off went from 4 to 0, and the anon role went from reading 2 rows of a granted table to 0. All 4 then showed up in the second query. The table that already had a policy was left alone, and so was a table in another schema.

How do you enable RLS on every new table automatically?

With an event trigger. Supabase's event triggers guide gives a function rls_auto_enable() and a trigger ensure_rls that runs after create table, create table as and select into in public. I installed it as published and got:

  • A table created afterwards with create table had RLS on without any alter. The public key got 200 [] on select and 401 on insert.
  • A table created with create table as select also had RLS on.
  • A table created before the trigger stayed off. The trigger isn't retroactive.

Without the trigger, a second table created next to the protected one had RLS off, and once granted, the public key read and wrote it freely. It also covers only public, other exposed schemas need their own line in the function.

Does FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY help?

Not for the roles you would worry about. alter table ... force row level security makes RLS apply to the table owner too. On Supabase both postgres and service_role have BYPASSRLS, so after force the owner still counted 3 rows, the secret key still saw everything, and a view owned by postgres still leaked. It only changed something for an owner role I created without BYPASSRLS: 2 rows before, 0 after.

How do you check your own project?

  • In the SQL editor, list the tables in public with RLS off: 
select c.relname as table_name
from pg_class c
join pg_namespace n on n.oid = c.relnamespace
where n.nspname = 'public'
  and c.relkind in ('r', 'p')
  and not c.relrowsecurity
order by 1;
  • The Advisor in the dashboard reports the same as rls_disabled_in_public, what that error means is in the RLS disabled in public note.
  • A scanner can't know which rows belong to whom. To prove that, send requests as two users, as above. The full method for an app with roles is in how to test Supabase RLS.

How I tested

  • Supabase CLI 2.109.1 on a laptop: Postgres 17.6, PostgREST 14.14, Auth 2.192.0. Two users signed in with a password, plus the local publishable and secret keys.
  • One table, public.todos, reseeded to the same 3 rows before every request. Each step was applied as SQL, and each request went over the REST API, with its status code and body recorded.
  • Grants for steps 2 to 5 were added by hand, to match a project created before 30 October 2026.

Limits. One local stack, made-up data, 28 October 2026. The dashboard steps are quoted from Supabase's docs, not clicked through. Tables created by the dashboard's own role may get different default grants. I didn't test that, or Storage, Realtime or GraphQL.

title: Self-Correcting RAG With LangGraph
description:
Short answer: A self-correcting RAG agent searches for evidence, checks whether the passages can answer the original question, and rewrites the search query when evidence is weak. LangGraph makes each decision explicit. If the evidence remains insufficient after the allowed attempts, return an honest abstention.

How does the agent decide that evidence is enough?

Relevance and sufficiency answer different questions. A passage can discuss the right product without stating the price the user asked for. One authoritative policy paragraph can be enough for a direct lookup. A comparison may require evidence for both items. Grade against the original question, then return a structured verdict with the IDs of the supporting passages. Validate the verdict and reject unknown IDs.

Sources: LangGraph agentic RAG tutorial · LangGraph Graph API · Structured output

How do you build a self-correcting RAG graph in LangGraph?

The Python example keeps the original question separate from the search query, deduplicates passages by stable ID, and stops when the rewrite is blank or repeats a previous query. MAX_ATTEMPTS counts retrieval calls, including the first search. Save the example as rag_demo.py, install langgraph, and run python rag_demo.py. The offline demonstration needs no provider key and produces a supported answer after one rewrite. On LangGraph 1.2.22 it prints Refunds within 14 days. ['refund-policy'] 2: the answer, its citation and the number of retrieval attempts.

from collections.abc import Callable
from typing import Literal, TypedDict

from langgraph.graph import END, START, StateGraph

class Passage(TypedDict):
    id: str
    text: str

class Grade(TypedDict):
    sufficient: bool
    evidence_ids: list[str]

class RagState(TypedDict):
    question: str
    query: str
    seen_queries: list[str]
    passages: list[Passage]
    evidence: list[Passage]
    attempts: int
    answer: str
    citations: list[str]

MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3

def build_graph(
    search: Callable[[str], list[Passage]],
    assess: Callable[[str, list[Passage]], Grade],
    rephrase: Callable[[str, str], str],
    write_answer: Callable[[str, list[Passage]], str],
):
    def retrieve(state: RagState) -> dict:
        passages = search(state["query"])
        by_id = {p["id"]: p for p in passages}
        return {
            "passages": list(by_id.values()),
            "attempts": state["attempts"] + 1,
        }

    def grade(state: RagState) -> dict:
        if not state["passages"]:
            return {"evidence": []}
        check = assess(state["question"], state["passages"])
        ids = set(check["evidence_ids"]) if check["sufficient"] else set()
        if not ids.issubset({p["id"] for p in state["passages"]}):
            return {"evidence": []}
        return {"evidence": [p for p in state["passages"] if p["id"] in ids]}

    def after_grade(state: RagState) -> Literal["answer", "rewrite", "abstain"]:
        if state["evidence"]:
            return "answer"
        return "abstain" if state["attempts"] >= MAX_ATTEMPTS else "rewrite"

    def rewrite(state: RagState) -> dict:
        query = rephrase(state["question"], state["query"]).strip()
        key = " ".join(query.casefold().split())
        if not key or key in state["seen_queries"]:
            return {"query": ""}
        return {"query": query, "seen_queries": [*state["seen_queries"], key]}

    def answer(state: RagState) -> dict:
        evidence = state["evidence"]
        return {
            "answer": write_answer(state["question"], evidence),
            "citations": [p["id"] for p in evidence],
        }

    def abstain(_: RagState) -> dict:
        return {"answer": "I could not find enough evidence.", "citations": []}

    graph = StateGraph(RagState)
    graph.add_node("retrieve", retrieve)
    graph.add_node("grade", grade)
    graph.add_node("rewrite", rewrite)
    graph.add_node("answer", answer)
    graph.add_node("abstain", abstain)
    graph.add_edge(START, "retrieve")
    graph.add_edge("retrieve", "grade")
    graph.add_conditional_edges("grade", after_grade)
    graph.add_conditional_edges(
        "rewrite", lambda state: "retrieve" if state["query"] else "abstain",
        {"retrieve": "retrieve", "abstain": "abstain"},
    )
    graph.add_edge("answer", END)
    graph.add_edge("abstain", END)
    return graph.compile()

def initial_state(question: str) -> RagState:
    return {
        "question": question, "query": question,
        "seen_queries": [" ".join(question.casefold().split())],
        "passages": [], "evidence": [], "attempts": 0,
        "answer": "", "citations": [],
    }

if __name__ == "__main__":
    refund: Passage = {"id": "refund-policy", "text": "Refunds within 14 days."}
    demo = build_graph(
        search=lambda query: [refund] if query == "refund window" else [],
        assess=lambda question, passages: {
            "sufficient": True, "evidence_ids": [passages[0]["id"]],
        },
        rephrase=lambda question, query: "refund window",
        write_answer=lambda question, evidence: evidence[0]["text"],
    )
    run = demo.invoke(
        initial_state("Can I return this?"), {"recursion_limit": 20},
    )
    print(run["answer"], run["citations"], run["attempts"])

The mock assesses a tiny fixture. In a live adapter, give the grader both the question and candidate passages, require the sufficient and evidence_ids fields, and handle invalid output explicitly. Use an evaluation suite to distinguish missing evidence from grader or retriever failure. Report failures as errors, rather than as evidence that the documents lack the answer.

The example returns the selected evidence IDs for traceability. In a real product, carry a document ID, title or URL, and chunk location. Render only authorized source links. If the generator supplies claim-level citations, verify that each ID belongs to the selected evidence and each claim is supported. A list of selected IDs alone does not prove the answer is grounded.

How do you handle conversation state, cost and latency?

Checkpointing stores thread-scoped graph state. Configure a persistent checkpointer and pass an authorized thread_id for production continuity. Resolve ambiguous follow-ups using authorized conversation history, then start each new question with its own attempts, evidence and seen_queries. Set the graph recursion_limit as a separate guard on graph execution, and use upstream timeouts to enforce the request’s latency budget.

Keep the number of candidate passages and retrieval attempts small enough to fit the latency budget. Batch or limit concurrency for grading, depending on measured quality and cost. Trace retrieval and grading separately and measure p95 latency, attempts per question, and the share of questions recovered by rewriting. If rewrites often fail, inspect retrieval coverage, filters, chunking and the evaluation set before increasing the cap.

Sources: LangGraph persistence · LangSmith RAG evaluation tutorial

How do you evaluate a self-correcting RAG agent?

Keep a labeled set of directly answerable, rewrite-dependent, and unanswerable questions. Add tests for duplicate chunks, unsupported comparisons, invalid source IDs, and a repeated rewrite. Compare baseline retrieval with the corrective workflow on evidence recall@k, groundedness, correct abstentions, latency, and cost. Run the production tests on your own sources and models.

Related guides

  • MongoDB vs PostgreSQL for a LangGraph RAG agent: what the agent stores and how to choose the database.
  • RAG evaluation metrics: how to build the test set that checks this loop.
  • pgvector hybrid search in PostgreSQL: a stronger retrieval step to feed the grader.

Frequently asked questions

What is corrective RAG?

It is a common name for this pattern: check the retrieved passages and correct the search when they are weak, before generating an answer.

How many retry attempts should I allow?

Start with two or three, and log the number of attempts per question. If most questions need a rewrite, the problem is usually in indexing or chunking, and the loop is hiding it.

Does self-correction replace evaluation?

No. It improves what the pipeline does at run time. You still need a test set that includes questions the documents cannot answer, as described in the RAG evaluation guide.

Where to go next

If you want a full application with a FastAPI backend and a Next.js chat interface, see the RAG starter kits.

The idea in short

The question is searched, each retrieved passage is graded for relevance, and a routing function decides what happens next: generate an answer if enough passages pass, rewrite the query and search again if not, or stop with a not-found answer once the attempt limit is reached.

Patterns covered: Corrective retrieval · State graph · Conditional routing · Attempt limit
