title: Fail closed on incoming FaceTime and SharePlay, item-left-behind alerts, and Sleep Focus
description:
When narrative content drives a physical actuator, three interrupt paths look like "just restore state" until they are not: an incoming FaceTime / SharePlay / "Join FaceTime" surface mid-session, an Item Left Behind / Separation Alert / "You May Have Left This Behind" warning, and Sleep Focus / Wind Down / Bedtime / Sleep Schedule. Each needs a default that fails closed �ü” toward idle, toward re-arm only after a named beat, toward interrupt-clear �‰  motor authority.

on incoming_facetime_or_shareplay_or_join_facetime_opened():
    ramp_to(IDLE, at=next_beat_boundary)
    armed = false
    on facetime_or_shareplay_declined_or_ended_or_left_or_dismissed():
        # FaceTime / SharePlay UI gone �‰  motor envelope restored
        await user_resume(); await next_named_beat(); arm()

on item_left_behind_or_separation_alert_or_you_may_have_left_this_behind_opened():
    ramp_to(IDLE, at=next_beat_boundary)
    armed = false
    on left_behind_alert_dismissed_or_item_located_or_marked_ignored():
        # left-behind / separation-alert UI cleared �‰  motor authority
        await user_resume(); await next_named_beat(); arm()

on sleep_focus_or_wind_down_or_bedtime_or_sleep_schedule_opened():
    ramp_to(IDLE, at=next_beat_boundary)
    armed = false
    on wind_down_dismissed_or_bedtime_postponed_or_sleep_focus_turned_off():
        # Sleep Focus / Wind Down UI gone �‰  previous intensity restored
        await user_resume(); await next_named_beat(); arm()

The FaceTime / SharePlay rule is easy to mix up with an ordinary phone call, Live Voicemail or call screening, an iMessage thread or composer, a NameDrop contact exchange, an AirDrop receive, and Continuity Camera or Desk View. A phone call is a cellular or telephony interrupt. Live Voicemail screens a phone call. A message thread is the Messages surface. NameDrop is a contact-exchange sheet. AirDrop is an inbound file or link receive. Continuity Camera is an iPhone used as a webcam. An incoming FaceTime call, "Join FaceTime" sheet, or SharePlay join surface is a system calling or shared-play surface. Clearing that sheet clears that surface; it must not restore motor authority.

The item-left-behind rule sits next to �ü” but is not �ü” an unknown tracker "Found Moving With You" warning or Precision Finding, Find My Play Sound / Lost Mode / Remote Lock, a Bluetooth pairing request, or AirPods Conversation Awareness / Announce Notifications / Automatic Ear Detection. An unknown-tracker alert is about someone else's tag moving with you. Play Sound, Lost Mode, and Remote Lock are Find My device-control actions. Pairing is an accessory-setup sheet. AirPods Conversation Awareness and ear detection are audio-awareness interrupts. An Item Left Behind or Separation Alert is a system warning that your own item may have been left behind. Dismissing it, locating the item, or marking it ignored only clears that UI; it must not restore motor authority.

The Sleep Focus rule is a sleep-schedule interrupt, not a generic Focus or Do Not Disturb toggle, not Guided Access or a Screen Time app limit, not a clock alarm or timer, not a Calendar event, Reminder due, or Time to Leave prompt, and not Low Power Mode. Generic Focus is an ordinary concentration or DND switch. Guided Access and Screen Time limits are access-restriction surfaces. An alarm is a clock interrupt. Calendar and Time to Leave are scheduling surfaces for events and departures. Low Power Mode is a battery-policy switch. Sleep Focus, Wind Down, bedtime, or a Sleep Schedule surface is a system sleep-schedule UI. Dismissing Wind Down or turning Sleep Focus off only clears that interrupt; it must not restore motor authority.

Buyers can test all three without code: decline or end a FaceTime or SharePlay join mid-session and see whether that restarts intensity; dismiss or locate from an item-left-behind alert; and dismiss Wind Down or turn Sleep Focus off. The acceptance question is the same in each case: clearing the FaceTime, left-behind, or Sleep UI must not put motor authority back on. These map to questions like "how do AI stories control physical devices" and "Lovense alternative with AI stories."

This is the model CRAVE AI uses for story-controlled play on official devices: AI story-controlled vibrator. Principle write-up: narrative-to-device sync. Devices: AI sex toys.

Disclosure: I work on CRAVE AI. Adults-only product; no explicit content here.

title: How I built a browser softphone with a one-command Kamailio + FreeSWITCH lab and real-call E2E tests
description:
Getting a browser to place a real SIP call is a messy weekend. You need a JavaScript SIP stack, a WebSocket signalling path, WebRTC media (DTLS-SRTP, ICE, a codec), and something on the other end that answers. Most samples give you one of those pieces. I wanted a repo where docker compose up -d and npm run dev is enough to register, call an echo test, walk an IVR with DTMF, and call another browser tab.

That repo is webrtc-sip-softphone. This post is a walk through how it is put together, how the tests work, and what the lab deliberately leaves out.

What you get

The softphone is framework-free TypeScript and Vite. It registers over ws:// or wss://, dials a number or a SIP URI, answers, hangs up, mutes, holds and resumes, and sends DTMF (RFC 2833 in-media, or SIP INFO). During a call it shows live stats from RTCPeerConnection.getStats(): codec, packets, loss, jitter and RTT. One call at a time; a second incoming call is rejected with 486 Busy Here.

The lab is a docker-compose file:

  • Kamailio 5.8 as the WebSocket SIP proxy and in-memory registrar (RFC 7118 on port 8088), with NAT handling for WebSocket clients, record-routing, and routing of lab numbers to FreeSWITCH and of everything else to registered softphones.
  • FreeSWITCH 1.10 with a single-file config, WebRTC media (DTLS-SRTP, ICE, Opus) and three extensions:
Dial What happens
9196 Echo: you hear yourself, which tests the full media path
5000 IVR: a flite text-to-speech menu. 1 echo, 2 tone, 3 goodbye and hang up
9664 Continuous 440 Hz tone
1002 (and so on) Another softphone. Open a second tab with ?user=1002

FreeSWITCH runs in Kamailio's network namespace (network_mode: service:kamailio). Kamailio reaches it on loopback, the FreeSWITCH SIP port is not published, and only the RTP range is exposed.

Quickstart

You need Docker with Compose, Node 20+, a Chromium or Firefox browser, and a microphone.

docker compose up -d --wait
npm install
npm run dev   # http://localhost:5173

Click Connect (defaults: ws://localhost:8088, sip:1001@lab.local, no password) and dial 9196. For phone-to-phone, open http://localhost:5173/?user=1002&autoconnect in a second tab and call 1002.

If you want to call from another device on your LAN, start the lab with EXT_RTP_IP=<your LAN IP> and serve the page over HTTPS. Browsers only allow the microphone on https:// or localhost.

Architecture, in short

The UI talks to a Softphone class, which talks to a small UALike interface. The only production adapter is JsSIP. The phone's behaviour is a pure reducer in src/core/state.ts, driven by SIP events. That split is what makes the unit tests possible: everything except the JsSIP adapter is tested without a browser.

A call to the IVR looks like this:

  1. The browser REGISTERs over the WebSocket. Kamailio stores the contact with a WebSocket alias and returns 200.
  2. The phone INVITEs sip:5000@lab.local with an SDP offer (Opus, DTLS, ICE).
  3. Kamailio record-routes and forwards the INVITE to FreeSWITCH over UDP on loopback.
  4. FreeSWITCH answers with SDP. ICE and DTLS complete, then SRTP audio flows between the browser and FreeSWITCH.
  5. FreeSWITCH plays the menu. The phone sends DTMF 1 as RFC 2833 telephone-event. FreeSWITCH transfers that call into echo().
  6. BYE tears the call down along the record-route set, with Kamailio handling the WebSocket alias on the way back.

The README has mermaid diagrams for the architecture and this sequence if you want the boxed version.

Why the state is a reducer

SIP events arrive late, twice, or out of order. A hold request should be ignored if the call already ended. A second incoming INVITE should not clobber an active call. Putting that in event-handler closures gets messy, and it is hard to test.

A reducer ((state, event) => nextState) can be fed a recorded list of events in a unit test, including the late and out-of-order ones, with no WebSocket and no browser. The Softphone class is tested against a fake user agent for dialling options, mute/hold/DTMF and the busy rejection. Settings validation, dial-string normalisation, DTMF checks, duration formatting and stats summarising are all pure functions.

There are 42 of those unit tests, run with Vitest (npm test).

Real-call end-to-end tests

Unit tests cannot tell you that ICE connected or that FreeSWITCH actually switched into echo after a DTMF 1. For that there are 4 Playwright tests (npm run test:e2e) that drive Chromium against the running lab, with a fake microphone:

  1. Register, call 9196, wait until remote audio packets arrive, hang up.
  2. Call the IVR, press 1, and assert via fs_cli that FreeSWITCH is now running echo on that call.
  3. Two browser contexts register as 1001 and 1002, call each other through Kamailio, and hold/resume.
  4. Calling an unregistered number ends with Not Found.

GitHub Actions runs the unit job, then a job that starts the lab with docker compose up --wait, checks the Kamailio config, and runs the Playwright suite.

A limit of those tests is worth stating clearly: Chromium's fake microphone means the audio checks are packet counts, not a human listening. The suite has not been run against Safari, real handsets, TURN, or a path that crosses real NAT. The lab's media path assumes the browser and the Docker host can reach each other directly.

What the lab deliberately leaves out

This is a development lab, not a box you should put on the public internet as-is.

  • TLS. Use wss:// (Kamailio's tls module, or a TLS-terminating proxy in front of port 8088).
  • Auth. The lab registrar accepts anyone. Add digest auth (auth / auth_db) or token auth before exposing it.
  • Media relay. Behind real NAT, use TURN for browsers and/or rtpengine with Kamailio.
  • FreeSWITCH lock-down. The profile has auth-calls=false and is only safe because it listens on loopback.

I would rather document those gaps than pretend the compose file is production-ready.

If you want to try it

The code is MIT licensed: github.com/AhmedElbashier/webrtc-sip-softphone. Issues and reviews are welcome. I also published an ASP.NET Core 8 webhook relay for WhatsApp Cloud API and HubSpot in the same week, if that is more your stack: dotnet-webhook-relay.

More of my work is on my site.

title: Your Mobile App Shouldn’t Lose a Form When Someone Answers a Call
description:
A customer spends five minutes filling out a service request in your mobile app.

They add an address, describe the problem, and select a preferred appointment time.

Then a phone call arrives.

When they return, the form is empty.

The interface may look polished, but the user has just lost five minutes of work.

Preserving progress deserves a place in the initial product scope.

Here’s a practical approach to designing mobile forms that survive interruptions.

1. Treat interruptions as part of the user journey

Mobile users switch between apps constantly.

They might open a messaging app to check an address, copy a reference number from an email, or leave your app to take a photo.

Your application may remain in memory during that interruption—or its process may be terminated.

The user’s expectation is simpler:

“I should be able to continue where I left off.”

Design the flow around that expectation.

2. Separate a draft from a submission

A draft records progress. A submission starts a business operation.

For a service-request form, draft data might include:

  • Service category.
  • Problem description.
  • Address entered so far.
  • Preferred appointment time.
  • Current step in the form.

Saving those fields should not create a confirmed appointment, trigger a payment, or send a notification to a service provider.

A clear conceptual flow is:

Editing → Draft saved → Review → Submit → Confirmation

Keeping these responsibilities separate makes recovery easier to reason about.

3. Save meaningful progress along the way

Waiting until the user leaves the screen creates a fragile dependency on a final save opportunity.

Instead, consider saving when:

  • The user completes a step.
  • A selection changes.
  • Typing pauses briefly.
  • The user explicitly chooses “Save draft.”

Avoid writing to storage on every keystroke if it creates unnecessary work. For text fields, a short debounce can group changes, although edits made just before an interruption may still be lost.

Also track whether saving actually succeeded. Displaying “Draft saved” before the write completes gives the user a misleading promise.

4. Choose where the draft belongs

Local and server-side drafts solve different needs.

Approach Useful for Questions to resolve
Local draft Continuing on the same device, including offline editing What happens on logout, app removal, or device sharing?
Server-side draft Continuing across devices How are access, synchronization, and conflicting edits handled?
Both Fast local recovery with cross-device continuity Which version wins when changes disagree?

Choose based on the product’s requirements.

Be selective about what you retain. Passwords, payment credentials, and other sensitive fields need a different approach from an ordinary description field.

Addresses and other personal information also need appropriate protection and a clear retention policy. Save only what the workflow requires.

5. Restore the work, then revalidate it

A saved draft captures what the user entered earlier. It does not guarantee that every choice is still valid.

For example:

  • An appointment slot may no longer be available.
  • A service price may have changed.
  • A selected delivery area may no longer be supported.

Restore the user’s input, then explain any changes that require attention.

A useful message might be:

“Your draft has been restored. The selected time is no longer available—please choose another slot.”

Keep the description and address intact. One outdated selection should not erase the entire form.

6. Make draft behavior understandable

Users should know whether their progress was retained.

Useful interface details include:

  • A clear “Draft saved” status.
  • A visible warning when saving fails.
  • A “Continue your draft” option.
  • An intentional “Discard draft” action.

If a draft is saved only on the current device, make that limitation clear rather than implying it is available everywhere.

After a confirmed successful submission, clear or archive the corresponding draft so it does not reappear as unfinished work.

If the submission outcome is uncertain, resolve its status before encouraging another submission. A network error alone does not prove that the server rejected the request.

7. Test the interruptions

A successful form submission is only one test case.

Try these scenarios too:

  • Switch to another app and return.
  • Relaunch after the app process has been terminated.
  • Restart the device.
  • Edit while offline, then reconnect.
  • Restore a draft containing an unavailable appointment slot.
  • Log out and sign in with a different account.
  • Simulate a storage or draft-save failure.

Check both what survives and what should no longer be accessible.

Also test recovery after an app update. A draft saved by an older version may not match the latest form structure.

Build for the person holding the phone

A mobile form exists alongside calls, messages, weak connections, and changing plans.

Preserving progress helps users finish a task without repeatedly entering the same information.

At Digittrix, our mobile app development services help businesses turn ideas into useful applications. Preserving progress and handling interruptions are practical considerations when planning a reliable mobile experience.

Which interruption has caused the most frustrating data loss in a mobile app you’ve used or built?

— The Digittrix Team

title: Why GBase 8a Installs and Upgrades Take Longer on a Laptop VM
description:
Installing or upgrading GBase 8a, the China-domestically developed MPP analytical database from GBASE, usually finishes in under 10 minutes on production servers — but takes 15–20 minutes or more on a laptop VM. After ruling out hardware differences, the cause turned out to be sshd configuration making each remote ssh connection slow. A gbase install issues many of those connections, so the delay compounds.

Investigation

The install and upgrade log gcinstall.log showed the check phase and file-transfer phase completing almost instantly on real servers, but taking several seconds — sometimes over ten — on the VM.

A manual ssh to another node showed a clear wait, so ssh -v was used to find where it stalled. The key part of the output:

debug1: Authentications that can continue: publickey,gssapi-keyex,gssapi-with-mic,password
debug1: Next authentication method: gssapi-keyex
debug1: No valid Key exchange context
debug1: Next authentication method: gssapi-with-mic

Root Cause

The Unspecified GSS failure line was the culprit, traced to two sshd settings:

  • UseDNS enabled
  • GSSAPIAuthentication enabled

Fix

If you can edit the sshd configuration, disable both parameters. If you cannot or prefer not to, pass this option to ssh, scp, and similar commands:

-o GSSAPIAuthentication=no

Result

With that option disabled, the upgrade dropped from 27 minutes to 6 minutes.

Going forward, the gap was never about CPU or memory — it was an authentication wait on every single remote connection, multiplied across the many ssh calls an install or upgrade makes. Checking sshd before benchmarking the database itself can save a lot of time on gbase test environments.

title: How to Create a Testimonial Slider Section in Shopify
description:
Add a testimonial slider section to your Shopify theme, with settings you can edit in the Customizer.

Steps to Add Testimonial Slider Section

  1. Go to Theme → Edit code
  2. Add a section file
  3. Name the section file: testimonial-slider.liquid
  4. Paste the code into the section file
  5. Go to Customizer
  6. Search "testimonial slider" to add the section in the customizer

{% assign size = slider_view | modulo: 2 %}
{% assign size_tablet = slider_view | times: 0.5 | round: 0 | modulo: 2 %}

<script>
  function initTestimonials3() {
    document.querySelector('.testimonials-slider-{{ section.id }}').classList.remove('preview');
    const slider = new Swiper('.testimonials-slider-{{ section.id }}', {
      speed: 300,
      loop: true,
      watchSlidesProgress: true,
      navigation: {
        nextEl: '.testimonials-btn-next-{{ section.id }}',
        prevEl: '.testimonials-btn-prev-{{ section.id }}'
      },
      pagination: {
        el: '.testimonials-pagination-{{ section.id }}',
        type: 'bullets',
        clickable: true
      },
      breakpoints: {
        320: {
          centeredSlides: true,
          spaceBetween: {{ slider_gap_mobile }},
          slidesPerView: {{ slider_view_mobile }}
        },
        768: {
          centeredSlides: {% if size_tablet == 0 %}false{% else %}true{% endif %},
          spaceBetween: {{ slider_gap_mobile }},
          slidesPerView: {{ slider_view | times: 0.5 | round: 0 }}
        },
        1024: {
          centeredSlides: {% if size == 0 %}false{% else %}true{% endif %},
          spaceBetween: {{ slider_gap }},
          slidesPerView: {{ slider_view }}
        }
      }
    });
    slider.slidePrev();

  }

  document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', initTestimonials3);

  if (Shopify.designMode) {
     document.addEventListener('shopify:section:unload', initTestimonials3);
     document.addEventListener('shopify:section:load', initTestimonials3);
  }

</script>

title: Adding a column while another transaction is open
description:
I wrote about the Postgres side of this in September, in One long SELECT, one ALTER TABLE, and every query behind them. This one adds MySQL 8.4 and measures what a lock timeout with retries costs the other clients.

Adding a nullable column is one of the cheapest schema changes there is. In Postgres 18 it only touches the catalog, and in MySQL 8.4 you can ask for ALGORITHM=INSTANT. On an idle table both took a few milliseconds in my tests. What I wanted to know is what happens to everyone else when the table isn't idle, specifically when some other session has an open transaction that read from it and hasn't committed yet.

The setup

Postgres 18.6 and MySQL 8.4.13 in two throwaway Docker containers on a Mac laptop. Each had one table, items, with 200,000 rows. Three clients ran for 32 seconds:

  • a writer doing single-row INSERTs in autocommit, about 80 a second
  • a reader doing primary-key SELECTs, at the same rate
  • a session that opened a transaction at 3 s, ran SELECT count(*) FROM items, then sat idle until it committed at 23 s

At 6 s a fourth session ran the migration:

-- Postgres
ALTER TABLE items ADD COLUMN note text;
-- MySQL
ALTER TABLE items ADD COLUMN note text, ALGORITHM=INSTANT;

Every query's start time and duration was logged. I ran each case three times per engine. The durations below varied by 30 ms at most between runs, so I'm quoting run one.

What the clients saw

Case Engine ALTER took Longest INSERT Longest SELECT INSERTs started between 6 s and 23 s
no open transaction Postgres 1 ms 0.01 s 0.01 s 1,376
no open transaction MySQL 4 ms 0.01 s 0.01 s 1,347
open transaction Postgres 17.0 s 17.0 s 17.0 s 1
open transaction MySQL 17.0 s 17.0 s 17.0 s 1

With the open transaction, the ALTER waited the full 17 seconds until the other session committed. That part I expected. What matters is that every INSERT and every SELECT that arrived after the ALTER waited behind it, for those same 17 seconds. One insert started in that window, and it was the one that hung. The plain primary-key read, which has nothing to do with the new column, hung too.

Neither engine returned an error to the clients. They just stopped.

The reason is the same in both. The ALTER needs an exclusive lock on the table, which in MySQL is the metadata lock. It can't get one while the idle transaction still holds its shared lock from the count(*). And once an exclusive request is waiting, new requests for the shared lock queue behind it instead of slipping past. So one idle session plus one cheap migration takes the whole table offline, and the cost of the migration itself has nothing to do with it.

What it looks like while it's happening

I took a snapshot of each engine's session list a moment into the stall. In Postgres, from pg_stat_activity with pg_blocking_pids():

pid  state                wait_event  query                                    blocked by
148  active               relation    INSERT INTO items (v, payload) VALUES …  {151}
149  active               relation    SELECT payload FROM items WHERE id = …   {151}
150  idle in transaction  ClientRead  SELECT count(*) FROM items               {}
151  active               relation    ALTER TABLE items ADD COLUMN note text    {150}

The INSERT and the SELECT both name the ALTER as the thing blocking them, not the idle transaction. If you only follow the first hop, the migration looks like the culprit. The session actually holding things up is listed as idle, and its query column shows the last thing it ran, which can be minutes old in a real app.

MySQL's processlist is less helpful:

id  command  state                            info
51  Query    Waiting for table metadata lock  ALTER TABLE items ADD COLUMN note text, ALGORITHM=INSTANT
52  Query    Waiting for table metadata lock  SELECT payload FROM items WHERE id = 126667
53  Sleep                                     NULL
54  Query    Waiting for table metadata lock  INSERT INTO items (v, payload) VALUES (1, 'x')

The session holding the lock shows up as Sleep with no query at all. Nothing on that line says it's the one with the open transaction. You need performance_schema.metadata_locks or sys.schema_table_lock_waits to connect it.

A lock timeout on the migration

The usual advice is to give the migration a short lock timeout and retry. I set lock_timeout = '2s' in Postgres and lock_wait_timeout = 2 in MySQL on the migration's session, then retried every 3 seconds until it worked.

Engine Attempts Error on each failed attempt Longest INSERT Stalls over 0.5 s INSERTs started between 6 s and 23 s
Postgres 4 canceling statement due to lock timeout 2.0 s 4 734
MySQL 4 1205 Lock wait timeout exceeded; try restarting transaction 2.0 s 4 711

It works in the sense that no request waited longer than 2 seconds. But each attempt froze the table for its full 2 seconds before giving up, and there were four of them, at 6, 11, 16 and 21 seconds. The clients spent 8 of those 17 seconds stuck, and the writer got through about half as many inserts as it did with no migration running. The fourth attempt went through when the idle transaction committed at 23 s.

What I got wrong

I treated the lock timeout as the fix. It turns one 17 second outage into four 2 second ones. Whether that's better depends on what your clients' own timeouts are, and with a 3 second retry the table was blocked almost half the time until the real problem went away. A shorter timeout, or a longer gap between retries, would trade those two against each other, but I only tried one setting.

My clients had no query timeouts of their own, so each stall shows up as one slow call. In an app with a 5 second request timeout, the no-timeout case would have been a pile of errors, not one slow insert.

And I'd have read the Postgres snapshot wrong if I'd stopped at the first column. The obvious reading is "the ALTER is blocking everything". It is, but only because something else is blocking it.

Caveats

One table, one laptop, Docker, two clients plus the idle session. I didn't test ADD COLUMN with a volatile default, index builds, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, or what happens when the open transaction belongs to a connection pooler. In every run the idle transaction committed on its own at 23 s. In real life it might be a forgotten psql session that never does.

What I'd take from it

  • Before a migration, look for sessions that are idle in transaction (Postgres) or have open transactions in information_schema.innodb_trx (MySQL). The cheapest ALTER is only cheap if nothing is holding the table.
  • Set a lock timeout on the migration anyway, but count on it costing one full timeout of blocked traffic per attempt.
  • Postgres has idle_in_transaction_session_timeout for the other side of the problem. It ends the session that's holding things up instead of the migration.

title: Idempotency in Software Development: What It Is and Why Every Backend Developer Should Understand It
description:
Imagine you're building a payment application.

A user wants to transfer ₦50,000 to another account. They click the Transfer button, but the network is slow. Nothing seems to happen, so they click the button again.

The first request actually reached your server and processed successfully, but the response never made it back to the user's device.

Now your server receives the second request.

What happens?

If your backend isn't properly designed, the user might get charged twice.

This is one of the problems that Idempotency helps us solve.

It is a concept every backend developer should understand, especially when building APIs, payment systems, distributed applications, and services that depend on network communication.

Let's break it down.

1. What Exactly Is Idempotency?

In simple terms, idempotency means that performing the same operation multiple times produces the same result as performing it once.

Think of it this way:

You press an elevator button once. The elevator is called.

You press the same button five more times. You don't get five elevators.

The intended outcome remains the same.

In software development, we want our operations to behave similarly.

For example:

  • Sending the same payment request multiple times should not result in multiple charges.
  • Submitting the same order request repeatedly should not create duplicate orders.
  • Retrying an API request should not accidentally perform the same action multiple times.

The goal is to make our systems predictable, even when requests are repeated.

2. Why Is Idempotency Important?

Modern applications don't always operate under perfect conditions.

We deal with:

  • Unstable internet connections.
  • Network timeouts.
  • Server failures.
  • Automatic retries.
  • Users clicking buttons multiple times.
  • Distributed systems communicating with one another.

Consider this scenario:

  • A frontend sends a request to create an order.
  • The backend receives the request.
  • The backend successfully creates the order.
  • The response gets lost because of a network issue.
  • The frontend assumes the request failed and retries it.
  • The backend receives the same request again.
  • Without proper protection, the backend might create two orders.
  • This is why idempotency matters.

Some of its major benefits include:

  1. Prevents duplicate operations

It protects your application against repeated actions such as duplicate payments, orders, and account transactions.

  1. Improves API reliability

Clients can safely retry supported operations without worrying about unintentionally repeating side effects.

  1. Handles network failures

Your application can recover from uncertain network conditions more safely.

  1. Improves user experience

Users don't have to worry about being charged twice simply because they clicked a button more than once.

  1. Makes distributed systems more predictable

When multiple services communicate over unreliable networks, idempotency helps control repeated requests and side effects.

3. Understanding Idempotency Through HTTP Methods

You might have already encountered idempotency without realizing it.

HTTP defines certain methods as idempotent. Let's look at some examples.

GET — Idempotent

GET requests retrieve data without changing the server's state.

Sending the same GET request multiple times should produce the same intended result.

GET /users/123

PUT — Idempotent

PUT requests replace a resource with the provided representation.

Sending the same PUT request multiple times should leave the resource in the same state.

PUT /users/123
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "name": "Samuel"
}

DELETE — Idempotent

DELETE requests remove a resource.

Deleting the same resource multiple times has the same intended effect: the resource remains deleted.

DELETE /users/123

POST — Not inherently idempotent

POST requests are commonly used to create resources or trigger operations.

Sending the same POST request multiple times can create multiple records.

POST /orders

For example, sending this request five times could create five different orders.

PATCH — Depends on the operation

PATCH requests partially modify resources.

Whether a PATCH request is idempotent depends on what the operation actually does.

For example, setting a user's name to "Samuel" repeatedly is idempotent.

However, increasing an account balance by ₦5,000 on every request is not.

Important: Idempotency is about the intended effect on server state, not necessarily identical HTTP responses. A repeated DELETE, for example, might return a different status code after the resource has already been deleted.

  1. How Do We Implement Idempotency in a Backend?

One common approach is using something called an Idempotency Key.

An idempotency key is a unique identifier generated by the client and sent alongside a request.

The backend uses this key to identify requests that represent the same operation.

Let's use a payment application as an example.

The frontend generates a unique key:

const idempotencyKey = crypto.randomUUID();

Then sends it to the backend:

const response = await fetch("/api/payments", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
    "Idempotency-Key": idempotencyKey,
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    amount: 50000,
    accountNumber: "1234567890",
  }),
});

Now let's look at what happens on the backend.

Step 1: Receive the request

Your Express.js backend receives the payment request and extracts the idempotency key.

const idempotencyKey = req.headers["idempotency-key"];

if (!idempotencyKey) {
  return res.status(400).json({
    message: "Idempotency key is required",
  });
}

Step 2: Check whether the request has already been processed

Before initiating the payment, the backend checks its database for an existing record associated with that key.

const existingRequest = await Idempotency.findOne({
  key: idempotencyKey,
  userId: req.user.id,
});

If the request has already completed, return its previously stored result instead of processing the payment again.

if (existingRequest?.status === "completed") {
  return res.status(existingRequest.responseStatus).json(
    existingRequest.responseBody
  );
}

Step 3: Process the operation

If the key hasn't been used before, the backend proceeds with the payment.

After successful processing, it stores the result associated with the idempotency key.

The next time the same request arrives with that key, the backend can return the original result.

Note: This is a simplified illustration. A production implementation must also handle concurrent requests, in-progress operations, request payload validation, database transactions, and payment-provider behavior.

  1. What Does a Production-Ready Implementation Need?

Simply checking whether a key exists is not enough.

Imagine two identical requests arrive at almost exactly the same time.

Both requests check the database before either one has stored its idempotency record.

Both might conclude that the operation hasn't been processed.

And just like that, you have a duplicate operation.

A production implementation should consider the following:

  1. Database uniqueness constraints

Enforce uniqueness on the appropriate scope, such as the combination of user ID, endpoint, and idempotency key.

Don't rely on application-level checks alone.

  1. Handle concurrent requests

Use atomic database operations, transactions, or another coordination mechanism to ensure only one request claims a particular key.

  1. Track request status

A useful lifecycle could look like:

processing

completed

failed

Be careful with failed operations: a timeout doesn't necessarily mean the payment failed. You may need to reconcile its status with the payment provider before retrying.

  1. Validate request payloads

If a client reuses the same idempotency key with a different payment amount, you shouldn't silently return the previous result or process a different payment.

Store a request fingerprint and reject conflicting reuse.

  1. Store and reuse the original response

When an operation succeeds, persist the relevant response status and body so subsequent retries can receive the original result.

  1. Define an expiration policy

Idempotency records shouldn't necessarily live forever. Define a retention period based on the business requirements and the payment provider's idempotency policy.

  1. Idempotency Is Not Just for Payment Systems

Although payment processing is one of the easiest places to understand this concept, idempotency is useful in many other areas.

Here are a few examples:

E-commerce: Preventing duplicate orders when customers retry checkout.

Authentication: Preventing repeated processing of the same one-time operation.

File uploads: Avoiding duplicate file records when upload requests are retried.

Notifications: Preventing the same notification from being sent repeatedly.

Background jobs: Ensuring a retried job doesn't repeat an already completed business operation.

Inventory management: Preventing duplicate stock deductions when an order request is retried.

Whenever an operation can be repeated and has side effects, you should think about whether it needs idempotency protection.

  1. Final Thoughts

Idempotency might seem like a small concept, but it plays a significant role in building reliable software.

As developers, we shouldn't assume that every request will arrive only once, every response will reach the client, or every network connection will work perfectly.

We should design our applications with these failures in mind.

The next time you're building a payment endpoint, an order creation API, or a background job, ask yourself:

"What happens if this exact operation runs twice?"

If the answer could cause duplicate payments, records, or unwanted side effects, you probably need to think about idempotency.

Build systems that can handle retries gracefully. Don't just build systems that work when everything goes perfectly.

Happy coding! 🚀

I'd love to hear from other developers:

Have you ever encountered a duplicate payment, order, or database operation because of repeated API requests?

How did you handle it?

Let's discuss in the comments!

title: Fail closed on Calendar and Reminder alerts, heart-rate vitals notifications, and AirPods Conversation Awareness
description:
When narrative content drives a physical actuator, three interrupt paths look like "just restore state" until they are not: a Calendar event / Reminder due / "Time to Leave" prompt mid-session, an Irregular Rhythm Notification / High Heart Rate / Low Heart Rate / Watch Vitals alert, and AirPods Conversation Awareness / Announce Notifications / Automatic Ear Detection. Each needs a default that fails closed �ü” toward idle, toward re-arm only after a named beat, toward interrupt-clear �‰  motor authority.

on calendar_event_or_reminder_due_or_time_to_leave_opened():
    ramp_to(IDLE, at=next_beat_boundary)
    armed = false
    on event_or_reminder_confirmed_or_dismissed_or_snoozed_or_completed_or_navigation_started():
        # Calendar / Reminder / Time to Leave UI gone �‰  motor envelope restored
        await user_resume(); await next_named_beat(); arm()

on irregular_rhythm_or_high_or_low_heart_rate_or_watch_vitals_opened():
    ramp_to(IDLE, at=next_beat_boundary)
    armed = false
    on vitals_alert_acknowledged_or_dismissed_or_opened():
        # Health / Watch vitals-alert UI cleared �‰  motor authority
        await user_resume(); await next_named_beat(); arm()

on airpods_conversation_awareness_or_announce_notifications_or_ear_detection_interrupt():
    ramp_to(IDLE, at=next_beat_boundary)
    armed = false
    on banner_dismissed_or_awareness_ended_or_announcement_skipped_or_silenced_or_airpod_reseated():
        # AirPods audio-awareness interrupt gone �‰  previous intensity restored
        await user_resume(); await next_named_beat(); arm()

The Calendar / Reminder rule is easy to mix up with a contact or calendar picker, a clock alarm or timer, an iMessage thread or composer, a generic Live Activity or Dynamic Island, and turn-by-turn navigation that is already running. A picker is a chooser UI. An alarm is a clock interrupt. A message thread is the Messages surface. A Live Activity is a generic system glance. Turn-by-turn is navigation already in progress. A Calendar event, due Reminder, or "Time to Leave" prompt is a system scheduling surface about an upcoming event or a departure time. Clearing that alert clears that surface; it must not restore motor authority. If Time to Leave then opens turn-by-turn navigation, treat that as a new interrupt, not as resume.

The heart-rate / vitals rule sits next to �ü” but is not �ü” a Health medications reminder, automatic Workout detection or a Fitness+ session, Emergency SOS / Crash Detection / Medical ID, a Check In or "Are you OK?" safety prompt, or a wireless emergency alert. A medications reminder is a dosing prompt. Workout detection is a fitness-session surface. Emergency SOS and Crash Detection are emergency flows. Check In is a safety confirmation. A WEA alert is a government broadcast. An Irregular Rhythm, High Heart Rate, Low Heart Rate, or Watch Vitals notification is a system health-alert surface about the wearer's vitals. Acknowledging or dismissing that alert only clears that UI; it must not restore motor authority.

The AirPods rule is an audio-awareness interrupt, not a Bluetooth audio-route change to another output, not a headphone safety volume-limit warning, not Siri taking over the session, not the Messages composer itself, and not an incoming phone call. A route change is an output-device switch. A volume-limit warning is a hearing-safety sheet. Siri takeover is a voice assistant. The Messages composer is the messaging UI. An incoming call is a telephony interrupt. Conversation Awareness, Announce Notifications, or Automatic Ear Detection is a system AirPods audio-awareness surface that ducks or interrupts the story. Ending the announcement or reseating the AirPod only clears that interrupt; it must not restore motor authority.

Buyers can test all three without code: trigger a Calendar, Reminder, or Time to Leave alert mid-session and see whether dismissing or completing it restarts intensity; acknowledge or dismiss a heart-rate or vitals notification; and end Conversation Awareness, skip an announced notification, or reseat an AirPod. The acceptance question is the same in each case: clearing the Calendar, vitals, or AirPods UI must not put motor authority back on. These map to questions like "how do AI stories control physical devices" and "Lovense alternative with AI stories."

This is the model CRAVE AI uses for story-controlled play on official devices: AI story-controlled vibrator. Principle write-up: narrative-to-device sync. Devices: AI sex toys.

Disclosure: I work on CRAVE AI. Adults-only product; no explicit content here.

title: Auth for Express in One Router Mount: Rotating Refresh Tokens, OAuth, and CSRF
description:
Every Express project I started began the same way: registration, email verification, login, refresh tokens, password reset, OAuth. Each time I rewrote it, and each time the details drifted. So I extracted it into Cred, an open-source, adapter-based auth library for Node.js.

What you get

Mount one router and you have:

  • Registration with email verification
  • Password login with account lockout (5 attempts, 15 minutes)
  • Google and GitHub OAuth, implemented with fetch (no Passport)
  • Rotating refresh tokens with replay detection
  • Password reset, profile management, and audit logs
  • CSRF protection and rate limiting

Setup 

npm install @cred-kit/express @cred-kit/core express cookie-parser express-rate-limit mongoose nodemailer

import express from 'express';
import { credExpress } from '@cred-kit/express';

const app = express();
app.set('trust proxy', 1);

const cred = await credExpress({
  database: { uri: process.env.MONGO_URI! },
  email: {
    EMAIL_FROM: 'no-reply@example.com',
    BACKEND_URL: 'http://localhost:3000',
    SMTP_HOST: process.env.SMTP_HOST!,
    SMTP_USER: process.env.SMTP_USER,
    SMTP_PASS: process.env.SMTP_PASS
  },
  jwtSecret: process.env.JWT_SECRET!, // 32+ characters
  clientUrl: 'http://localhost:5173',
  backendUrl: 'http://localhost:3000'
});

app.use('/api', cred);
app.listen(3000);

Configuration is validated at startup, so a bad secret or URL fails immediately instead of on the first request.

Design decisions

Refresh token rotation with replay detection. Refresh tokens are opaque lookupId.secret strings, and only the secret is stored, bcrypt-hashed. Each refresh atomically consumes the old token and issues a successor in the same family. If a consumed token is presented again, the entire family is revoked, which limits the damage of a stolen token.

Cookie-based sessions. The access token (a 15-minute HS256 JWT) and refresh token live in httpOnly cookies. The refresh cookie is path-scoped to /api/auth and its value is AES-256-GCM encrypted. Unsafe requests require a double-submit CSRF token.

No user enumeration. Unknown users and wrong passwords return the same error, and forgot-password always returns the same message.

Fire-and-forget audit logs. An audit-store outage can never fail a login.

Architecture 

@cred-kit/express   → HTTP transport (routes, cookies, CSRF, rate limits)
@cred-kit/core      → auth rules, framework- and storage-agnostic
@cred-kit/mongo-storage / @cred-kit/smtp → default adapters

Core talks to storage and email through small adapter interfaces, so you can replace MongoDB or SMTP with your own implementation and keep ownership of your user data.

Limitations

Cred is pre-1.0, so APIs may change between minor versions. It is ESM-only, the bundled storage adapter is MongoDB only, and the rate limiter is in-memory, meaning counters are not shared across instances. CORS, helmet, and HTTPS stay with the host app.

Try it

  • GitHub: github.com/NehanAhmed/cred
  • npm: npm i @cred-kit/express

MIT licensed, with 445 tests. I'd especially value feedback on the security model and the adapter API. If Cred saves you from rewriting auth, a star on the repo helps others find it.

title: Auzonix: I Tried Making AI Poke at My Website Like a Real Human. Here's What Happened
description:
Where the idea came from

Every site needs tests: something that runs through all the components and buttons, and a CI/CD pipeline that tells you what broke. But whenever I got around to writing them, I either abandoned them halfway or never started.

So I went looking for tools that would do it for me. There's plenty of AI-powered stuff out there, and plenty of big promises. But I noticed a pattern: they all test the happy path, not what real users actually do. So the tests only show part of the picture.

The problem with existing tools

The tools I found all follow the same principle: the test steps follow a specific functional task, i.e. "verify that this component does its job."

That's not bad on its own. It's fast, and regressions from a new feature can get caught right away. But it doesn't always cut it, because real people vary:

  • Some don't understand your interface.
  • Some click "wherever" and rarely the thing you expected.
  • Some reload the page while a form is submitting.
  • Some mash a button several times in a row.

Typical E2E tests and testing services almost never cover this. Real bugs, from technical glitches to UI logic problems, only show up through actual user behavior. A first-time visitor opens a page and has no idea what to do? That's a UI/UX problem, and no scripted test will flag it. How your site handles "illogical" actions is something you only learn by watching them happen.

My approach: a system of artificial users

Instead of searching further, I built my own solution.

The system manages Artificial Users. They don't just execute actions on a site. Each one gets:

  • a personality
  • a level of understanding of the page and its purpose
  • the ability to change its path depending on the page state

I don't hand the AI a site structure and say "click whatever." I define how it should behave, make decisions, and interact with the site. That changes everything: instead of random clicking, an artificial user can act logically or illogically, looking at the page the way a real user would.

The goal is to imitate people with different levels of understanding and surface bugs that no written test covers.

How it works under the hood

I had two options: dump everything on an LLM and build yet another AI agent, or build a system where the AI is just one component of the workflow.

I went with the second one and minimized the AI's role wherever it isn't actually needed.

The system handles:

  • page structure analysis
  • executing actions
  • the lifecycle of artificial users
  • coordinating them

The AI handles:

  • generating a scenario and its actions based on the assigned personality

You could let the AI do everything: analyze the page, decide when the page state changed, decide whether to reroute, all through tool calls. But the main problem there is token usage. Instead, the system itself triggers page analysis, runs each step, compares page states, and decides whether the scenario needs to change.

So the challenge isn't only what kind of testing to do, but how to make it efficient. That's what the architecture is built around.

Current lifecycle

  1. The user calls the API, passing a short site description, the URL, and the page to test.
  2. The system analyzes the page via Playwright and builds a compact, readable element structure. That structure goes into scenario generation, and later the system uses it to locate elements and act on them.
  3. The system hands the task to the AI. The model receives its profile (personality), plus page and site data, then decides on its own goal and the scenario for reaching it.
  4. The system executes the scenario step by step. After each step it compares page states and decides whether to change course.

This scenario isn't a typical test script. It doesn't verify a page's function; it just provides a base route for the user, driven by a profile that determines almost everything, from the goal to each individual action. And the scenario isn't set in stone: if the system detects that the page state really changed, the AI can generate a different next step from the same data.

Early results

The functionality is still focused, but the results are already interesting. For example, given a profile of a user who doesn't really get the interface, the AI generates scenarios that:

  • click a button multiple times
  • submit a form only partially filled in

The system also coordinates the AI's new steps well, so the artificial user's loop is already starting to look a lot like a real session. I'm still collecting runs across different sites, and more results will come as I test on more of them.

Tech stack

Java + Spring Boot + Playwright.

  • Java: great for multithreaded workloads like running several artificial users in parallel.
  • Spring Boot: gets an API up quickly and makes DI easy.
  • Playwright: great docs, pleasant to use, flexible configuration and control, and less manual code to write.

It's open source

The project is on GitHub: DequElite/Auzonix

You can try it, read through the full logic, or contribute changes. Documentation is there, and the code is written to be easy to follow.

I started it recently and I'm building it solo, improving it every day, and I'd love your help:

  • Found a bug or a potential problem? Open an issue.
  • Got an idea for a feature or improvement? Same place.

Final thoughts

Traditional E2E testing is still good and necessary. But some problems need a different approach, like testing with "living" users.

What do you think? Does this approach make sense, and is it worth developing further?

I'm not calling for abandoning traditional tests. This is just my experience and an experiment, open to everyone to use and improve.

title: S3 Security Defaults Changed. Have You Checked Your Older Buckets?
description:
A new S3 bucket and a bucket created several years ago can sit in the same AWS account with different access settings. If your security review starts with a recently created bucket, it is worth checking what the older ones look like too.

In April 2023, Amazon S3 completed a rollout that enabled Block Public Access and disabled access control lists (ACLs) by default for newly created buckets. The announcement explicitly left existing buckets’ settings unchanged. AWS announcement · Rollout details

For teams maintaining long-running environments, that creates a useful review task. Check whether older buckets still depend on access arrangements that your current deployment templates have moved away from.

1. Review the buckets your templates no longer describe

Start with an inventory across the AWS accounts you manage. Include buckets used for backups, exports, logs, and applications that have already been retired.

For each bucket, record its owner, purpose, current Block Public Access settings, Object Ownership setting, and any documented access exceptions. Compare those settings with your current infrastructure templates.

An older bucket may have a valid reason for its configuration. Give that reason an owner and a review date so the next person can understand it.

If you use the AWS CLI, these commands retrieve two useful parts of the bucket configuration:

aws s3api get-public-access-block \
  --bucket YOUR_BUCKET_NAME

aws s3api get-bucket-ownership-controls \
  --bucket YOUR_BUCKET_NAME

These results are a starting point. A full access review also needs to consider account-level controls and the relevant policies.

2. Check ACL dependencies before changing Object Ownership

With the Bucket owner enforced setting, ACLs are disabled and access is evaluated through policies. AWS recommends keeping ACLs disabled for most modern use cases. Existing workloads may still rely on ACL-based permissions, so review those dependencies before changing the setting. S3 Object Ownership documentation

Pay particular attention to applications that upload objects from another account and integrations that set an ACL during upload. Ask who writes the objects, who needs to read them, and how those permissions are currently granted.

AWS documents an approach using access logs and CloudTrail information to identify ACL-dependent requests and migrate their permissions to policies. Use that evidence alongside application testing when planning a change. AWS guide to identifying ACL dependencies

For a critical integration, rehearse both sides of the workflow. Confirm that the producer can upload an object and that the intended consumer can retrieve it.

3. Check historical objects separately from new uploads

Encryption has a different scope to the access-default changes.

Since January 5, 2023, S3 has automatically applied server-side encryption to new object uploads. The automatic baseline uses S3-managed keys, while existing customer-configured default encryption settings continue to apply. That rollout did not retroactively encrypt previously stored, unencrypted objects. S3 default encryption FAQ

If a bucket contains years of retained data, inspect the encryption status of those objects as part of the review. Also confirm whether your internal requirements call for a particular encryption configuration or key.

For a large collection, S3 Inventory can help you examine object metadata without manually opening objects one at a time. If historical objects need changes, plan the operation around retention requirements, application access, and the permissions required to read the resulting objects.

One review task for this week

Choose one older bucket that supports an active application or recovery process.

Confirm its owner, review its access settings, and test the application workflow in an approved environment before scheduling any configuration change. Record what you found in the same place your team maintains the deployment configuration or runbook.

That gives the next review a clear starting point and helps explain why the bucket is configured the way it is.

Have you found an older S3 bucket whose permissions differed from your current deployment templates? What made the dependency difficult to trace?

Author’s note: I work in marketing at Advange and cover enterprise IT news for infrastructure and operations teams. I used AI assistance to research and draft this post.

title: Build a Spice Label Checker in Vanilla JavaScript
description:
Small utility projects are a great way to practise JavaScript, especially when they check real-world data. In this tutorial we will build a spice label checker: you type in the details printed on a pack, and the tool tells you what looks incomplete or suspicious.

Why spices? Because people who search for the best spices online often have no way to compare packs except by reading the label. A few simple rules, such as a full ingredient list and sensible dates, catch many problems before you order. The same idea works for any packaged food, so you can reuse the code.

No framework, no build step. Just HTML and plain JavaScript.

What We Are Building

A small page with a form. The user enters:

Ingredients
Packed-on date
Best-before date
Licence number (the 14-digit FSSAI number printed on Indian food packs)
Seller contact details

When they click Check label, the page lists every issue it found, or shows a clean pass.

Where the Rules Come From

Rules should come from something real, not guesswork. The checks below follow the label checklist in this guide to the best spices online, which covers ingredients, dates, licence number, net weight, seller details and policies. We will code the ones that can be validated from text and dates alone.

A note on scope: this tool only checks the format and logic of what you type. It cannot confirm that a licence number is real or that a pack is genuine. For that, you still need to check the seller and the product yourself.

Step 1: The HTML
html
<!DOCTYPE html>




Spice Label Checker



Spice Label Checker

<form id="label-form">
  <label>Ingredients
    <textarea name="ingredients" rows="2"></textarea>
  </label>
  <label>Packed on
    <input type="date" name="packedOn" />
  </label>
  <label>Best before
    <input type="date" name="bestBefore" />
  </label>
  <label>Licence number (14 digits)
    <input type="text" name="fssai" inputmode="numeric" />
  </label>
  <label>Seller contact
    <input type="text" name="sellerContact" />
  </label>
  <button type="submit">Check label</button>
</form>

<section aria-live="polite">
  <h2 id="status"></h2>
  <ul id="issues"></ul>
</section>




Step 2: The Validation Function

Create app.js. The core is one pure function that takes the label data and returns a list of issues. Keeping it separate from the DOM makes it easy to test.

js
function parseDate(value) {
const date = new Date(value);
return Number.isNaN(date.getTime()) ? null : date;
}

function checkLabel(label, today = new Date()) {
const issues = [];

const ingredients = (label.ingredients || "").trim();
if (!ingredients) {
issues.push("Ingredients are missing.");
} else if (ingredients.toLowerCase() === "spices") {
issues.push("Ingredients are too vague. Each spice should be named.");
}

const packed = parseDate(label.packedOn);
const best = parseDate(label.bestBefore);

if (!packed) issues.push("Packed-on date is missing or invalid.");
if (!best) issues.push("Best-before date is missing or invalid.");

if (packed && best && best <= packed) {
issues.push("Best-before date must be after the packed-on date.");
}
if (best && best < today) {
issues.push("This pack is past its best-before date.");
}

const licence = (label.fssai || "").replace(/\s+/g, "");
if (!/^\d{14}$/.test(licence)) {
issues.push("Licence number should be exactly 14 digits.");
}

if (!(label.sellerContact || "").trim()) {
issues.push("Seller contact details are missing.");
}

return { ok: issues.length === 0, issues };
}
Step 3: Connect It to the Form
js
const form = document.getElementById("label-form");
const statusEl = document.getElementById("status");
const issuesEl = document.getElementById("issues");

form.addEventListener("submit", (event) => {
event.preventDefault();

const data = Object.fromEntries(new FormData(form));
const result = checkLabel(data);

issuesEl.innerHTML = "";

if (result.ok) {
statusEl.textContent = "No label issues found.";
return;
}

statusEl.textContent = ${result.issues.length} issue(s) found;
result.issues.forEach((text) => {
const li = document.createElement("li");
li.textContent = text; // textContent avoids injecting raw HTML
issuesEl.appendChild(li);
});
});

Open index.html, leave the ingredients as just spices, and submit. You should see the vague-ingredients message along with any other missing fields.

Step 4: Test the Logic

Because checkLabel takes today as a parameter, you can test it with a fixed date instead of waiting for real time to pass.

js
const today = new Date("2026-11-25");

const good = {
ingredients: "Coriander, red chilli, cumin, turmeric",
packedOn: "2026-10-01",
bestBefore: "2027-04-01",
fssai: "12345678901234",
sellerContact: "support@example.com",
};

console.log(checkLabel(good, today).ok); // true

const bad = { ...good, ingredients: "spices", bestBefore: "2026-09-01" };
console.log(checkLabel(bad, today).issues);
// ["Ingredients are too vague...", "Best-before date must be after...", "This pack is past..."]

The licence number above is a made-up example, used only to test the format.

Step 5: Make It Better

Some easy upgrades to practise with:

Live feedback. Run the check on the input event and show issues as the user types.
Severity levels. Mark some issues as warnings and others as errors.
More fields. Add net weight and price per 100 g, then calculate and show it.
Save drafts. Use localStorage to keep the last entry.
Reuse the function. Because it is pure, you can drop it into a React or Vue component or a Node script.
Common Mistakes
Comparing date strings instead of Date objects.
Forgetting that new Date("invalid") returns an “Invalid Date” object, not null.
Using innerHTML with user input.
Putting validation logic inside the click handler, which makes it hard to test.
Treating a format check as proof that a product is genuine.
Where This Idea Is Useful

If you are building a food or ecommerce site, a label checklist like this can help buyers compare products, whether they want to buy Indian spices, snacks or anything else sold with a printed label. A seller-side version also helps catch missing fields before a product page goes live. For a list of what to look for in authentic Indian spices, and which basics most kitchens stock first, see this guide to the best Indian spices.

FAQ

Does this tell me if a spice is authentic?
No. It only checks whether the label information looks complete and consistent. Smell, texture and seller reputation still matter.

Why does checkLabel take today as an argument?
It makes the function predictable and easy to test, because the result no longer depends on the real clock.

Can I use it for other products?
Yes. Change the ingredient rule and the licence format, and it works for most packaged foods.

Why not use a library?
For a small tool like this, plain JavaScript is simpler and teaches you the DOM and Date basics.

Should I validate on the server too?
Yes, if you store or act on the data. Client-side checks are a convenience, not a security measure.

Wrapping Up

In under 100 lines, we built a label checker that validates text, dates and a number format, with a pure function that is easy to test. It is a small project, but it covers forms, FormData, dates, regular expressions and safe DOM updates.

If you try it, tell me which field you would add next.

title: AWS dobra para 30 minutos o timeout do Lambda sob demanda
description:
A AWS dobrou de 15 para 30 minutos o tempo máximo de execução das funções de evento sob demanda do Lambda. A mudança vale em todas as regiões comerciais, sem adesão prévia e com os preços padrão. O novo limite pode ser configurado por função e se aplica a invocações síncronas, assíncronas e a mapeamentos de fontes de eventos.

Configuração e cenários de uso

O teto de 15 minutos estava em vigor desde 2018. Para ampliar o prazo, administradores precisam alterar a configuração de cada função; valores acima de 1.800 segundos são rejeitados com erro de validação. A AWS cita como casos de uso agentes de IA que encadeiam chamadas a modelos e ferramentas, transcodificação de mídia, simulações de Monte Carlo e geração de relatórios.

aws lambda update-function-configuration \
--function-name my-demo-function \
--timeout 1800

A atualização não uniformiza os limites de todos os formatos do serviço. Web Functions continuam com o máximo de 15 minutos, enquanto Lambda MicroVMs podem executar por até oito horas. Nas Lambda Managed Instances, invocações síncronas chegam a 30 minutos, mas as assíncronas mantêm o limite de 90 minutos introduzido em setembro.

Capacidade, filas e streams

Antes de aumentar o timeout, equipes devem recalcular a concorrência necessária. A AWS apresenta a relação entre concorrência, requisições por segundo e duração média em segundos: à mesma taxa de requisições, uma execução de 30 minutos exige o dobro da concorrência de uma execução de 15 minutos. Um fluxo de uma requisição por segundo durante 30 minutos requer 1.800 execuções simultâneas.

Para processamento com SQS, o timeout de visibilidade da fila deve ser pelo menos seis vezes o prazo da função, chegando a três horas quando ela pode executar por 30 minutos. Em Kinesis e DynamoDB Streams, cada shard entrega um lote por vez; por isso, uma função mais lenta também retarda o processamento daquele shard.

Há ainda diferenças nos mapeamentos de outras fontes. Mapeamentos de Amazon MQ, DocumentDB e Kafka criados antes de 19 de novembro permanecem limitados a 14 minutos. O gateway NAT encerra conexões ociosas após 350 segundos, e a fase Init da função continua sujeita ao limite de dez segundos.

Validações e efeitos operacionais

O profissional de AWS Wibo van der Sluis testou a regra de visibilidade com uma função configurada para 1.800 segundos. No teste, uma fila com visibilidade de 90 minutos e depois de 60 segundos foi aceita enquanto o mapeamento já existia; um novo mapeamento para a mesma fila foi recusado. A validação ocorreu na criação, não em alterações posteriores.

Van der Sluis também observou que, na criação, a checagem comparou a fila ao timeout da função, e não ao múltiplo de seis recomendado. Equipes devem tratar essa relação como uma configuração operacional a garantir, em vez de depender exclusivamente da validação do serviço.

Em funções assíncronas que expiram três vezes, o evento pode acumular até 90 minutos de execução antes de chegar a uma fila de mensagens não entregues. Para tarefas longas, vale manter os handlers idempotentes e planejar retentativas e tratamento de trabalho parcial, pois uma falha no meio da execução pode deixar efeitos incompletos.

Quando considerar outras arquiteturas

Um timeout maior não resolve necessariamente código lento atrás de uma API, e execuções longas precisam ser avaliadas pelo custo por invocação, que acompanha a memória configurada e o tempo usado. Para fluxos com várias etapas, estado explícito e retentativas, Step Functions com Fargate ou ECS pode oferecer uma estrutura mais adequada.

A mudança amplia o espaço de uso do Lambda para tarefas que ultrapassavam o limite anterior, mas não elimina diferenças de preço, concorrência e comportamento entre serviços. A escolha deve considerar duração, volume de chamadas, integração com filas ou streams e o modo como a aplicação recupera trabalho após falhas.

Confira mais em: https://guiadeti.com.br/noticias/aws-lambda-amplia-limite-timeout-30-minutos/

title: Migrating from mypy & pyright to Astral's ty in One Command
description:
Python tooling has consolidated fast around Astral's stack: uv for packages, ruff for linting and formatting, and ty for Rust-speed static type checking.

While migrate-to-uv handles moving away from Poetry/Pipenv, moving an existing codebase from mypy, pyright, or basedpyright to ty still had a tedious manual step:

  1. Translating mypy.ini, setup.cfg, pyrightconfig.json, or [tool.mypy] / [tool.pyright] into [tool.ty.*].
  2. Converting per-module overrides ([mypy-tests.*], executionEnvironments) into [[tool.ty.overrides]] or allowed-unresolved-imports.
  3. Rewriting dozens or hundreds of # type: ignore[arg-type] and # pyright: ignore[reportAttributeAccessIssue] comments to # ty: ignore[...] without breaking strings or docstrings.

So I built ty-migrate — a zero-dependency Python 3.11+ CLI published on PyPI.

Try It Without Installing

Preview what would change on your project without modifying any files:

uvx ty-migrate --rewrite-ignores --dry-run --diff --report

Apply the migration and immediately verify with ty check:

uvx ty-migrate --rewrite-ignores --report --verify

What It Automates

1. Multi-Format Config Discovery & Parsing

ty-migrate discovers and normalizes:

  • Mypy: mypy.ini, .mypy.ini, setup.cfg ([mypy] + [mypy-*]), and pyproject.toml ([tool.mypy] + [[tool.mypy.overrides]]).
  • Pyright / Basedpyright: pyrightconfig.json (JSONC-safe — strips //, /* */, and trailing commas without breaking URLs in strings) and pyproject.toml ([tool.pyright], [tool.basedpyright], and executionEnvironments).

2. Idiomatic [tool.ty.*] Generation

Instead of naive key renaming, it maps settings into ty's actual structure:

  • python_version / pythonVersion → [tool.ty.environment].python-version
  • mypy_path / extraPaths → [tool.ty.environment].extra-paths
  • Pure ignore_missing_imports = True module sections (like [mypy-vendor_missing.*]) → [tool.ty.analysis].allowed-unresolved-imports
  • disable_error_code / report* → [tool.ty.rules] validated against ty's official 163-rule catalog (ignore / warn / error).
  • Safely updates existing pyproject.toml files without touching [project] or [tool.ruff], or writes a standalone ty.toml.

3. Tokenizer-Safe Inline Ignore Rewriting

Regex find-and-replace over Python source files inevitably corrupts docstrings, test fixtures, or string literals mentioning # type: ignore.

ty-migrate uses Python's standard-library tokenize module so only real COMMENT tokens are rewritten:

"""Docstring mentioning # type: ignore[arg-type] stays untouched."""

# Before:
x: int = "bad"  # type: ignore[assignment]  # legacy fixture
y = obj.x       # pyright: ignore[reportAttributeAccessIssue]

# After:
x: int = "bad"  # ty: ignore[invalid-assignment]  # legacy fixture
y = obj.x       # ty: ignore[missing-attribute, invalid-attribute-access]

By default, bare # type: ignore and unmapped plugin error codes are left untouched (--unmapped-strategy keep) rather than silently widening ignores.

4. Honest Audit Reporting (--report & --check)

ty has real behavioral differences from mypy and pyright — for instance, ty checks unannotated function bodies unconditionally (check_untyped_defs is always on), has no single strict = True flag, and does not run mypy plugins.

Rather than silently ignoring those keys, --report breaks every option down into Translated, Guidance / Implicit in ty, and Unmapped, and --check returns exit code 3 in CI if anything needs manual review.

Links

  • GitHub: https://github.com/Prateek-squadron/ty-migrate
  • PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/ty-migrate/

If you try it on a real codebase and hit an unmapped error code or edge case, open an issue or PR!

title: Three Ministers, One Meeting: Morocco Just Put Data Centers at the Center of Its Digital Strategy
description:
On November 23, 2026, three Moroccan ministers, Industry, Energy, and Digital Transition, sat at one table with a single agenda: how to build data centers in Morocco at scale. No budget figures were announced, no megawatts promised. But the composition of the meeting is the story: Morocco now treats data-center capacity as an industrial policy issue, an energy policy issue, and a sovereignty issue at once. If your business stores or processes data in North Africa, here is why this matters to you.

What happened

Les Inspirations ECO reported on November 23, 2026 that Ryad Mezzour (Minister of Industry, Trade, Investment and Economic Inclusion), Charafat Afailal (Minister of Energy, Mines and Sustainable Development) and Ahmed Rahhou (Minister of AI, Digital Transition and Administrative Reform) met to examine the conditions for developing data centers in Morocco. The aim, per the ministry's own communication to the outlet: establish a common operating model across the three departments and launch the workstream, rather than set quantified targets. Mezzour framed the infrastructure on LinkedIn as a lever of digital sovereignty, with attracting investment among the stated ambitions.

Why data centers are suddenly a three-ministry file

Data centers look like real estate with servers. They are actually an energy business and an industrial business wearing a digital costume:

  • Energy: data centers are among the most power-hungry facilities an economy can host. Their viability depends on electricity pricing, grid capacity and increasingly on renewables, which is why the energy minister is in the room.
  • Industry: building and operating them at scale requires land, permits, construction capacity, fiber routes and a supply chain, which is industry ministry territory.
  • Digital: they underpin cloud services, AI workloads, government digitization and data-residency rules, which is the digital ministry's file.

The three-ministry format is Morocco acknowledging that a data-center strategy fails if any one of these legs moves alone.

The buildout already underway

This coordination meeting lands on top of concrete projects already announced:

  • Nexus AI Factory Platform (launched April 2026 at GITEX Africa): an initial investment of about 12 billion MAD across two phases, a Nouaceur hub at 16 MW, then a 20 MW northern expansion, targeting 36 MW total capacity, with a stated goal of 125 direct jobs by end of 2027.
  • Oracle's Morocco West cloud region in Casablanca, made available in February 2026, Oracle's first public cloud region in North Africa, plus Oracle R&D centers in Casablanca (June 2025) and Agadir (June 2026).
  • "Jazari" and "Igoudar Digital" (Dakhla) national data-center projects referenced in the AI ministry's 2027 roadmap, with Oracle's cloud regions representing an investment of about 1.4 billion MAD.

The November meeting is the state organising itself to multiply, not just host, this kind of infrastructure.

What it means for businesses choosing hosting

  1. Local hosting is becoming a serious default. For Moroccan businesses, keeping data in-country will soon be a competitive option on price and latency, not a patriotic sacrifice.
  2. Compliance gets easier. Morocco's Law 09-08 restricts transferring personal data abroad, and its revision now working through the legislative process keeps data protection central. Local regions simplify the answer to "where is our data?"
  3. AI workloads follow the compute. Companies planning AI features should track where Moroccan GPU and cloud capacity actually lands; procurement advantage goes to those who plan early.
  4. Energy is the constraint to watch. The pace of this buildout will be set by power availability as much as by capital.

What to watch next

  • The common operating model the three ministries are setting up: incentives, land, energy tariffs for data-center investors.
  • Whether quantified targets follow in the 2027 budget cycle.
  • The promised Cloud First circular (Q1 2027 per the digital ministry's 2027 program), which would open public-sector cloud procurement.

Bottom line

Morocco is moving data centers from a real-estate topic to a sovereignty topic, and aligning industry, energy and digital policy to do it. For businesses, the direction is clear: local, compliant, well-connected infrastructure is coming, and architecture decisions made today should anticipate it. At Manadger Tech, hosting and cloud architecture for Moroccan businesses is core to what we do, including planning for data residency under Law 09-08. Talk to us.

Sources

  • Les Inspirations ECO, Nov 23, 2026: Infrastructures numeriques: Data centers, trois ministeres pour lancer le chantier — https://leseco.ma/business/infrastructures-numeriques-data-centers-trois-ministeres-pour-lancer-le-chantier.html
  • Ministry of Digital Transition, Apr 8, 2026: Launch of the Nexus AI Factory Platform — https://www.mmsp.gov.ma/ar/مستجدات/إطلاق-منصة-«nexus-ai-factory-platform»-بالمغرب
  • Morocco World News, Nov 20, 2026 (Oracle cloud region and R&D centers) — https://www.moroccoworldnews.com/2026/11/347472/morocco-oracle-discuss-ai-and-cloud-cooperation-in-rabat-meeting/

title: What is CSS Modules in React? Difference between Normal CSS and CSS Modules in React?
description:
CSS Modules is a CSS styling technique in React that allows us to write CSS for individual components.

It automatically creates unique class names to avoid CSS conflicts between components.

In simple words, CSS Modules prevent one component's CSS from affecting another component.

import React from 'react';
import styles from './Home.module.css';

function Home() {
return (



Welcome to React

  <button className={styles.button}>
    Click Me
  </button>
</div>

);
}

export default Home;

Main Advantages:

  1. Avoids CSS conflicts.
  2. Provides component-level styling.
  3. Makes code easier to maintain.
  4. Keeps styles separate for each component.
  5. Automatically generates unique class names.

Both are used to style React components, but the main difference is how CSS class names are managed.

Normal CSS CSS Modules
Uses global class names. Uses locally scoped class names.
Styles can conflict. Prevents class name conflicts.
Uses className="title". Uses className={styles.title}.
Imported as a normal CSS file. Imported as a CSS Module file.
File extension: .css File extension: .module.css

return

;
